Select X coupled to the original carrier P, the only option satisfying both conditions.
keyConcept: Linked (cognate) recognition requires the hapten and the primed carrier to be physically joined so one B cell binds the hapten and receives carrier-specific T help.
commonMistake: Assuming any carrier works, or that co-administering unlinked hapten and carrier is equivalent to covalent linkage.

optionExplanations.1: Carrier P alone has no hapten X, so the anti-X B cells are never engaged and no anti-X antibody is boosted.
optionExplanations.2: A free hapten is too small to be processed and presented, so it cannot recruit helper T-cell help for a class-switched response.
optionExplanations.4: Coupling X to a novel carrier Q finds no memory helper T cells against Q, giving only a slow primary-strength response.

shortExplanation: The herd-immunity threshold is 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75. At 60% efficacy, required coverage V = 0.75/0.60 = 1.25 (125%), so even vaccinating everyone immunises only 0.60 < 0.75 and the threshold cannot be reached.
solutionSteps: Compute the threshold immune fraction: 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75.
Relate coverage to immunity: vaccinating fraction V immunises 0.60 x V.
Since coverage cannot exceed 100%, even full coverage immunises only 0.60 < 0.75, so the threshold is unattainable.
keyConcept: Required vaccination coverage equals the herd-immunity threshold divided by vaccine efficacy; if this exceeds 1, herd immunity is impossible with that vaccine.
commonMistake: Equating coverage with the immune fraction and ignoring imperfect vaccine efficacy.

optionExplanations.0: 75% is the threshold immune fraction and equals required coverage only for a 100%-effective vaccine; at 60% efficacy, 75% coverage immunises just 0.45.
optionExplanations.3: 60% is the vaccine efficacy, not the required coverage; vaccinating 60% at 60% efficacy immunises only 0.36.
optionExplanations.4: 0.45 = 0.60 x 0.75 multiplies efficacy by the threshold, but efficacy should divide, not multiply, the threshold.

shortExplanation: With aminopterin blocking de novo nucleotide synthesis, survival requires the HGPRT-dependent salvage pathway. Only the hybrid unites the B cell's functional HGPRT (salvage competence) with the myeloma's immortality, so only hybrids proliferate in HAT medium.
solutionSteps: Note aminopterin blocks de novo synthesis, so survival depends on HGPRT-driven salvage.
Unfused myeloma cells are HGPRT-deficient, so they die despite being immortal.
Unfused B cells have HGPRT but are mortal, so they die within days.
Only the hybrid combines HGPRT from the B cell and immortality from the myeloma, so only hybrids grow.
keyConcept: HAT selection uses genetic complementation, so only cells possessing both HGPRT (salvage) and immortality survive.
commonMistake: Believing the HAT medium immortalises cells or that selection targets antibody secretion.

optionExplanations.0: HAT does not immortalise cells; unfused normal B cells remain mortal and die within days.
optionExplanations.1: Aminopterin blocks nucleotide synthesis in every cell regardless of antibody secretion; hybrids survive by HGPRT complementation.
optionExplanations.3: HAT actively kills both unfused parent populations, so it is a genuine selection step, not a neutral medium.
optionExplanations.4: Unfused myeloma cells are HGPRT-deficient and cannot use salvage, so they die despite being immortal.

shortExplanation: Each of the n homologous pairs orients independently at metaphase I, giving an independent maternal-or-paternal choice, so the number of chromosomally distinct gametes is 2^n. With 2n = 8, n = 4, so 2^4 = 16.
solutionSteps: Recall each homologous pair aligns independently at metaphase I.
Each pair contributes an independent two-way (maternal/paternal) choice.
The count of distinct gametes from independent assortment is 2^n.
Set n = 4 from 2n = 8, giving 2^4 = 16.
keyConcept: Independent assortment gives 2^n genetically distinct gametes, where n is the haploid number of chromosome pairs.
commonMistake: Using the exponent 2n instead of n, or applying n! or n rather than a power of 2.

optionExplanations.0: 256 = 2^(2n) treats all eight chromosomes as independent, but the two homologues of a pair are not independent, so the exponent is n = 4.
optionExplanations.1: 8 is the diploid number 2n, confusing chromosome count with the number of distinct gamete types.
optionExplanations.4: 4 is the haploid number n; each pair adds an independent factor of 2, so the count is 2^n, not n.

shortExplanation: A drug that blocks initiation of replication lets each cell finish its current cycle (dividing if past S), but the progeny then halt at the G1/S boundary because they cannot start S. Since S phase is never performed, the arrested cells keep the unreplicated 2C content of a G1 cell.
solutionSteps: Recall DNA is duplicated only in S phase: G1 = 2C, G2/M = 4C.
The block prevents entry into S but allows cells already past it to finish the cycle.
Progeny cells then stall at the G1/S boundary, unable to start replication.
Because S is never carried out, arrested cells retain the unreplicated 2C content of a G1 cell.
keyConcept: Blocking replication initiation funnels the whole population to the G1/S boundary with unreplicated 2C DNA, unlike a spindle poison that arrests at 4C in mitosis.
commonMistake: Assuming DNA is still replicated to 4C, or equating unreplicated 2C with the haploid 1C content of a gamete.

optionExplanations.0: Metaphase arrest at 4C is produced by a spindle poison via the spindle-assembly checkpoint, and wrongly assumes the DNA has doubled.
optionExplanations.2: The arrest point is right, but a diploid unreplicated somatic cell contains 2C; 1C is the content of a haploid gamete.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes cells still replicate to 4C and stall at G2/M, but the drug blocks entry into S so DNA is never duplicated.
optionExplanations.4: A specific block synchronises the population at one transition rather than leaving cells spread across all phases.

shortExplanation: Three paired bivalents at the plate identify this cell as metaphase I. Anaphase I is reductional: whole homologues separate while sister chromatids stay joined, producing two haploid cells that each keep three still-replicated chromosomes.
solutionSteps: Recognise metaphase I by the presence of bivalents (paired homologous chromosomes) at the equator.
Note that anaphase I separates homologues, not sister chromatids (reductional division).
Distinguish mitotic metaphase (single chromosomes at the diploid number, 6) from metaphase II (single chromosomes at the haploid number, 3).
Conclude the bivalent-showing cell is meiosis I, yielding two haploid cells each with three two-chromatid chromosomes.
keyConcept: Bivalents at the metaphase plate mark meiosis I; anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes while sister chromatids remain attached.
commonMistake: Assuming every anaphase separates sister chromatids, which ignores the reductional first meiotic division.

optionExplanations.0: Anaphase I of meiosis separates homologous chromosomes and keeps sister chromatids joined, so the claim that anaphase always separates sister chromatids fails.
optionExplanations.1: Six single chromosomes aligned individually is mitotic metaphase; meiosis I is identified by bivalents, not merely by chromosome number.
optionExplanations.2: A cell with three single chromosomes is haploid, so it is metaphase II rather than mitosis, and a mitotic cell here would show six chromosomes.

shortExplanation: Two coexisting cell lines (46 normal and 47,+21) within one person point to an error AFTER fertilisation. Mitotic non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in an early division of a normal 46-chromosome zygote creates a 47,+21 daughter line alongside the surviving 46 line: post-zygotic mosaicism.
solutionSteps: Identify the clue: the child has both a normal 46,XY line and a trisomic 47,XY,+21 line, from a single conception with two normal parents.
Reason about timing: if the error were meiotic (in a gamete), every cell of the embryo would inherit the abnormality, so there would be no normal 46 line.
Therefore the error must be post-zygotic (mitotic), after a normal zygote had already formed.
Mechanism: during an early mitosis of the 46-chromosome embryo, chromosome 21 fails to separate. One daughter gains an extra 21 (47,+21) and one loses it (45, usually lost).
The descendants of the 47 cell and of the unaffected 46 cells form the two coexisting lines seen in the karyotype.
keyConcept: Mosaicism = two genetically different cell lines arising from ONE conception via a post-zygotic mitotic error. A whole-body (non-mosaic) trisomy instead reflects a meiotic error present from the zygote onward.
commonMistake: Blaming a parental meiotic non-disjunction, which would make every embryonic cell trisomic and could not leave a normal 46 line behind.

optionExplanations.0: Crossing over is the normal exchange of segments between homologues; it does not change chromosome number and cannot create an extra whole chromosome 21, so it cannot produce aneuploidy or mosaicism.
optionExplanations.1: A meiotic non-disjunction in a parent would put the extra 21 in every cell of the embryo from the zygote onward, giving a uniform 47 karyotype, not a mix with a normal line.
optionExplanations.2: Fusion of two separate zygotes describes chimaerism, which requires two independent fertilisation events; here there is a single conception with two normal parents.
optionExplanations.4: A translocation reattaches chromosome-21 material onto another chromosome but does NOT raise the count to 47; the abnormal line here has 47 chromosomes, i.e. an extra free chromosome.

shortExplanation: Down syndrome is caused by three DOSES of chromosome-21 genes, not by the chromosome count. Here two of those doses ride on a single fused chromosome, so the child has three-21 dosage while the total count stays at 46.
solutionSteps: First, separate two ideas that sound the same but aren't: the NUMBER of chromosomes you can count, and the DOSE of genes present. Down syndrome depends on dose — having chromosome-21 genes in three copies instead of two.

Understand the mother. A Robertsonian translocation glues two chromosomes together end-to-end — here one chromosome 14 and one chromosome 21 become a single fused chromosome, der(14;21). She still has one free 14 and one free 21 as well.

So her genes are all in the right dose (two 14s worth, two 21s worth of material), but they sit on 45 chromosomes instead of 46 because two of them share one physical chromosome. That is why she is healthy: balanced carrier.
Now the risky gamete. When she makes an egg, that egg can end up carrying BOTH her free chromosome 21 AND the der(14;21) fusion. That single egg already holds two copies of chromosome-21 material.
The father contributes a normal chromosome 21. Add it up: fusion-21 + free-21 (from mum) + normal-21 (from dad) = three doses of chromosome-21 genes.

Now count the physical chromosomes in the child: the der(14;21) fusion counts as ONE chromosome, plus the two free 21s, plus everything else — that comes to 46, not 47, because two of the 21 doses are packed onto one fused chromosome.
So the child has trisomy-21 dosage hidden inside a normal-looking count of 46. That extra dose of chromosome-21 genes is what produces Down syndrome.
keyConcept: Down syndrome comes from gene DOSAGE — three copies of chromosome-21 material — not from the raw chromosome number. A Robertsonian translocation lets a parent pass on that extra dose while the count still reads 46, so trisomy 21 can be inherited from a healthy balanced-carrier parent.
commonMistake: Assuming a chromosome count of 46 must mean normal gene dosage and therefore a healthy child. The count and the dose are different things: two doses of chromosome 21 can hide on one fused chromosome, giving a total of 46 but a genetic dose of three.

optionExplanations.0: A translocation fuses whole chromosomes together; it does not rewrite a single letter of DNA. Down syndrome is a whole-chromosome dosage effect (three copies of the chromosome-21 genes), not a point mutation, so this misnames the cause.
optionExplanations.1: This is the count-equals-dose trap. Translocation Down syndrome is exactly the case where 46 chromosomes carry THREE doses of chromosome 21, so a count of 46 does not guarantee a healthy balanced carrier — you have to check the dose, not just the number.
optionExplanations.2: The father's karyotype is normal, and a paternal non-disjunction would make a 47-chromosome child. Here the count is 46 and the extra dose is maternal, hidden on the der(14;21) fusion — so the source and the count both rule this out.
optionExplanations.3: Correct: the child holds three doses of chromosome-21 genes — a normal 21 from the father, a free 21 from the mother, and a third copy fused into the mother's der(14;21). Two doses sharing one fused chromosome keep the total at 46 while the dose is three, which is Down syndrome.
optionExplanations.4: This is the most tempting distractor because it correctly counts only two 'free' chromosome 21s and forgets the third dose is fused onto the der(14;21). It then blames chromosome 14, but chromosome 14 dosage is normal here — the fusion still delivers a full extra chromosome-21, giving three 21 doses in total. Down syndrome comes from that third 21, not from anything happening to 14.

shortExplanation: The intrinsic (denervated) rate is 100/min, but the innervated resting rate is only 70/min, so at rest the sinoatrial node is held back by tonic vagal (parasympathetic) tone acting via muscarinic receptors. Atropine blocks those receptors, removing the brake, so the rate climbs towards about 100/min.
solutionSteps: Compare the two rates: denervated intrinsic = 100/min, normally innervated resting = 70/min.
Since innervation LOWERS the rate below intrinsic, the resting autonomic balance must be net inhibitory, i.e. dominant vagal (parasympathetic) tone.
Recall the mechanism of vagal slowing: acetylcholine acting on muscarinic (M2) receptors at the sinoatrial node.
Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist, so it blocks this vagal acetylcholine signal.
Removing the vagal brake lets the intrinsic pacemaker run, so the rate rises towards ~100/min.
keyConcept: When the resting rate sits BELOW the intrinsic pacemaker rate, tonic parasympathetic (vagal) tone dominates. Muscarinic blockade removes that brake and unmasks the intrinsic rate.
commonMistake: Assuming the resting node has no autonomic tone, or that any drug speeding the heart must be acting through sympathetic (adrenergic) receptors.

optionExplanations.0: The resting rate (70) is far below the intrinsic rate (100), which can only happen if the node is being actively slowed; the vagal supply is not silent at rest.
optionExplanations.1: Atropine is an ANTAGONIST at muscarinic receptors; it has no agonist action at beta1-adrenergic receptors, so it cannot directly stimulate the node.
optionExplanations.2: Atropine acts on muscarinic (parasympathetic) receptors, not on noradrenaline or adrenergic transmission; it does not block sympathetic signalling, and blocking the accelerator would slow, not describe, this effect.
optionExplanations.3: Ganglionic transmission (both sympathetic and parasympathetic) uses acetylcholine on NICOTINIC receptors, which atropine (a muscarinic blocker) does not affect, so it cannot act there.

shortExplanation: Total time is the sum of each segment's time (t = distance / velocity). The intact 0.95 m at 50 m/s takes 19 ms; the 0.050 m lesion at 2.0 m/s takes 25 ms. Total = 44 ms, more than double the normal 20 ms.
solutionSteps: Split the axon into two segments: healthy length = 1.00 - 0.050 = 0.95 m at 50 m/s; lesion = 0.050 m at 2.0 m/s.
Healthy segment time: 0.95 / 50 = 0.019 s = 19 ms.
Lesion segment time: 0.050 / 2.0 = 0.025 s = 25 ms.
Total = 19 + 25 = 44 ms.
Compare with normal: 1.00 / 50 = 0.020 s = 20 ms, so 44 ms is more than double.
keyConcept: Conduction time adds up over segments and depends on BOTH length and local speed. A short segment that is 25x slower can dominate the total, so you cannot dismiss it by length alone.
commonMistake: Judging the 5 cm lesion negligible because it is short, while ignoring that its speed dropped from 50 to 2 m/s (25x slower).

optionExplanations.0: Ignores the speed drop: at 2 m/s the 0.050 m patch takes 25 ms, which alone exceeds the entire healthy axon's time, so the effect is far from negligible.
optionExplanations.2: Comes from a decimal slip reading 0.050 / 2.0 as ~1-2 ms; done correctly it is 25 ms, so the lesion adds 25 ms, not 1 ms.
optionExplanations.3: Double-counts the lesion length: it takes the FULL 1.00 m at 50 m/s (20 ms) and then adds the lesion time (25 ms), but the fast part is only 0.95 m; the lesion's 0.050 m must not be counted at both speeds.
optionExplanations.4: Uses only the 25 ms lesion time and forgets the healthy 0.95 m still takes 19 ms; conduction times add, so the total is 44 ms, not 25 ms.

formulaNotes: time = distance / velocity, summed over segments: t_total = 0.95/50 + 0.050/2.0 = 0.019 + 0.025 = 0.044 s.

shortExplanation: In the presynaptic defect, faulty voltage-gated Ca2+ channels reduce transmitter release, but a high-frequency train lets residual Ca2+ accumulate in the terminal (facilitation), transiently boosting acetylcholine release and improving strength.
solutionSteps: Recall that Ca2+ entering through voltage-gated channels triggers vesicle fusion and transmitter release.
Identify the presynaptic defect (blocked Ca2+ channels) as reducing acetylcholine released per impulse.
Note that high-frequency firing allows residual Ca2+ to build up in the terminal (facilitation).
Conclude this transient rise in Ca2+ increases release and briefly improves strength in the presynaptic disorder.
keyConcept: A presynaptic Ca2+-channel defect shows facilitation with high-frequency stimulation, whereas a postsynaptic receptor defect fatigues.
commonMistake: Swapping the presynaptic and postsynaptic disorders, or assuming acetylcholinesterase inhibitors create new receptors.

optionExplanations.0: The postsynaptic patient lacks functional receptors, so releasing more transmitter cannot fully correct the weakness once receptors are limiting.
optionExplanations.2: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors prolong existing acetylcholine; they do not create new receptors and chiefly help the postsynaptic defect.
optionExplanations.3: Only the presynaptic patient releases less acetylcholine per impulse; in the postsynaptic patient release is normal.
optionExplanations.4: In the postsynaptic patient the scarce receptors are the bottleneck, so sustained stimulation causes fatigue rather than improvement.

shortExplanation: Preserved pin-prick sensation rules out any sensory or mixed lesion, while absent reflex, absent voluntary contraction, and flaccidity are classic lower-motor-neuron signs. Only section of the purely motor ventral root spares all sensation yet removes both the reflex's efferent limb and the sole motor path to the muscle.
solutionSteps: Apply the Bell-Magendie law: the dorsal root is sensory and the ventral root is motor.
Use preserved pin-prick to exclude lesions of the sensory limb or of a mixed nerve.
Recognise absent reflex, no voluntary contraction, and flaccidity with reduced tone as lower-motor-neuron signs.
Identify the ventral root as the only structure whose loss spares sensation while removing both the efferent reflex limb and the motor pathway.
keyConcept: The ventral root is the purely motor efferent limb; its section gives a lower-motor-neuron picture with fully preserved sensation.
commonMistake: Assuming an absent reflex must come from the sensory limb, or confusing upper- with lower-motor-neuron signs.

optionExplanations.1: Cutting the sensory dorsal root would abolish cutaneous sensation, but pin-prick is preserved here.
optionExplanations.2: A dorsal-column lesion impairs fine touch and proprioception but leaves the local reflex and voluntary power intact.
optionExplanations.3: An upper-motor-neuron lesion causes increased tone and exaggerated reflexes, not areflexia with flaccidity.
optionExplanations.4: A mixed peripheral nerve carries sensory fibres too, so its section would also abolish sensation.

shortExplanation: With equal Na+ and K+ conductance, net current is zero when the membrane potential equals the average of the two equilibrium potentials: V = (E_Na + E_K)/2 = (+60 + (-90))/2 = -15 mV. The end-plate depolarises from -80 mV towards this reversal potential.
solutionSteps: Write net current I = g_Na(V - E_Na) + g_K(V - E_K).
Set g_Na = g_K = g because the channel is equally permeable to both ions.
Set I = 0, giving (V - E_Na) + (V - E_K) = 0, so V = (E_Na + E_K)/2.
Substitute: V = (+60 + (-90))/2 = -15 mV, which lies between the two single-ion equilibrium potentials.
keyConcept: The reversal potential of a channel equally permeable to two ions is the average of their equilibrium potentials.
commonMistake: Treating the channel as selective for a single ion, driving V to only E_Na or only E_K.

optionExplanations.0: This value arises from a sign error such as (-90 - 60)/2; the correct mean is (+60 - 90)/2 = -15 mV.
optionExplanations.1: At -80 mV the inward Na+ driving force greatly exceeds the outward K+ driving force, so net current is inward and the membrane depolarises.
optionExplanations.2: The K+ equilibrium potential applies only to a K+-selective channel; here simultaneous Na+ influx pulls the reversal potential up.
optionExplanations.3: The Na+ equilibrium potential applies only to a Na+-selective channel; simultaneous K+ efflux pulls the reversal potential far below +60 mV.

shortExplanation: Loading the lumen to pH 4 and raising the outside to pH 8 creates an artificial proton gradient of the same polarity the light reactions build. Protons flow out through ATP synthase and make ATP in darkness with no electron transport, showing the proton-motive force alone is sufficient.
solutionSteps: Note the imposed gradient: lumen at pH 4 (high H+), stroma side at pH 8 (low H+).
Recognise this polarity matches the physiological gradient built by the light reactions.
Protons flow out of the lumen through ATP synthase, and this free energy phosphorylates ADP.
Because ATP is made in darkness with no electron transport, conclude the proton gradient alone drives synthesis.
keyConcept: Chemiosmosis: a proton-motive force across the thylakoid membrane is by itself sufficient to drive ATP synthesis; light only builds the gradient.
commonMistake: Believing light or electron transport is required for the phosphorylation step itself rather than just for creating the gradient.

optionExplanations.1: The result shows the opposite of an artefact: once a gradient exists, ATP synthesis proceeds in the dark.
optionExplanations.2: No electron transport can occur here, as there is no light and no added electron donor or acceptor.
optionExplanations.3: Protons flow from the acidic lumen outward through ATP synthase to drive synthesis, not inward.

shortExplanation: Releasing one O2 requires oxidising two water molecules, yielding four electrons. In linear flow each electron is energised twice (once per photosystem), so 4 x 2 = 8 photons. Since NADPH carries two electrons, four electrons make 2 NADPH.
solutionSteps: Write the photolysis of water: 2 H2O -> O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e-, giving four electrons per O2.
Count photons: each electron absorbs one photon at each of two photosystems, so 4 x 2 = 8 photons.
Recall NADPH is a two-electron carrier: NADP+ + 2 e- + H+ -> NADPH.
Divide four electrons by two per NADPH to get 2 NADPH.
keyConcept: One O2 corresponds to four electrons; linear flow needs two photons per electron and NADPH accepts two electrons.
commonMistake: Counting one photon per electron (ignoring the second photosystem) or treating NADPH as a one-electron carrier.

optionExplanations.0: The NADPH count of 2 is right, but 4 photons counts only one photon per electron, ignoring re-energising at photosystem I.
optionExplanations.1: The 8 photons is correct, but treating each electron as reducing one NADP+ overstates NADPH; four electrons make only 2 NADPH.
optionExplanations.2: Producing one O2 requires oxidising two water molecules and moving four electrons, not one.
optionExplanations.3: This combines one photon per electron and one NADPH per electron, both errors.

shortExplanation: Cyclic flow normally adds ATP without NADPH, raising the ATP:NADPH output to the 3:2 the Calvin cycle needs. Without it, linear flow alone supplies too little ATP per NADPH, so ATP becomes limiting while unused NADPH accumulates and carbon fixation is restricted.
solutionSteps: Note the Calvin cycle needs 3 ATP per 2 NADPH.
Recall linear flow supplies these in a ratio below 3:2 (too little ATP).
Recall cyclic flow normally tops up ATP with no NADPH to reach the required ratio.
Remove cyclic flow: ATP runs short and NADPH accumulates, throttling carbon fixation.
keyConcept: Cyclic electron flow balances the chloroplast's ATP:NADPH output to match the Calvin cycle's 3:2 demand.
commonMistake: Assuming linear flow alone self-balances the coenzyme budget, when its ATP:NADPH ratio is below 3:2.

optionExplanations.1: The stem states linear flow's ratio is below 3:2, which is exactly why cyclic flow is normally needed.
optionExplanations.2: The electrons that reduce NADP+ come from water splitting via linear flow, so O2 evolution continues without cyclic flow.
optionExplanations.3: Cyclic flow supplies extra ATP, so its loss makes ATP scarce and NADPH plentiful, not the reverse.
optionExplanations.4: Linear flow also pumps protons into the lumen, so cyclic flow is not the only proton source, and losing it would not acidify the stroma.

shortExplanation: Track the carbons. Three turns fix 3 CO2 (3 C) onto 3 RuBP (15 C) = 18 C, which appear as six 3-carbon G3P (18 C). Five G3P (15 C) regenerate the 3 RuBP and one G3P (3 C) is exported. So 3 CO2 fixed and 6 G3P produced in total.
solutionSteps: Each turn fixes 1 CO2 onto 1 RuBP; to net one exported 3-carbon G3P you need enough carbon, so use 3 turns.
Carbon in: 3 CO2 (3 C) + 3 RuBP (3 x 5 = 15 C) = 18 carbons.
These 18 carbons emerge as six molecules of the 3-carbon G3P (6 x 3 = 18 C). Total G3P produced = 6.
Regeneration: 5 G3P (5 x 3 = 15 C) are recycled to rebuild the 3 RuBP (3 x 5 = 15 C).
Net export: the remaining 1 G3P (3 C) leaves the cycle. Answer: 3 CO2 fixed, 6 G3P made.
keyConcept: The Calvin cycle balances carbon: 3 turns fix 3 CO2 and make 6 G3P, of which 5 regenerate RuBP and only 1 is exported. One net G3P is NOT one CO2.
commonMistake: Assuming one fixed CO2 gives one exportable sugar, forgetting that G3P has 3 carbons and that most G3P must be recycled to regenerate RuBP.

optionExplanations.1: One CO2 (1 C) plus one RuBP (5 C) = 6 C = two G3P, but both are needed to rebuild RuBP; nothing is left to export, so 1 CO2 cannot yield a net G3P.
optionExplanations.2: 6 CO2 / 12 G3P is exactly double: it produces TWO net G3P (one hexose). One net G3P needs half of this.
optionExplanations.3: The 3 CO2 is right, but 5 G3P counts only the recycled molecules and omits the one exported G3P; the total made is 6.
optionExplanations.4: Fails the carbon balance: 2 CO2 (2 C) + 2 RuBP (10 C) = 12 C = four G3P, but regenerating 2 RuBP needs 10 C (over three G3P), leaving only ~1 C, not a whole 3-carbon G3P to export. The cycle only balances cleanly in multiples of 3 turns.

shortExplanation: Net uptake already has respiration subtracted, so gross photosynthesis = net uptake + respiration = 15 + 5 = 20 units per hour. Zero net exchange at the lower intensity means gross photosynthesis exactly equals respiration, the light compensation point.
solutionSteps: Recognise that measured net uptake equals gross photosynthesis minus respiration.
Add respiration back: gross = 15 + 5 = 20 units per hour at the higher intensity.
At the lower intensity, net exchange is zero, so gross photosynthesis equals respiration (both 5 units).
Identify this balance point as the light compensation point, where respiration still continues.
keyConcept: Gross photosynthesis = net CO2 uptake + respiration; the light compensation point is where they cancel, not where respiration stops.
commonMistake: Subtracting respiration from net uptake, or believing respiration ceases at the compensation point.

optionExplanations.0: Subtracting respiration (15 - 5 = 10) is the wrong operation, and the compensation point is not the saturation point.
optionExplanations.2: The gross rate of 20 is right, but respiration does not stop; net exchange is zero because 5 offsets 5.
optionExplanations.3: This reports only the respiration rate as gross photosynthesis and confuses light with CO2 compensation.
optionExplanations.4: Taking net uptake (15) as gross forgets ongoing respiration, and zero net exchange means balance, not that photosynthesis stopped.

shortExplanation: The two enzymes share a GATC overhang so their ends ligate, but joining a G-side end to the other regenerates hybrid junctions (GGATCT and AGATCC) that are neither a BamHI site (GGATCC) nor a BglII site (AGATCT). Neither enzyme can re-cut them, so the insert cannot be excised by either.
solutionSteps: Note both enzymes leave an identical 5'-GATC overhang, so their cut ends anneal and ligate.
Recognise the recognition sequences differ only in the flanking base.
Combine a BamHI G-end with a BglII end to get top-strand GGATCT and reciprocal AGATCC.
Compare with BamHI (GGATCC) and BglII (AGATCT): both junctions are hybrids neither enzyme recognises.
keyConcept: Ligation requires complementary overhangs, not identical recognition sequences; compatible-end ligation can destroy both parental sites.
commonMistake: Assuming compatible overhangs restore an original recognition site, or that one parental site is selectively preserved.

optionExplanations.0: Both junctions are destroyed, so no BglII site survives; the supposed asymmetry does not exist.
optionExplanations.1: Ligation depends on complementary overhangs, not identical recognition sequences, and both enzymes leave a GATC overhang.
optionExplanations.2: Joining a BamHI end to a BglII end yields a hybrid junction that BamHI cannot regenerate or cut.
optionExplanations.4: A circular recombinant must join the vector at both insert ends; a single-stranded end could not circularise.

shortExplanation: The multiplicity of infection is 1x10^7 / 5x10^8 = 0.02, so essentially every adsorbed phage infects a separate cell and infected cells equal the 1x10^7 adsorbed phage. Burst size = 8x10^8 progeny / 1x10^7 infected cells = 80.
solutionSteps: Compute the multiplicity of infection: 1x10^7 / 5x10^8 = 0.02.
Conclude at most one phage per cell, so infected cells equal adsorbed phage, 1x10^7.
Note the infecting phage are eclipsed inside cells, so all 8x10^8 particles after lysis are progeny.
Divide progeny by infected cells: 8x10^8 / 1x10^7 = 80.
keyConcept: Burst size = progeny released / number of infected cells, where infected cells equal the adsorbed phage at low multiplicity.
commonMistake: Dividing progeny by the total bacteria instead of only the infected cells.

optionExplanations.0: This divides progeny by the total bacteria (8x10^8 / 5x10^8 = 1.6), but only 1x10^7 cells were infected.
optionExplanations.1: This subtracts the input phage first, but the infecting phage are eclipsed inside cells, not free particles to subtract.
optionExplanations.3: This divides bacteria by phage (5x10^8 / 1x10^7 = 50), swapping the two counts.
optionExplanations.4: This just reads off the mantissa of the final titre and ignores the number of infected cells.

shortExplanation: The amplicon spans the 5' end of the forward primer (position 201) to the 5' end of the reverse primer (position 497), a core of 497 - 201 + 1 = 297 bp, plus the reverse primer's 6-nucleotide non-templated tail. Total = 303 bp.
solutionSteps: Locate the forward primer's 5' end at position 201.
The reverse primer's 18 template-matching bases cover 480-497, so its 5' end corresponds to position 497.
Compute the template-defined core: 497 - 201 + 1 = 297 bp.
Add the reverse primer's 6-nt tail (copied in from the second cycle): 297 + 6 = 303 bp.
keyConcept: The final amplicon runs from the 5' end of one primer to the 5' end of the other and includes any non-templated 5' tails.
commonMistake: Omitting the non-annealing 5' tail, or measuring to a primer's 3' extension end instead of its 5' end.

optionExplanations.0: 297 counts the template core correctly but omits the 6-nt tail that becomes part of the amplicon.
optionExplanations.1: This measures to the reverse primer's 3' end (480) instead of its 5' end (497); the amplicon extends to the 5' ends.
optionExplanations.2: This adds a 6-nt tail at both ends, but only the reverse primer carries a tail.
optionExplanations.4: 497 - 201 = 296 makes an off-by-one error and also omits the 6-nt tail.

shortExplanation: For a single length, migration reflects conformation. A single nick relaxes supercoils to open-circular, which is the slowest band; a single double-strand cut gives full-length linear, the intermediate band. The remaining fastest band is supercoiled, so migration runs supercoiled > linear > open-circular.
solutionSteps: Note all molecules are the same length, so migration depends on conformation.
The nicking control yields open-circular DNA and runs as the slowest band, so the slowest band is open-circular.
The single-cut control yields full-length linear DNA and runs as the intermediate band, so that band is linear.
Assign the remaining fastest band to the compact supercoiled form.
keyConcept: For DNA of one length, agarose migration is set by conformation: supercoiled (fastest) > linear > open-circular (slowest).
commonMistake: Assuming more compact supercoiled DNA migrates slowly, or that cutting a circle changes its length.

optionExplanations.0: Supercoiling makes the molecule more compact so it migrates faster, and the nicking product is the slowest band.
optionExplanations.2: The single-cut linear product is the intermediate band, and cutting a circle does not change its contour length.
optionExplanations.3: The treatments interconvert the bands, proving all three are conformations of one molecule, not three plasmids.
optionExplanations.4: The nicking treatment produces open-circular DNA and gives the slowest band, so the open circle is not the fastest.

shortExplanation: A circular molecule cut at n distinct sites is divided into exactly n fragments (unlike a linear molecule, which gives n+1). The two enzymes together cut at 3 + 2 = 5 distinct sites, so a complete double digest yields 5 fragments.
solutionSteps: Count the distinct cut sites: 3 EcoRI + 2 BamHI = 5.
Recall that a circular molecule cut at n sites gives n fragments (the first cut only opens the circle).
Apply the rule: 5 sites give 5 fragments.
keyConcept: A circular DNA molecule cut at n distinct sites yields exactly n linear fragments; a linear molecule would give n+1.
commonMistake: Applying the linear-molecule rule (n+1) to a circle, or counting only one enzyme's sites.

optionExplanations.0: 3 counts only the EcoRI sites and ignores the two BamHI sites in the same digest.
optionExplanations.1: 4 undercounts the sites; there are five distinct cut sites, giving one fragment per site.
optionExplanations.2: 6 applies the linear-molecule rule (n+1); a circle has no free ends, so n cuts give n fragments.
optionExplanations.3: 2 counts only the BamHI sites and ignores the three EcoRI sites.

shortExplanation: The sub-atmospheric pleural pressure keeps a positive transpulmonary gradient holding the lung expanded against its inward recoil. Opening the pleura raises pressure to atmospheric, abolishing the gradient, so the lung collapses inward under its own recoil while the chest wall springs outward toward its larger resting volume.
solutionSteps: Recall the sealed sub-atmospheric pleural pressure creates a positive transpulmonary pressure holding the lung open.
Note this balance depends on the lung's inward recoil opposing the chest wall's outward recoil across a sealed space.
Open the pleura: air enters until intrapleural pressure equals atmospheric, abolishing the transpulmonary gradient.
Conclude the lung recoils inward and collapses, while the released chest wall springs outward.
keyConcept: The transpulmonary pressure from a sealed sub-atmospheric pleural space holds the lung expanded; losing the seal lets the lung and chest wall recoil in opposite directions.
commonMistake: Treating the chest wall's recoil as inward; the relaxed chest wall's resting volume is larger, so it recoils outward.

optionExplanations.0: The balance depended on the sealed sub-atmospheric space, so removing the seal does change the geometry.
optionExplanations.1: The relaxed chest wall recoils outward, not inward, so the two structures do not collapse together.
optionExplanations.2: The lung's elastic tissue and surface tension give a net inward recoil, so it does not spring outward.
optionExplanations.3: This reverses both recoils; the lung recoils inward and the relaxed chest wall recoils outward.

shortExplanation: In the lung the chloride shift reverses: plasma bicarbonate re-enters the red cell (chloride leaves) so that intracellular carbonic anhydrase can act. Inside, bicarbonate combines with H+ to reform CO2, which diffuses out to the alveolus.
solutionSteps: Recall that reconverting bicarbonate to CO2 requires carbonic anhydrase, which is inside the red cell.
So bicarbonate must re-enter the red cell, exchanged for chloride leaving (the reverse chloride shift).
Inside, bicarbonate combines with H+ (released as haemoglobin oxygenates) to form carbonic acid.
Carbonic anhydrase converts this to CO2, which diffuses out to the alveolus to be exhaled.
keyConcept: In the lungs the chloride shift runs in reverse: bicarbonate enters the red cell and chloride leaves so CO2 can be regenerated and exhaled.
commonMistake: Applying the tissue (forward) chloride-shift directions to the lung, or assuming both anions move the same way through an antiport.

optionExplanations.0: The transport is an electroneutral antiport, so both anions cannot enter at once without an equal counter-movement.
optionExplanations.1: Carbonic anhydrase is intracellular, so bicarbonate must re-enter the cell; plasma-only conversion is far too slow.
optionExplanations.2: This describes the tissue chloride shift; in the lung the process reverses so CO2 can be regenerated and exhaled.
optionExplanations.4: Both anions leaving ignores the antiport nature and would leave no bicarbonate to regenerate the CO2.

shortExplanation: Once 2,3-BPG is removed the two curves coincide, showing the intrinsic oxygen affinities are essentially equal. The in-blood difference must therefore arise because 2,3-BPG lowers HbA's affinity more than it lowers HbF's.
solutionSteps: Recall 2,3-BPG binds between the beta chains and stabilises the low-affinity T state, lowering oxygen affinity.
Note the gamma chains of HbF lack some cationic residues, so 2,3-BPG binds and depresses HbF less.
Observe that removing 2,3-BPG makes both curves coincide, so intrinsic affinities are essentially equal.
Conclude the physiological difference comes from 2,3-BPG lowering HbA's affinity more than HbF's.
keyConcept: HbF's higher affinity in blood is an allosteric effect: 2,3-BPG depresses HbA more than HbF, not an intrinsic difference in the haem.
commonMistake: Attributing the difference to intrinsic haem chemistry, which the coinciding BPG-free curves directly contradict.

optionExplanations.0: Both HbA and HbF have four haem groups (one per chain); the gamma chains add no extra haems.
optionExplanations.2: This reverses the binding: HbF actually binds 2,3-BPG more weakly, which is why its affinity is lowered less.
optionExplanations.3: The coinciding curves after 2,3-BPG removal show the intrinsic affinities are nearly identical, not greater for HbF.
optionExplanations.4: Oxygen binds the same ferrous haem iron in both haemoglobins, so the binding chemistry is not different.

shortExplanation: The urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising CO2. Hyperventilation lowers arterial CO2, so it takes longer to climb back to the breakpoint, delaying the urge; meanwhile oxygen keeps falling unchecked, so the swimmer can become severely hypoxic and black out before the urge forces a breath.
solutionSteps: Recall the dominant stimulus to breathe during a breath-hold is a rise in arterial PCO2.
Hyperventilation blows off CO2, driving PCO2 far below normal while adding little O2 (haemoglobin already ~97% saturated).
During the breath-hold, PCO2 must climb from a low start, delaying the breakpoint and the urge to breathe.
Meanwhile PO2 falls unchecked and can reach loss-of-consciousness levels, causing hypoxic blackout.
keyConcept: A single mechanism explains both effects: lowering CO2 delays the CO2-driven breakpoint while oxygen falls to hypoxic levels.
commonMistake: Thinking hyperventilation raises CO2 or meaningfully enlarges the oxygen store, or that the urge to breathe is driven by falling O2.

optionExplanations.0: Hyperventilation lowers arterial CO2, and blackout is from hypoxia, not CO2 toxicity.
optionExplanations.1: Haemoglobin is already about 97% saturated and cannot rise far above that, and the urge is driven by CO2, not O2.
optionExplanations.2: At normal pressure the oxygen dissolved in plasma is negligible, so hyperventilation adds little oxygen store.
optionExplanations.4: Hyperventilation does not lower arterial oxygen, and low oxygen does not relax the respiratory muscles to delay breathing.

shortExplanation: Both halve carrying capacity, but carbon monoxide also shifts the remaining haemoglobin toward the high-affinity state through cooperativity, so it unloads less oxygen at the tissues. Anaemia leaves the remaining haemoglobin normal, so the CO patient delivers oxygen less effectively.
solutionSteps: Note both conditions halve the haemoglobin available, halving oxygen-carrying capacity.
Recall haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively, so CO on some subunits shifts the rest toward the high-affinity R state.
This left-shifts the remaining haemoglobin's dissociation curve, so it unloads less at low tissue PO2.
Anaemia's remaining haemoglobin is normal and unloads normally, so the CO patient delivers oxygen worse.
keyConcept: CO poisoning is a double hit: reduced carrying capacity plus a leftward shift that impairs unloading of the remaining haemoglobin.
commonMistake: Treating the two as equivalent by counting only carrying capacity, ignoring CO's leftward affinity shift.

optionExplanations.0: CO increases the affinity of the remaining subunits (leftward shift), so oxygen is released less, not more, readily.
optionExplanations.2: This asserts the reverse: removing whole molecules preserves normal unloading, whereas CO impairs it.
optionExplanations.3: This counts only capacity and PO2, omitting the extra leftward shift that CO produces in the functional haemoglobin.
optionExplanations.4: Arterial PO2 (dissolved oxygen) is normal in both, and peripheral chemoreceptors sense PO2, not oxygen content, so they are not strongly stimulated.

shortExplanation: Net filtration pressure is favoured by capillary hydrostatic pressure and opposed by capsular hydrostatic pressure and plasma oncotic pressure: 48 - 8 - 30 = 10 mmHg. GFR = Kf x net pressure = 12.5 x 10 = 125 mL/min.
solutionSteps: Identify the driving force: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure = 48 mmHg.
Identify the opposing forces: capsular hydrostatic pressure (8) and plasma oncotic pressure (30); capsular oncotic pressure is 0.
Compute net filtration pressure: 48 - 8 - 30 = 10 mmHg.
Multiply by Kf: GFR = 12.5 x 10 = 125 mL/min.
keyConcept: GFR = Kf x net filtration pressure, where net pressure = capillary hydrostatic - capsular hydrostatic - plasma oncotic pressure.
commonMistake: Adding the plasma oncotic pressure as if it favoured filtration, or omitting one of the opposing pressures.

optionExplanations.1: This uses the capillary hydrostatic pressure alone (48) as the net pressure, ignoring both opposing pressures.
optionExplanations.2: This adds the oncotic pressure (48 - 8 + 30 = 70) as though it favoured filtration, but it opposes filtration.
optionExplanations.3: This uses 48 - 8 = 40, ignoring the plasma oncotic pressure that opposes filtration.
optionExplanations.4: This uses 48 - 30 = 18, omitting the capsular hydrostatic pressure that also opposes filtration.

shortExplanation: Filtered load = GFR x plasma concentration = 0.120 L/min x 25 mmol/L = 3.0 mmol/min. Because this exceeds the transport maximum, reabsorption saturates at 2.0 mmol/min and the excess is excreted: 3.0 - 2.0 = 1.0 mmol/min.
solutionSteps: Compute filtered load: 0.120 L/min x 25 mmol/L = 3.0 mmol/min.
Compare with the transport maximum (2.0 mmol/min); the load exceeds it.
Reabsorption saturates at Tm = 2.0 mmol/min.
Excreted = filtered load - reabsorbed = 3.0 - 2.0 = 1.0 mmol/min.
keyConcept: When filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, reabsorption saturates at Tm and the surplus is excreted.
commonMistake: Confusing the reabsorbed amount (Tm) with the excreted amount, or assuming reabsorption stops entirely once the threshold is passed.

optionExplanations.0: 2.0 mmol/min is the reabsorbed rate (the Tm), not the excreted rate.
optionExplanations.1: Assuming a constant 50% reabsorption ignores that glucose transport saturates at a fixed maximum.
optionExplanations.2: Assuming full reabsorption ignores that the filtered load (3.0) exceeds the transport maximum (2.0).
optionExplanations.3: Assuming no reabsorption once the threshold is exceeded is wrong; reabsorption continues at the Tm.

shortExplanation: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the medulla without letting water follow, building the corticomedullary osmotic gradient. Blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter collapses that gradient, so the collecting duct cannot reabsorb water even when ADH is present, producing a large volume of dilute urine.
solutionSteps: Recall that the thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl but is impermeable to water (the 'single effect').
The countercurrent multiplier amplifies this into a steep medullary osmotic gradient.
Furosemide blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, removing solute from the interstitium.
The medullary gradient dissipates, so the collecting duct has no osmotic driving force to reabsorb water.
Even with ADH and aquaporins present, little water is reabsorbed, giving a large volume of dilute urine.
keyConcept: The medullary osmotic gradient, built by NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, is what lets the collecting duct concentrate urine; abolishing the gradient causes a diuresis.
commonMistake: Assuming diuretics act by suppressing ADH, or that solute transport in the ascending limb also drives water reabsorption there.

optionExplanations.0: The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water regardless of transporter activity, so it never reabsorbs water there.
optionExplanations.1: Blocking solute reabsorption makes the fluid leaving the loop less hypo-osmotic, and the urine is dilute rather than concentrated.
optionExplanations.2: Furosemide acts on the tubular cotransporter, not on ADH secretion or its receptor.
optionExplanations.4: The active NaCl pump is in the thick ascending limb; the descending limb has no active NaCl transport and is permeable to water.

shortExplanation: Because desmopressin restores concentrating ability in patient X, that collecting duct is competent and the defect is a lack of endogenous ADH (central diabetes insipidus). Patient Y's urine stays dilute despite ADH, showing the collecting duct cannot respond (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus).
solutionSteps: Recall that ADH inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting-duct cells to allow water reabsorption and urine concentration.
Patient X concentrates urine after desmopressin, so the collecting duct works and only endogenous ADH was missing.
Classify patient X as central (ADH-deficient) diabetes insipidus.
Patient Y fails to concentrate despite desmopressin, so the collecting duct cannot respond to ADH.
Classify patient Y as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
keyConcept: A response to exogenous ADH distinguishes central (hormone-deficient) from nephrogenic (receptor/aquaporin-unresponsive) diabetes insipidus.
commonMistake: Reversing the interpretation, or attributing patient Y's failure to a missing medullary gradient rather than to receptor unresponsiveness.

optionExplanations.1: A fully ADH-responsive collecting duct would concentrate urine after desmopressin, which patient Y does not; and patient X is ADH-deficient, not an over-secretor.
optionExplanations.2: Patient Y does not respond to desmopressin, which is incompatible with simple ADH deficiency.
optionExplanations.3: In primary polydipsia the kidney can concentrate urine after water deprivation, yet both patients failed to.
optionExplanations.4: This reverses the interpretation; the patient whose urine concentrates after desmopressin has central, not nephrogenic, diabetes insipidus.

shortExplanation: Inulin concentration rises only as water is reabsorbed, so the fraction of filtered water remaining is 1/(TF/P inulin) = 1/3. The fraction of X remaining is TF/P(X)/TF/P(inulin) = 1.2/3.0 = 0.4, so the fraction reabsorbed is 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 = 60%.
solutionSteps: Since inulin is neither reabsorbed nor secreted, its amount is constant and its rise reflects water removal only.
Fraction of filtered water still in the tubule = 1/(TF/P inulin) = 1/3.
Fraction of X remaining = TF/P(X)/TF/P(inulin) = 1.2/3.0 = 0.4.
Fraction of X reabsorbed = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 = 60%.
keyConcept: Inulin acts as a volume marker; dividing a solute's TF/P by inulin's TF/P gives the fraction of that solute's filtered load still remaining.
commonMistake: Reading the concentration ratio directly as a reabsorbed fraction, or forgetting to subtract the remaining fraction from 1.

optionExplanations.0: 1/(TF/P inulin) = 1/3 is the fraction of filtered water still in the tubule, not the fraction of X reabsorbed.
optionExplanations.1: 1 - 1/3 = 67% is the fraction of water reabsorbed and wrongly assumes X is reabsorbed in the same proportion as water.
optionExplanations.2: Reading a TF/P of 1.2 as a '20% reabsorption' ignores that concentration also rises simply because water was removed.
optionExplanations.4: 1.2/3.0 = 0.4 is the fraction of X still remaining, not the fraction reabsorbed.

shortExplanation: Extra circulating T3 acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary just like the body's own hormone, so negative feedback suppresses TSH. Loss of TSH lowers the gland's own T4 output and causes the thyroid to atrophy, so all three variables fall together.
solutionSteps: Note that tablet T3 is indistinguishable from endogenous hormone to feedback receptors, and total activity is kept slightly high.
Negative feedback therefore suppresses pituitary TSH secretion.
TSH is the trophic hormone driving T4 synthesis and maintaining follicular-cell mass.
Sustained low TSH reduces endogenous T4 secretion and causes the gland to shrink.
keyConcept: Exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses TSH by negative feedback, and low TSH reduces both endogenous hormone output and gland size.
commonMistake: Believing a goitre must form, or that hormone taken as a tablet is not sensed by the feedback receptors.

optionExplanations.1: Endogenous T4 does fall, but extra hormone lowers rather than raises TSH, and the gland atrophies rather than enlarging.
optionExplanations.2: Exogenous hormone is indistinguishable to the feedback receptors and does suppress TSH, so TSH does not stay constant.
optionExplanations.3: This reverses negative feedback; extra thyroid hormone does not raise TSH or stimulate the gland.
optionExplanations.4: Low TSH means less stimulation, so endogenous T4 falls and the gland shrinks rather than enlarging.

shortExplanation: Months of high glucocorticoid chronically suppress CRH and ACTH by negative feedback, so the adrenal cortex atrophies. When the drug is stopped abruptly, the atrophied cortex cannot make cortisol and the suppressed pituitary cannot quickly restore ACTH, causing acute cortisol deficiency.
solutionSteps: Sustained high glucocorticoid suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH by negative feedback.
Without ACTH stimulation, the cortisol-producing zona fasciculata atrophies.
While the drug is present it substitutes for cortisol, masking the problem.
Abrupt withdrawal leaves the atrophied cortex unable to make cortisol and the pituitary slow to restore ACTH.
Acute cortisol deficiency produces hypotension, weakness and hypoglycaemia.
keyConcept: Chronic exogenous steroid suppresses the HPA axis and atrophies the adrenal cortex, so therapy must be tapered rather than stopped suddenly.
commonMistake: Thinking the drug chemically destroys the cortex, or that withdrawal triggers an ACTH surge; the cortex is atrophied through disuse and recovers gradually.

optionExplanations.0: The adrenal medulla and its adrenaline output are controlled by sympathetic nerves, not by the cortisol/ACTH feedback loop.
optionExplanations.2: There is no permanent resetting of pituitary sensitivity; the axis is transiently suppressed and recovers over time.
optionExplanations.3: The drug does not chemically destroy the cortex; the gland is atrophied through disuse and can recover if ACTH is restored gradually.
optionExplanations.4: After withdrawal ACTH is suppressed and slow to recover, not surging.

shortExplanation: If the parathyroid glands respond normally, a high blood calcium should switch PTH off, and that is exactly what is seen (PTH is low). The glands are behaving appropriately, so the calcium excess must come from a PTH-independent source.
solutionSteps: Apply the feedback rule: high blood calcium should suppress PTH in normally responsive glands.
The observed low PTH is therefore the appropriate response, not a defect.
Conclude the parathyroids are not the cause of the high calcium.
Attribute the calcium excess to a PTH-independent mechanism (for example a PTH-related peptide, excess vitamin D or bone breakdown).
keyConcept: A hormone level that is consistent with its feedback rule points the diagnosis away from that gland; low PTH with high calcium indicates a non-parathyroid source.
commonMistake: Assuming a hormone and its controlled variable must move in the same direction, and reflexively blaming the parathyroids.

optionExplanations.1: Parathyroid failure gives low PTH and therefore low, not high, calcium.
optionExplanations.2: PTH promotes renal calcium reabsorption, so a low PTH would reduce reabsorption rather than raise calcium.
optionExplanations.3: An autonomous PTH-secreting tumour would show a high, inappropriate PTH, not a low one.
optionExplanations.4: Low PTH with high calcium is precisely what functioning feedback predicts, not a laboratory error.

shortExplanation: Amino acids stimulate insulin, which lowers blood glucose, and after a carbohydrate-free meal no dietary glucose offsets this. The safeguard is that the same amino acids also release glucagon, which mobilises hepatic glucose; blocking glucagon leaves insulin unopposed, so blood glucose falls to hypoglycaemic levels.
solutionSteps: Amino acids stimulate insulin secretion, which lowers blood glucose.
A protein-only meal supplies no dietary glucose to offset this insulin action.
Normally the same amino acids also release glucagon, which makes the liver release glucose and balances the insulin.
With glucagon blocked, insulin acts unopposed on circulating glucose.
Blood glucose therefore falls to abnormally low (hypoglycaemic) levels.
keyConcept: Glucagon released alongside insulin after a protein meal prevents hypoglycaemia by mobilising hepatic glucose to balance insulin's glucose-lowering effect.
commonMistake: Believing a protein meal cannot change blood glucose because it contains no glucose, ignoring that amino-acid-driven insulin still acts on circulating glucose.

optionExplanations.0: The insulin response is intact and beta-cell secretion does not require glucagon.
optionExplanations.1: This reverses glucagon's action; glucagon raises glucose, so blocking it cannot make the liver release more glucose.
optionExplanations.2: Amino acids do not directly raise glucose here, and glucagon raises rather than lowers glucose, so removing it would not cause a rise.
optionExplanations.4: Insulin secreted in response to the amino acids continues to act on the glucose already circulating, so glucose does not stay constant.

shortExplanation: Cutting the stalk removes all hypothalamic signals reaching the anterior pituitary. The hormones under stimulatory releasing-hormone control fall, but prolactin, whose dominant hypothalamic signal is inhibitory dopamine, rises once that brake is removed.
solutionSteps: Severing the stalk stops all portal-vessel signals from the hypothalamus.
ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH and growth hormone lose their releasing hormones, so their secretion falls.
Prolactin's dominant hypothalamic signal is inhibitory dopamine.
Removing dopamine lifts the brake, so prolactin secretion rises.
keyConcept: Prolactin is under tonic inhibitory (dopamine) control while other anterior-pituitary hormones are under stimulation, so stalk section raises prolactin but lowers the rest.
commonMistake: Treating every anterior-pituitary hormone as stimulated by the hypothalamus, overlooking that prolactin is inhibited by dopamine.

optionExplanations.0: The anterior pituitary is not autonomous; its secretion depends on hypothalamic hormones arriving through the portal vessels.
optionExplanations.2: Most anterior-pituitary hormones are stimulated, not inhibited, so cutting their supply lowers them.
optionExplanations.3: This is the exact inversion of the correct pattern; prolactin is the one that rises, not the one that falls.
optionExplanations.4: Prolactin is under inhibitory control, so losing that signal makes it rise, not fall.

shortExplanation: Enteropeptidase makes the first trypsin, which then activates all the other pancreatic protease zymogens. Without it the whole cascade stays inactive, so protein digestion is severely impaired; amylase is secreted active and needs no proteolytic activation, so starch digestion continues normally.
solutionSteps: Enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, the single physiological trigger of the cascade.
Trypsin normally activates further trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase.
With no enteropeptidase, the initiating trypsin is never formed and the whole cascade remains inactive.
Protein digestion in the small intestine therefore collapses despite normal enzyme secretion.
Amylase is secreted active and is not a zymogen, so starch digestion is essentially unaffected.
keyConcept: Enteropeptidase initiates the entire pancreatic protease cascade, so its absence blocks protein digestion while leaving non-zymogen amylase-dependent carbohydrate digestion intact.
commonMistake: Assuming trypsinogen autoactivates spontaneously, or that amylase or lipase depend on the trypsin cascade for activation.

optionExplanations.0: Spontaneous trypsinogen autoactivation is negligible in vivo, which is why a dedicated activator is required.
optionExplanations.1: Pancreatic lipase is secreted active and is not part of the trypsin activation cascade.
optionExplanations.2: Amylase is not a zymogen and needs no proteolytic activation, so carbohydrate digestion does not depend on the cascade.
optionExplanations.3: Pepsin performs only limited gastric protein breakdown and cannot replace the trypsin-headed cascade.

shortExplanation: Bile salts physically emulsify fat, greatly increasing the lipid-water surface area but hydrolysing no ester bonds, so they alone release essentially no fatty acids. Lipase does the chemical hydrolysis but only at the interface, so the tube with both bile salts and lipase releases fatty acids fastest.
solutionSteps: Bile salts are amphipathic and break large fat globules into tiny droplets (physical emulsification).
Emulsification breaks no chemical bonds, so bile salts alone release essentially no fatty acids.
Lipase performs the chemical hydrolysis but can act only at the water-lipid interface.
On a single large fat mass the interfacial area is small, so lipase alone works slowly.
With bile salts increasing the surface area, the same lipase has far more interface, so the combined tube is fastest.
keyConcept: Bile salts and lipase act synergistically: bile provides interfacial surface area physically, while lipase supplies the hydrolysis chemically.
commonMistake: Treating bile salts as digestive enzymes that hydrolyse fat, or denying that surface area affects the enzyme's rate.

optionExplanations.0: Lipase acts only at the lipid-water interface, so emulsification markedly speeds hydrolysis; the combined tube is faster than lipase alone.
optionExplanations.1: Bile salts emulsify fat physically and hydrolyse no ester bonds, so the bile-only tube releases essentially no fatty acids.
optionExplanations.2: Pancreatic lipase is secreted active and works at duodenal pH; it needs no acid activation.
optionExplanations.4: Bile salts alone produce no hydrolysis, so the enzyme-plus-emulsification tube cannot equal the emulsification-only tube.

shortExplanation: The three features multiply in series, so the healthy amplification is 3 x 10 x 20 = 600. In disease only the folds remain, leaving 3, so the reduction factor is 600/3 = 200 (the lost villi and microvilli contribute 10 x 20 = 200).
solutionSteps: The features act in series, so their contributions multiply.
Healthy amplification = 3 x 10 x 20 = 600, giving area 600A.
In disease only the circular folds persist, giving 3 x A = 3A.
Reduction factor = 600A / 3A = 200.
keyConcept: Serially acting surface-amplifying features multiply, so losing the villi (x10) and microvilli (x20) reduces area by their product, 200-fold.
commonMistake: Adding the factors instead of multiplying, or counting only one of the two lost layers.

optionExplanations.1: 33 comes from adding the three factors (3 + 10 + 20) instead of multiplying them.
optionExplanations.2: 20 counts only the lost microvilli and forgets that the villi are also flattened.
optionExplanations.3: 30 multiplies only two factors (3 x 10) and misidentifies which layers are retained versus lost.
optionExplanations.4: 600 is the full healthy amplification and wrongly assumes the retained circular folds are also lost.

shortExplanation: Excess amino acids are deaminated to ammonia, which the liver normally converts to urea for excretion. In cirrhosis, hepatocyte failure plus portosystemic shunting lets ammonia bypass detoxification, so blood ammonia rises (causing confusion) while urea synthesis falls.
solutionSteps: Excess dietary amino acids are deaminated, chiefly in the liver, releasing toxic ammonia.
Normally portal blood delivers ammonia to hepatocytes, which convert it to urea via the urea cycle.
In cirrhosis many hepatocytes are lost and portosystemic shunts let portal blood skip the liver.
Ammonia escapes conversion and accumulates in the systemic blood, causing encephalopathy.
Urea production falls because the failing or bypassed liver makes less of it; a high-protein meal worsens this.
keyConcept: The liver detoxifies deamination-derived ammonia into urea; hepatocyte failure with shunting raises blood ammonia (neurotoxic) and lowers urea.
commonMistake: Identifying urea as the neurotoxin, or blaming low urea on faster renal excretion rather than reduced hepatic synthesis.

optionExplanations.0: Urea is low because the failing or bypassed liver synthesises less of it, not because the kidneys clear it faster.
optionExplanations.1: Urea is relatively non-toxic and is low here; the neurotoxic agent is ammonia.
optionExplanations.2: Transamination transfers an amino group without releasing free ammonia, and the liver disposes of ammonia as urea, not unchanged in bile.
optionExplanations.3: Urea synthesis is effectively unidirectional, so the liver does not regenerate ammonia from urea; the rise reflects failure to detoxify.

shortExplanation: With the bile duct blocked the liver still conjugates bilirubin, but the water-soluble conjugated form backs up into the blood and is filtered into the urine, making it dark. No bilirubin reaches the gut, so stools are pale and urinary urobilinogen falls.
solutionSteps: The liver still conjugates bilirubin normally; only its excretion is blocked.
Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood.
Because it is water-soluble, it is filtered by the kidney, giving dark urine (bilirubinuria).
No bilirubin reaches the gut, so bacteria form no stercobilin, giving pale stools.
Little urobilinogen is made, so reabsorbed urinary urobilinogen falls.
keyConcept: Obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice raises water-soluble conjugated bilirubin in blood and urine while cutting off the gut supply that makes stercobilin and urobilinogen.
commonMistake: Thinking obstruction blocks conjugation (it blocks excretion), or that unconjugated bilirubin appears in urine (it is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound).

optionExplanations.0: Urobilinogen is made by gut bacteria from bilirubin reaching the intestine; obstruction cuts off that supply, so urinary urobilinogen falls.
optionExplanations.1: Conjugation occurs normally in the hepatocytes; it is excretion that is blocked, so conjugated bilirubin rises.
optionExplanations.3: Obstruction stops bilirubin reaching the gut, so less stercobilin forms and stools become pale, not dark.
optionExplanations.4: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound, so it is not filtered into the urine.

shortExplanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase needs thiamine pyrophosphate to convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. A glucose load raises glycolytic flux and pyruvate production, but with the enzyme impaired the extra pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+, worsening the lactic acidosis.
solutionSteps: Pyruvate dehydrogenase uses thiamine pyrophosphate for the link reaction converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
With the cofactor deficient, pyruvate cannot enter the Krebs cycle.
A glucose infusion increases glycolytic flux, generating more pyruvate.
Glycolysis needs continuous NAD+, so the excess pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+.
Blood lactate rises, worsening the acidosis; thiamine must be given before or with glucose.
keyConcept: When pyruvate dehydrogenase is blocked, a glucose load drives excess pyruvate into lactate to regenerate NAD+, worsening lactic acidosis.
commonMistake: Attributing the acidosis to CO2 from an accelerated Krebs cycle, when the cycle is actually under-supplied and the acidosis is lactic.

optionExplanations.0: The acidosis is lactic, not a CO2 (respiratory) acidosis, and the Krebs cycle is under-supplied here.
optionExplanations.2: Glycogen stores glucose, not lactate, and its breakdown yields glucose phosphates rather than free lactate.
optionExplanations.3: Lactate is produced by reducing pyruvate within glycolysis; glucose cannot become lactate without passing through the pathway.
optionExplanations.4: Glucose is a respiratory substrate, not an inhibitor of the electron transport chain.

shortExplanation: In a single turn the two carbons lost as CO2 come from the four-carbon oxaloacetate already present, not from the newly added acetyl group. The labelled acetyl carbons stay within the four-carbon intermediates, so no labelled CO2 is released during this turn.
solutionSteps: The two decarboxylations occur as isocitrate becomes alpha-ketoglutarate and as alpha-ketoglutarate becomes succinyl-CoA.
Atom-mapping shows both released CO2 carbons originate from the pre-existing oxaloacetate, not the acetyl group.
The labelled acetyl carbons remain in the four-carbon pool.
Succinate is symmetrical, so their positions become scrambled but stay in the four-carbon intermediates.
After exactly one turn no labelled CO2 is produced.
keyConcept: The carbons released as CO2 in the first turn of the cycle come from oxaloacetate, so the entering acetyl carbons are retained until later turns.
commonMistake: Assuming the two carbons entering as the acetyl group are the ones immediately released as CO2.

optionExplanations.0: The link reaction decarboxylates pyruvate, not acetyl-CoA, so it cannot release the acetyl-group label.
optionExplanations.2: Neither of the two CO2 released in the first turn comes from the acetyl carbons.
optionExplanations.3: NADH and FADH2 carry hydrogen and electrons, not carbon atoms.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes the entering acetyl carbons are immediately decarboxylated, but they are retained in the first turn.

shortExplanation: Electrons dam up behind the Complex III block, so the upstream carriers (NADH pool and ubiquinone) become reduced while the downstream carriers (cytochrome c and Complex IV) drain to oxygen and stay oxidised. With no electron flow to oxygen, oxygen uptake stops and the proton gradient collapses.
solutionSteps: Antimycin A blocks electron transfer within Complex III, before cytochrome c.
Carriers upstream of the block accumulate electrons and become fully reduced.
Carriers downstream drain their remaining electrons to oxygen and then stay oxidised, as none arrive.
With no electron flow to oxygen, oxygen consumption stops.
No protons are pumped, so the existing gradient dissipates through the membrane's natural leak.
keyConcept: An electron-transport-chain block reduces upstream carriers, oxidises downstream ones, halts oxygen uptake, and lets the proton gradient decay.
commonMistake: Confusing an inhibitor (which stops oxygen uptake) with an uncoupler (which collapses the gradient but raises oxygen uptake), or thinking the gradient can rise when pumping has stopped.

optionExplanations.0: A block does not oxidise the upstream carriers, and once electron flow ceases oxygen consumption stops rather than slowing.
optionExplanations.2: Downstream carriers cannot become reduced, and the gradient cannot rise when pumping has stopped.
optionExplanations.3: This reverses the pattern; electrons pile up before, not after, the block, so downstream carriers become oxidised.
optionExplanations.4: A Complex III block necessarily changes the carriers' redox state and cannot raise the gradient.

shortExplanation: Aerobically the fibre uses 96/32 = 3 mmol glucose per minute; anaerobically it must use 96/2 = 48 mmol per minute for the same ATP. The rate rises by 48/3 = 16-fold.
solutionSteps: Aerobic glucose use = ATP demand / aerobic yield = 96/32 = 3 mmol/min.
Anaerobic glucose use = ATP demand / anaerobic yield = 96/2 = 48 mmol/min.
Factor change = 48/3 = 16-fold increase.
keyConcept: A factor change is a ratio of the two yields (32/2 = 16), so a much lower ATP yield per glucose demands proportionally more glucose.
commonMistake: Using the difference of the yields (32 - 2) instead of their ratio, or inverting the ratio.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the difference 32 minus 2 rather than the ratio 32/2; a factor comes from division, not subtraction.
optionExplanations.2: This seizes on the anaerobic yield of 2 rather than forming the ratio of the two yields.
optionExplanations.3: This inverts the ratio; a lower yield per glucose means more, not less, glucose is consumed.
optionExplanations.4: Glycolysis alone contributes only 2 of the 32 ATP made aerobically, so losing the aerobic stages is far from negligible.

shortExplanation: From the proton budget each NADH gives 10/4 = 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 gives 6/4 = 1.5 ATP, so chemiosmotic ATP = (10 x 2.5) + (2 x 1.5) = 28. Adding the 4 substrate-level ATP gives 32 total, and 28/32 = 87.5% is chemiosmotic.
solutionSteps: Each NADH yields 10/4 = 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 yields 6/4 = 1.5 ATP.
Chemiosmotic ATP = (10 x 2.5) + (2 x 1.5) = 25 + 3 = 28 ATP.
Add the 4 substrate-level ATP: total = 28 + 4 = 32 ATP.
Chemiosmotic fraction = 28/32 = 0.875 = 87.5%.
keyConcept: Convert the proton budget into ATP per coenzyme, sum the chemiosmotic ATP, then add substrate-level ATP for the total and take the ratio.
commonMistake: Using the older whole-number values (3 ATP per NADH, 2 per FADH2), or counting substrate-level ATP as chemiosmotic.

optionExplanations.1: This uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2, not the proton budget given here.
optionExplanations.2: The 4 substrate-level ATP are not made by chemiosmosis, so the chemiosmotic fraction is less than 100%.
optionExplanations.3: This omits the substrate-level ATP from the total, treating the 28 chemiosmotic ATP as the whole yield.
optionExplanations.4: This forgets the 2 ATP (GTP) made in the citric acid cycle, giving 30 total instead of 32.

shortExplanation: The cross X^D X+ by X+ Y gives four equally likely conceptuses: affected daughter, normal daughter, affected son (dies before birth) and normal son. Removing the non-viable affected son leaves three liveborn children, one of whom is affected, giving 1/3.
solutionSteps: Set the cross as X^D X+ (mother) by X+ Y (father).
The four equally likely conceptuses are affected daughter, normal daughter, affected son and normal son.
The hemizygous affected son (X^D Y) dies before birth, so it is not liveborn.
Three equally likely liveborn children remain, one affected.
Proportion affected among liveborn = 1/3.
keyConcept: Prenatal lethality of one genotype removes it from the liveborn denominator, so probabilities must be renormalised over surviving offspring.
commonMistake: Failing to remove the non-viable affected sons from the denominator, which would give 1/4 instead of 1/3.

optionExplanations.0: 2/3 is the proportion of liveborn children that are unaffected, the complement of the required value.
optionExplanations.1: 1/4 uses affected daughters over all conceptions without removing the non-viable affected sons from the denominator.
optionExplanations.2: 1/6 results from an extra, unjustified halving; the affected class among survivors is already 1/3.
optionExplanations.3: 1/2 ignores the prenatal death of affected males, which removes them from the liveborn count.

shortExplanation: The affected brother and unaffected father make the mother an obligate carrier, so the unaffected woman is a carrier with probability 1/2. A carrier passes the mutant allele to a son with probability 1/2, giving 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
solutionSteps: The affected brother is X^a Y and the father is X^A Y, so the mother must be a carrier (X^A X^a).
The unaffected woman is X^A X^A or X^A X^a with equal probability, so she is a carrier with probability 1/2.
A carrier transmits the mutant allele to a son with probability 1/2.
The child is specified as a son, so no extra sex factor applies: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
keyConcept: Chain the probability that the woman is a carrier with the transmission probability; because the child is already specified as a son, no further sex factor is applied.
commonMistake: Assuming the woman is certainly a carrier, or adding an extra 1/2 for the child being a son when a son is already specified.

optionExplanations.1: 1/2 assumes the woman is certainly a carrier, but she inherited the allele with only 1/2 probability.
optionExplanations.2: 1/16 over-multiplies the 1/2 factors; only two independent 1/2 factors are justified.
optionExplanations.3: 1/3 misapplies a conditional adjustment; the straightforward carrier-then-transmission calculation gives 1/4.
optionExplanations.4: 1/8 adds an extra 1/2 for the child being a son, but a son is already specified.

shortExplanation: The colour-blind grandfather and non-carrier grandmother make every daughter an obligate carrier. Each of her sons is colour-blind with probability 1/2, so P(at least one of two) = 1 - (1/2)^2 = 3/4.
solutionSteps: The grandfather is X^c Y and the grandmother is X^C X^C.
Every daughter receives X^c from her father and X^C from her mother, so she is an obligate carrier.
Each son of this carrier receives X^c (colour-blind) with probability 1/2.
P(neither of two sons colour-blind) = (1/2)^2 = 1/4.
P(at least one colour-blind) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4.
keyConcept: For 'at least one' outcomes, compute 1 minus the probability that none occur, using the daughter's certain carrier status.
commonMistake: Treating the daughter as only a probable carrier, or computing the probability for a single son or for both sons instead of 'at least one'.

optionExplanations.0: 1/8 introduces an unjustified third 1/2 factor; the daughter is an obligate carrier, so only the two son-transmissions apply.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 1 assumes every son of a carrier is affected, but transmission is only 1/2 per son.
optionExplanations.2: 1/2 is the probability for a single son and ignores that there are two sons and the 'at least one' requirement.
optionExplanations.4: 1/4 is the probability that both sons are colour-blind, not that at least one is.

shortExplanation: Being colour-blind, the boy carries the recessive allele on both X chromosomes. His normal-vision father contributes only X^C, so both X^c must be maternal and identical, which arises when sister chromatids fail to separate at meiosis II of a c-bearing oocyte.
solutionSteps: The colour-blind boy must be X^c X^c Y, carrying the recessive allele on both X chromosomes.
His normal-vision father can contribute only X^C, so a paternal X would make the boy a carrier, contradicting his phenotype.
Therefore both X^c chromosomes are maternal and identical.
His carrier mother (X^C X^c) produces two identical X^c only if sister chromatids fail to separate at meiosis II.
Fertilisation of that X^c X^c egg by a Y sperm gives 47,XXY: maternal meiosis II.
keyConcept: Two identical X chromosomes in one gamete indicate a meiosis II sister-chromatid non-disjunction; the colour-blind phenotype pins the origin to the mother.
commonMistake: Choosing maternal meiosis I, which would place the two different homologues (X^C and X^c) in the egg, giving a normal-vision son.

optionExplanations.0: A post-zygotic mitotic error would create a mosaic, not a uniformly colour-blind XXY individual.
optionExplanations.1: Maternal meiosis I would place the two different homologues in the egg, producing a normal-vision son.
optionExplanations.2: A paternal meiosis I error yields an XY sperm carrying the father's X^C, so the son could not be colour-blind.
optionExplanations.3: Paternal meiosis II produces XX or YY sperm, not XY, and any paternal X is X^C anyway.

shortExplanation: A resource split into two distinct types favours both bill extremes while disfavouring intermediates, which is disruptive selection. It removes intermediate phenotypes, produces a bimodal distribution and increases phenotypic variance.
solutionSteps: The seed supply is split into two distinct, non-overlapping types.
Deep-billed and shallow-billed birds each exploit one type efficiently; intermediates fit neither.
Both extremes are favoured over the middle, defining disruptive (diversifying) selection.
Intermediate phenotypes are removed, giving a bimodal distribution.
Phenotypic variance increases as the distribution spreads toward both extremes.
keyConcept: Disruptive selection favours both phenotypic extremes over intermediates, producing bimodality and increasing phenotypic variance.
commonMistake: Assuming any strong selection narrows a distribution, or attributing the systematic loss of intermediates to random genetic drift.
