optionExplanations.3: The immune system does not selectively inactivate antibiotics during viral illness; the drug simply lacks a target.

shortExplanation: The enormous variation between independent cultures is the fluctuation-test signature of random mutation before exposure: a mutation arising early gives a large clone of resistant descendants, while a late one gives few. The antibiotic selects pre-existing resistant cells rather than inducing resistance.
solutionSteps: Consider the two predictions: induced resistance gives similar counts, random mutation gives hugely variable counts.
The observed counts vary enormously between cultures, including jackpot cultures.
This fits random mutation occurring at different times during growth before drug exposure.
An early mutation is inherited by a large clone (high count); a late one leaves few resistant cells (low count).
Conclude resistance pre-exists the drug, which merely selects the already-resistant cells.
keyConcept: The fluctuation test shows resistance arises by random mutation before exposure; large between-culture variation reflects the timing of the mutation.
commonMistake: The Lamarckian idea that contact with the antibiotic induces or directs resistance, which would predict uniform counts.

optionExplanations.0: Induced resistance would give low, uniform counts across cultures, the opposite of the observed huge variation.
optionExplanations.2: Timing of division at exposure would still give comparable counts between equal cultures and cannot explain jackpot cultures.
optionExplanations.3: If the drug raised the mutation rate only after being added, counts would be similar, not hugely variable.
optionExplanations.4: Cells individually sensing and deciding is directed Lamarckian adaptation, which predicts uniform rather than wildly variable counts.

shortExplanation: Opsonisation works because the antibody physically bridges bacterium to phagocyte: its Fab arms grip the bacterial surface while its Fc region engages the phagocyte's Fc receptor. Removing the Fc leaves the bacterium coated but breaks the bridge, so only intact antibody enhances engulfment.
solutionSteps: Recall the two functional ends of an antibody: the Fab arms bind antigen, the Fc region binds phagocyte Fc receptors.
In condition (ii) the Fab fragments still coat the bacterium, so the loss of enhancement is NOT due to the bacterium becoming uncoated.
The only element removed in condition (ii) is the Fc region, so the enhancement in condition (iii) must depend on that Fc-to-receptor link.
Conclude: intact antibody acts as a molecular bridge, tethering the coated bacterium to the phagocyte and triggering engulfment; cut the Fc and the tether is gone.
keyConcept: Opsonisation boosts phagocytosis by bridging pathogen to phagocyte: Fab binds antigen, Fc binds the phagocyte's Fc receptor.
commonMistake: Thinking removal of the Fc stops the antibody binding the bacterium, when the stem states the Fab fragments remain attached.

optionExplanations.0: Antibodies do not generally kill bacteria on contact, and phagocytes readily engulf live pathogens, so 'engulf only dead bacteria' is false.
optionExplanations.1: This is the complement-only trap. The experiment isolates the antibody: the only difference between conditions (ii) and (iii) is the presence of the Fc region, and phagocytes carry Fc receptors specifically for antibody. If recognition depended solely on complement, intact versus Fc-stripped antibody would make no difference, yet only intact antibody enhances engulfment. So the effect is antibody-Fc driven, not complement-only.
optionExplanations.3: The antigen-binding sites are in the Fab arms, not the Fc region, so this misassigns the parts of the antibody.

shortExplanation: Antibodies act in blood and tissue fluid to neutralise extracellular pathogens and their toxins, while cytotoxic T cells kill the body's own cells that harbour intracellular pathogens. So the antibody-deficient patient is most vulnerable to the extracellular toxin-producing bacterium, and the cytotoxic-T-cell-deficient patient is most vulnerable to the intracellular virus.
solutionSteps: Locate each pathogen: bacterium X multiplies outside cells and harms via a secreted toxin; virus Y replicates inside host cells.
Match effectors to location: antibodies reach extracellular pathogens and toxins; cytotoxic T cells clear intracellular pathogens by killing infected cells.
Patient 1 lacks antibodies, so is most vulnerable to the extracellular bacterium X and its toxin.
Patient 2 lacks cytotoxic T cells, so is most vulnerable to the intracellular virus Y.
keyConcept: The humoral (antibody) and cell-mediated (cytotoxic T cell) arms are specialised for extracellular versus intracellular pathogens respectively.
commonMistake: Reversing the pairing, assigning intracellular defence to antibodies and extracellular defence to cytotoxic T cells.

optionExplanations.0: Cytotoxic T cells cannot neutralise a secreted toxin or extracellular bacteria, so they are not required for every response.
optionExplanations.2: This reverses the correct pairing between pathogen location and effector arm.
optionExplanations.4: Antibodies cannot clear an established intracellular virus, so they are not the only effective defence.

shortExplanation: The new strain's surface protein has mutated exactly where the earlier antibodies bind, so those memory antibodies can no longer neutralise it despite intact memory (antigenic drift). Effective protection therefore needs a vaccine updated to match the current surface protein, or one aimed at a conserved region.
solutionSteps: Recall that antibody memory is specific to particular epitopes on the surface protein.
The new strain differs at the exact recognised region, so existing antibodies bind poorly and fail to neutralise.
The conserved internal nucleoprotein is hidden inside the virion and inaccessible to neutralising antibody, so it cannot rescue protection.
Conclude the vaccine must be reformulated to the current surface antigen, or target a conserved accessible region.
keyConcept: Antigenic drift: mutation of surface epitopes lets a virus escape existing specific antibodies, requiring updated vaccines.
commonMistake: Assuming any conserved internal protein automatically confers antibody protection, ignoring that it is not exposed on the intact virus.

optionExplanations.0: The internal nucleoprotein is inaccessible to antibody on the intact virus, so its conservation gives no neutralisation.
optionExplanations.1: Viruses escape by mutating their own antigens, not by acquiring bacterial resistance plasmids.
optionExplanations.2: The stem states memory and antibodies are still present and functional, so waning memory cannot be the cause.

shortExplanation: An effector is the structure that carries out the corrective response. When core temperature rises, sweat glands secrete sweat whose evaporation removes heat, so the sweat glands are the effector.
solutionSteps: Identify the roles: receptor detects the stimulus, hypothalamus compares with the set point, effector carries out the response.
For a temperature rise the corrective response is heat loss by sweating.
The structure that produces sweat is the sweat gland, so it is the effector.
keyConcept: In negative feedback the effector is the structure that performs the corrective action, distinct from receptor, control centre and signalling pathway.
commonMistake: Confusing the efferent nerve pathway or the hypothalamic receptors with the effector, or picking a heat-conserving response to a rise in temperature.

optionExplanations.1: These sympathetic neurones form the efferent pathway carrying the command, not the structure that produces the response.
optionExplanations.2: Hypothalamic thermoreceptors are receptors that detect the stimulus, not effectors.
optionExplanations.3: Vasoconstriction conserves heat and belongs to the response to a fall in temperature, not a rise.

shortExplanation: This is positive feedback because more stretch causes more oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions and yet more stretch, driving the system further from its start rather than back to a set point. Because there is no set point to restore, the loop is ended by an external event: birth of the baby removes the cervical stretch.
solutionSteps: Check the direction of the loop: the response (contractions) reinforces the stimulus (cervical stretch), so it is positive feedback.
Note that positive feedback escalates and has no set point pulling it back.
Identify the terminating event: delivery of the baby removes the cervical stretch, ending oxytocin secretion.
keyConcept: Positive feedback amplifies the initiating stimulus and is halted by an external event, not by returning to a set point.
commonMistake: Importing negative-feedback logic (a set point or self-correction) into a positive-feedback loop.

optionExplanations.0: Positive-feedback loops do not regulate around a set point and are not self-terminating in that way.
optionExplanations.2: Opposing the stimulus and returning to a set point describes negative feedback, not this loop.
optionExplanations.3: Direct self-inhibition of oxytocin release would itself be negative feedback; the loop is broken by delivery removing the stimulus.

shortExplanation: To keep temperature constant the heat lost must equal the heat produced. Heat produced in one hour is 600 W x 3600 s = 2.16 x 10^6 J, and each kilogram of sweat removes 2.4 x 10^6 J, so mass = 2.16 x 10^6 / 2.4 x 10^6 = 0.90 kg.
solutionSteps: Calculate heat produced in one hour: 600 W x 3600 s = 2.16 x 10^6 J.
Recall each kilogram evaporated removes the latent heat, 2.4 x 10^6 J.
Divide energy by latent heat: 2.16 x 10^6 / 2.4 x 10^6 = 0.90 kg.
keyConcept: Mass evaporated = (power x time) / latent heat of vaporisation.
commonMistake: Failing to convert to the correct time (using 60 s or 60 min instead of 3600 s in an hour).

optionExplanations.0: 0.00025 kg is the mass per second; it omits multiplying by the seconds in an hour.
optionExplanations.3: 0.015 kg uses only 60 seconds instead of 3600 seconds for one hour.
optionExplanations.4: 6.5 kg divides by the latent heat of fusion, not vaporisation, confusing melting with evaporation.

shortExplanation: The hypothalamus generates its command from the error signal (actual temperature minus set point), not from whether the effector succeeds. With sweating disabled, less heat is lost, core temperature rises further above the set point, and the larger error drives a stronger command along the sympathetic pathway even though the glands cannot respond.
solutionSteps: Recognise sweating is the main heat-loss effector in a hot environment; blocking it means less heat is lost.
So core temperature rises higher than in a normal individual.
The hypothalamic output depends on the error (actual temperature minus set point), which is now larger.
Therefore both core temperature and the hypothalamic output along that pathway are higher.
keyConcept: A control centre sets its output from the size of the error signal, independent of whether the effector actually corrects the variable.
commonMistake: Believing the hypothalamus detects the effector's failure and reduces (or zeroes) its command.

optionExplanations.0: The control centre's output tracks the error signal, not the effector's success, so it does not fall.
optionExplanations.1: The block is distal to the hypothalamus, so it still fires along the pathway; output is not zero and is in fact raised.
optionExplanations.4: Blocking a heat-loss effector in a hot environment cannot make core temperature fall.

shortExplanation: Skin temperature is a leading indicator of a cold disturbance that will later cool the core. Starting vasoconstriction and shivering as soon as the skin cools opposes the disturbance before the regulated core temperature has deviated much, making the eventual fall in core temperature smaller.
solutionSteps: Recognise that a cooled skin will soon draw heat away from the core.
The skin signal therefore predicts a coming fall in core temperature.
Acting on it early triggers heat conservation and generation in advance of core deviation.
This anticipatory correction reduces the size of the eventual core temperature change.
keyConcept: Anticipatory (feed-forward) correction within a negative-feedback system uses a leading indicator to act before the regulated variable deviates.
commonMistake: Mislabelling this early, heat-conserving response as positive feedback.

optionExplanations.0: The responses oppose the cooling, so the loop remains negative feedback, not positive feedback.
optionExplanations.1: Core temperature is the ultimately regulated variable; the skin signal is an early warning, not a replacement.
optionExplanations.2: The early response is not due to the skin receptors having a different set point; both feed the same integrator.

shortExplanation: Mature mRNA has already had its introns spliced out, so the cDNA copied from it is a continuous intron-free coding sequence. E. coli, a prokaryote, has no splicing machinery, so it could not remove introns from a genomic copy.
solutionSteps: The human insulin gene in genomic DNA contains introns interrupting the coding sequence.
In human cells splicing removes these introns to produce the mature mRNA.
Reverse transcriptase copies that mature mRNA into cDNA, which therefore lacks introns.
E. coli cannot splice, so only an intron-free coding sequence can be transcribed and translated into functional insulin.
keyConcept: cDNA made from mature mRNA is intron-free, which is essential in a prokaryotic host because bacteria lack RNA-splicing machinery.
commonMistake: Believing RNA is more stable than DNA, or that reverse transcription amplifies the gene the way PCR does.

optionExplanations.0: RNA is in fact less chemically stable than DNA and is readily degraded, so stability is not the reason.
optionExplanations.1: Reverse transcriptase makes essentially one DNA copy per template; it does not amplify the gene like PCR.
optionExplanations.2: Splicing removes the introns before the mRNA is made, so the cDNA is a continuous coding sequence the bacterium can express.
optionExplanations.3: cDNA carries only the coding sequence; a bacterial promoter is not included and must be supplied by the plasmid vector.
optionExplanations.4: Bacterial ribosomes do not perform the eukaryotic post-translational modifications, so starting from mRNA cannot guarantee them.

shortExplanation: Each heterozygous genotype has Hardy-Weinberg frequency 2pq, giving 0.040, 0.100 and 0.010 at the three loci. Because the loci assort independently, the probabilities multiply: 0.040 x 0.100 x 0.010 = 4 x 10^-5, about 1 in 25,000.
solutionSteps: For each heterozygous locus compute 2pq: Locus 1 = 2(0.20)(0.10) = 0.040; Locus 2 = 2(0.25)(0.20) = 0.100; Locus 3 = 2(0.10)(0.05) = 0.010.
Because the loci are on different chromosomes and independent, multiply the single-locus frequencies.
keyConcept: Independent loci combine by the product rule, each heterozygote scored as 2pq under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
commonMistake: Forgetting the factor of 2 for a heterozygote, or adding instead of multiplying the single-locus frequencies.

optionExplanations.0: About 1 in 250 uses only two of the three loci, omitting the third locus frequency.
optionExplanations.1: About 1 in 200,000 uses pq instead of 2pq, forgetting the factor of 2 for a heterozygote.
optionExplanations.4: About 1 in 7 comes from adding the three frequencies instead of multiplying them.

shortExplanation: Growth on ampicillin shows a plasmid was taken up, but the insert lies within the tetracycline-resistance gene, disrupting it. So recombinant cells stay ampicillin-resistant but become tetracycline-sensitive: they grow on ampicillin yet fail to grow when replica-plated onto tetracycline.
solutionSteps: Ampicillin selection identifies all cells that took up any plasmid.
The human gene is inserted inside the tetracycline-resistance gene, disrupting it (insertional inactivation).
A recombinant plasmid therefore keeps ampicillin resistance but loses tetracycline resistance.
Recombinant colonies grow on ampicillin but fail to grow on tetracycline.
keyConcept: Insertional inactivation of a second marker distinguishes recombinant plasmids from re-circularised empty vector.
commonMistake: Assuming ampicillin resistance alone proves the insert is present, when empty re-circularised vector is also ampicillin-resistant.

optionExplanations.0: Ampicillin resistance only shows a plasmid was taken up; empty vector is also resistant.
optionExplanations.2: This reverses which marker is disrupted; every plasmid-bearing cell must be ampicillin-resistant to survive the first plate.
optionExplanations.4: Resistance to both antibiotics means an intact tetracycline gene, so the plasmid has no insert.

shortExplanation: The disorder is a recessive loss of function, so adding a single working copy of the gene supplies the missing enzyme and restores activity, with no need to remove the mutant alleles. Because only somatic bone-marrow cells are modified, the correction cannot be passed to the child's own offspring.
solutionSteps: Note the disorder is recessive loss of function: the two inherited alleles make no working enzyme.
A recessive loss-of-function phenotype needs only some functional protein, so one added copy is enough (gene addition, not replacement).
The cells treated are somatic bone-marrow stem cells, not germ cells.
Therefore the correction restores enzyme production but is not heritable by the patient's children.
keyConcept: Somatic gene addition can rescue a recessive loss-of-function disorder without altering the germ line, so it is not inherited.
commonMistake: Confusing somatic gene therapy with germline correction, or thinking the mutant alleles must be removed.

optionExplanations.0: This is gene addition, not replacement; the vector adds a functional copy rather than excising the mutant alleles.
optionExplanations.1: A single functional copy produces enough enzyme, which is why loss-of-function alleles are recessive; it is not masked.
optionExplanations.2: Only somatic cells are modified, so the germ line and future offspring are unaffected.

shortExplanation: Repeated spraying is a strong selection pressure that kills susceptible weeds but spares the few already carrying resistance alleles, whether from spontaneous mutation or transgene flow from the crop. The survivors reproduce, so resistance-allele frequency rises over generations and the herbicide loses effectiveness.
solutionSteps: Recognise natural variation: a few weeds already carry resistance alleles (from mutation or pollen-borne transgene flow).
Spraying kills susceptible weeds but resistant ones survive and reproduce.
Resistance-allele frequency therefore rises generation after generation (directional selection).
Eventually resistant weeds dominate and the herbicide loses effectiveness.
keyConcept: Herbicide use is directional natural selection acting on pre-existing variation, not a cause of adaptive mutation.
commonMistake: Believing the herbicide directs weeds to mutate, or that individuals acquire and inherit resistance within their lifetime.

optionExplanations.0: The herbicide does not direct adaptive mutation; mutations arise independently of need and are only selected.
optionExplanations.1: Transgenes can move into wild or weedy relatives by cross-pollination; being artificial does not prevent gene flow.
optionExplanations.4: This describes inheritance of an acquired characteristic; populations change in allele frequency, individuals do not acquire heritable resistance.

shortExplanation: In a nested hierarchy the lower the shared rank, the more recent the common ancestor. Species K and L share ranks down to family (both Vulpa), whereas K and M share only their order (Terra), so K and L are more closely related to each other than either is to M.
solutionSteps: Compare K and L: both share class, order and family (Vulpa), differing only in genus.
Compare K and M: they share only the order (Terra); their families differ (Vulpa vs Wroe).
The lower shared rank for K and L means a more recent common ancestor.
Therefore K and L are the more closely related pair.
keyConcept: Relatedness is judged from the lowest shared rank in a nested classification, not from table adjacency or a single higher rank.
commonMistake: Assuming that sharing a higher rank forces sharing of a lower rank, or judging relatedness by row proximity.

optionExplanations.1: M is in order Terra and N in order Sella, so they are in different orders.
optionExplanations.3: K and M share the order Terra but sit in different families (Vulpa vs Wroe).
optionExplanations.4: All four species are in class Malia, so they are not four different classes.

shortExplanation: The lack of peptidoglycan plus branched, ether-linked lipids identify organism Y as an archaeon, while the nuclear envelope identifies Z as a eukaryote. Like eukaryotes, archaea wrap their DNA around histone(-like) proteins, so Y and Z share this DNA-packaging mechanism, reflecting that Archaea are closer to Eukarya than to Bacteria.
solutionSteps: Identify X: peptidoglycan and unbranched ester-linked lipids, no histones, so a bacterium.
Identify Y: no peptidoglycan, branched ether-linked lipids, histone-like DNA packaging, so an archaeon.
Identify Z: nuclear envelope present, so a eukaryote.
Note both Y and Z package DNA around histone(-like) proteins, a shared feature reflecting archaea-eukaryote affinity.
keyConcept: X, Y and Z represent the three domains Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya; archaea share histone-based DNA packaging with eukaryotes.
commonMistake: Treating all cells without a nucleus as a single group, so grouping bacteria and archaea into one domain.

optionExplanations.0: X, Y and Z are three separate domains, not three kingdoms of one domain.
optionExplanations.1: Bacteria and Archaea are two separate domains, so lacking a nucleus does not place them together.
optionExplanations.3: The nuclear envelope makes Z a eukaryote regardless of lipid chemistry.

shortExplanation: The biological species concept counts populations that can potentially interbreed to give fertile offspring. The two fruit-fly populations produce fully fertile hybrids in the lab, so they are not reproductively isolated, and mere geographic distance does not split them into separate species.
solutionSteps: State the concept: a species is groups of actually or potentially interbreeding populations reproductively isolated from others.
The Group 2 fruit flies give fully fertile offspring when crossed, showing no reproductive isolation.
Geographic separation is not itself a biological reproductive barrier.
Therefore the two populations belong to the same biological species.
keyConcept: Reproductive isolation, not geographic separation, defines biological species; potential interbreeding counts.
commonMistake: Equating geographic separation (allopatry) with reproductive isolation.

optionExplanations.0: Geographic separation is not a biological reproductive barrier; the fertile lab cross shows potential interbreeding.
optionExplanations.1: A behavioural prezygotic barrier keeps the two bird populations as separate species despite sharing space and season.
optionExplanations.3: Apomictic dandelions reproduce asexually and do not interbreed, so the concept cannot be applied to them.

shortExplanation: A clade contains a common ancestor and all its descendants. The ancestor of S together with the (R, P, Q) group has exactly S, R, P and Q as descendants, because T branches off earlier, so {P, Q, R, S} is monophyletic.
solutionSteps: Recall a clade is an ancestor plus every one of its descendants.
T is sister to all the others, so it diverges before the node ancestral to S, R, P and Q.
The node ancestral to S and the (R, P, Q) group has descendants exactly S, R, P and Q.
Therefore {P, Q, R, S} is a clade.
keyConcept: A monophyletic group is a node and all descending tips; excluding a descendant or including a too-basal taxon breaks it.
commonMistake: Grouping adjacent tips in the tree that omit a descendant, or including T, whose only shared ancestor with the rest is the root.

optionExplanations.0: The common ancestor of Q and R also gave rise to P, so a clade there must include P.
optionExplanations.2: The only ancestor common to R, S and T is the root, which also produced P and Q, so this set is paraphyletic.
optionExplanations.3: The most recent common ancestor of S and T is the root, whose descendants are all five species.

shortExplanation: Reading each couplet in full: jointed legs give 1a, five pairs of legs is 'four or more' so 2b, the two-region body gives 4a, and five or more pairs of legs with two pairs of antennae gives 5b, which is Crustacea. The gills are consistent but not part of the key.
solutionSteps: Jointed legs present: couplet 1a leads to couplet 2.
Five pairs of walking legs counts as 'four or more', so couplet 2b leads to couplet 4.
Body in two regions (cephalothorax and abdomen), so couplet 4a leads to couplet 5.
Five or more pairs of legs plus two pairs of antennae is couplet 5b, giving Crustacea.
keyConcept: A dichotomous key must be followed couplet by couplet, checking every condition of the chosen option.
commonMistake: Mapping a high leg count straight to a myriapod without applying the body-region couplet.

optionExplanations.0: Diplopoda lies on the many-segment branch (4b), which the two-region body excludes.
optionExplanations.2: Insecta needs three pairs of legs and three body regions; the specimen has five pairs and two regions.
optionExplanations.3: Arachnida requires exactly four pairs of legs and no antennae; the specimen has five pairs and two pairs of antennae.

shortExplanation: iPSCs are reprogrammed from the patient's own cells, so their derivatives are genetically identical (autologous) and carry the patient's own self markers. They are therefore far less likely to be rejected than cells from an unrelated embryonic stem cell line.
solutionSteps: Note the iPSCs are made from the patient's own fibroblasts.
Cells derived from them are genetically identical to the patient.
They display the patient's own MHC (self) markers, so are not seen as foreign.
An unrelated hESC line is allogeneic and would trigger immune rejection, so the immune match is the key advantage.
keyConcept: Autologous iPSC-derived cells are genetically matched to the patient, minimising immune rejection.
commonMistake: Thinking stem cells express all their genes at once, or that reprogramming corrects the patient's disease alleles.

optionExplanations.0: Differentiated RPE cells express only a subset of the genome; no cell expresses all its genes simultaneously.
optionExplanations.2: iPSCs from the patient carry the same genome, including any disease alleles; reprogramming changes expression, not sequence.
optionExplanations.3: Cells that self-renew without differentiating would form tumours and supply no functional pigment; differentiation is required.

shortExplanation: A differentiated intestinal nucleus, placed in egg cytoplasm, can direct development of a whole fertile frog. This is only possible if that nucleus still contains the complete genome needed to specify every cell type, demonstrating genome equivalence.
solutionSteps: The transferred nucleus comes from a fully differentiated intestinal cell.
In egg cytoplasm it directs formation of a complete, fertile adult frog.
Building every tissue requires all the genes for every cell type.
Therefore the differentiated nucleus must have retained the complete genome.
keyConcept: Genome equivalence: differentiation is reversible differential gene expression, not loss or change of DNA.
commonMistake: Believing genes are deleted or mutated during differentiation.

optionExplanations.0: Differentiation is not caused by DNA mutations, and cytoplasmic DNA repair is fictional; the cytoplasm changes gene expression.
optionExplanations.1: In the body these cells are not totipotent; their potential is revealed only after nuclear transfer and reprogramming.
optionExplanations.2: If unused genes had been deleted, the nucleus could not direct formation of a complete frog.

shortExplanation: The 4-cell blastomere can form a complete individual including extra-embryonic tissues, so it is totipotent. The inner-cell-mass cell forms all body tissues but not the placenta alone, so it is pluripotent; the haematopoietic stem cell forms only blood lineages, so it is multipotent.
solutionSteps: Totipotent cells form the whole organism including extra-embryonic tissue: cell P, the 4-cell blastomere.
Pluripotent cells form all body tissues but not the placenta alone: cell Q, the inner-cell-mass cell.
Multipotent cells form a limited range of related cell types: cell R, restricted to blood cells.
Therefore P totipotent, Q pluripotent, R multipotent.
keyConcept: Potency ranks by breadth: totipotent (whole organism incl. placenta) > pluripotent (all body tissues) > multipotent (one lineage).
commonMistake: Assuming no single body cell can be totipotent, or swapping the pluripotent and multipotent labels.

optionExplanations.0: It underrates P as pluripotent, but a 4-cell blastomere can form a complete individual including placenta, which is totipotency.
optionExplanations.2: It inverts Q and R, labelling the broad inner-cell-mass cell multipotent and the blood-restricted stem cell pluripotent.
optionExplanations.3: It misclassifies R as pluripotent; a haematopoietic stem cell forms only blood lineages and is multipotent.

shortExplanation: All somatic cells share the same genome, so the fibroblasts already carried the muscle-protein genes but kept them silent. MyoD is a master regulatory transcription factor that binds regulatory DNA and switches on the whole set of muscle-specific genes, driving the fibroblast into the muscle programme.
solutionSteps: Recall genome equivalence: fibroblasts and muscle cells share the same genes.
The muscle-protein genes were therefore present in the fibroblasts but switched off.
MyoD is a master regulatory transcription factor.
When expressed it activates the muscle-specific gene programme, differentiating the fibroblast into muscle.
keyConcept: Differentiation is differential gene expression driven by master regulatory transcription factors, not a change in gene content.
commonMistake: Confusing a gene regulator with the enzyme that makes the product, or thinking cell types have different genomes.

optionExplanations.0: MyoD is a regulatory protein that activates transcription; it is not an enzyme that manufactures myosin.
optionExplanations.2: All somatic cells share one genome; genomes are not swapped between cell types.
optionExplanations.3: Transcription factors regulate genes already present; they do not insert new genes.

shortExplanation: Because the DNA sequence is identical in every cell type, the stable, heritable differences must be carried by epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and histone modifications, which are copied along with the DNA at each division. Reprogramming a hepatocyte to an iPSC must therefore erase and reset these marks to restore a pluripotent expression pattern.
solutionSteps: The DNA sequence is identical in hepatocytes and neurons, so sequence cannot explain their stable differences.
Epigenetic marks (DNA methylation, histone modifications) set which genes are active or silent.
These marks are copied when DNA replicates, giving a heritable cell memory transmitted to daughter cells.
Reprogramming to pluripotency must erase and reset these marks without altering the base sequence.
keyConcept: Heritable epigenetic marks maintain the differentiated state through mitosis; reprogramming resets them.
commonMistake: Thinking different cell types have different gene content, or that lineage identity is caused by mutation.

optionExplanations.1: By genome equivalence all cell types carry the same genes; nothing is deleted or inserted.
optionExplanations.2: The differentiated state is stably and reproducibly inherited, not re-set by chance each division.
optionExplanations.3: Lineage identity is not caused by DNA mutations; the sequences are identical and reprogramming corrects no bases.

shortExplanation: Having an affected (cc) child shows both parents are carriers (Cc), so a Cc x Cc cross gives 1 CC : 2 Cc : 1 cc. The daughter is unaffected, so the cc class is excluded, leaving 1 CC : 2 Cc, giving a 2/3 probability she is a carrier.
solutionSteps: The affected child (cc) shows both parents must be heterozygous carriers (Cc).
A Cc x Cc cross gives genotypes 1 CC : 2 Cc : 1 cc.
The daughter is unaffected, so remove the cc class.
Among the remaining 1 CC : 2 Cc, the probability of being a carrier is 2/3.
keyConcept: Conditional probability: renormalise the genotype ratio after excluding the impossible (affected) class.
commonMistake: Quoting the unconditional heterozygote frequency of 1/2 instead of conditioning on the child being unaffected.

optionExplanations.0: 1/2 is the unconditional Cc frequency; it ignores that the daughter is known to be unaffected.
optionExplanations.2: 1/4 is the frequency of a single homozygous class, not the heterozygote probability.
optionExplanations.4: 3/4 is the probability a child is unaffected, not the probability of being a carrier given she is healthy.

shortExplanation: Her prior risk of carrying the allele is 1/2. Being symptom-free at 50 is informative because only 50% of carriers are still asymptomatic then, whereas all non-carriers are. By Bayes' theorem, P(carrier | asymptomatic) = (1/2 x 0.5) / (1/2 x 0.5 + 1/2 x 1) = 0.25 / 0.75 = 1/3.
solutionSteps: Set the prior: father affected and heterozygous, mother not a carrier, so P(carrier) = 1/2.
Use penetrance: 50% of carriers are asymptomatic at 50, 100% of non-carriers are.
Simplify to 1/3.
keyConcept: Bayes' theorem updates a prior transmission risk using age-dependent penetrance evidence.
commonMistake: Treating being symptom-free at 50 as uninformative and keeping the 1/2 prior.

optionExplanations.0: 2/3 is P(non-carrier | asymptomatic), the complement of the required probability.
optionExplanations.1: 1/2 is the prior risk; it ignores the informative absence of symptoms at 50.
optionExplanations.2: 1/4 is the joint probability of carrier and asymptomatic, not renormalised by the total probability of being asymptomatic.

shortExplanation: Dominance is not fixed to an allele; it depends on the phenotype examined. For the disease, the heterozygote is healthy so HbS is recessive; at the protein level electrophoresis shows both HbA and HbS, so the alleles are codominant.
solutionSteps: Recognise that dominance is defined for a specific phenotype, not as a fixed property of an allele.
For the anaemia phenotype, note the heterozygote is essentially healthy, so HbS behaves as recessive.
For the protein phenotype, note electrophoresis reveals both HbA and HbS bands, so the alleles are codominant.
Conclude the dominance relationship changes with the phenotype being scored.
keyConcept: Dominance is relative to the phenotype and the level at which it is measured, not an intrinsic feature of an allele.
commonMistake: Assuming an allele has one fixed dominance status that applies to every phenotype.

optionExplanations.0: Treating HbS as dominant for all phenotypes would wrongly predict the heterozygote suffers sickle-cell anaemia.
optionExplanations.1: Calling HbS simply recessive ignores that electrophoresis shows both proteins, which is codominance at the protein level.
optionExplanations.3: This confuses the heterozygote's malaria fitness advantage with incomplete dominance, which means a blended intermediate phenotype.
optionExplanations.4: Codominance holds at the protein level but not for anaemia, where the heterozygote is not intermediate.

shortExplanation: The fraction as extreme as one parent is (1/4)^n, so (1/4)^n = 1/64 gives n = 3 loci. The active-allele dose runs from 0 to 2n, giving 2n + 1 = 7 phenotypic classes.
solutionSteps: Set the extreme-parent fraction equal to (1/4)^n = 1/64.
Solve 4^n = 64 to get n = 3 loci.
Note the number of active alleles ranges from 0 to 2n = 6.
Count the distinct doses: 2n + 1 = 7 classes.
keyConcept: For n additive loci, the extreme fraction is (1/4)^n and the number of phenotypic classes is 2n + 1.
commonMistake: Reporting the number of loci or forgetting the '+1' zero-dose class when counting phenotypic categories.

optionExplanations.0: 2n = 6 counts the intervals between doses, omitting the zero-dose class.
optionExplanations.1: 3 is the number of loci n, not yet converted into phenotypic classes.
optionExplanations.2: 2n - 1 = 5 drops one of the two extreme classes.
optionExplanations.4: n + 1 = 4 misapplies the rule; doses run from 0 to 2n, not from 0 to n.

shortExplanation: The two reaction norms cross: genotype X is tallest at low altitude, they are equal at medium, and genotype Y is tallest at high altitude. Because the ranking depends on altitude, no genotype is superior everywhere, demonstrating a genotype-environment interaction.
solutionSteps: Read each genotype's height across the three altitudes.
Note the two clones differ within the same environment, so genotype affects height.
Note each clone changes across altitudes, so environment affects height.
Observe the lines cross, so the genotype ranking reverses with altitude, i.e. a genotype-environment interaction.
keyConcept: Crossing reaction norms show that the effect of genotype on a trait depends on the environment (a genotype-environment interaction).
commonMistake: Concluding one genotype is simply superior, or that crossing norms mean zero heritability.

optionExplanations.0: An environment-only explanation fails because the clones reach different heights in the same environment.
optionExplanations.1: Picking the single tallest value is not overall genetic superiority once the reaction norms cross.
optionExplanations.2: A genotype-only explanation fails because each clone changes height across altitudes.
optionExplanations.4: Crossing norms do not make a trait non-heritable; heritability is defined within a given environment.

shortExplanation: Normal strength and sensation exclude the motor cortex and sensory pathways, and normal heart rate, breathing and temperature exclude the medulla and hypothalamus. Impaired coordination, past-pointing and loss of balance with intact power point to the cerebellum.
solutionSteps: Note strength and sensation are normal, excluding the motor cortex and sensory pathways.
Note heart rate, breathing and temperature are normal, excluding the medulla and hypothalamus.
Identify the remaining deficit: poorly coordinated movement, past-pointing and loss of balance.
Match this coordination and balance role to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: The cerebellum coordinates and smooths voluntary movement and maintains balance using sensory feedback, without generating force or sensation.
commonMistake: Assuming any movement disorder must come from the motor cortex, ignoring the cerebellum's coordinating role.

optionExplanations.0: The hypothalamus regulates temperature, water balance and endocrine output, none disturbed here, and has no role in limb coordination.
optionExplanations.2: Motor cortex damage would cause weakness or paralysis, but strength is explicitly normal.
optionExplanations.4: The medulla controls heart rate and breathing, which are stated to be normal.

shortExplanation: Bending at a surface depends on the difference in refractive index across it. The largest jump is from air (1.00) to the cornea (1.34), so the cornea does most of the focusing, while the lens, sitting between media of similar index, contributes less but provides adjustable fine focusing.
solutionSteps: Recall that refraction at a boundary depends on the change in refractive index, not the absolute value.
Compute the air-to-cornea step: 1.34 - 1.00 = 0.34, the largest change.
Compute the lens step: about 1.42 - 1.34 = 0.08 on each side, a small change.
Conclude the cornea dominates focusing while the lens provides variable fine adjustment.
keyConcept: The amount of refraction at a surface depends on the difference in refractive index across it, not on the absolute index on one side.
commonMistake: Confusing the structure that adjusts focus (the lens) with the structure that provides most of the focusing (the cornea).

optionExplanations.0: The ability to change shape governs how focus is adjusted, not how much refraction occurs.
optionExplanations.2: The retina detects the image; it is not a refracting surface, and refraction is complete before light reaches it.
optionExplanations.3: The cornea and lens do not refract equally; the cornea supplies roughly two-thirds of the converging power.
optionExplanations.4: A high refractive index alone does not cause strong bending; the lens sits between media of similar index.

shortExplanation: Bright light triggers parasympathetic contraction of the circular (sphincter) iris muscles, which actively constricts the pupil. Because the sensory signal from the lit eye is relayed centrally to the motor supply of both eyes, both pupils constrict together in the consensual reflex.
solutionSteps: Identify the two antagonistic iris muscles: circular (constrict, parasympathetic) and radial (dilate, sympathetic).
Note bright light drives parasympathetic contraction of the circular muscles, actively narrowing the pupil.
Recognise the afferent signal from the lit eye is relayed centrally to the motor supply of both eyes.
Conclude both pupils constrict together as the consensual reflex.
keyConcept: Pupil constriction is active parasympathetic contraction of the circular iris muscle, and central relay produces a consensual bilateral response.
commonMistake: Thinking constriction is passive, or that the shaded eye must itself receive light to respond.

optionExplanations.0: Constriction is an active muscle contraction, not passive closure from relaxation.
optionExplanations.2: The optic nerves do not fuse; the reflex is coordinated by central midbrain connections reaching both eyes.
optionExplanations.3: The shaded eye is not appreciably lit; its response is neural, via the consensual reflex.
optionExplanations.4: The radial muscles are dilators; their sympathetic contraction widens, not narrows, the pupil.

shortExplanation: The image distance is fixed at 0.020 m, so 1/v = 50 D always. For a distant object 1/u = 0, giving 50 D; for the object at 0.25 m, 1/u = 4 D, giving 54 D. The power must therefore increase by 4 dioptres.
solutionSteps: Convert the fixed image distance: v = 0.020 m, so 1/v = 50 D.
For a distant object, 1/u = 0, so P(far) = 50 D.
For the near object, 1/u = 1/0.25 = 4 D, so P(near) = 54 D.
Take the difference: 54 - 50 = an increase of 4 D.
keyConcept: Focusing a nearer object at a fixed image distance requires more converging power, supplied by accommodation as the lens becomes more curved.
commonMistake: Reporting an absolute power instead of the change, inverting the direction, or mis-converting the object distance.

optionExplanations.0: The direction is inverted; a nearer object needs more, not less, converging power.
optionExplanations.1: This uses 0.5 m instead of 0.25 m, giving 2 D instead of 4 D.
optionExplanations.2: 50 D is the total power for distant vision, not the change on accommodating.
optionExplanations.3: Although v is fixed, 1/u changes from 0 to 4 D, so the total power must change.

shortExplanation: Looking straight at the star focuses it on the cone-only fovea, which has low convergence and poor dim-light sensitivity. Looking to one side moves the image onto the rod-rich periphery, where many rods converge onto each nerve cell so their weak signals summate, giving greater sensitivity.
solutionSteps: Note the fovea contains only cones, wired with little convergence, giving high acuity but low sensitivity.
Note the periphery is rod-rich, with many rods converging onto each downstream nerve cell.
Explain that convergence lets weak rod signals summate and cross the detection threshold.
Conclude the faint star is best seen off-centre (averted vision) on the rod-rich periphery.
keyConcept: Convergence of rods gives high sensitivity through spatial summation, while low-convergence cones give high acuity but poor dim-light sensitivity.
commonMistake: Swapping the locations of rods and cones, or attributing summation to cones.

optionExplanations.0: One-to-one wiring gives cones high acuity, not high sensitivity, and the periphery is rod-rich, not cone-rich.
optionExplanations.1: The brain interprets the inverted retinal image correctly regardless of gaze; orientation does not affect visibility.
optionExplanations.2: This reverses the distribution and wrongly attributes summation to cones; the fovea is cone-only and the periphery rod-rich.
optionExplanations.4: Pupil size depends on overall light intensity, not on where a tiny faint source is imaged.

shortExplanation: The nutrient-rich pond supports a large photosynthetic and decomposer biomass. By day photosynthesis exceeds respiration and oxygen becomes supersaturated; after dark photosynthesis stops but respiration by algae and decomposers continues, drawing oxygen to a minimum just before dawn.
solutionSteps: Note the fertiliser bloom builds a large algal and decomposer biomass.
By day, gross photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so oxygen accumulates to supersaturation.
After dark, photosynthesis stops but respiration continues with no oxygen input.
Oxygen is consumed faster than it can diffuse in, reaching a pre-dawn minimum that kills fish.
keyConcept: In eutrophic water the bloom drives both daytime oxygen supersaturation and night-time depletion through continued respiration.
commonMistake: Believing photosynthesis occurs at night, or that gas exchange and respiration require light.

optionExplanations.1: Photosynthesis releases oxygen and cannot occur in the dark, so it cannot consume oxygen at night.
optionExplanations.2: Diffusion of atmospheric oxygen is a physical process independent of light and continues at night.
optionExplanations.3: Gas solubility rises as temperature falls, and the small change cannot explain a fall from 16 to 2 mg/L.
optionExplanations.4: Respiration is not driven by light and does not stop in the dark; it is what removes the oxygen.

shortExplanation: Total emissions are 9.0 + 1.0 = 10.0 Gt C and total sink uptake is 2.5 + 3.5 = 6.0 Gt C, so 4.0 Gt C accumulates. Dividing by 2.0 Gt C per ppm gives a rise of 2.0 ppm.
solutionSteps: Add anthropogenic sources: 9.0 + 1.0 = 10.0 Gt C.
Add sinks: 2.5 + 3.5 = 6.0 Gt C.
Subtract to find atmospheric accumulation: 10.0 - 6.0 = 4.0 Gt C.
Convert to concentration: 4.0 / 2.0 = 2.0 ppm.
keyConcept: Only the imbalance between emissions and sink uptake accumulates in the atmosphere, then converted from mass to concentration.
commonMistake: Skipping the mass-to-ppm conversion, ignoring sinks, or misclassifying deforestation as a sink.

optionExplanations.0: 4.0 is the net mass flux in Gt C reported as ppm without the required conversion.
optionExplanations.1: 5.0 ppm ignores all sinks and assumes every tonne emitted stays airborne.
optionExplanations.2: 1.5 ppm omits the 1.0 Gt C land-use emission, using only fossil fuels.
optionExplanations.3: 1.0 ppm treats deforestation as a sink rather than a source.

shortExplanation: For the dominated community, sum of squares is 0.80^2 + 4 x 0.05^2 = 0.65, so D = 0.35. For the even community, 4 x 0.25^2 = 0.25, so D = 0.75. The even community is more diverse because its greater evenness outweighs its lower richness.
solutionSteps: Compute the dominated community: 0.80^2 + 4 x 0.05^2 = 0.64 + 0.01 = 0.65, so D = 0.35.
Compute the even community: 4 x 0.25^2 = 0.25, so D = 0.75.
Compare the two indices: 0.75 exceeds 0.35.
Attribute the higher value to greater evenness outweighing the difference in richness.
keyConcept: Simpson's index reflects both species richness and evenness; heavy dominance by one species lowers diversity.
commonMistake: Equating diversity with species richness alone and ignoring evenness.

optionExplanations.0: This equates diversity with richness and ignores evenness, the factor that lowers the dominated community.
optionExplanations.1: Adding species does not always lower the dominance term; a community dominated by one species can still score high.
optionExplanations.3: Reaching the right community for the wrong reason: fewer species does not by itself raise D; evenness does.
optionExplanations.4: Simpson's index depends on proportional abundances, not merely on the number of species.

shortExplanation: Since S is proportional to A^z, the surviving fraction is (A_new/A_old)^z = (1/16)^0.25. Because 16 = 2^4, the fourth root gives 1/2, so about half the bird species persist.
solutionSteps: Write the ratio S_new/S_old = (A_new/A_old)^z.
Substitute A_new/A_old = 1/16 and z = 0.25.
Conclude the surviving fraction is 1/2.
keyConcept: The species-area power law means species loss is far less than proportional to area loss, set by the exponent z.
commonMistake: Using the wrong exponent (such as 1, 0.5 or 0.75) or assuming species number tracks area directly.

optionExplanations.0: 15/16 ignores the species-area relationship entirely and drastically underestimates extinction.
optionExplanations.1: 1/8 = (1/16)^0.75, using 0.75 instead of 0.25 for the exponent.
optionExplanations.3: 1/16 assumes z = 1, i.e. species number directly proportional to area.
optionExplanations.4: 1/4 = (1/16)^0.5, using a square root instead of the fourth root implied by z = 0.25.

shortExplanation: The per-generation retention factor is 1 - 1/(2 x 5) = 0.90. Over 3 generations this compounds: 0.90^3 = 0.729, so H3 = 0.80 x 0.729 = 0.58.
solutionSteps: Compute the retention factor: 1 - 1/(2 x 5) = 1 - 0.1 = 0.90.
Raise it to the number of generations: 0.90^3 = 0.729.
Multiply by the starting heterozygosity: 0.80 x 0.729 = 0.583.
Round to about 0.58.
keyConcept: Heterozygosity erodes multiplicatively with each generation at a rate set by the effective population size.
commonMistake: Using the wrong number of generations, dropping the factor of 2, or treating the loss as linear.

optionExplanations.0: 0.65 uses t = 2 (0.80 x 0.90^2) instead of t = 3.
optionExplanations.2: 0.72 applies the retention factor for only one generation (0.80 x 0.90).
optionExplanations.3: 0.41 uses 1/Ne instead of 1/(2Ne), overstating the loss.
optionExplanations.4: 0.56 treats the loss as a fixed 10% subtraction per generation rather than multiplicative decay.

shortExplanation: Only the phosphagen system responds instantly: creatine kinase transfers phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP, regenerating ATP almost as fast as myosin consumes it. This buffers ATP at nearly constant levels while phosphocreatine is drawn down, matching the data.
solutionSteps: Note ATP demand rises instantly but the ATP concentration barely falls while phosphocreatine falls sharply.
Compare response speeds: oxidative phosphorylation takes 1-2 minutes and glycolysis several seconds.
Identify the phosphagen system as the only essentially instantaneous source.
Explain that creatine kinase rephosphorylates ADP from phosphocreatine, buffering ATP as phosphocreatine is consumed.
keyConcept: The phosphocreatine system, via creatine kinase, instantly buffers ATP at the onset of intense exercise.
commonMistake: Assuming glycolysis or aerobic respiration ramps up instantly, or that ATP is spared by inhibiting demand.

optionExplanations.0: Glycolytic flux takes several seconds to reach maximum, so it cannot hold ATP constant in the first instant.
optionExplanations.1: ATP is held constant by regeneration, not by throttling hydrolysis; contraction continues at the high rate.
optionExplanations.2: Mitochondrial respiration is limited by oxygen delivery and takes 1-2 minutes to rise, not instantly.
optionExplanations.3: The sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump consumes ATP; it does not synthesise it.

shortExplanation: After the power stroke a myosin head stays bound to actin until a new ATP binds and triggers detachment. With calcium present the binding sites are exposed and heads attach, but with no ATP they cannot release, locking the fibre in a rigid state, the basis of rigor mortis.
solutionSteps: Recall that detachment of a myosin head requires binding of a new ATP molecule.
Note calcium is present, so troponin-tropomyosin exposes the binding sites and heads attach.
Note no ATP is available, so the attached heads cannot detach.
Conclude the fibre locks in a rigid, inextensible state (rigor).
keyConcept: Myosin detachment from actin depends on ATP binding, not hydrolysis; without ATP the fibre becomes rigid.
commonMistake: Assuming no ATP means no force and therefore relaxation.

optionExplanations.1: Calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum needs an ATP-driven pump, so without ATP calcium stays high.
optionExplanations.2: Tropomyosin position is controlled by calcium, which is present, so the sites stay exposed.
optionExplanations.3: Repeated cycling requires ATP to detach and re-cock the head; calcium alone cannot power it.
optionExplanations.4: Without ATP the attached heads cannot release, so the fibre is rigid, not relaxed.

shortExplanation: Calcium normally binds troponin C to shift troponin-tropomyosin off the actin binding sites. If troponin C cannot bind calcium, tropomyosin stays over the sites however much calcium is released, so no cross-bridges form and the fibre cannot contract.
solutionSteps: Recall that calcium triggers contraction by binding troponin C, not actin or myosin directly.
Note the mutation abolishes calcium binding to troponin C.
Conclude tropomyosin remains over the binding sites despite calcium release.
Therefore no cross-bridges form and the fibre fails to contract.
keyConcept: Calcium initiates contraction through troponin C; without that binding, the binding sites stay blocked.
commonMistake: Thinking calcium acts directly on actin or myosin, or confusing failure to bind calcium with failure to remove it.

optionExplanations.1: Calcium does not act on actin directly; it works through troponin.
optionExplanations.2: This describes a relaxation defect, but the mutation prevents calcium binding so contraction never starts.
optionExplanations.3: Calcium does not bind the myosin head; the power stroke follows phosphate and ADP release after ATP hydrolysis.
optionExplanations.4: Rigor needs heads attached to exposed sites, but here the sites stay blocked so no attachment occurs.

shortExplanation: High myoglobin, many mitochondria and dense capillaries all indicate reliance on aerobic respiration, and low myosin-ATPase means slow contraction. Together these mark fibre X as a slow-twitch oxidative fibre, fatigue-resistant and suited to endurance and postural activity.
solutionSteps: Interpret high myoglobin, many mitochondria and dense capillaries as markers of aerobic respiration.
Interpret low myosin-ATPase as slow cross-bridge cycling and slow contraction.
Combine these to classify fibre X as a slow-twitch, oxidative, fatigue-resistant fibre.
Match this profile to endurance and postural roles.
keyConcept: Slow-twitch oxidative fibres, rich in myoglobin, mitochondria and capillaries, resist fatigue and suit sustained endurance work.
commonMistake: Reversing the fibre types or equating fast, high-ATPase fibres with endurance capacity.

optionExplanations.0: Peak power in a brief effort is greater in the fast, high-ATPase fibre, not the oxidative one.
optionExplanations.2: A high myosin-ATPase consumes ATP faster and fatigues sooner; it is not more economical.
optionExplanations.3: Fibre X's abundant mitochondria and capillaries make it fatigue-resistant, so it outlasts the other fibre.
optionExplanations.4: Prolonged aerobic endurance is the province of the oxidative fibre, not the glycolytic one.

shortExplanation: Each half of the thick filament bears cross-bridges over (1.6 - 0.2)/2 = 0.7 um. At a sarcomere length of 2.9 um the thin filament overlaps this zone by 0.8 - (1.45 - 1.0) = 0.35 um, so tension is 0.35/0.7 = 50% of maximum.
solutionSteps: Place the sarcomere centre at the origin with Z-lines at plus and minus 1.45 um.
Find the cross-bridge zone on each half of the thick filament: (1.6 - 0.2)/2 = 0.7 um, reaching to 0.8 um.
Find the thin filament inner tip: 1.45 - 1.0 = 0.45 um from centre.
Compute overlap with the cross-bridge zone: 0.8 - 0.45 = 0.35 um.
Express as a fraction of the 0.7 um zone: 0.35/0.7 = 50%.
keyConcept: Active tension is proportional to overlap between the thin filament and the cross-bridge-bearing part of the thick filament, excluding the bare zone.
commonMistake: Ignoring the central bare zone or referencing overlap to the wrong length (whole thick or thin filament).

optionExplanations.0: The maximal plateau holds only up to 2.2 um; at 2.9 um the fibre is on the descending limb.
optionExplanations.1: 44% divides the overlap by 0.8 um, ignoring the 0.2 um bare zone that bears no cross-bridges.
optionExplanations.2: 35% references the overlap to the whole 1.0 um thin filament rather than the 0.7 um cross-bridge zone.
optionExplanations.4: Overlap reaches zero only at 3.6 um; at 2.9 um the filaments still overlap.

shortExplanation: Glucose consumed with lactate produced signals anaerobic glycolysis, and zero oxygen use shows no oxidative phosphorylation. Both follow from the mature red cell lacking mitochondria, which means it cannot burn the oxygen it carries, sparing it all for the tissues.
solutionSteps: Read the data: glucose consumed and lactate released, but no oxygen used.
Interpret glucose-in, lactate-out as anaerobic glycolysis.
Interpret zero oxygen consumption as no electron transport chain operating.
Attribute both to the absence of mitochondria and note the advantage: transported oxygen is spared for the tissues.
keyConcept: Mature mammalian red cells lack mitochondria, so they rely on anaerobic glycolysis and do not consume the oxygen they carry.
commonMistake: Choosing another true red-cell fact (biconcave shape, no ribosomes, no nucleus) that does not explain the metabolic data.

optionExplanations.0: The biconcave shape aids gas exchange but does not explain lactate production or zero oxygen use.
optionExplanations.1: Lacking ribosomes explains neither lactate production nor zero oxygen consumption.
optionExplanations.3: Carbonic anhydrase concerns carbon dioxide transport, not glycolysis or oxygen use.
optionExplanations.4: The nucleus is not the site of oxygen use; a cell can lack a nucleus yet respire aerobically if it keeps mitochondria.

shortExplanation: Stroke volume is 130 - 60 = 70 mL and ejection fraction is 70/130 = about 54%. During isovolumetric contraction both valves are shut, so the volume stays fixed at the end-diastolic value of 130 mL while pressure rises.
solutionSteps: Compute stroke volume: 130 - 60 = 70 mL.
Compute ejection fraction: 70/130 = 0.54, about 54%.
Recall that isovolumetric contraction follows mitral closure but precedes aortic opening.
Conclude the volume is constant at 130 mL during this phase as pressure climbs to 75 mmHg.
keyConcept: During isovolumetric contraction both valves are closed, so ventricular volume is fixed at the end-diastolic value while pressure rises.
commonMistake: Confusing the two isovolumetric phases or using the wrong denominator for ejection fraction.

optionExplanations.0: The stroke volume and ejection fraction are right, but the fall from 130 to 60 mL occurs during ejection, not isovolumetric contraction.
optionExplanations.1: 60 mL is the end-systolic volume, the volume during isovolumetric relaxation, not contraction.
optionExplanations.2: 60 mL is the residual volume, not the stroke volume, so both values are wrong.
optionExplanations.4: 117% divides stroke volume by end-systolic volume; an ejection fraction above 100% is impossible.

shortExplanation: The S1-S2 interval is systole; the rest of the cycle is diastole. During exercise the cycle length is 60/150 = 0.40 s and systole is 0.25 s, so diastole is 0.15 s, compared with 0.50 s at rest. Diastole is shortened far more than systole.
solutionSteps: Identify the S1-S2 interval as systole and the remainder as diastole.
Compute the exercise cycle length: 60/150 = 0.40 s.
Subtract systole: 0.40 - 0.25 = 0.15 s of diastole.
Compare with the resting diastole of 0.80 - 0.30 = 0.50 s.
keyConcept: As heart rate rises, the shortening of the cardiac cycle falls almost entirely on diastole, reducing filling time.
commonMistake: Equating the whole cycle with the filling period or assuming both phases shorten equally.

optionExplanations.0: 0.40 s is the whole cycle length, and diastole certainly is affected by heart rate.
optionExplanations.2: This reverses the phases; the data show systole nearly constant while diastole collapses.
optionExplanations.3: A 0.40 s cycle cannot contain a longer diastole than the resting 0.50 s; diastole must shorten.
optionExplanations.4: 0.25 s is the systolic interval; systole changes little while diastole falls steeply, so they do not scale equally.

shortExplanation: The AVN delay times ventricular contraction to begin only after atrial systole finishes filling the ventricles. Bypassing it makes the ventricles contract too early, losing the atrial top-up, so end-diastolic volume and, by the Frank-Starling mechanism, stroke volume fall.
solutionSteps: Recall the AVN delay lets atrial systole finish filling the ventricles before they contract.
Note the accessory pathway removes this delay, so the ventricles contract almost immediately.
Conclude the atrial contribution to filling is lost, lowering end-diastolic volume.
Apply the Frank-Starling relationship: a smaller end-diastolic volume gives a smaller stroke volume.
keyConcept: The AVN delay preserves the atrial-then-ventricular sequence, protecting ventricular filling and stroke volume.
commonMistake: Assuming faster atrioventricular conduction improves filling or output, or that it slows the pacemaker.

optionExplanations.0: Heart rate is set by the sino-atrial pacemaker, not by conduction speed to the ventricles.
optionExplanations.1: The ordered timing is exactly what the AVN delay provides; bypassing it destroys coordination.
optionExplanations.2: Contracting sooner removes the atrial contribution and lowers end-diastolic volume, so stroke volume falls.
optionExplanations.3: Filling requires the ventricle to stay relaxed until atrial systole is complete, not faster conduction.

shortExplanation: The heart follows whichever pacemaker reaches threshold first, i.e. the fastest. With the SAN slowed to 40 per minute, the AVN at 50 per minute now fires first and captures the heart, giving a junctional escape rhythm of about 50 per minute.
solutionSteps: Recall the fastest spontaneous pacemaker controls the heart and resets slower tissues.
Note the drug lowers the SAN's intrinsic rate to 40 per minute.
Compare with the AVN at 50 per minute, now the fastest site.
Conclude the AVN takes over, giving a heart rate of about 50 per minute.
keyConcept: Pacemaker dominance depends on relative firing rates, not a fixed anatomical ranking; the fastest site captures the heart.
commonMistake: Treating the SAN as an obligate pacemaker, averaging rival rates, or summing pacemaker rates.

optionExplanations.0: The SAN is dominant only while fastest; slowed below the AVN, it loses control.
optionExplanations.2: The controlling rate is that of the single fastest pacemaker, not an average of two.
optionExplanations.3: Pacemaker tissues do not add their rates; one fastest site captures and resets the others.
optionExplanations.4: An escape pacemaker is the fastest remaining tissue, the AVN at 50 per minute, not the ventricular tissue.

shortExplanation: Wobble only relaxes third-position pairing; the first two positions need strict Watson-Crick pairing. The UCN box needs 2 tRNAs (inosine reads UCU/UCC/UCA but not UCG) and the AGY box needs 1 (a G-wobble anticodon reads AGU and AGC), giving a minimum of 3.
solutionSteps: Note wobble applies only at the third codon position; the first two are read strictly.
Split the codons into two boxes: UCN (UCU, UCC, UCA, UCG) and AGY (AGU, AGC).
For the UCN box, inosine reads UCU/UCC/UCA but not UCG, so a second tRNA is needed: 2 tRNAs.
For the AGY box, one G-wobble anticodon reads AGU and AGC: 1 tRNA.
Add: 2 + 1 = 3 tRNAs minimum.
keyConcept: Only the third codon position tolerates wobble, so codons differing at the first two positions need separate tRNAs.
commonMistake: Ignoring wobble entirely, or assuming inosine reads all four third-position bases.

optionExplanations.1: A single tRNA cannot read all six; the two boxes differ at strictly-paired positions and no wobble base reads all four third bases.
optionExplanations.2: One tRNA per codon ignores wobble, which lets one tRNA read several codons differing only at the third position.
optionExplanations.3: This wrongly treats AGU and AGC as needing separate tRNAs; one G-wobble anticodon reads both.
optionExplanations.4: One tRNA per box fails because inosine reads at most three of four bases, so the UCN box needs two tRNAs.

shortExplanation: Peptidyl transfer moves the growing chain onto the A-site glycyl-tRNA, so it carries Met-Phe-Gly while the former P-site tRNA is deacylated. Translocation then shifts the peptidyl-tRNA to the P site, the deacylated tRNA (which read UUU) to the E site, and opens the A site over the His codon.
solutionSteps: During peptide-bond formation, transfer the chain from the P-site tRNA onto the A-site glycyl-tRNA, forming Met-Phe-Gly.
Note the former P-site tRNA-Phe is now deacylated.
During translocation, move the peptidyl-tRNA from A to P (over GGU).
Move the deacylated tRNA-Phe from P to E and open the A site over the His (CAU) codon.
keyConcept: Peptidyl transfer loads the chain onto the A-site tRNA, and translocation advances the ribosome one codon toward the 3' end.
commonMistake: Reversing the direction of peptidyl transfer or of ribosome movement, or misidentifying the deacylated tRNA.

optionExplanations.1: The ribosome translocates toward the 3' end, not the 5' end.
optionExplanations.2: The deacylated tRNA is the former peptidyl-tRNA (tRNA-Phe), not the glycine tRNA, which now holds the chain.
optionExplanations.3: After translocation the new peptidyl-tRNA moves from the A site to the P site; it does not stay in the A site.
optionExplanations.4: Peptidyl transfer moves the chain from the P-site tRNA onto the A-site tRNA, not the reverse.

shortExplanation: On cytoplasmic ribosomes the standard code treats the internal UGA as a stop codon, so translation terminates there and a truncated polypeptide is released. Inside the mitochondrion UGA is read as tryptophan, so translation continues to the downstream UAA and produces the full-length polypeptide.
solutionSteps: Recognise that the same triplet can be decoded differently in the two systems because the code is only near-universal.
Apply the standard code in the cytoplasm: the internal UGA is a stop codon, a release factor terminates translation, and a truncated chain is released.
Apply the mitochondrial reassignment: UGA is read by a Trp-tRNA, elongation continues to the UAA stop, and the full-length polypeptide is made.
keyConcept: The genetic code is near-universal, not truly universal: human mitochondria reassign UGA from stop to tryptophan, so identical mRNA can yield different products.
commonMistake: Assuming UGA is always a stop codon (or always tryptophan) everywhere, ignoring that the reassignment is specific to the mitochondrion.

optionExplanations.0: Over-applies universality by treating UGA as a stop codon in both systems, ignoring the mitochondrial reassignment of UGA to tryptophan.
optionExplanations.2: A stop codon terminates translation; it does not shift the reading frame, so no frameshift occurs.
optionExplanations.3: Over-generalises the mitochondrial exception to the cytoplasm, where UGA is a stop codon, not tryptophan.
optionExplanations.4: Reverses the two systems: it is the mitochondrion that reads UGA as tryptophan and the cytoplasm that stops there.

shortExplanation: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence recruits and positions the 30S subunit by pairing with the 16S rRNA so the AUG sits in the P site. Abolishing this pairing prevents proper positioning, so initiation fails and very little protein is made even though the coding sequence is intact.
solutionSteps: Note that the Shine-Dalgarno sequence lies upstream of AUG and is not itself translated.
Its role is to base-pair with the 16S rRNA to recruit and register the 30S subunit on the mRNA.
Removing the pairing means the 30S subunit cannot be positioned at the start codon, so the initiation complex does not form efficiently and protein output falls sharply.
keyConcept: In bacteria, ribosome recruitment depends on Shine-Dalgarno to 16S rRNA base-pairing; without it, initiation cannot proceed efficiently.
commonMistake: Thinking an intact AUG alone is enough to recruit the bacterial ribosome, which is actually the eukaryotic scanning mechanism.

optionExplanations.0: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence lies in the untranslated region and is not translated, so it does not encode the first amino acid; the initiator is fMet specified by AUG.
optionExplanations.2: Polypeptides are always synthesised N-to-C; ribosomes cannot build a chain in reverse.
optionExplanations.4: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence acts at initiation, not elongation or termination, so its loss impairs initiation rather than blocking later stages.

shortExplanation: Changing the stop codon UAA to the sense codon CAA removes the termination signal, so the ribosome inserts glutamine and reads through in the same frame. It continues until the next in-frame stop codon ten codons later, extending the protein by about ten amino acids at its C-terminus.
solutionSteps: Recognise that termination needs a stop codon in the A site recognised by a release factor.
Converting UAA to CAA (glutamine) removes the stop signal, so a tRNA decodes it and elongation continues.
Translation reads through in the same frame until the next in-frame stop codon, ten codons later, adding roughly ten residues at the C-terminus.
keyConcept: Loss of a stop codon causes read-through, extending the protein at its C-terminus until the next in-frame stop codon.
commonMistake: Confusing this with a nonsense mutation (which creates a premature stop and truncates), or thinking a single substitution causes a frameshift.

optionExplanations.0: Release factors recognise stop codons specifically; a sense codon such as CAA is decoded by a tRNA, not terminated by a release factor.
optionExplanations.2: The stated downstream in-frame stop codon does terminate translation, just ten codons later, so the ribosome does not run to the 3' end.
optionExplanations.3: The stop codon is removed, not created, so the protein is lengthened rather than truncated.
optionExplanations.4: A single base substitution does not change the reading frame; only insertions or deletions not in multiples of three cause frameshifts.

shortExplanation: Apply the Lincoln index with n1 = 84 marked, n2 = 90 in the second sample and 18 recaptured marked fish. N = (84 x 90)/18 = 7560/18 = 420.
solutionSteps: Identify n1 = 84 (marked and released) and n2 = 90 (second sample).
Identify the recapture count: 18 marked fish in the second sample.
keyConcept: The Lincoln index assumes the marked fraction in the second sample equals the marked fraction in the whole population, so N = (n1 x n2)/recaptured.
commonMistake: Putting the wrong number in the denominator (e.g. the unmarked fish 90-18 = 72) or forgetting to divide by the recapture count at all.

optionExplanations.0: Dividing by 2 x 18 = 36 double-uses the recapture number; it belongs in the denominator once, undivided.
optionExplanations.1: Dividing 7560 by the 72 unmarked fish is wrong; only the 18 recaptured marked fish belong in the denominator.
optionExplanations.3: 84 + 90 - 18 = 156 treats the samples as overlapping sets; the Lincoln index is a ratio estimate, not a union of sets.
optionExplanations.4: 84 x 90 = 7560 omits the division by the recapture count entirely.

shortExplanation: Since N = (n1 x n2)/recaptured, N is underestimated only when the recapture count is inflated. Trap-happy marked animals enter traps more readily, raising the recapture count and making N come out too small.
solutionSteps: Write N = (n1 x n2)/recaptured and note N falls when the recapture count rises.
Look for the single factor that inflates the recapture count.
Trap-happy marked animals are overrepresented in the second sample, inflating the denominator and underestimating N.
Confirm every other option lowers the recapture count, which would overestimate N.
keyConcept: An underestimate of N requires an inflated recapture count; only over-representation of marked animals in the second sample achieves this.
commonMistake: Assuming that fewer marked animals recaptured means an underestimate; the algebra gives the opposite (fewer recaptures raise N).

optionExplanations.0: Faded, unreadable marks lower the recapture count, which raises N to an overestimate.
optionExplanations.1: Incomplete mixing with sampling away from the release point lowers the recapture count, again overestimating N.
optionExplanations.2: Emigration of marked animals replaced by unmarked immigrants dilutes the marked fraction, lowering recaptures and overestimating N.
optionExplanations.3: Extra predation on conspicuous marked animals lowers the recapture count, increasing N to an overestimate.

shortExplanation: Each quadrat covers 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 m^2, so density = 3.0/0.25 = 12 plants per m^2. The meadow area is 80 x 50 = 4000 m^2, giving a total of 12 x 4000 = 48000 plants.
solutionSteps: Find the quadrat area: 0.5 m x 0.5 m = 0.25 m^2.
Convert the mean count to a density: 3.0/0.25 = 12 plants per m^2.
Find the meadow area: 80 x 50 = 4000 m^2.
Multiply density by area: 12 x 4000 = 48000 plants.
keyConcept: Scaling a quadrat count to a whole area requires dividing by the quadrat area to get a density per m^2, then multiplying by the total area.
commonMistake: Using the quadrat side length (0.5) as the area instead of the side squared (0.25 m^2), or re-applying the number of quadrats after the mean is already averaged.

optionExplanations.0: Taking the quadrat area as 0.5 m^2 (side length instead of side squared) gives 24000; the area is 0.25 m^2.
optionExplanations.2: 3.0 x 4000 treats each quadrat as 1 m^2, but it is 0.25 m^2, so the density is 12 per m^2, not 3.
optionExplanations.3: Dividing 48000 by 20 averages a second time; the averaging is already contained in the mean of 3.0 per quadrat.
optionExplanations.4: Squaring the area (0.25^2) gives a spurious density of 48 per m^2; the area must be used once, not squared again.

shortExplanation: With counts 5, 3, 2 the total N = 10. Sum n(n-1) = 20 + 6 + 2 = 28 and N(N-1) = 90, so D = 1 - 28/90 = 0.69. On the 0 to 1 scale a value near 1 indicates relatively high diversity.
solutionSteps: Total the individuals: N = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.
Compute N(N-1) = 10 x 9 = 90.
Apply D = 1 - 28/90 = 0.69, which is near the maximum, indicating high diversity.
keyConcept: Simpson's Index of Diversity runs from 0 to 1 with higher values meaning greater diversity; use the supplied count form n(n-1)/N(N-1) and remember the leading 1 minus.
commonMistake: Using the proportion (p^2) form instead of the defined count form, or dropping the '1 -' and reporting a dominance value.

optionExplanations.0: 0.62 uses the proportion form 1 - sum (n/N)^2 rather than the defined count form; the interpretation is right but the formula used is not the one given.
optionExplanations.1: 2.63 is Simpson's Reciprocal Index (an effective number of species), not the 0 to 1 Index of Diversity defined here.
optionExplanations.2: 0.31 drops the '1 -' and reports Simpson's index of dominance, not diversity.
optionExplanations.4: 0.38 is a dominance measure (sum of (n/N)^2), the chance two individuals are the same species, mislabelled as diversity.

shortExplanation: Only 80% of truly-marked beetles are recognised, so the 20 scored marks represent 20/0.80 = 25 genuinely marked beetles. Applying the Lincoln index with the true recapture number gives N = (200 x 150)/25 = 1200.
solutionSteps: Recognise that faded marks make the recapture count too small.
Correct the recapture count: 20 scored marks / 0.80 = 25 truly marked beetles.
Apply the Lincoln index: N = (200 x 150)/25 = 1200.
Note the corrected value is lower than the naive 1500 because the naive figure was inflated by missed recaptures.
keyConcept: Mark loss undercounts recaptures, so correct the recapture number upward before applying the Lincoln index; this lowers the estimate.
commonMistake: Scaling the naive estimate up for mark loss, or applying the 20% correction to the whole second sample rather than only to the recaptured animals.

optionExplanations.1: 1875 scales the naive estimate up for mark loss, but mark loss makes recaptures too few, so the estimate must be scaled down.
optionExplanations.2: 1500 is the naive estimate that ignores mark loss entirely, undercounting the true recaptures.
optionExplanations.3: 600 applies the 20% loss to all 150 beetles rather than only to the marked animals in the recapture count.
optionExplanations.4: 960 applies the 20% correction a second time; the factor should be used only once.

shortExplanation: The normal gene is a proto-oncogene encoding a receptor that promotes division only when its ligand binds. The point mutation makes the receptor constitutively active (a gain of function), producing an oncogene that signals dominantly even with a normal copy present.
solutionSteps: Identify the normal gene as a proto-oncogene: it promotes division when its ligand binds.
Recognise the mutation makes the receptor signal continuously without ligand: a gain of function.
A gain-of-function change in one allele is enough to produce the abnormal signal, so it acts dominantly and the activated gene is an oncogene.
keyConcept: Activating (gain-of-function) mutations convert a proto-oncogene into an oncogene and act dominantly at the cellular level, unlike tumour-suppressor loss which is recessive and needs both copies knocked out.
commonMistake: Applying the two-hit tumour-suppressor rule to an oncogene, or treating an activating mutation as a recessive loss-of-function change.

optionExplanations.0: An activated oncogene drives the signal by itself; simultaneous loss of both tumour-suppressor copies is not a prerequisite.
optionExplanations.1: It inverts the terminology: the growth-promoting gene is the proto-oncogene and its activated version the oncogene, and the two-copy rule applies to tumour suppressors.
optionExplanations.3: The mutant receptor signals independently of ligand, so it is dominant; the behaviour of the normal allele is irrelevant.
optionExplanations.4: This is an activating, division-promoting change, not a loss-of-function that blocks the cycle; it pushes cells into S phase.

shortExplanation: DNA damage stabilises p53, which switches on a gene for a CDK inhibitor that halts the cycle at the G1/S boundary so the breaks can be repaired. In the p53-null line Y no arrest occurs, so the damaged DNA is replicated and mutations are passed to daughter cells.
solutionSteps: Identify p53 as a tumour-suppressor transcription factor stabilised by DNA damage.
It induces a CDK inhibitor (p21) that blocks the G1 cyclin-CDK complexes, arresting the cell for repair.
