In line X this checkpoint operates; in line Y, lacking p53, no arrest signal forms.
Line Y replicates the damaged template, fixing errors as inherited mutations.
keyConcept: p53 acts at the DNA-damage checkpoint by inducing a CDK inhibitor to arrest the cycle; losing it removes the arrest and raises the mutation rate.
commonMistake: Casting p53 as a repair enzyme, a growth factor, or an oncogene, or reversing which line arrests.

optionExplanations.0: p53 is a transcription factor that induces arrest and repair genes; it does not itself carry out the enzymatic repair, and line Y keeps dividing.
optionExplanations.1: p53 arrests the cycle after damage rather than accelerating it, so its loss removes a brake and does not slow the cycle.
optionExplanations.2: p53 is a tumour suppressor, not an oncogene; the 'switched-off oncogene' framing misclassifies it.
optionExplanations.4: Arrest occurs in the p53-competent line X, and p53 induces a CDK inhibitor, so it is not required to activate cyclin-CDK complexes.

shortExplanation: Growth 2 is malignant: its cells have invaded through the basement membrane and identical cells appear in a distant lymph node (metastasis). Growth 1 is encapsulated, well-differentiated and localised, so it is benign.
solutionSteps: Note that uncontrolled division is common to all tumours and does not distinguish benign from malignant.
Recognise the defining features of malignancy: invasion through the basement membrane and metastasis to distant sites.
Classify Growth 1 (encapsulated, localised, resembling normal tissue) as benign.
Classify Growth 2 (breached basement membrane, cells in a distant lymph node) as malignant.
keyConcept: Malignancy is defined by invasion through the basement membrane and metastasis, not merely by uncontrolled division.
commonMistake: Treating uncontrolled division or a fibrous capsule as the criterion, when a capsule and localisation actually indicate a benign tumour.

optionExplanations.1: A fibrous capsule and localisation are hallmarks of a benign tumour, not malignancy, and division rate is not the classifying criterion.
optionExplanations.2: Benign tumours also divide beyond normal control yet stay benign; malignancy needs invasion and metastasis, which only Growth 2 shows.
optionExplanations.3: Behaviour (invasion and metastasis) classifies tumours and is directly observable here; the first mutated gene need not be known.
optionExplanations.4: Identical cells in a distant lymph node are exactly the evidence of metastasis and therefore of malignancy.

shortExplanation: Rb is a tumour suppressor, so a tumour needs both copies lost in the same cell. Inherited-form children carry one faulty copy in every cell, so a single further somatic hit suffices, giving early, multiple, often bilateral tumours; the sporadic form needs two independent hits in one cell, so it is later and usually single.
solutionSteps: Establish that Rb is a tumour suppressor requiring loss of both copies in the same cell (recessive at the cellular level).
In the inherited form the germline supplies the first hit in every cell.
Only one further somatic hit is then needed in any retinal cell, so tumours arise early and at multiple sites.
In the sporadic form both hits must occur independently in the same cell, which is rare, so tumours are later and usually single.
keyConcept: The two-hit hypothesis: tumour-suppressor loss is recessive within a cell, but inheriting one defective copy makes the predisposition dominant at the level of the organism.
commonMistake: Treating the inherited predisposition as if one hit transforms the cell directly, or classifying Rb as an oncogene.

optionExplanations.0: The predisposition is inherited dominantly, but a retinal cell still needs its second Rb copy knocked out; one hit does not transform the cell alone.
optionExplanations.1: The inherited form needs only one somatic hit because the germline supplies the first, so earlier onset follows from the pre-existing hit, not faster division.
optionExplanations.2: Rb is a tumour suppressor whose loss (not activation) causes the tumour; cells do not divide uncontrollably until both copies are lost.
optionExplanations.3: Inheriting one faulty copy so only one further hit is needed describes the inherited form, not the sporadic form, which starts with two working copies.

shortExplanation: Losing p53 removes the DNA-damage checkpoint that would arrest or destroy damaged cells, so the mutant clone becomes genetically unstable and accumulates further mutations. Cancer develops as successive advantageous mutations build up within a single cell lineage until it becomes invasive and metastasises.
solutionSteps: Recall that cancer arises by a series of mutations accumulating in one cell lineage, each giving a growth or survival advantage.
The polyp already had an activated oncogene and lost a tumour suppressor but stayed benign.
Losing p53 removes the DNA-damage checkpoint, so the clone becomes genetically unstable and gains mutations rapidly.
Some new mutations enable invasion and metastasis, converting the benign adenoma into a malignant carcinoma.
keyConcept: Multi-step carcinogenesis: cancer results from several mutations accumulating within a single clonal lineage, and p53 loss accelerates this by abolishing the DNA-damage checkpoint.
commonMistake: Collapsing multi-step progression into a single p53 event, or thinking mutations from different cells can be pooled into one cell.

optionExplanations.0: The scenario requires prior hits plus several further mutations after p53 loss; one mutation does not by itself produce a metastatic cancer.
optionExplanations.2: Cancer arises within one clonal lineage; mutations in separate neighbouring cells are not combined into a single cell.
optionExplanations.3: Malignancy (invasion and metastasis) appeared only after p53 loss and later mutations, so p53 loss clearly did change the lesion's behaviour.
optionExplanations.4: p53 is a tumour suppressor, so inactivating both copies is a loss of function, not the creation of a migration-driving oncogene.

shortExplanation: Each expected class is 400/4 = 100, giving chi-squared = 4 + 4 + 2.25 + 2.25 = 12.5. For a goodness-of-fit test the degrees of freedom are (4 - 1) = 3, so the critical value is 7.815; since 12.5 exceeds it, independent assortment is rejected and the loci are linked.
solutionSteps: Compute each expected value: 400/4 = 100 per class.
Sum to get chi-squared = 12.5.
Use df = (classes - 1) = 3, critical value 7.815; since 12.5 > 7.815, reject independent assortment, so the loci are linked.
keyConcept: In a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test, df = (number of classes - 1) and exceeding the critical value rejects the null hypothesis.
commonMistake: Using df equal to the number of classes, or misreading the decision rule so that exceeding the critical value is taken to support the null hypothesis.

optionExplanations.0: Degrees of freedom are (classes - 1) = 3, not 4, and rejecting independent assortment implies linkage, not independence.
optionExplanations.1: 25.0 is twice the correct value, from double-counting deviations or dividing by 50; the correct statistic is 12.5.
optionExplanations.3: Exceeding the critical value means the deviation is too large for chance, so independent assortment is rejected, not supported.
optionExplanations.4: 3.13 averages the four terms instead of summing them; the chi-squared statistic is their sum, 12.5.

shortExplanation: In the repulsion arrangement A b / a B the parental gametes are A b and a B, so A B is a recombinant gamete. Recombinants total the 16% recombination frequency split equally between the two recombinant classes, so A B = 16%/2 = 8%.
solutionSteps: Identify the arrangement as repulsion: A with b, and a with B, on the two homologues.
The parental gametes are therefore A b and a B; the recombinant gametes are A B and a b.
Recombinants total the recombination frequency of 16%, shared equally between the two recombinant classes.
keyConcept: Map distance equals total recombination frequency; each of the two recombinant gamete classes gets half of it, and which classes are recombinant depends on the coupling or repulsion arrangement.
commonMistake: Treating A B as a parental class (as in coupling) or dividing the recombination frequency by 4 among all gamete types.

optionExplanations.1: 16% is the combined frequency of both recombinant gametes; each of the two equal classes is half of this.
optionExplanations.2: 42% is a parental-gamete frequency; A B is parental only in coupling, but here it is recombinant.
optionExplanations.3: The 16% recombination frequency is shared between the two recombinant classes (divide by 2), not among all four gamete types.
optionExplanations.4: 25% for every gamete type assumes independent assortment, but the loci are linked 16 cM apart.

shortExplanation: A double crossover (one exchange in each interval) swaps q but leaves p and r in their parental combination, so it is not scored as a p-r recombinant. These undetected events make the measured 32% an underestimate; the accurate map distance is the sum of the two short intervals, 20 + 20 = 40 cM.
solutionSteps: Consider a meiosis with a crossover in the p-q interval and another in the q-r interval.
This double crossover exchanges q but restores the parental p-r combination, so it is not counted as a p-r recombinant.
Undetected double crossovers make the directly measured 32% too low.
Build the map by summing the short additive intervals: 20 + 20 = 40 cM.
keyConcept: Over larger distances, recombination frequency underestimates map distance because undetected double crossovers restore the parental arrangement; genetic maps sum short additive intervals.
commonMistake: Invoking interference incorrectly, or thinking recombination frequency always equals the exact map distance.

optionExplanations.0: Positive interference reduces double crossovers, which would raise the observed p-r frequency toward 40%, not lower it.
optionExplanations.1: Sub-additivity is the expected signature of double crossovers between linked genes, not evidence they are on different chromosomes.
optionExplanations.2: The observed shortfall is twice the double-crossover frequency (2 x 4% = 8%), and the map distance is the sum of intervals, 40 cM, not 36 cM.
optionExplanations.3: Recombination frequency equals map distance only for closely linked genes; over larger separations it underestimates the true additive distance.

shortExplanation: Recombinant offspring for the A/B loci arise at the recombination frequency, 10% (this already covers both reciprocal recombinant classes). Gene D assorts independently, so P(dd) = 0.5. The events are independent, so multiply: 0.10 x 0.5 = 0.05 = 5%.
solutionSteps: P(recombinant for A/B) equals the recombination frequency, 0.10.
D is on a separate chromosome, so a Dd x dd cross gives P(dd) = 0.5.
The two requirements are independent, so multiply the probabilities: 0.10 x 0.5 = 0.05 = 5%.
keyConcept: Combine independent probabilities by multiplying; the recombination frequency already sums both reciprocal recombinant classes.
commonMistake: Treating A and B as assorting independently (P = 0.5) instead of using the 10% recombination frequency, or halving the recombination frequency unnecessarily.

optionExplanations.0: 50% is only P(dd) and ignores the requirement to also be recombinant for A and B.
optionExplanations.1: 'Recombinant for A and B' includes both reciprocal classes and equals the full 10%, not a single 5% class.
optionExplanations.2: 25% treats A and B as independent (P = 0.5), but they are linked 10 cM apart, so P(recombinant) = 0.10.
optionExplanations.4: 10% is P(recombinant for A/B) alone and omits the independent condition at the D locus.

shortExplanation: With no crossing over the plant makes only A B and a b gametes in equal numbers. Self-fertilisation gives 1 AABB : 2 AaBb : 1 aabb, which is three both-dominant plants to one both-recessive: a 3:1 ratio, as if the loci were a single gene.
solutionSteps: With complete linkage in coupling, only A B and a b gametes form, in equal numbers.
Self-fertilisation randomly fuses these gametes, giving 1 AABB : 2 AaBb : 1 aabb.
Phenotypically AABB and AaBb both show both dominant traits, so the ratio is 3 both-dominant to 1 both-recessive.
keyConcept: Completely linked genes in coupling are inherited as a single unit, so a self-cross gives a monohybrid-style 3:1 phenotypic ratio.
commonMistake: Applying the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio (which needs independent assortment) or confusing coupling with the repulsion 1:2:1 outcome.

optionExplanations.0: 1:2:1 is the repulsion arrangement A b / a B outcome; here the alleles are in coupling, giving 3:1.
optionExplanations.1: 1:1:1:1 is a testcross outcome, but this is a self-cross where every gamete type can fuse with every other.
optionExplanations.2: The gametes occur 1:1, but random fusion gives genotypes 1:2:1 and phenotypes 3:1; the gamete ratio is not the phenotype ratio.
optionExplanations.3: 9:3:3:1 requires independent assortment; complete linkage in coupling gives 3:1.

shortExplanation: On the plateau of curve P, adding more light does nothing, so light is in excess, not limiting. At that same light intensity the culture with more carbon dioxide (Q) reaches a higher rate, showing that carbon-dioxide concentration was limiting curve P.
solutionSteps: A factor is limiting only if increasing it raises the rate.
On P's plateau the curve is horizontal, so more light does not help; light is in excess.
At the same light intensity, curve Q (more CO2) gives a higher rate.
Therefore carbon-dioxide concentration was limiting curve P at its plateau.
keyConcept: A limiting factor is the one whose increase raises the rate; a horizontal plateau shows that variable is no longer limiting.
commonMistake: Thinking a levelling light-response curve means light has become limiting, when a plateau actually means light is in excess.

optionExplanations.0: Water is almost never limiting for a submerged aquatic plant and was not the variable that raised the rate.
optionExplanations.2: Nothing in the data shows temperature is limiting; the direct evidence is that raising CO2, not temperature, increased the rate.
optionExplanations.3: Chlorophyll was not varied and is not a raw material whose shortage is shown; more pigment cannot help when light is already saturating.
optionExplanations.4: On a plateau the rate no longer responds to light, so light is in excess and cannot be the limiting factor.

shortExplanation: Recover the solvent-front distance from carotene: solvent front = 76/0.95 = 80 mm. Then the second pigment's Rf = 36/80 = 0.45.
solutionSteps: Use carotene's known Rf: solvent front = pigment distance / Rf = 76/0.95 = 80 mm.
Apply Rf to the second pigment: Rf = 36/80 = 0.45.
Note that carotene (Rf 0.95) has not reached the front, so its spot cannot be used as the solvent front.
keyConcept: Rf = distance moved by pigment / distance moved by solvent front; a known Rf lets you back-calculate the missing solvent-front distance.
commonMistake: Assuming the fastest-moving pigment marks the solvent front, or reading a travel distance directly as an Rf.

optionExplanations.0: 0.95 simply restates carotene's Rf, ignoring that the second spot moved a shorter distance.
optionExplanations.2: 2.22 inverts the definition (80/36); an Rf can never exceed 1.
optionExplanations.3: 0.47 divides 36 by the carotene distance (76), wrongly treating the fastest pigment as the solvent front.
optionExplanations.4: 0.36 reads the pigment's travel distance directly as an Rf, forgetting to divide by the solvent-front distance.

shortExplanation: At low light, raising the temperature barely changes the rate (10 to 11), so the temperature-insensitive photochemical (light-dependent) reactions limit. At high light, the same temperature rise increases the rate sharply (18 to 31), so the temperature-sensitive enzyme-catalysed Calvin cycle limits.
solutionSteps: Compare the two low-light rows: 15 to 25 degrees C changes the rate only from 10 to 11.
Conclude that at low light the rate is set by photochemical reactions, which are temperature-insensitive.
Compare the two high-light rows: 15 to 25 degrees C raises the rate from 18 to 31.
Conclude that at high light the rate is set by enzyme-catalysed reactions, which are temperature-sensitive.
keyConcept: Photosynthesis has a temperature-insensitive photochemical stage (limiting at low light) and a temperature-sensitive enzyme-catalysed stage (limiting at saturating light).
commonMistake: Assuming every step of photosynthesis is enzyme-limited, or overgeneralising that temperature always raises the rate.

optionExplanations.0: The light-dependent reactions are photochemical and largely temperature-independent; the Calvin reactions are the enzyme-catalysed, temperature-sensitive ones.
optionExplanations.1: At 15 degrees C, raising light from low to high lifts the rate from 10 to 18, so light clearly does affect the rate.
optionExplanations.3: At low light the temperature change barely moved the rate, so temperature is not the main limiting factor there; light is.
optionExplanations.4: At low light the increase (10 to 11) is negligible, so temperature does not always raise the rate.

shortExplanation: CO2 combines with RuBP to make GP. Removing CO2 stops this step, so RuBP is no longer consumed and accumulates, while GP stops being produced. Because bright light continues, ATP and NADPH keep reducing the existing GP to triose phosphate, so GP falls. Hence RuBP rises and GP falls.
solutionSteps: Recall that CO2 fixation combines CO2 with RuBP to form GP.
Removing CO2 halts that step, so RuBP is no longer used up and accumulates.
GP is no longer produced, but continuing light still supplies ATP and NADPH to reduce existing GP.
Therefore RuBP increases and GP decreases.
keyConcept: Cutting off CO2 blocks the RuBP-to-GP fixation step while light-driven GP reduction continues, so RuBP rises and GP falls (the opposite of switching off the light).
commonMistake: Assuming the whole Calvin cycle freezes so all intermediates build up, or swapping this pattern with the switch-off-light experiment.

optionExplanations.0: The RuBP-to-GP step is exactly the one that stops, and GP continues to be consumed, so not every intermediate builds up.
optionExplanations.1: This is the switch-off-light pattern (GP accumulates, RuBP falls); the two experiments have been swapped.
optionExplanations.2: CO2 is the substrate of the light-independent reactions, so removing it directly halts fixation; the cycle is not independent of CO2.
optionExplanations.3: RuBP regeneration continues while its consumption ceases, so RuBP rises rather than being used up.

shortExplanation: Being on the plateau of the light-response curve means light was already saturating, so doubling it cannot raise the rate. The rise from 20 to 35 bubbles per minute is therefore due to relieving the carbon-dioxide limitation.
solutionSteps: Note the plant starts on the plateau of its light-response curve, so light is already in excess.
Doubling saturating light cannot increase the rate.
The only change that could raise the rate is the higher CO2, which had been limiting.
So the whole increase is attributable to relieving the CO2 limitation.
keyConcept: On a light-response plateau light is saturating, so only the previously limiting factor (here CO2) can raise the rate.
commonMistake: Assuming that raising any factor must help, or that the rate always tracks photon supply even above light saturation.

optionExplanations.0: A plant on a plateau is not light-limited; if light had been limiting the rate would still be rising with light.
optionExplanations.1: Lowering temperature would slow the enzyme-controlled Calvin reactions and reduce the rate; enzymes do not work faster when cooler.
optionExplanations.2: Above light saturation the plant cannot use extra photons, so the rate does not track photon supply.
optionExplanations.4: On the plateau light is already in excess, so the extra light contributed nothing to the rise.

shortExplanation: Immobilising the lactase on the insoluble beads keeps the enzyme in the column while the milk flows through, so the same enzyme molecules are reused continuously and the treated milk emerges free of enzyme.
solutionSteps: Recognise that binding the enzyme to insoluble beads anchors it in the column.
The milk flows past while the enzyme stays behind, so it is recovered automatically and reused for many batches.
The product stream leaves free of enzyme, which matters for a food product.
keyConcept: Immobilising an enzyme allows continuous reuse and gives an enzyme-free product, without changing the enzyme's catalytic properties or specificity.
commonMistake: Believing immobilisation lowers activation energy, changes specificity, removes the need for substrate, or alters the reaction's thermodynamics.

optionExplanations.1: An enzyme still needs substrate present; immobilisation only changes where the enzyme is, not the requirement for a reactant.
optionExplanations.2: Specificity is retained; a loss of specificity would be a disadvantage, not an advantage.
optionExplanations.3: Immobilisation does not lower activation energy; if anything it slightly slows the reaction because substrate must diffuse to the fixed enzyme.
optionExplanations.4: Enzymes do not change the reaction's free-energy change; lactose hydrolysis is already favourable and the catalyst only affects the rate.

shortExplanation: At high glucose concentration the immobilised enzyme becomes saturated and works at its maximum rate, so the current cannot rise further. Fructose gives no current because glucose oxidase's active site is specific for glucose and does not bind fructose.
solutionSteps: The current is proportional to the enzyme's reaction rate.
At low glucose the rate and current rise with concentration; at high glucose all active sites are occupied (saturation), so the rate and current plateau.
Fructose gives no current because the active site is complementary to glucose and does not bind a structurally different sugar.
Saturation plus specificity explain both observations together.
keyConcept: Enzyme saturation explains the plateau in a rate-against-substrate curve, and active-site specificity explains why a non-substrate gives no signal.
commonMistake: Attributing the plateau to substrate depletion, oxygen exhaustion, or substrate inhibition, or thinking the signal comes from the sugar's electric charge.

optionExplanations.0: In a fresh high-glucose standard the substrate is not depleted during the brief reading; the plateau reflects saturation, and fructose is highly soluble.
optionExplanations.1: A fixed oxygen shortage would not give a glucose-proportional rise at low concentration, and fructose does not denature the enzyme; it is simply not a substrate.
optionExplanations.3: Glucose is the substrate and the plateau is saturation, not non-competitive inhibition; fructose gives no signal because it is not bound at all.
optionExplanations.4: Glucose and fructose are both neutral; the current comes from the enzyme-catalysed oxidation, not from a charge on the sugar.

shortExplanation: A competitive inhibitor is outcompeted at saturating substrate, so its plateau matches the control. A non-competitive inhibitor takes enzyme permanently out of action and lowers the maximum, while doubling the enzyme adds active sites and raises the maximum.
solutionSteps: Recall that raising substrate to saturation crowds a competitive inhibitor off the active site, so the competitive-inhibitor run reaches the same maximum as the control.
Note that a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and cannot be displaced by substrate, so it lowers the maximum rate.
Note that doubling the enzyme doubles the number of active sites at saturation, raising the maximum rate.
Match same / lower / higher to the three runs.
keyConcept: At saturating substrate, competitive inhibition is overcome (same Vmax), non-competitive inhibition lowers Vmax, and more enzyme raises Vmax.
commonMistake: Believing the maximum rate is fixed regardless of enzyme amount, or that adding substrate can overcome a non-competitive inhibitor.

optionExplanations.0: This reverses the effects: it wrongly raises the non-competitive plateau and lowers the more-enzyme plateau.
optionExplanations.1: This swaps the two inhibitors, wrongly lowering the competitive plateau and holding the non-competitive one unchanged.
optionExplanations.3: This wrongly lowers the competitive plateau and holds the doubled-enzyme plateau constant.
optionExplanations.4: This wrongly lets the non-competitive inhibitor be overcome by substrate, returning it to the control maximum.

shortExplanation: Ethanol and methanol share the same active site and the enzyme prefers ethanol, so ethanol acts as a reversible competitive inhibitor: methanol is oxidised only slowly and the intact methanol is excreted before it forms toxic products. Because the inhibition is competitive, a large methanol excess could still outcompete the ethanol, so the ethanol level must be maintained.
solutionSteps: Note that ethanol and methanol bind the same active site, so ethanol is a competitive inhibitor of methanol metabolism.
Because the enzyme prefers ethanol, it occupies the site and methanol is oxidised slowly, forming little toxic formaldehyde/formic acid.
The unconverted methanol is excreted by the kidneys (or removed by dialysis).
Recognise that competitive inhibition can be overcome by excess substrate, so the ethanol concentration must be sustained.
keyConcept: Competitive inhibition by a preferred substrate slows metabolism of a toxic substrate but can be overcome by excess of that substrate.
commonMistake: Thinking ethanol speeds methanol clearance or permanently blocks the enzyme, rather than reversibly slowing methanol conversion.

optionExplanations.0: Ethanol does not act at an allosteric site or raise affinity for methanol, and faster methanol conversion would be harmful, not protective.
optionExplanations.1: This reverses the mechanism: ethanol slows, not speeds, methanol metabolism, which is why it protects.
optionExplanations.2: Same-site competition is competitive, not non-competitive, inhibition; it is reversible and cannot give permanent one-dose protection.
optionExplanations.3: Competitive inhibition is reversible binding, not denaturation; the enzyme works normally once ethanol is cleared.

shortExplanation: A non-competitive inhibitor and a halved enzyme amount both lower the maximum rate while leaving the half-maximal substrate concentration unchanged, so they can produce the same curve shape. A competitive inhibitor instead keeps the reference maximum but requires a higher substrate concentration for half-maximal rate.
solutionSteps: The non-competitive inhibitor removes catalytic capacity that substrate cannot restore, lowering the maximum without changing the half-maximal substrate concentration.
Halving the enzyme lowers the maximum (fewer active sites) but also leaves the half-maximal substrate concentration unchanged.
Conclude these two share the same curve shape.
The competitive inhibitor is overcome by substrate, so it keeps the reference maximum but needs more substrate for half-maximal rate.
keyConcept: Lowering Vmax cannot by itself distinguish less enzyme from non-competitive inhibition; only competitive inhibition preserves Vmax while raising the apparent Km.
commonMistake: Assuming all inhibitors act alike, or that an inhibitor never changes the maximum rate.

optionExplanations.0: Competitive and non-competitive inhibitors give different curves, so the two inhibitor samples are not identical.
optionExplanations.2: Both the non-competitive inhibitor and the reduced enzyme lower the maximum, so not all three reach the reference maximum.
optionExplanations.3: This swaps the inhibitor effects; the competitive case retains the maximum and the non-competitive case lowers it.
optionExplanations.4: A non-competitive inhibitor does lower the maximum, so the non-competitive sample also reaches a reduced plateau.

shortExplanation: With acetylcholinesterase irreversibly inhibited, released acetylcholine is not hydrolysed, so it lingers in the cleft and repeatedly binds nicotinic receptors, holding the postsynaptic membrane depolarised and causing prolonged, repetitive stimulation.
solutionSteps: Recall that acetylcholinesterase normally hydrolyses acetylcholine to terminate its action.
If the enzyme is inhibited, acetylcholine is not destroyed and accumulates in the cleft.
The transmitter keeps binding and rebinding nicotinic receptors.
Conclude the postsynaptic membrane is held depolarised, giving prolonged/repetitive stimulation.
keyConcept: Blocking the transmitter-degrading enzyme increases, not decreases, transmitter action at the synapse.
commonMistake: Assuming the enzyme supplies or delivers acetylcholine, so that inhibiting it reduces transmission.

optionExplanations.0: Cholinergic transmission is ended by enzymatic hydrolysis in the cleft, not by reuptake of intact acetylcholine.
optionExplanations.1: The enzyme destroys the transmitter, so inhibiting it raises, not lowers, the amount acting on receptors.
optionExplanations.2: Acetylcholine still binds normally and the response is excitatory depolarisation, not hyperpolarisation.
optionExplanations.4: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor acts on the cleft enzyme and does not control presynaptic calcium entry.

shortExplanation: Threshold is 15 mV above rest, so three +5 mV EPSPs must add. At 200 Hz the 5 ms interval between EPSPs is much shorter than the ~20 ms decay time, so successive EPSPs overlap and summate (temporal summation), driving the membrane past -55 mV.
solutionSteps: Calculate the depolarisation needed: -70 mV to -55 mV is 15 mV, requiring three +5 mV EPSPs.
Calculate the interspike interval at 200 Hz: 1/200 s = 5 ms.
Compare with the ~20 ms EPSP decay time; the interval is much shorter, so EPSPs overlap.
Conclude overlapping EPSPs from one neuron summate over time (temporal summation) and reach threshold.
keyConcept: Temporal summation lets repeated subthreshold EPSPs from a single neuron add when they arrive faster than they decay.
commonMistake: Thinking higher firing frequency enlarges each EPSP, or that reaching threshold always needs several different neurons.

optionExplanations.0: Individual EPSP amplitude is fixed; frequency lets EPSPs sum but does not enlarge them.
optionExplanations.1: Subthreshold EPSPs summate when they overlap in time, so the membrane can reach threshold.
optionExplanations.2: Repeated firing of one neuron is temporal, not spatial, summation; spatial summation needs different neurons.
optionExplanations.4: A single neuron firing rapidly can reach threshold by temporal summation without other inputs.

shortExplanation: Drug Z is a depolarising agonist that holds the end plate depolarised, which drives the muscle's voltage-gated Na+ channels into persistent inactivation and causes flaccid paralysis. Because acetylcholine acts the same way, adding an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor cannot reverse the block and may deepen it.
solutionSteps: Identify Drug Z as a nicotinic agonist that opens receptors and depolarises the end plate (the initial twitching).
Because it is not cleared by acetylcholinesterase, the end plate stays depolarised.
Sustained depolarisation inactivates the surrounding voltage-gated Na+ channels, so no new action potentials fire (depolarising block).
Adding an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor raises acetylcholine, another depolarising agonist, so it cannot relieve and may worsen the block.
keyConcept: A depolarising blocker holds the end plate depolarised and inactivates Na+ channels; unlike a competitive antagonist, its block is not reversed by raising acetylcholine.
commonMistake: Treating Drug Z as a competitive antagonist (like curare) whose block is relieved by more acetylcholine.

optionExplanations.0: Drug Z acts on postsynaptic receptors; the initial twitching shows agonist action at the end plate, not blocked release.
optionExplanations.1: Drug Z activates receptors and causes twitching, so it is an agonist, not a competitive antagonist; more acetylcholine does not reverse its block.
optionExplanations.2: The end plate is held depolarised by an excitatory agonist, not hyperpolarised by opening K+ channels.
optionExplanations.4: The stem states Drug Z binds and activates receptors; it is not an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

shortExplanation: Strychnine is a competitive antagonist that prevents glycine from opening the inhibitory Cl- channels, abolishing the normal IPSPs. Removing this inhibition leaves the motor neuron's excitatory inputs unopposed, so it becomes more easily excited.
solutionSteps: Recall that glycine opens Cl- channels and, because ECl (-75 mV) is below rest (-70 mV), produces a small hyperpolarising IPSP.
As a competitive antagonist, strychnine occupies the glycine receptor without opening the channel.
This abolishes the inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (disinhibition).
With inhibition removed, excitatory inputs drive the motor neuron to threshold more readily, causing hyperexcitability.
keyConcept: Blocking an inhibitory receptor removes inhibition (disinhibition), making the postsynaptic neuron hyperexcitable.
commonMistake: Treating the antagonist as if it opened Cl- channels or strengthened inhibition, rather than removing it.

optionExplanations.0: Strychnine blocks the glycine receptor rather than opening Cl- channels, so it removes inhibition instead of adding it.
optionExplanations.1: Strychnine acts on the postsynaptic receptor, and glycine is inhibitory, so blocking it releases the neuron from inhibition.
optionExplanations.2: The glycine receptor is Cl--selective and inhibitory; strychnine does not create a depolarising Na+ current.
optionExplanations.3: Blocking the receptor abolishes the IPSP; an antagonist cannot enlarge it.

shortExplanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release, so almost no transmitter reaches the cleft. An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor only preserves transmitter that has been released, so it gives little benefit here, unlike in myasthenia gravis where release is normal and raising acetylcholine can activate the scarce receptors.
solutionSteps: Identify the lesion: botulinum toxin acts presynaptically, blocking vesicle fusion and acetylcholine release.
Recall that an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor only slows breakdown of already-released transmitter.
In botulism there is essentially no released transmitter to preserve, so the drug helps little.
Contrast with myasthenia gravis, where release is normal but receptors are scarce, so raising acetylcholine improves activation.
keyConcept: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor can only preserve transmitter that is released; it cannot help when the defect is blocked presynaptic release.
commonMistake: Assuming an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor corrects any neuromuscular weakness regardless of whether transmitter is being released.

optionExplanations.0: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor acts only in the cleft and cannot restore vesicle fusion when SNARE proteins are cleaved.
optionExplanations.1: Botulinum toxin acts presynaptically on vesicle fusion, so there is no receptor competition to worsen.
optionExplanations.2: The drug needs transmitter to be released; a release block leaves nothing to preserve, so the two conditions are not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: With release blocked there is essentially no transmitter to preserve, so no extra benefit; this also confuses fusion with recycling.

shortExplanation: Both extremes (lightest and heaviest) are removed while intermediates survive best, which is stabilising selection. Because body mass is heritable, the survivors' offspring cluster more tightly around the original mean, giving a similar mean but a smaller variance.
solutionSteps: Identify which phenotypes survive: intermediates survive best, both extremes are removed.
Classify this as stabilising selection (selection against both tails).
Recall that stabilising selection keeps the mean roughly unchanged and reduces the variance.
Apply heritability: offspring of intermediate survivors form a narrower distribution around the original mean.
keyConcept: Stabilising selection removes both extremes, keeping the mean about the same while narrowing the spread of a heritable trait.
commonMistake: Confusing selection against extremes with disruptive selection (which favours the extremes and widens or splits the distribution).

optionExplanations.1: A larger variance results from disruptive selection favouring extremes, but here both extremes are selected against.
optionExplanations.2: A bimodal distribution is the signature of disruptive selection; favouring intermediates forms no two peaks.
optionExplanations.3: A rightward shift of the mean is directional selection; symmetric removal of both extremes leaves the mean about the same.

shortExplanation: Sustained spraying is directional selection that raises the frequency of pre-existing resistance alleles, shifting the mean resistance up. The plateau occurs because those alleles become nearly fixed, so little heritable variation remains for selection to act on.
solutionSteps: Recognise a single sustained pressure favouring one extreme as directional selection.
The mean resistance rises as pre-existing resistance alleles increase in frequency.
Selection needs heritable variation to act; as the beneficial alleles approach fixation, that variation is used up.
Conclude the response slows and the trait plateaus even though spraying continues.
keyConcept: Directional selection raises a favourable allele's frequency until it nears fixation, at which point the loss of heritable variation ends further response.
commonMistake: Believing the insecticide induces the specific resistance mutations, or that mutation simply switches off to create the plateau.

optionExplanations.0: Surrounding unsprayed populations carry mostly susceptibility alleles, and the stem states the population is isolated, so gene flow cannot explain the rise.
optionExplanations.2: The insecticide selects among pre-existing alleles rather than inducing beneficial mutations, and mutation does not switch off to produce a plateau.
optionExplanations.3: Drift is random and would not repeatably raise resistance alleles under strong sustained selection; the tight link to spraying indicates selection.
optionExplanations.4: Stabilising selection maintains an intermediate optimum, but the mean is driven to a high extreme, which is directional.

shortExplanation: Mating, gamete transfer and fertilisation all succeed and embryos begin to develop, so every prezygotic barrier has failed. Isolation is postzygotic: hybrid embryos die (reduced hybrid viability) and the rare survivors are sterile (hybrid sterility), and together these still prevent gene flow.
solutionSteps: Note that the frogs breed together, gametes are transferred and eggs are fertilised, so all prezygotic barriers are absent.
Note that hybrid embryos begin to develop but nearly all die: reduced hybrid viability.
Note that the few survivors are sterile: hybrid sterility.
Classify both as postzygotic barriers that still block gene flow.
keyConcept: Isolating mechanisms are prezygotic if they act before zygote formation and postzygotic if they act after; hybrid inviability and sterility are postzygotic.
commonMistake: Labelling a barrier prezygotic (temporal, mechanical, behavioural, gametic) without checking that mating and fertilisation actually succeeded.

optionExplanations.0: Mechanical isolation would block gamete transfer, but transfer and fertilisation clearly occur here.
optionExplanations.1: Temporal isolation means breeding at different times, yet both species breed in the same ponds in the same season.
optionExplanations.3: Behavioural isolation would prevent mating, but the frogs readily attempt to mate.
optionExplanations.4: Gametic isolation would prevent fertilisation, yet the eggs are fertilised and embryos develop.

shortExplanation: The F1 hybrid has 7 + 9 = 16 chromosomes with no homologous partners, so meiosis fails and it is sterile. Doubling the whole set gives an allopolyploid (2n = 32) in which every chromosome has a homologue, restoring fertile meiosis; the polyploid cannot cross with either parent, so it has speciated sympatrically in one generation.
solutionSteps: Count the hybrid's chromosomes: 7 from A plus 9 from B = 16, none with a pairing partner.
Unpaired chromosomes cannot align at meiosis, so the F1 is sterile (a postzygotic effect).
Spontaneous doubling gives two A sets and two B sets, 2n = 32, so every chromosome now has a homologue and meiosis is regular.
A cross to either 2n parent gives unbalanced sterile offspring, so the polyploid is reproductively isolated and arose in place (sympatric).
keyConcept: Allopolyploidy restores meiotic pairing in a sterile hybrid and produces a reproductively isolated new species sympatrically in a single generation.
commonMistake: Calling the hybrid's sterility a prezygotic barrier, or taking the new chromosome number as the average of the parents rather than the doubled hybrid count.

optionExplanations.0: Allopatric speciation requires geographic separation, but the new species arose in place among its parents.
optionExplanations.1: The F1 grew as an adult, so its sterility is a postzygotic failure of meiotic pairing, not a prezygotic mating barrier.
optionExplanations.2: The stem states the new plants cannot make fertile offspring with A or B, so they are reproductively isolated.
optionExplanations.4: 2n = 16 is the sterile hybrid's count; the fertile species has the doubled complement, 2n = 32, not the arithmetic mean.

shortExplanation: Because the allele is neutral, selection is absent and each small pond's frequency follows an independent random walk (genetic drift), intensified by the small founder number and population size. The replicate ponds therefore diverge widely, some fixing the allele and others losing it, while heterozygosity within each pond declines.
solutionSteps: Note the allele is neutral, so selection cannot change its frequency.
Attribute frequency changes to genetic drift, which is random in direction.
Recall drift is strongest with small founder numbers and small population sizes.
Conclude replicate ponds diverge from one another (some fix, some lose the allele) while each loses heterozygosity internally.
keyConcept: Genetic drift makes replicate small populations diverge from one another while losing variation within each, the diagnostic signature that distinguishes drift from selection.
commonMistake: Assuming a neutral allele's frequency cannot change without selection, or that random founder choice freezes the frequency.

optionExplanations.0: A consistent same-direction shift across independent replicates is the signature of selection, not drift.
optionExplanations.2: Random sampling sets the average starting frequency but does not freeze it; drift changes it every generation.
optionExplanations.3: In finite populations a neutral allele drifts randomly, so 'no selection means no change' ignores drift.
optionExplanations.4: The allele starts common (0.5), and neutral alleles are not systematically eliminated; drift is as likely to fix as to lose it.

shortExplanation: Read each species' mixed-culture density against its own monoculture: S benefits (820 to 1150) while T is unchanged (610 to 590, non-significant). A benefit-to-one, no-effect-on-the-other outcome is commensalism, with S the commensal and T the unaffected host.
solutionSteps: Compare S in mixed versus monoculture: 1150 vs 820, a significant increase (benefit).
Compare T in mixed versus monoculture: 590 vs 610, within random variation (no significant effect).
Assign signs: S is +, T is 0.
Classify a +/0 interaction as commensalism.
keyConcept: Ecological interactions are classified by the sign of the effect on each partner; a benefit to one with no effect on the other is commensalism.
commonMistake: Over-reading the trivial 610 to 590 dip as harm, or treating a higher combined total or a one-sided benefit as mutualism.

optionExplanations.0: Parasitism requires the host to be harmed, yet T's density is essentially unchanged.
optionExplanations.1: Predation predicts a marked fall in prey density, but T changes only within random variation.
optionExplanations.2: Mutualism requires both partners to benefit, but T shows no significant change.
optionExplanations.3: Competition would depress both densities, yet S rises well above its monoculture value.

shortExplanation: Leghaemoglobin buffers the free oxygen concentration to a very low level, protecting the oxygen-labile nitrogenase, while its rapid loading and unloading still delivers oxygen fast enough to fuel the respiration that supplies the large ATP demand. In the mutant, free oxygen rises and inactivates nitrogenase, so fixation collapses despite normal bacteroid numbers.
solutionSteps: Note the oxygen paradox: nitrogenase is destroyed by O2, yet the ATP-costly reaction needs aerobic respiration.
Leghaemoglobin binds O2, keeping the free dissolved concentration very low to protect nitrogenase.
Its rapid binding and release maintains a high O2 flux to the bacteroid for ATP-generating respiration.
In the mutant, free O2 rises and inactivates nitrogenase, so fixation fails even though bacteroid numbers are normal.
keyConcept: Leghaemoglobin resolves the oxygen paradox by holding free O2 low while delivering bound O2 for respiration, protecting nitrogenase yet fuelling fixation.
commonMistake: Assuming the nodule must be strictly anaerobic, ignoring that bacteroids need aerobic respiration for the ATP fixation demands.

optionExplanations.0: The nitrogen in ammonia comes from N2, not from leghaemoglobin, which binds oxygen rather than nitrogen.
optionExplanations.1: Leghaemoglobin binds oxygen, not ammonia, and ammonia export does not depend on it.
optionExplanations.2: The catalyst that reduces N2 is nitrogenase; leghaemoglobin is an oxygen-transport protein, not the fixing enzyme.
optionExplanations.3: Bacteroids must respire aerobically for ATP, so oxygen cannot be excluded completely; leghaemoglobin buffers it low rather than eliminating it.

shortExplanation: Bare glacial rock has no soil, so Area 1 is primary succession and is slow because pioneers must first weather rock and accumulate nitrogen (partly via nitrogen-fixers) before larger plants establish. Area 2 keeps its soil, nutrients and seed bank after the fire, so it is secondary succession and reaches climax much sooner.
solutionSteps: Apply the criterion: primary succession starts where there is no soil; secondary succession starts where soil and its seed bank persist.
Classify bare glacial rock as primary succession.
Explain its slowness: pioneers must build soil and accumulate nitrogen and organic matter (facilitation) before later species can grow.
Classify the burnt field with intact soil and seed bank as secondary succession, which skips the slow start-up and reaches climax faster.
keyConcept: The primary/secondary distinction depends on whether soil and its seed bank persist, not on whether vegetation was destroyed.
commonMistake: Equating any recolonisation after destruction with primary succession, or swapping the primary/secondary criteria.

optionExplanations.0: The definitions are reversed: intact soil after fire is secondary, and bare glacial rock is primary despite a few lichens.
optionExplanations.2: The stem states Area 2 is faster, and bare rock is slow because soil and nutrients must be built first, not because competitors are absent.
optionExplanations.3: The climax is set largely by climate and soil, not fixed by the identity of the first colonisers.
optionExplanations.4: Primary versus secondary is defined by whether soil persists; Area 2 retains soil and is therefore secondary.

shortExplanation: L is the predator: it is less numerous (peak 30 vs H's 70) and its peak lags H's by one year. Its numbers keep rising after H starts falling because abundant prey still supports predator reproduction, and H falls once predator density is high enough that predation losses exceed H's reproduction.
solutionSteps: Compare abundances: H peaks at 70, L at 30, so the more numerous H is the prey and L the predator.
Compare phase: L's peak (year 4) lags H's peak (year 3).
Explain the lag: the predator keeps growing while prey remain plentiful, so it peaks after the prey.
H falls once predation losses outstrip its reproduction, then L declines as prey become scarce.
keyConcept: In predator-prey cycles the prey are usually more numerous and the predator peak lags the prey peak by about a quarter-cycle.
commonMistake: Believing predators outnumber their prey, or expecting the two populations to peak simultaneously with no time lag.

optionExplanations.0: The consistent one-year lag is a signature of coupling, not coincidence.
optionExplanations.1: The data show a lag, not instantaneous control; H is already falling while L still rises.
optionExplanations.2: Prey are typically more numerous than predators, so the more abundant H is the prey, not the predator.
optionExplanations.4: H's decline coincides with high and still-rising predator numbers, so predation cannot be dismissed.

shortExplanation: This is overshoot-and-dieback: while food was plentiful the herbivores grew rapidly, but because the density-dependent brake (food depletion from overgrazing) acted with a delay, numbers overshot the carrying capacity. The resulting food shortage sharply raised the death rate, causing the crash before numbers settled near a carrying capacity of about 2000.
solutionSteps: Recognise the trajectory: rapid rise, a peak well above the final level, a crash, then settling.
Attribute early rapid growth to abundant, non-limiting food.
Note that overgrazing's effect on the food supply lags the rise in numbers, so the population overshoots K.
The density-dependent food shortage raises mortality sharply, causing dieback to settle around K (~2000).
keyConcept: Overshoot-and-dieback occurs when delayed density-dependent limitation lets a population exceed carrying capacity before mortality pulls it back.
commonMistake: Reading the highest count (6000) as the carrying capacity, or thinking exponential growth continues indefinitely.

optionExplanations.0: Exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely because food limitation intensifies with density; the crash is real.
optionExplanations.2: The peak of 6000 is a transient overshoot, not the sustainable carrying capacity, and the decline follows from the population's own excess density.
optionExplanations.3: The stem specifies no predators, so a predator increase cannot explain the crash.
optionExplanations.4: The crash reflects density-dependent starvation, so density strongly affects the death rate; a density-independent balance cannot produce an overshoot-and-crash.

shortExplanation: The rise in acid on seeing and smelling food is a nervous reflex (the cephalic phase) carried by the vagus, so cutting the vagus abolishes it. Food placed directly in the stomach still triggers secretion through other pathways (the hormone gastrin and local reflexes), which do not depend on the vagus.
solutionSteps: Note that in the healthy volunteer, sight and smell of food raise acid secretion (the cephalic phase).
Cutting the vagus abolishes this response, showing it is a nervous vagal reflex.
Placing food in the stomach still causes secretion in the vagotomised person.
Conclude the gastric-phase response works through non-vagal pathways (gastrin and local reflexes).
keyConcept: The cephalic phase of gastric secretion is a vagal nervous reflex, while the gastric phase is driven largely by gastrin and local reflexes independent of the vagus.
commonMistake: Over-generalising the vagus as the sole pathway for all acid secretion, ignoring gastrin and local reflexes.

optionExplanations.0: The vagotomised person still secretes acid when food is placed in the stomach, so the vagus is not required for all secretion.
optionExplanations.1: The sight/smell response is abolished by cutting the vagus, proving it is nervous, not purely hormonal.
optionExplanations.3: Sight and smell clearly stimulate, not inhibit, acid secretion in the healthy volunteer.
optionExplanations.4: If gastric-phase secretion depended only on a vagal stretch reflex, cutting the vagus would abolish it too, yet it persists.

shortExplanation: Without secretin the pancreas and liver do not release bicarbonate, so the duodenum stays acidic; without CCK, pancreatic enzymes and bile are not delivered. The low pH further disables the pH-8 enzymes, so both fat and protein digestion are impaired.
solutionSteps: Note the pancreas, liver and gall bladder are intact but no longer receive their hormonal signals.
Loss of secretin means no bicarbonate release, so the duodenum stays acidic.
Loss of CCK means pancreatic enzymes are not released and the gall bladder does not contract to deliver bile.
The low pH disables trypsin and lipase (optimum ~8), impairing digestion of both protein and fat.
keyConcept: Secretin and CCK are the stimulatory signals that neutralise duodenal acid and deliver pancreatic enzymes and bile; losing the endocrine cells removes both.
commonMistake: Treating the hormones as inhibitory, or assuming pancreatic lipase and bicarbonate are secreted automatically without hormonal control.

optionExplanations.0: Secretin and CCK are stimulatory, so losing them decreases, not increases, pancreatic secretion.
optionExplanations.2: Pancreatic lipase is also under CCK control and is pH-sensitive, so fat digestion is impaired too.
optionExplanations.3: Bicarbonate release is driven by secretin, so without the endocrine cells the duodenum stays acidic.
optionExplanations.4: Gall-bladder contraction is triggered by CCK, not automatically by fat, so bile is not delivered.

shortExplanation: Salivary amylase is redundant (destroyed by stomach acid and duplicated by pancreatic amylase), and both amylases only produce maltose. The final, non-redundant step from maltose to absorbable glucose is done by brush-border maltase, so lacking it most severely blocks starch digestion.
solutionSteps: Trace the pathway: amylases break starch only to maltose and short chains.
Note salivary amylase is redundant because pancreatic amylase does the same job.
Identify the non-redundant final step: brush-border maltase converts maltose to glucose.
Conclude losing maltase blocks completion of starch digestion regardless of amylase activity.
keyConcept: The rate-limiting loss is the step with no back-up; brush-border maltase is the only route from maltose to absorbable glucose.
commonMistake: Over-rating salivary amylase as essential, or matching proteases (pepsin) or bile to starch digestion.

optionExplanations.0: Salivary amylase is destroyed by stomach acid and duplicated by pancreatic amylase, so its absence has little effect.
optionExplanations.1: Bile salts emulsify fats and play no part in starch digestion.
optionExplanations.3: Stomach acid does not digest starch; its absence would if anything let salivary amylase survive longer.
optionExplanations.4: Pepsin digests protein, not starch, so its absence does not affect carbohydrate digestion.

shortExplanation: The terminal ileum is where bile salts are reabsorbed and recycled to the liver. Removing it lets bile salts escape in the faeces faster than the liver's limited synthesis can replace them, so the bile-salt pool shrinks, micelle formation fails, and fat is malabsorbed (fatty stools).
solutionSteps: Recall the terminal ileum reabsorbs bile salts and returns them to the liver (enterohepatic circulation).
Removing that segment means bile salts are lost in the faeces on each pass.
The liver's limited synthesis cannot replace the whole recycled amount, so the pool shrinks.
A depleted bile-salt pool cannot form enough micelles, so fat is malabsorbed.
keyConcept: Enterohepatic recycling in the terminal ileum sustains a large bile-salt pool from small daily synthesis; losing that segment depletes the pool and impairs fat absorption.
commonMistake: Assuming the liver can compensate without limit, or that lipase alone makes bile salts unnecessary.

optionExplanations.0: Pancreatic lipase alone is not enough; bile salts are needed to emulsify fat and form micelles.
optionExplanations.1: Removing the ileum removes the reabsorption site, so bile salts are lost faster, not retained longer.
optionExplanations.3: Sugars and amino acids are absorbed mainly in the proximal small intestine, so their absorption is largely preserved.
optionExplanations.4: Hepatic synthesis is limited and cannot fully replace the recycled amount, so the pool falls.

shortExplanation: A highly lipophilic drug is packaged into chylomicrons and released into the lacteals with the products of fat digestion, then travels in the lymph to the systemic circulation. This route bypasses the hepatic portal vein and the liver on the first pass, so more drug reaches the general circulation unchanged.
solutionSteps: Recall water-soluble products enter the villus capillaries and the hepatic portal vein, passing through the liver first (first-pass metabolism).
Fat-digestion products are packaged into chylomicrons and released into the lacteal (lymph).
The lymph drains into a neck vein and thus into the systemic circulation, bypassing the portal vein.
A lipophilic drug taken with a fatty meal follows this lymphatic route, escaping first-pass metabolism.
keyConcept: Fats and lipophilic substances are absorbed via the lacteals into lymph, bypassing the hepatic portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism.
commonMistake: Believing chylomicrons travel in the portal blood to the liver, or that a first-pass bypass means the drug is never metabolised.

optionExplanations.0: Chylomicrons enter the lacteals and lymph, not the hepatic portal vein, so this route is anatomically incorrect.
optionExplanations.2: The liver does metabolise lipophilic drugs; the drug only escapes the first pass by routing through lymph, not forever.
optionExplanations.3: Lipophilic substances cross the lipid membranes readily, and less absorption would lower the systemic amount, contradicting the data.
optionExplanations.4: Fat actually slows stomach emptying, and enzyme exposure time is not what determines hepatic destruction.

shortExplanation: The showy scented petals, nectar guides and small amount of sticky pollen with a sticky stigma all identify an insect-pollinated flower. However, because the anthers and receptive stigma lie at the same level, nothing described prevents the flower's own pollen from reaching its stigma, so self-pollination is still possible.
solutionSteps: Identify the insect-pollination features: bright scented petals, nectar guides, and sticky pollen with a sticky stigma.
Contrast with wind-pollinated flowers (reduced petals, no scent, exposed feathery stigmas, abundant smooth pollen).
Note that attracting an insect only makes cross-pollination possible, not guaranteed.
Note the anthers and stigma are at the same level, so self pollen can reach the stigma; no anti-selfing device is described.
keyConcept: Insect-pollination features promote but do not guarantee outcrossing; preventing selfing requires an extra device such as spatial separation, timing differences, or self-incompatibility.
commonMistake: Equating animal pollination with obligate cross-pollination, or reading anthers and stigma at the same level as forcing self-fertilisation.

optionExplanations.0: Insect visitation promotes but does not guarantee outcrossing, and level anthers and stigma let self pollen reach the stigma.
optionExplanations.1: Level anthers and stigma merely permit selfing; the costly insect-attracting features would be pointless in an obligate selfer.
optionExplanations.2: Wind-pollinated flowers have reduced petals and feathery stigmas; the scent, nectar guides and sticky pollen contradict wind pollination.
optionExplanations.4: Petal colour and nectar guides function in visual attraction of pollinators, not in photosynthesis or heating the ovary.

shortExplanation: The central cell of the aa mother contributes two polar nuclei (each a) and the AA father's sperm contributes one A, giving a triploid Aaa endosperm that is coloured because A is dominant. The seed develops on the maternal aa plant, so coloured kernels appear on the colourless mother this generation (xenia).
solutionSteps: Identify the endosperm's parental contributions: two maternal polar nuclei (a + a) plus one sperm nucleus (A).
Combine to give a triploid endosperm of genotype Aaa.
Because one dominant A is present, the endosperm is coloured.
The seed develops on the maternal aa plant, so coloured kernels appear on the colourless mother in the current season (xenia).
keyConcept: Endosperm is triploid (two maternal polar nuclei + one sperm), and a dominant paternal allele can show immediately in the seed on the maternal plant (xenia).
commonMistake: Treating the endosperm as a diploid embryo, or thinking the endosperm inherits only from the mother.

optionExplanations.0: The endosperm is triploid, not diploid Aa, and seeds form on the female/seed parent, not the pollen parent.
optionExplanations.1: The two maternal polar nuclei supply a and a and the single sperm supplies one A, giving Aaa, not AAa.
optionExplanations.3: A sperm nucleus (A) fuses with the polar nuclei, so the endosperm is not purely maternal; it is Aaa and coloured.
optionExplanations.4: The paternal allele is expressed in the endosperm now, so coloured kernels are visible this season, not only later.

shortExplanation: In gametophytic self-incompatibility each haploid pollen grain carries one S-allele and is rejected if it matches either allele in the pistil. On an S1S2 pistil, S2 pollen is rejected and only S3 pollen fertilises, giving S1S3 and S2S3 offspring in equal numbers.
solutionSteps: Note the genotypes: pistil is S1S2; the S2S3 pollen parent makes equal numbers of S2 pollen and S3 pollen.
Apply the rule: a pollen grain fails if its single S-allele matches EITHER pistil allele.
S2 pollen matches the pistil's S2 allele, so it is rejected and forms no seeds.
S3 pollen matches neither S1 nor S2, so it is accepted and fertilises.
Each successful seed gets S3 from the father and either S1 or S2 from the mother, giving S1S3 and S2S3 in a 1:1 ratio.
keyConcept: Gametophytic self-incompatibility acts on each individual pollen grain by its own haploid S-allele; it blocks only the matching pollen, not the whole cross.
commonMistake: Assuming a shared S-allele blocks the entire cross, or reversing which pollen grain is rejected.

optionExplanations.0: S2 pollen is incompatible on an S1S2 pistil, so it cannot fertilise; no S2S2 offspring can form and not all pollen is effective.
optionExplanations.1: This applies the rule backwards. The compatible grain is the one that matches NEITHER pistil allele (S3), while the matching grain (S2) is the one rejected, so the successful offspring carry S3, not S2 from the father.
optionExplanations.2: There is no 'preferential transmission' of the shared allele; the mechanism does the opposite. The S2 grain is precisely the one blocked, so S2 from the father is transmitted LESS, not more. Offspring are S1S3 and S2S3 (S3 always from the father), never uniformly S2S3.
optionExplanations.4: Sharing the S2 allele blocks only the S2 pollen; the compatible S3 pollen still fertilises, so seeds do form.

shortExplanation: Embryo-free grain halves make no amylase in water alone but do so when gibberellin is added, identifying GA as the embryo's signal. A protein-synthesis inhibitor blocks the amylase even with GA present, showing the enzyme is made new by the aleurone, which then digests the starch stored in the endosperm.
solutionSteps: Water alone gives no amylase, so the embryo normally supplies a signal.
Adding GA restores amylase and starch breakdown, identifying GA as that signal (a hormone, not an enzyme).
Adding a protein-synthesis inhibitor with GA abolishes the amylase, showing the enzyme is synthesised de novo, not released from a store.
The responding living tissue is the aleurone, which secretes amylase into the starchy endosperm where the starch reserves lie.
keyConcept: Gibberellin from the embryo induces de novo alpha-amylase synthesis in the aleurone layer, mobilising endosperm starch.
commonMistake: Treating GA as the starch-digesting enzyme, or assuming amylase is stored ready-made rather than newly synthesised.

optionExplanations.0: GA is a signalling hormone; the molecule that hydrolyses starch is amylase produced by the aleurone in response to GA.
optionExplanations.1: The starch reserves lie in the dead starchy endosperm, while the living aleurone is the source of the enzyme, not the starch.
optionExplanations.3: The inhibitor blocks amylase even with GA present, so the enzyme must be newly made, not merely released from a store.

shortExplanation: The shoot perceives gravity in its own tissues, so it still curves upward as the lower-side auxin promotes elongation. The root perceives gravity in the cap, so removing the cap deletes its sensor: no lateral auxin gradient forms and the root grows straight.
solutionSteps: Identify where gravity is sensed: the root cap (columella) for the root, and the shoot's own tissues for the shoot.
In the shoot, lower-side auxin promotes elongation, so it bends upward (negative gravitropism).
Removing the root cap deletes the root's gravity sensor, so no auxin gradient forms in the root.
With no gradient the root elongates evenly and grows straight, while the shoot is unaffected and still curves upward.
keyConcept: Root graviperception resides in the cap, whereas the shoot senses gravity independently in its own tissues.
commonMistake: Assuming a single whole-plant gravity sensor in the root cap, or that auxin promotes elongation in the root as it does in the shoot.

optionExplanations.0: In roots the raised lower-side auxin inhibits elongation, so an intact root bends downward; with the cap removed it does not curve at all.
optionExplanations.1: Auxin is made mainly in the shoot apex, so cap removal does not stop auxin supply; the shoot still bends upward.
optionExplanations.4: The root's gravity sensor is the cap's columella, not the elongation zone, so removing the cap abolishes root curvature.

shortExplanation: For a cube of side a, surface-area-to-volume ratio is 6/a, giving 60 per mm for P and 6 per mm for Q. The larger organism Q has a ten-times-smaller ratio, so with the same demand per unit volume its surface cannot supply enough oxygen by diffusion and it needs a specialised gas-exchange surface.
solutionSteps: Write SA:V for a cube: 6a^2 / a^3 = 6/a.
Compute for P (a = 0.1 mm): 6/0.1 = 60 per mm.
Compute for Q (a = 1.0 mm): 6/1.0 = 6 per mm.
Note demand scales with volume, so the organism with the smaller SA:V struggles to meet demand.
Q has the smaller ratio, so Q is the one needing a specialised gas-exchange surface.
keyConcept: As a body grows, volume (and demand) rises faster than surface area, so SA:V falls as 1/length.
commonMistake: Reversing the ratio to think the smaller organism has the lower SA:V, or believing shape alone fixes SA:V.

optionExplanations.0: This reverses the ratio: the smaller organism P actually has the larger SA:V (60 versus 6), so it copes better with diffusion.
optionExplanations.1: SA:V depends on absolute size, not shape alone; two cubes of different side length have different ratios.
optionExplanations.2: This correctly identifies Q but reverses the reasoning: larger similar bodies have a smaller SA:V, not a larger one.

shortExplanation: Countercurrent flow keeps the water's oxygen partial pressure above the blood's along the whole lamella, so oxygen diffuses into the blood over its entire length. At the water-entry end the blood meets the freshest water at 15 kPa and can be loaded until it approaches roughly 14 kPa.
solutionSteps: Recognise that blood and water flow in opposite directions (countercurrent).
This maintains a favourable water-above-blood gradient at every point along the lamella.
The blood leaves at the water-entry end, where it meets water at 15 kPa.
The blood is loaded until it approaches, but stays just below, 15 kPa, i.e. about 14 kPa.
keyConcept: Countercurrent exchange sustains a diffusion gradient along the whole surface, letting blood exceed the outgoing-water partial pressure.
commonMistake: Applying parallel-flow logic (blood limited to the outgoing water value) or assuming complete equilibration to exactly the inflow value.

optionExplanations.1: Over a finite lamella the blood can approach but not fully reach the incoming water's 15 kPa, so it does not fully equilibrate.
optionExplanations.2: A favourable gradient exists at every point, so net diffusion does occur and blood partial pressure rises well above 4 kPa.
optionExplanations.4: Being limited to the outgoing-water value of 6 kPa is parallel-flow reasoning; countercurrent flow lets the blood exceed it.

shortExplanation: Withdrawing fluid from the tracheole tips lets the air column extend closer to the mitochondria of the active muscle. Because oxygen diffuses far faster in air than in fluid, shortening the slow fluid-phase path increases the rate of oxygen delivery.
solutionSteps: Note that fluid is drawn out of the tracheole tips into the muscle cells.
This allows the air-filled column to extend further along the tracheole, nearer the mitochondria.
Oxygen diffuses about ten thousand times faster in air than in fluid.
Replacing fluid-filled length with air-filled length shortens the slow diffusion path, so oxygen delivery rises (Fick's law).
keyConcept: Shortening the fluid-phase diffusion distance in the tracheoles speeds oxygen delivery to active tissue.
commonMistake: Reinterpreting the fluid movement as water conservation, carbon dioxide expulsion, or reliance on a respiratory pigment.

optionExplanations.1: Carbon dioxide leaves by diffusion, not by being pushed out by fluid; the described pH change is unrelated.
optionExplanations.2: The insect tracheal system delivers gaseous oxygen directly, so no dissolved oxygen-carrying pigment is involved.
optionExplanations.3: This describes water conservation, whereas the effect is on shortening the oxygen diffusion path to the muscle.

shortExplanation: The spongy mesophyll's air spaces are the pathway by which carbon dioxide diffuses in and dissolves on a large moist internal surface before reaching the cells. Packing the cells together removes this pathway and reduces the moist surface, so with light and water ample, carbon dioxide supply becomes limiting.
solutionSteps: Recall that carbon dioxide enters through stomata and diffuses through intercellular air spaces.
It dissolves on the large moist cell-wall surface and reaches the photosynthesising cells over a short path.
Removing the air spaces cuts both the diffusion pathway and the moist internal surface area.
With light and water ample, carbon dioxide delivery becomes the limiting factor for photosynthesis.
keyConcept: Intercellular air spaces provide the diffusion pathway and moist surface for carbon dioxide uptake into the mesophyll.
commonMistake: Blaming light penetration, oxygen accumulation, or water build-up instead of impaired carbon dioxide supply.

optionExplanations.1: Photosynthetic oxygen does not simply accumulate and shut off the light-dependent reactions as described.
optionExplanations.2: Light absorption occurs mainly in the palisade layer; in bright light the constraint here is carbon dioxide diffusion, not light.
optionExplanations.3: Reduced air spaces do not create a harmful excess of cell water; the real limit is impaired carbon dioxide supply.

shortExplanation: Diffusive supply scales as (surface area / diffusion distance) = L^2/L = L, while oxygen demand scales as volume = L^3. So supply relative to demand scales as L / L^3 = L^-2, and for a 4-fold increase this is (1/4)^2 = 1/16.
solutionSteps: Let every linear dimension scale by factor L (here L = 4).
Surface area scales as L^2 and the body-wall thickness (diffusion distance) scales as L, with concentration difference unchanged.
By Fick's law, supply scales as area/distance = L^2/L = L.
Demand scales as volume = L^3.
Supply/demand scales as L/L^3 = L^-2 = (1/4)^2 = 1/16.
keyConcept: Under isometric growth, diffusive supply per unit demand falls as the square of linear size because the wall also thickens.
commonMistake: Ignoring the thickening diffusion path (giving 1/4) or treating supply as fixed while demand grows (giving 1/64).

optionExplanations.0: Area scales as L^2 and volume as L^3, so their ratio must change as the organism grows; it is not unchanged.
optionExplanations.1: 1/64 treats supply as fixed, but the larger surface still raises supply in proportion to L, giving exponent -2, not -3.
optionExplanations.2: 1/4 uses only the surface-area-to-volume ratio and ignores that the thicker body wall lengthens the diffusion path.

shortExplanation: Cervical carcinoma is non-communicable because the tumour cells cannot pass between people, but its cause, HPV, is a communicable virus. Vaccinating against HPV removes the upstream infectious cause and so lowers the incidence of the non-communicable cancer.
solutionSteps: Define communicable: the diseased state or its pathogen is transmitted host to host.
Note the tumour cell mass itself cannot transfer between people, so the cancer is non-communicable.
Recognise its main cause, HPV, is a transmissible virus.
Conclude that blocking HPV by vaccination removes the cause and reduces cervical-carcinoma incidence.
keyConcept: A non-communicable disease with an infectious cause can be prevented by vaccinating against that transmissible agent.
commonMistake: Equating an infectious cause with transmission of the disease itself, or assuming any non-communicable disease can be vaccinated against.

optionExplanations.0: HPV can pass between people, but the tumour cells are not transferred, so the carcinoma itself is not communicable.
optionExplanations.1: Both communicable and non-communicable diseases have identifiable risk factors, and infection is not a random event.
optionExplanations.2: Social risk factors raise susceptibility, but tuberculosis is still spread by an airborne bacterium and remains communicable.

shortExplanation: Relative risk compares incidences, not raw counts: 80/4000 = 2.0% in smokers versus 20/8000 = 0.25% in non-smokers, giving a relative risk of 8. The absolute risk difference is 2.0% minus 0.25% = 1.75 percentage points.
solutionSteps: Compute incidence in smokers: 80/4000 = 0.020 (2.0%).
Compute incidence in non-smokers: 20/8000 = 0.0025 (0.25%).
Relative risk = 0.020 / 0.0025 = 8.
Absolute risk difference = 0.020 - 0.0025 = 0.0175 = 1.75 percentage points.
keyConcept: A large relative risk can coexist with a small absolute difference when the baseline risk is low; the two measures are distinct.
commonMistake: Dividing raw case counts instead of incidences, or confusing the relative risk with the absolute percentage-point difference.

optionExplanations.0: This inverts the ratio (0.0025/0.020 = 0.125), wrongly suggesting protection instead of increased risk.
optionExplanations.1: Dividing raw counts (80/20 = 4) ignores that the smoker cohort is half the size, halving the true ratio.
optionExplanations.3: The relative risk of 8 is a ratio; quoting it as 8 percentage points confuses it with the absolute difference of 1.75.

shortExplanation: A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one time, so it cannot establish which came first. Heavier people may adopt artificial sweeteners to cut energy intake (reverse causation), so the data cannot support the claim that sweeteners cause weight gain.
solutionSteps: Note that a cross-sectional design records exposure and outcome at the same moment.
Recognise the temporal order of the two variables is therefore unknown.
Consider the reverse explanation: already-heavier people choose non-caloric sweeteners to control weight.
Conclude the design cannot support a directional causal claim.
keyConcept: A single-time-point study cannot establish temporal order, so it cannot distinguish causation from reverse causation.
commonMistake: Treating a statistically significant correlation as proof of causation, or assuming a survey removes all confounding.

optionExplanations.1: Asserting the opposite effect from a lack of calories ignores the data, which show a positive association.
optionExplanations.2: This is the correlation-equals-causation error; significance argues against chance, not for causation.
optionExplanations.4: Cross-sectional adjustment cannot remove all confounding or fix temporal order; a randomised trial is what is needed.

shortExplanation: Because the investigator fixes the numbers of cases and controls, incidence and relative risk cannot be measured directly; only the odds ratio can be calculated. Here the odds ratio is (150x150)/(50x50) = 9, which for a rare disease closely approximates the relative risk.
solutionSteps: Note the case and control group sizes were fixed by the investigator, so sample disease frequency is artificial.
Conclude that incidence and relative risk cannot be measured, but the odds ratio can.
Odds of exposure in cases = 150/50 = 3; odds in controls = 50/150 = 1/3.
Odds ratio = 3 / (1/3) = 9, equivalently (150x150)/(50x50) = 9.
Because the disease is rare, this odds ratio approximates the relative risk.
keyConcept: A case-control study yields an odds ratio, which approximates relative risk when the disease is rare.
commonMistake: Reading case-control data as if from a cohort study to compute incidence, absolute risk, or relative risk.

optionExplanations.0: Treating 150/50 as a relative risk uses group sizes that were arbitrarily fixed at 200 each, so it is not a relative risk.
optionExplanations.2: 150/200 is the proportion of cases who were exposed, not the probability of developing disease given exposure.
optionExplanations.4: The odds ratio is precisely the association measure a case-control study is designed to provide, so it is not incalculable.

shortExplanation: BMI = 100 / (1.75^2) = about 33, which is nominally in the obese range. But BMI uses only mass and height and cannot separate muscle from fat, so a low-body-fat weightlifter's high BMI need not indicate excess adiposity or high metabolic risk.
solutionSteps: Compute BMI = mass / height^2 = 100 / (1.75 x 1.75) = 100 / 3.0625 = about 32.7, i.e. about 33.
Note this value nominally falls in the obese range.
Recognise BMI cannot distinguish lean (muscle, bone) mass from fat mass.
Conclude the muscular athlete's high BMI reflects muscularity, not necessarily excess fat or high risk.
keyConcept: BMI is a mass/height^2 index that cannot distinguish muscle from fat, so it can misclassify muscular individuals.
commonMistake: Dividing by height instead of height squared, or treating BMI as a definitive individual risk verdict.

optionExplanations.0: Dividing by height instead of height squared gives about 57; the correct value using height squared is about 33.
optionExplanations.1: A population association does not make a low-body-fat muscular person high-risk; BMI misclassifies him.
optionExplanations.3: Heavy muscle raises mass and therefore BMI, which is exactly why this athlete scores as obese despite low body fat.
