optionExplanations.1: 8 x 0.25 = 2.0 mg applies the haem efficiency to all the iron, ignoring the lower non-haem efficiency.
optionExplanations.2: (3x0.25)+(5x0.05) = 1.0 mg handles haem correctly but ignores the vitamin C enhancement of non-haem iron.
optionExplanations.3: 8 mg assumes the entire iron content is absorbed, ignoring bioavailability altogether.

shortExplanation: Vitamin D, made by sunlight on skin and supplemented by diet, is required for calcium absorption from the gut. With minimal sun exposure and negligible dietary vitamin D, little calcium is absorbed despite the calcium-rich diet, so bone is poorly mineralised and rickets develops.
solutionSteps: Recall vitamin D is needed for efficient intestinal calcium absorption.
Note the child has minimal sun exposure and negligible dietary vitamin D.
So despite abundant calcium intake, little calcium is absorbed and plasma calcium is inadequate.
Poorly mineralised bone results, producing the soft, bowing bones of rickets; the limiting step is absorption, not intake.
keyConcept: Vitamin D is required for intestinal calcium absorption, so its deficiency causes rickets even when dietary calcium is plentiful.
commonMistake: Attributing rickets to insufficient dietary calcium, dairy phosphate, or protein/vitamin C deficiency rather than to impaired calcium absorption from lack of vitamin D.

optionExplanations.0: Dairy phosphate does not clinically sequester dietary calcium to cause rickets; this ignores the central role of vitamin D.
optionExplanations.1: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with defective collagen, not rickets.
optionExplanations.2: This misattributes rickets to the protein/collagen matrix, and the dairy-rich diet supplies ample protein.
optionExplanations.3: The diet is explicitly calcium-rich, so intake is not the limiting factor.

shortExplanation: Editing a single-cell zygote is germ-line: every cell of the resulting individual, including the cells that form the gametes, descends from that one edited cell, so the change is heritable. Correcting a patient's haematopoietic stem cells is somatic; those cells make blood cells but never gametes, so the change cannot be passed on.
solutionSteps: Distinguish somatic gene therapy (non-reproductive cells, not heritable) from germ-line modification (cells giving rise to gametes, heritable).
In Strategy 2 the edited zygote is totipotent, so all its descendants, including the future germ line, carry the change.
In Strategy 1 the corrected bone-marrow stem cells divide only into blood cells, never gametes.
Conclude only Strategy 2 can transmit the gene to future generations.
keyConcept: Germ-line edits made in a zygote are heritable because the germ line descends from that cell, whereas somatic cell edits are confined to the patient.
commonMistake: Assuming any stem cell belongs to the germ line, or conflating ordinary cell division with germ-line transmission.

optionExplanations.0: This reverses the labels; bone-marrow stem cells are somatic and the zygote is the germ-line target.
optionExplanations.1: Corrected bone-marrow stem cells divide, but their progeny are blood cells, not gametes, so Strategy 1 is not heritable.
optionExplanations.2: Integrating viral vectors can insert the gene into a host chromosome, so heritability is possible in principle.
optionExplanations.3: Somatic bone-marrow cells never become gametes at any age, so developmental timing relative to puberty is irrelevant.

shortExplanation: An antibiotic-resistance marker gene could, in principle, be taken up by gut or soil bacteria through horizontal gene transfer, adding to the pool of antibiotic-resistance genes. This is a biologically coherent concern, unlike the other objections which rest on misconceptions.
solutionSteps: Recall the resistance gene is a selectable marker, letting only transformed cells survive on antibiotic medium.
Consider that this gene, once in food or the environment, could be acquired by bacteria.
Horizontal gene transfer to gut or soil bacteria is a real, if low-probability, route for spreading resistance.
Identify this as the objection with the soundest biological basis.
keyConcept: Antibiotic-resistance marker genes in GM crops could in principle spread to bacteria by horizontal gene transfer, adding to the resistance gene pool.
commonMistake: Believing eating DNA rewrites the consumer's genome, that a bacterial gene is a pathogen, that transformation causes sterility, or that a resistance gene makes the antibiotic itself.

optionExplanations.0: Inserting a transgene does not inherently sterilise a plant; sterility only arises if a specific sterility trait is engineered.
optionExplanations.1: The resistance gene encodes an enzyme that inactivates kanamycin; it does not direct synthesis of the antibiotic.
optionExplanations.2: Dietary DNA is digested to nucleotides and is not incorporated into the consumer's genome.
optionExplanations.4: A transferred gene is a length of DNA, not a living pathogen, so it cannot cause infection.

shortExplanation: SCNT places P's diploid nucleus into an enucleated egg from D, which supplies cytoplasm and mitochondria carrying D's mitochondrial DNA. The stem cells therefore have P's nuclear genome and D's mitochondrial DNA; since rejection is governed by nuclear-encoded MHC, cells matched to P are unlikely to be rejected by P.
solutionSteps: Note the somatic nucleus (P) supplies all chromosomal genes; the enucleated egg (D) supplies no nuclear DNA.
The egg cytoplasm supplies mitochondria carrying D's mitochondrial DNA.
So the stem cells have P's nuclear genome and D's mitochondrial genome.
Because transplant rejection depends on nuclear-encoded MHC/HLA molecules matched to P, the cells are unlikely to be rejected by P.
keyConcept: In SCNT the nuclear genome comes from the somatic donor and the mitochondrial DNA from the egg donor; MHC matching to the somatic donor gives the therapeutic advantage.
commonMistake: Thinking the egg donor's cytoplasm triggers rejection, that reprogramming rewrites the DNA sequence, or that the egg contributes nuclear chromosomes.

optionExplanations.1: Rejection is determined by nuclear-encoded MHC/HLA proteins, which match P, not by the egg donor's cytoplasm.
optionExplanations.2: A blastocyst in culture does not become an individual; only implantation into a surrogate can do that.
optionExplanations.3: Reprogramming changes gene expression, not the DNA sequence, so the cells carry P's genotype, not D's.
optionExplanations.4: The egg is enucleated, so it contributes no nuclear chromosomes; all nuclear DNA is P's diploid genome.

shortExplanation: The panel misses some carriers, so a negative result lowers but does not abolish risk. Among 1000 people, 100 are carriers; the test detects 90 and misses 10, and all 900 non-carriers test negative, so the negative group has 10 carriers among 910, giving a residual risk of 10/910 = 1/91.
solutionSteps: Take 1000 people: 100 are carriers (1 in 10) and 900 are not.
The test detects 90% of carriers, so it identifies 90 and misses 10.
With no false positives, all 900 non-carriers also test negative.
The test-negative group has 10 carriers among 910 people, so the residual carrier probability is 10/910 = 1/91.
keyConcept: After a negative screen of limited sensitivity, use conditional probability (missed carriers over all who test negative) to find the residual risk.
commonMistake: Multiplying the prior by the miss rate to get 1/100, or inverting the conditional and confusing detection rate with the chance a negative is a carrier.

optionExplanations.0: 1/100 is the naive product of the prior and miss rate; it omits the conditional denominator, so it is not the residual risk for one negative test.
optionExplanations.1: A negative result is not proof of non-carrier status, because the panel cannot detect every mutation.
optionExplanations.2: The negative result does update her risk downward from 1/10 to about 1/91; it is not uninformative.
optionExplanations.4: This inverts the conditional; 90% detection does not mean 90% of negatives are carriers.

shortExplanation: Adding 12.5 mL of base neutralises exactly half the acetic acid, reaching the half-equivalence point where [acid] = [conjugate base]. There the pH equals the pKa, which is 4.74.
solutionSteps: Initial acid = 25.0 mL x 0.100 mol/L = 2.50 mmol.
Base added = 12.5 mL x 0.100 mol/L = 1.25 mmol, exactly half the acid.
Equal amounts of acetic acid and acetate remain (half-equivalence point).
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = pKa + log 1 = pKa.
keyConcept: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration, the buffer has equal acid and conjugate base, so pH = pKa.
commonMistake: Assuming the pH is 7 at this point, which only holds at the equivalence point of a strong acid-strong base titration.

optionExplanations.1: A pH of 7.00 applies to a strong acid-strong base equivalence point, not a weak-acid buffer at half-equivalence.
optionExplanations.3: A pH of 2.87 is roughly the pH of the original 0.100 mol/L acetic acid before any base is added.
optionExplanations.4: A pH of 8.72 is the basic pH at the full equivalence point, where only acetate remains.

shortExplanation: Dissociating a fraction alpha raises the total pressure to P0(1 + alpha). Setting this equal to 1.5 P0 gives alpha = 0.50, so half the N2O4 has dissociated.
solutionSteps: Let initial pressure be P0 and fraction dissociated be alpha.
At equilibrium: p(N2O4) = P0(1 - alpha), p(NO2) = 2 P0 alpha.
Total pressure = P0(1 - alpha) + 2 P0 alpha = P0(1 + alpha).
Set P0(1 + alpha) = 1.5 P0, so 1 + alpha = 1.5.
Solve: alpha = 0.50.
keyConcept: Because each mole of N2O4 gives two moles of NO2, the total pressure scales as (1 + alpha) times the initial pressure.
commonMistake: Writing the total pressure as P0(1 + 2 alpha) and solving, which mishandles the mole change.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 0.25 comes from wrongly writing the total pressure as P0(1 + 2 alpha).
optionExplanations.1: A value of 0.75 would require a total pressure of 1.75 P0, not 1.5 P0.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 0.33 comes from mis-scaling the 1.5-fold pressure increase instead of using the (1 + alpha) factor.

shortExplanation: Heating an endothermic reaction shifts it towards NO2, while compression favours the side with fewer gas moles, N2O4. The two stresses oppose each other, so the net shift cannot be stated without their relative magnitudes.
solutionSteps: Heat acts as a reactant for an endothermic reaction, so heating shifts equilibrium towards products (NO2).
Halving the volume raises the pressure; equilibrium favours the side with fewer gas moles.
The reactant side has 1 mole of gas versus 2 moles on the product side, so compression favours N2O4.
The two effects act in opposite directions, so the net result is indeterminate without magnitudes.
keyConcept: Temperature and pressure changes can each shift an equilibrium in opposite directions; the net effect requires quantitative comparison.
commonMistake: Inverting the temperature effect for an endothermic reaction, or assuming higher pressure favours the product side.

optionExplanations.0: This inverts the pressure effect and wrongly denies that heating shifts an endothermic equilibrium.
optionExplanations.3: This reads the pressure effect correctly but inverts the temperature effect, treating heating as if it favoured reactants.
optionExplanations.4: This identifies heating correctly but wrongly claims higher pressure favours products; compression favours the fewer-moles side, N2O4.

shortExplanation: With 20% dissociation, equilibrium concentrations are [N2O4] = 0.40 M and [NO2] = 0.20 M. Then Kc = (0.20)^2/0.40 = 0.10 mol/L.
keyConcept: Kc uses equilibrium molarities with the NO2 term squared per its stoichiometric coefficient of 2.
commonMistake: Forgetting the factor of 2 for NO2 formed, or failing to square the NO2 concentration.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 0.20 comes from omitting the square on [NO2] or using raw moles for NO2.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 0.40 comes from treating moles as molarities without dividing by volume consistently.
optionExplanations.2: A value of 0.050 comes from forgetting the stoichiometric factor of 2 for NO2.

shortExplanation: Adding 0.050 mol NaOH converts 0.050 mol acid into conjugate base, leaving 0.15 mol acid and 0.25 mol acetate. Then pH = 4.74 + log(0.25/0.15) = 4.74 + 0.22 = 4.96.
solutionSteps: NaOH neutralises acid: n(acetic acid) = 0.20 - 0.05 = 0.15 mol.
Conjugate base increases: n(acetate) = 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.25 mol.
Same volume lets the mole ratio be used directly in Henderson-Hasselbalch.
keyConcept: Strong base added to a buffer converts weak acid into its conjugate base, and the new mole ratio sets the pH.
commonMistake: Ignoring that NaOH consumes acid and creates conjugate base, or applying the log ratio in reverse.

optionExplanations.0: A pH of 9.00 treats the system as pure acetate hydrolysis, ignoring the large remaining buffer.
optionExplanations.3: A pH of 4.52 applies the ratio in reverse, subtracting the log term instead of adding it.
optionExplanations.4: A pH of 4.74 assumes the acid/base ratio stays 1:1, ignoring that NaOH shifts it.

shortExplanation: By Hess's law with combustion enthalpies, the reaction enthalpy is the sum for the reactants minus that for the product: (-1411 - 286) - (-1560) = -137 kJ/mol.
solutionSteps: Combustion-enthalpy Hess cycle: DH(rxn) = sum DHc(reactants) - sum DHc(products).
Sum for reactants = -1411 + (-286) = -1697 kJ/mol.
DH(rxn) = -137 kJ/mol, exothermic.
keyConcept: When using combustion enthalpies, the reaction enthalpy is reactants minus products, opposite to the formation-enthalpy expression.
commonMistake: Applying the products-minus-reactants convention (used with formation enthalpies) to combustion data, which flips the sign.

optionExplanations.2: A value of -1685 comes from mis-signing one term while reversing the reactant-product order.
optionExplanations.3: A value of -3257 comes from summing all three combustion enthalpies instead of subtracting the product term.
optionExplanations.4: A value of +137 has the correct magnitude but reversed sign, from using products minus reactants.

shortExplanation: Forming 0.500 mol Cl2 consumes 0.500 mol PCl5 and forms 0.500 mol PCl3, so all three species are 0.0500 M. Then Kc = (0.0500 x 0.0500)/0.0500 = 0.0500 mol/L.
solutionSteps: Divide each by V = 10.0 L: all three concentrations = 0.0500 M.
Kc = 0.0500 mol/L.
keyConcept: Convert every equilibrium amount to molarity before forming the Kc ratio.
commonMistake: Using raw moles for some species, or forgetting that PCl5 is reduced to 0.500 mol.

optionExplanations.1: A value of 0.100 comes from mixing raw moles and molarities in the expression, doubling the true value.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 0.0125 treats n(PCl5) as 1.00 mol, forgetting the 0.500 mol consumed.
optionExplanations.4: A value of 0.500 comes from using moles without dividing by volume, inflating Kc tenfold.

shortExplanation: The data give second order in A and first order in B, so rate = k[A]^2[B] with k = 2.0 M^-2 s^-1. At [A] = 0.30 M and [B] = 0.30 M, rate = 2.0 x 0.09 x 0.30 = 5.4 x 10^-2 M/s.
solutionSteps: Doubling [A] at fixed [B] quadruples the rate, so order in A is 2.
Doubling [B] at fixed [A] doubles the rate, so order in B is 1.
keyConcept: Reaction orders come only from experimental rate data, not from the stoichiometric coefficients.
commonMistake: Taking the order in A as 1, or equating it to the stoichiometric coefficient, instead of reading order 2 from the data.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 1.6 x 10^-1 comes from over-counting the overall order beyond 2 in A and 1 in B.
optionExplanations.2: A value of 1.8 x 10^-2 takes the order in A as 1 rather than 2.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 6.0 x 10^-3 simply triples the Experiment-1 rate instead of applying the rate law.

shortExplanation: Aluminium is the limiting reagent (0.200 mol Al versus 0.150 mol Fe2O3, which needs only 0.100 mol). This gives 0.200 mol Fe theoretical (11.17 g), and at 80% yield the mass is 8.9 g.
solutionSteps: Ratio 2 Al : 1 Fe2O3 means 0.200 mol Al needs only 0.100 mol Fe2O3, so Al is limiting.
From 2 Al -> 2 Fe, n(Fe) = n(Al) = 0.200 mol; theoretical mass = 0.200 x 55.85 = 11.17 g.
keyConcept: Identify the limiting reagent by comparing mole ratios to stoichiometry, then apply the percentage yield.
commonMistake: Treating Fe2O3 as limiting, or forgetting to apply the 80% yield factor.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 13.4 g arises from wrongly using Fe2O3 as limiting plus an arithmetic slip.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 11.2 g is the theoretical 100% yield of Fe, ignoring the 80% factor.
optionExplanations.2: A value of 16.8 g uses Fe2O3 as limiting with no yield correction.

shortExplanation: Decomposing 90% of 0.125 mol CaCO3 releases 0.1125 mol CO2. At 300 K and 1.00 atm, PV = nRT gives V = 2.77 L.
solutionSteps: Convert temperature: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
keyConcept: Use only the fraction that reacts to find moles of gas, and convert Celsius to kelvin before applying the ideal gas law.
commonMistake: Forgetting the 90% conversion, or using the Celsius value directly as the absolute temperature.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 2.52 L uses 273 K instead of 300 K for the temperature.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 5.54 L doubles the moles of CO2, as if 2 mol CO2 formed per mol CaCO3.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 3.08 L ignores the 90% conversion and uses the full 0.125 mol.

shortExplanation: Each Cr2O7 2- accepts 6 electrons (2 Cr each gaining 3), while each Fe2+ loses 1 electron. So 6 mol Fe2+ react per mol dichromate, giving 0.0200 x 6 = 0.120 mol.
solutionSteps: Cr goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons per Cr.
Two Cr per Cr2O7 2- means 6 electrons accepted per dichromate ion.
Each Fe2+ -> Fe3+ loses 1 electron, so 6 mol Fe2+ balance 1 mol dichromate.
keyConcept: Balance a redox reaction by equating total electrons gained by the oxidant with those lost by the reductant.
commonMistake: Counting only 3 electrons (one Cr) per dichromate, or assuming a 1:1 mole ratio.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 0.0600 mol uses a 3:1 ratio, counting only one Cr per dichromate.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 0.0200 mol assumes a 1:1 ratio, ignoring the differing electron counts.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 0.0400 mol uses a 2:1 ratio, counting the two Cr atoms but not the 3 electrons each.

shortExplanation: Nitrogen's half-filled 2p3 configuration is extra stable, so removing an electron from it costs more than removing one from oxygen's paired 2p4. Thus nitrogen has a higher first ionization energy than oxygen despite oxygen's greater nuclear charge.
solutionSteps: First ionization energy generally rises across a period with nuclear charge.
Oxygen (2p4) has a spin-paired electron whose removal relieves electron-electron repulsion, lowering its ionization energy.
Nitrogen (2p3) has a stable half-filled subshell with all p electrons unpaired.
Therefore IE1(N) > IE1(O), giving the order B < C < O < N.
keyConcept: The half-filled 2p3 subshell of nitrogen creates a dip in the ionization-energy trend at oxygen.
commonMistake: Assuming ionization energy increases strictly with nuclear charge, missing the anomaly at oxygen.

optionExplanations.0: Carbon actually has a higher first ionization energy than boron, so this reverses the order.
optionExplanations.2: Equating highest nuclear charge with highest ionization energy ignores the half-filled stability that puts nitrogen above oxygen.
optionExplanations.4: A strictly monotonic increase misses the oxygen dip; the real order is B < C < O < N.

shortExplanation: XeF4 is square planar (four bonding pairs plus two axial lone pairs), so its four equal bond dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel exactly, making it non-polar despite polar Xe-F bonds.
solutionSteps: XeF4 has 6 electron domains: 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs.
The two lone pairs occupy opposite axial positions, leaving the four bonds square planar.
The four equal Xe-F dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel.
The other molecules lack such cancelling symmetry, so they are polar.
keyConcept: A molecule is non-polar when its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry, as in square-planar geometry.
commonMistake: Assuming any molecule with polar bonds must be polar, ignoring how molecular geometry can cancel the dipoles.

optionExplanations.0: SF4 is see-saw shaped from one equatorial lone pair, so its dipoles do not cancel and it is polar.
optionExplanations.2: ClF3 is T-shaped with two lone pairs, an asymmetric arrangement that leaves a net dipole.
optionExplanations.3: NF3 is trigonal pyramidal, so its three N-F dipoles and lone pair give a net moment.

shortExplanation: C3H6O has one degree of unsaturation, and open-chain structures give six constitutional isomers: propanal, acetone, prop-2-en-1-ol, two enols (prop-1-en-1-ol and prop-1-en-2-ol), and methyl vinyl ether.
solutionSteps: C3H6O has one degree of unsaturation (a C=C or C=O); cyclic forms are excluded.
Carbonyl structures: propanal and propan-2-one (acetone).
Unsaturated alcohols: prop-2-en-1-ol, prop-1-en-1-ol, and prop-1-en-2-ol (two of these are enols).
Ether: methyl vinyl ether, CH2=CH-O-CH3.
Total distinct open-chain constitutional isomers = 6.
keyConcept: Systematically enumerate open-chain isomers by the position of the double bond (C=O or C=C) and the oxygen (alcohol, enol, or ether).
commonMistake: Omitting one of the enol isomers, or including excluded cyclic structures such as oxirane.

optionExplanations.1: A count of 8 overcounts by including cyclic species or counting cis/trans of an enol separately.
optionExplanations.2: A count of 5 usually omits one enol isomer, such as prop-1-en-1-ol.
optionExplanations.4: A count of 4 omits the two enol isomers.

shortExplanation: Bonds broken are one C=C and one H-H (612 + 436 = 1048 kJ); bonds formed are one C-C and two new C-H (348 + 824 = 1172 kJ). DeltaH = 1048 - 1172 = -124 kJ/mol.
solutionSteps: Only changed bonds matter; the four original C-H bonds cancel.
Bonds broken: C=C + H-H = 612 + 436 = 1048 kJ.
Bonds formed: C-C + 2 C-H = 348 + 2(412) = 1172 kJ.
DeltaH = bonds broken - bonds formed = 1048 - 1172 = -124 kJ/mol.
keyConcept: From bond enthalpies, DeltaH equals the energy of bonds broken minus the energy of bonds formed.
commonMistake: Counting only one new C-H bond, or forgetting to break the H-H bond, or inverting the broken-minus-formed convention.

optionExplanations.0: A value of +288 counts only one of the two new C-H bonds.
optionExplanations.2: A value of -560 forgets that the H-H bond must also be broken.
optionExplanations.3: A value of +124 reverses the convention, computing bonds formed minus bonds broken.

shortExplanation: The rate ratio is exp[(Ea,uncat - Ea,cat)/RT] = exp[(75000 - 50000)/(8.314 x 300)] = exp(10.0), which is about 2.2 x 10^4.
solutionSteps: Rate constant follows k = A e^(-Ea/RT), with A and T fixed.
Ratio k_cat/k_uncat = exp[(Ea,uncat - Ea,cat)/RT].
exp(10.0) is about 2.2 x 10^4.
keyConcept: Lowering the activation energy multiplies the rate by an exponential Boltzmann factor, not a linear one.
commonMistake: Reporting the exponent (10) instead of exponentiating it, or treating the rate as inversely proportional to Ea.

optionExplanations.0: A factor of 1.5 comes from 75/50, treating rate as inversely proportional to activation energy.
optionExplanations.2: A factor of 1.5 x 10^2 (e^5) halves the exponent, as if only 12.5 kJ/mol of barrier reduction applied.
optionExplanations.3: A factor of 10 is the exponent itself, forgetting to exponentiate it.

shortExplanation: The SO3 partial pressure by difference is 0.40 atm. Then Kp = (0.40)^2/[(0.10)^2 x 0.20] = 0.16/0.002 = 80 atm^-1.
solutionSteps: Kp = p(SO3)^2 / [p(SO2)^2 x p(O2)] with coefficients as exponents.
keyConcept: Kp places products over reactants with each partial pressure raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.
commonMistake: Using the total pressure as the SO3 partial pressure, or omitting the squared exponents.

optionExplanations.1: A value of 245 uses the total pressure 0.70 atm as the SO3 partial pressure.
optionExplanations.2: A value of 0.0125 inverts the expression, placing reactants over products.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 8 squares SO3 but not SO2, dropping the coefficient of 2 on the reactant.

shortExplanation: First-order decay multiplies the concentration by the same factor over equal intervals. The factor for 40 s is 0.36/0.60 = 0.60, so after another 40 s the concentration is 0.36 x 0.60 = 0.216 mol/L.
solutionSteps: For first order, [A] = [A]0 e^(-kt), so equal intervals give a constant multiplying factor.
First 40 s factor = 0.36/0.60 = 0.60.
Apply the same factor for the next 40 s: 0.36 x 0.60.
[A] at 80 s = 0.216 mol/L.
keyConcept: In a first-order reaction, concentration is multiplied by the same constant fraction during each equal time interval.
commonMistake: Treating the drop from 0.60 to 0.36 as a half-life, or subtracting a fixed amount as in zero-order kinetics.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 0.13 applies the decay factor twice more instead of once.
optionExplanations.2: A value of 0.18 halves 0.36, wrongly treating the first interval as a half-life.
optionExplanations.4: A value of 0.12 subtracts the same fixed amount lost in the first interval, assuming zero-order behaviour.

shortExplanation: DeltaG = DeltaH - T DeltaS = -60000 + 150T (in J/mol), which is negative when T < 400 K. So the forward reaction is spontaneous only below the crossover temperature of 400 K.
solutionSteps: Spontaneity requires DeltaG = DeltaH - T DeltaS < 0.
Substitute: DeltaG = -60000 - T(-150) = -60000 + 150T J/mol.
DeltaG < 0 when 150T < 60000, i.e. T < 400 K.
Crossover T = DeltaH/DeltaS = 60000/150 = 400 K.
keyConcept: When DeltaH and DeltaS are both negative, the reaction is spontaneous only below the crossover temperature DeltaH/DeltaS.
commonMistake: Assuming a negative DeltaH guarantees spontaneity at all temperatures, or using 298 K as the boundary.

optionExplanations.0: Spontaneity at all temperatures ignores the unfavourable negative entropy term that dominates at high T.
optionExplanations.1: Claiming it is never spontaneous ignores the favourable enthalpy term that dominates below 400 K.
optionExplanations.3: Placing spontaneity above 400 K reverses the temperature dependence for a negative DeltaS.

shortExplanation: The two-point van't Hoff equation gives DeltaH = R ln(K2/K1) x [T1 T2/(T2 - T1)] = 8.314 x 2.303 x 1200, about +23 kJ/mol. The positive sign matches K rising with temperature (endothermic).
solutionSteps: van't Hoff: ln(K2/K1) = -(DeltaH/R)(1/T2 - 1/T1).
Rearrange: DeltaH = R ln(K2/K1) x T1 T2/(T2 - T1).
DeltaH = 8.314 x 2.303 x 1200 is about +23000 J/mol = +23 kJ/mol.
keyConcept: The two-point van't Hoff relation links the change in equilibrium constant with temperature to the reaction enthalpy.
commonMistake: Using the temperature difference instead of T1 T2/(T2 - T1), or using log10 instead of ln, or reversing the sign.

optionExplanations.1: A value of +1.9 uses the temperature difference (100 K) instead of the factor 1200 K.
optionExplanations.3: A value of +6.7 inserts a single average temperature of 350 K rather than the two-point term.
optionExplanations.4: A value of -23 has the correct magnitude but reversed sign; rising K with temperature indicates an endothermic reaction.

shortExplanation: Total chloride is 0.100 mol from NaCl plus 0.060 mol from CaCl2 (two Cl per formula unit) = 0.160 mol. Divided by the combined 0.400 L, the concentration is 0.40 mol/L.
solutionSteps: From NaCl: 0.250 L x 0.40 mol/L = 0.100 mol Cl-.
From CaCl2: 0.150 L x 0.20 mol/L = 0.030 mol, giving 2 x 0.030 = 0.060 mol Cl-.
Total volume = 250 + 150 = 400 mL = 0.400 L.
keyConcept: Sum the moles of each ion (accounting for formula stoichiometry) and divide by the total combined volume.
commonMistake: Forgetting that CaCl2 releases two chloride ions, or failing to account for the mutual dilution on mixing.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 0.80 adds the chloride molarities before dilution, ignoring the mixing.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 0.30 is the arithmetic mean of the two molarities, ignoring volumes and ion counts.
optionExplanations.2: A value of 0.33 counts only one Cl- per CaCl2.

shortExplanation: The charge is 18000 C, giving 0.1865 mol electrons. Since Al3+ needs 3 electrons each, 0.0622 mol Al forms, with mass 0.0622 x 27.0 = 1.68 g.
solutionSteps: Moles of electrons = Q/F = 18000/96500 = 0.1865 mol.
Al3+ + 3e- -> Al, so moles Al = 0.1865/3 = 0.0622 mol.
keyConcept: Faraday's law relates charge to moles of electrons, then the ion charge sets the moles of metal deposited.
commonMistake: Forgetting to divide by 3 for Al3+, or mis-converting the 1 hour to seconds.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 0.028 g uses 60 s instead of 3600 s for the time.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 5.04 g omits dividing by the number of electrons, treating the ion as Al+.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 2.52 g divides by 2 instead of 3, treating the ion as Al2+.

shortExplanation: By Graham's law, effusion time is proportional to the square root of molar mass. So M_unknown = 32 x (90/60)^2 = 32 x 2.25 = 72.
solutionSteps: Graham's law: rate is proportional to 1/sqrt(M), so time is proportional to sqrt(M).
t_unknown/t_O2 = sqrt(M_unknown/M_O2).
M_unknown = M_O2 x (t_unknown/t_O2)^2 = 32 x (90/60)^2.
M_unknown = 32 x 2.25 = 72.
keyConcept: Under identical conditions, the heavier gas effuses more slowly, with time proportional to the square root of molar mass.
commonMistake: Taking the square root of the time ratio instead of squaring it, or inverting the ratio.

optionExplanations.1: A value of 39 takes the square root of the time ratio instead of squaring it.
optionExplanations.3: A value of 48 applies a linear proportionality, omitting the square root in Graham's law.
optionExplanations.4: A value of 21 inverts the time ratio, wrongly implying the heavier gas effuses faster.

shortExplanation: The successive ionization energies rise modestly for the first three, then jump sharply between the 3rd (2745) and 4th (11580). This shows three easily removed valence electrons, so the element is the period-3 Group-13 element aluminium.
solutionSteps: Track successive ionization energies for a large jump signalling a broken noble-gas core.
Values 578, 1817, 2745 rise gradually; the 4th (11580) is more than four times the 3rd.
The jump after the 3rd electron means three valence electrons, i.e. Group 13.
The period-3 Group-13 element is aluminium.
keyConcept: A large jump in successive ionization energies marks the point where removal breaks into a stable inner core, revealing the number of valence electrons.
commonMistake: Misreading which electron removal precedes the big jump, and thus the group number.

optionExplanations.1: Magnesium has two valence electrons, so its big jump would come after the 2nd ionization energy.
optionExplanations.2: Silicon has four valence electrons, so its jump would appear after the 4th, not the 3rd.
optionExplanations.3: Phosphorus has five valence electrons and would rise smoothly through all five listed values.

shortExplanation: The reaction quotient Q = [Zn2+]/[Cu2+] = 100, so log Q = 2, and n = 2. The Nernst equation gives E = 1.10 - (0.059/2)(2) = 1.04 V.
solutionSteps: Q includes only aqueous species: Q = [Zn2+]/[Cu2+] = 1.0/0.010 = 100.
log Q = 2; two electrons are transferred, so n = 2.
keyConcept: The Nernst equation adjusts the standard potential for non-standard concentrations using Q and the electron count n.
commonMistake: Omitting the division by n, or getting the sign of the correction term wrong.

optionExplanations.0: A value of 1.10 V is just E, neglecting the Nernst correction entirely.
optionExplanations.1: A value of 1.16 V adds instead of subtracts the correction term (a sign error).
optionExplanations.2: A value of 0.98 V omits the division by n, using 0.059 x 2.

shortExplanation: The permanganate delivered is 0.0200 mol/L x 0.0240 L = 4.80e-4 mol. The 5:1 mole ratio gives 2.40e-3 mol Fe2+, which in the 25.0 mL sample is 0.096 mol/L.
solutionSteps: Moles MnO4- = 0.0200 mol/L x 0.0240 L = 4.80e-4 mol.
Balanced equation gives 5 mol Fe2+ per 1 mol MnO4-, so moles Fe2+ = 5 x 4.80e-4 = 2.40e-3 mol.
Divide by the original sample volume: [Fe2+] = 2.40e-3 mol / 0.0250 L = 0.096 mol/L.
keyConcept: In a redox titration, multiply titrant moles by the stoichiometric ratio, then divide by the analyte (sample) volume.
commonMistake: Using a 1:1 ratio and ignoring the factor of 5, or dividing by the titrant volume instead of the sample volume.

optionExplanations.1: This uses a 1:1 permanganate-to-iron ratio, ignoring the stoichiometric factor of 5 in the balanced equation.
optionExplanations.2: This divides the permanganate moles by 5 instead of multiplying, inverting the direction of the 5:1 ratio.
optionExplanations.3: This divides the correct moles of Fe2+ by the titrant volume (24.0 mL) rather than the sample volume.

shortExplanation: The molecule has two independent stereocentres (C2 and C3) and one stereogenic C4=C5 double bond with no internal symmetry, so 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 distinct stereoisomers.
solutionSteps: Identify the two stereocentres at C2 and C3, each bearing OH, H and two different chain fragments.
Identify the stereogenic double bond C4=C5, disubstituted with different groups so it shows E/Z isomerism.
Confirm the two halves are constitutionally different, so there is no internal mirror plane and no meso reduction.
Multiply the independent stereogenic units: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.
keyConcept: Total stereoisomers equal 2^n for n independent stereogenic units (stereocentres plus stereogenic double bonds) when the molecule has no symmetry.
commonMistake: Forgetting that a disubstituted C=C is also stereogenic, or wrongly assuming a meso form reduces the count.

optionExplanations.1: Counting 2^2 ignores that the disubstituted double bond is also stereogenic and contributes a factor of 2.
optionExplanations.2: Assuming the OH-bearing carbons are equivalent creates a meso form, but this asymmetric molecule has no internal symmetry.
optionExplanations.4: Counting 2^4 treats each doubly bonded carbon as a separate stereocentre; the whole C=C contributes only one factor of 2.

shortExplanation: SN1 rate follows carbocation stability. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane ionises to a tertiary carbocation, the most stable of the set, so it solvolyses fastest.
solutionSteps: Recognise that the SN1 rate-determining step is ionisation, so it tracks carbocation stability.
Rank the cations: tertiary (from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane) > secondary and resonance-stabilised allyl > primary; aryl cannot ionise.
Select the substrate giving the most stable cation: the tertiary bromide.
keyConcept: SN1 reactivity is governed by the stability of the carbocation intermediate, with tertiary the most stabilised.
commonMistake: Applying SN2 steric logic (least hindered reacts fastest) or overrating resonance stabilisation over a tertiary centre.

optionExplanations.0: An aryl C-Br bond will not ionise under solvolytic conditions because a phenyl cation is prohibitively unstable.
optionExplanations.1: This applies SN2 reasoning; a primary carbocation is far too unstable to form readily under SN1 conditions.
optionExplanations.4: The allyl cation is resonance-stabilised only to about secondary-cation stability, still less than the tertiary centre.

shortExplanation: At pH 7 both carboxyls (pKa 2.0 and 3.9) are deprotonated (-1 each) and the alpha-ammonium (pKa 9.9) stays protonated (+1), giving a net -1, so the anion migrates toward the anode.
solutionSteps: Compare each ionisable group to pH 7: groups with pKa below 7 are deprotonated, those above are protonated.
Both carboxyls are deprotonated (-1 each); the alpha-ammonium remains protonated (+1).
Sum the charges: -1 + -1 + +1 = -1.
A net-negative ion migrates toward the positive electrode, the anode.
keyConcept: Net charge at a given pH is found by comparing each group's pKa to the pH; anions migrate to the anode.
commonMistake: Forgetting the ammonium group is still protonated at pH 7, or reversing which electrode attracts an anion.

optionExplanations.0: A net charge of -2 deprotonates both carboxyls but ignores the still-protonated ammonium group that adds +1.
optionExplanations.3: The net charge -1 is correct but the migration is reversed; anions travel to the anode, not the cathode.
optionExplanations.4: A net charge of 0 assumes the isoelectric point, but aspartate's pI is near 3.0, far below pH 7.

shortExplanation: Reducing behaviour and mutarotation both require a free anomeric carbon that can ring-open. In this disaccharide both anomeric carbons are locked in the glycosidic bond, so no hemiacetal remains.
solutionSteps: Note that a positive Tollens' test and mutarotation both require a free hemiacetal (anomeric) carbon that can open to a carbonyl.
Recognise that joining both anomeric carbons (glucose C1 and fructose C2) in the glycosidic bond locks both rings closed.
Conclude that with no free hemiacetal, no aldehyde forms, so the sugar is non-reducing and shows no mutarotation.
keyConcept: A non-reducing disaccharide has its glycosidic bond between both anomeric carbons, leaving no free hemiacetal to ring-open.
commonMistake: Attributing the lack of reduction to the linkage type, ring form, or ketose identity rather than to the absence of a free anomeric carbon.

optionExplanations.1: Beta-linkages do not block reduction; lactose has a beta(1->4) bond yet is a reducing sugar with a free anomeric carbon.
optionExplanations.3: Fructose is a reducing ketose that gives a positive test via isomerisation, so ketose identity is not the cause.
optionExplanations.4: The molecule has many free hydroxyls; reduction is specific oxidation of the hemiacetal, not generic -OH oxidation.

shortExplanation: Removing a beta-H from C1 gives but-1-ene, and from C3 gives (E)- and (Z)-but-2-ene: three alkenes. The small ethoxide base follows Zaitsev, and the more stable (E)-but-2-ene predominates.
solutionSteps: Identify the beta-hydrogens: C1 gives terminal but-1-ene, C3 gives but-2-ene.
Note but-2-ene exists as (E) and (Z), so there are three distinct alkenes.
Apply Zaitsev selectivity for the small ethoxide base: the more-substituted but-2-ene dominates.
Between geometric isomers, the more stable (E)-but-2-ene is formed preferentially.
keyConcept: E2 with a small base gives Zaitsev (more-substituted) alkenes; the more stable (E) isomer predominates.
commonMistake: Missing the E/Z isomers of but-2-ene, choosing the Hofmann product, or assigning geometric isomerism to terminal but-1-ene.

optionExplanations.0: But-1-ene predominating reflects Hofmann selectivity, which requires a bulky base, not the small ethoxide.
optionExplanations.1: Counting only two products overlooks that but-2-ene forms as two separate geometric isomers.
optionExplanations.3: Four products wrongly assigns E/Z isomerism to terminal but-1-ene, whose terminal carbon bears two identical hydrogens.

shortExplanation: Acidity tracks conjugate-base stability: ethanol < phenol (ring resonance) < 4-nitrophenol (added -NO2 withdrawal) < ethanoic acid (symmetric carboxylate) < chloroethanoic acid (extra -Cl induction).
solutionSteps: Rank the alcohols and phenols: ethoxide has no delocalisation (weakest); phenoxide is resonance-stabilised; the para-nitro group further stabilises phenoxide.
Note carboxylic acids are stronger than the nitrophenol because the carboxylate spreads charge over two oxygens.
Among carboxylic acids, electron-withdrawing chlorine stabilises the carboxylate, making chloroethanoic acid strongest.
Assemble increasing order: ethanol < phenol < 4-nitrophenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid.
keyConcept: Greater conjugate-base stabilisation (resonance and electron withdrawal) means a stronger acid.
commonMistake: Ranking ethanol above phenol, placing the nitrophenol below phenol, or reversing the chlorine inductive effect.

optionExplanations.1: This ranks ethanol as stronger than phenol, but phenoxide's ring resonance makes phenol the stronger acid.
optionExplanations.2: Placing 4-nitrophenol below phenol implies -NO2 lowers acidity, whereas it stabilises the phenoxide and raises acidity.
optionExplanations.4: This places 4-nitrophenol above ethanoic acid, but a nitrophenol (pKa about 7) is weaker than a carboxylic acid (pKa about 4.8).

shortExplanation: H+ = 0.060 mol and OH- = 0.040 mol (two per Ba(OH)2), leaving 0.020 mol excess H+ in 0.400 L, so [H+] = 0.050 M and pH = 1.30.
solutionSteps: Moles H+ = 0.200 L x 0.30 M = 0.060 mol.
Moles OH- = 0.200 L x 0.10 M x 2 = 0.040 mol (each Ba(OH)2 gives two OH-).
Divide by total volume 0.400 L: [H+] = 0.050 M, pH = -log(0.050) = 1.30.
keyConcept: Neutralise strong acid and base by moles, doubling hydroxide for a dihydroxide base, then divide excess by combined volume.
commonMistake: Treating Ba(OH)2 as giving one OH-, assuming the mix is neutral, or forgetting to divide by the total volume.

optionExplanations.1: This assumes any strong acid/base mixture neutralises exactly to pH 7, ignoring the stoichiometric excess of acid.
optionExplanations.2: This uses the 0.020 mol of excess acid directly as the molarity, never dividing by the 0.400 L total volume.
optionExplanations.3: This treats Ba(OH)2 as giving one OH- per formula unit, leaving too much excess H+ and [H+] = 0.10 M.

shortExplanation: With Ksp = [M2+][OH-]^2 and [OH-] fixed at 0.20 M by the NaOH, solubility s = Ksp/[OH-]^2 = 4.0e-12 / 0.040 = 1.0e-10 M.
solutionSteps: Write the dissolution: M(OH)2 gives M2+ + 2 OH-, so Ksp = [M2+][OH-]^2.
Set [OH-] = 0.20 M, dominated by the added NaOH (common ion).
Solve for solubility s = [M2+] = Ksp/[OH-]^2 = 4.0e-12 / (0.20)^2 = 1.0e-10 M.
keyConcept: The common-ion effect fixes [OH-] from the added base, and solubility follows from the Ksp expression with the squared hydroxide term.
commonMistake: Omitting the square on [OH-], ignoring the added NaOH, or using the pure-water expression Ksp = 4s^3.

optionExplanations.0: This divides Ksp by [OH-] to the first power, treating the salt as 1:1 and omitting the square.
optionExplanations.1: This takes s = sqrt(Ksp) for a 1:1 salt and ignores the added NaOH entirely.
optionExplanations.3: This is the solubility in pure water from Ksp = 4s^3, ignoring the common-ion suppression.

shortExplanation: At equivalence all HA becomes A- at 0.050 M. With Kb = Kw/Ka = 2.0e-9, [OH-] = sqrt(Kb x C) = 1.0e-5 M, so pH = 9.00, matching phenolphthalein.
solutionSteps: Find moles A- = 0.10 M x 0.0250 L = 2.5e-3 mol in 50.0 mL, so [A-] = 0.050 M.
Compute Kb = Kw/Ka = 1.0e-14 / 5.0e-6 = 2.0e-9.
Find [OH-] = sqrt(Kb x C) = sqrt(2.0e-9 x 0.050) = 1.0e-5 M, so pOH = 5.00 and pH = 9.00.
Choose an indicator bracketing pH 9: phenolphthalein (8.2-10.0).
keyConcept: The equivalence point of a weak acid with strong base is basic because the conjugate base hydrolyses; pick an indicator spanning that pH.
commonMistake: Assuming pH 7 at equivalence, using Ka instead of Kb, or choosing an indicator that does not bracket the equivalence pH.

optionExplanations.0: This assumes a neutral equivalence point, but the conjugate base makes the solution basic (pH about 9).
optionExplanations.1: This inserts Ka in place of Kb without the Kw conversion, overestimating the pH.
optionExplanations.2: The equivalence pH of about 9 is right, but methyl orange changes colour near pH 3-4, signalling the endpoint far too early.

shortExplanation: pH >= pKa requires [HCOO-] >= [HCOOH]. Adding x mol HCl gives 0.80 - x and 0.20 + x; setting them equal gives x = 0.30 mol.
solutionSteps: From Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH >= pKa is equivalent to [HCOO-] >= [HCOOH].
Added HCl converts formate to formic acid: [HCOO-] = 0.80 - x, [HCOOH] = 0.20 + x.
Set the limiting case 0.80 - x = 0.20 + x, giving 0.60 = 2x, so x = 0.30 mol.
keyConcept: pH equals pKa when the conjugate base and acid concentrations are equal; solve for the acid added that reaches this 1:1 point.
commonMistake: Using the total formate present, the pKa +/- 1 buffer range, or reporting a concentration instead of moles of HCl.

optionExplanations.0: 0.80 is the total conjugate base present, but the pH falls below pKa well before all of it is consumed.
optionExplanations.2: 0.71 uses the 10:1 (pKa - 1) buffer limit rather than the stated pH >= pKa condition.
optionExplanations.4: 0.60 is the initial excess of base over acid (0.80 - 0.20), not the amount of HCl that reaches the 1:1 point.

shortExplanation: AgCl precipitates first. When [Ag+] rises to 1.05e-5 M (onset of Ag2CrO4), remaining [Cl-] = Ksp(AgCl)/[Ag+] = 1.7e-5 M, so the fraction is 1.7e-5/0.010 = 1.7e-3.
solutionSteps: Find [Ag+] to start AgCl: Ksp(AgCl)/[Cl-] = 1.8e-10/0.010 = 1.8e-8 M.
Find [Ag+] to start Ag2CrO4: sqrt(Ksp/[CrO4]) = sqrt(1.1e-12/0.010) = 1.05e-5 M.
Since AgCl needs far less Ag+, it precipitates first.
At the chromate onset, remaining [Cl-] = 1.8e-10/1.05e-5 = 1.7e-5 M.
Fraction remaining = 1.7e-5 / 0.010 = 1.7e-3.
keyConcept: In fractional precipitation, the second salt begins at its own [Ag+] threshold; use that to find the residual first-ion concentration and divide by the initial value.
commonMistake: Comparing Ksp values directly across different stoichiometries, or reporting the residual molarity instead of the fraction.

optionExplanations.0: This divides the onset [Ag+] by the initial [Cl-] rather than computing surviving chloride via Ksp(AgCl)/[Ag+].
optionExplanations.2: This compares Ksp magnitudes directly and wrongly concludes chromate precipitates first, leaving chloride untouched.
optionExplanations.4: This is the residual chloride concentration (1.7e-5 M) reported as though it were the fraction, without dividing by 0.010 M.

shortExplanation: With [Cl-] fixed near 0.10 M by the NaCl common ion, s = [Ag+] = Ksp/[Cl-] = 1.8e-10 / 0.10 = 1.8e-9 mol/L.
solutionSteps: Write Ksp = [Ag+][Cl-] for AgCl.
Set [Cl-] = 0.10 mol/L, dominated by the added NaCl.
keyConcept: The common-ion effect from added chloride suppresses AgCl solubility far below its pure-water value.
commonMistake: Using sqrt(Ksp) as if in pure water, or dividing by the wrong chloride concentration.

optionExplanations.0: 1.8e-8 divides Ksp by 0.01 instead of 0.10.
optionExplanations.3: 1.8e-10 is Ksp itself, not a solubility.
optionExplanations.4: 1.3e-5 is the pure-water solubility (sqrt of Ksp), ignoring the common-ion suppression by the added chloride.

shortExplanation: Zinc's configuration fills seven subshells (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d, 4s). Each subshell has exactly one ml = 0 orbital holding 2 electrons, giving 7 x 2 = 14.
solutionSteps: Write the ground-state configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2, seven fully filled subshells.
Note every subshell contains exactly one orbital with ml = 0.
Each filled ml = 0 orbital holds 2 electrons, so total = 7 x 2 = 14.
keyConcept: Each subshell (any l value) has one orbital with ml = 0, holding up to two electrons when filled.
commonMistake: Excluding the d subshell's ml = 0 orbital, or counting one electron per orbital instead of two.

optionExplanations.0: This excludes the filled 3d subshell, wrongly assuming d has no ml = 0 orbital (6 subshells x 2 = 12).
optionExplanations.3: This states the total number of electrons in the atom, ignoring the ml = 0 restriction.
optionExplanations.4: This counts the seven ml = 0 orbitals but records only one electron per orbital, though each is doubly occupied.

shortExplanation: Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6; six d-electrons under Hund's rule give one paired plus four singly occupied orbitals, so exactly four unpaired electrons.
solutionSteps: Remove 4s electrons before 3d: Fe is [Ar]3d6 4s2, so Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6.
Distribute six electrons across five 3d orbitals by Hund's rule: one orbital doubly occupied, four singly.
Count four unpaired electrons.
keyConcept: For transition-metal ions, remove 4s before 3d, then apply Hund's rule to count unpaired electrons.
commonMistake: Forgetting the third electron removed from Fe3+ comes from 3d, giving a false 3d6 with four unpaired.

optionExplanations.0: Cr3+ is [Ar]3d3 with three unpaired electrons.
optionExplanations.3: Fe3+ is [Ar]3d5 with five unpaired; assuming only the two 4s electrons are lost wrongly gives 3d6.
optionExplanations.4: Ni2+ is [Ar]3d8 with only two unpaired electrons due to forced pairing.

shortExplanation: In an isoelectronic series the radius shrinks as nuclear charge rises. So increasing radius is Ca2+ < K+ < Cl- < S2- < P3-.
solutionSteps: Note all five ions share 18 electrons, so radius is set only by nuclear charge.
List protons: Ca 20 > K 19 > Cl 17 > S 16 > P 15.
More protons pull the electron cloud tighter, so the ion is smaller.
Order by increasing radius: Ca2+ < K+ < Cl- < S2- < P3-.
keyConcept: Within an isoelectronic series, ionic radius decreases as nuclear charge increases.
commonMistake: Ordering by atomic number directly, or thinking greater negative charge contracts the ion.

optionExplanations.0: This inverts the cations, treating fewer protons (K+) as giving a smaller ion.
optionExplanations.2: This orders by increasing atomic number, implying larger nuclear charge gives a larger radius, the reverse of the trend.
optionExplanations.4: This uses neutral-atom periodic sizes, ignoring that these isoelectronic ions are sized by nuclear charge.

shortExplanation: H2S has two lone pairs and a large, weakly electronegative sulfur bonding through nearly pure p orbitals, giving an angle of about 92 degrees, the smallest of the set.
solutionSteps: Rank by geometry: BF3 is 120 degrees, CH4 is 109.5, NH3 about 107, H2O about 104.5.
Note H2O and H2S both have two lone pairs, so lone-pair count cannot separate them.
Recognise sulfur is larger and less electronegative, using nearly pure p orbitals, so H2S is about 92 degrees.
Select H2S as the smallest angle.
keyConcept: Lone pairs compress bond angles, and a larger, less electronegative central atom with little s-p mixing gives angles near 90 degrees.
commonMistake: Stopping at H2O by the 'most lone pairs = smallest angle' rule and overlooking the larger central atom in H2S.

optionExplanations.0: BF3 is trigonal planar at 120 degrees, the largest angle here.
optionExplanations.3: NH3 is about 107 degrees; one lone pair compresses it less than the two in H2O and H2S.
optionExplanations.4: H2O is about 104.5 degrees; its central oxygen is smaller than sulfur, so its angle stays larger than H2S.

shortExplanation: The CH3 carbon has four sigma bonds (sp3); nitrogen has two sigma bonds plus a lone pair (sp2); the central carbon has two cumulated double bonds and only two domains (sp).
solutionSteps: Count domains on the CH3 carbon: four sigma bonds gives sp3.
Count domains on nitrogen: two sigma bonds plus one lone pair gives three domains, sp2.
Count domains on the central carbon: two sigma bonds (to N and O) with two pi bonds gives two domains, sp.
keyConcept: Hybridisation is set by the number of electron domains (sigma bonds plus lone pairs); a carbon with two cumulated double bonds is sp.
commonMistake: Treating nitrogen as an ordinary sp3 amine, or labelling the cumulated central carbon sp2.

optionExplanations.1: This treats nitrogen as sp3 by ignoring its pi bond and the central carbon as sp2.
optionExplanations.2: This demotes the CH3 carbon to sp2, mis-counting its four sigma bonds.
optionExplanations.4: This labels the central carbon sp2, missing that two cumulated double bonds leave only two electron domains.

shortExplanation: In 2-nitrophenol the adjacent OH and NO2 form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, tying up the O-H internally and reducing intermolecular bonding, so it is more volatile; the para isomer hydrogen-bonds between molecules.
solutionSteps: In the ortho isomer, the OH sits next to NO2 and forms a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen-bonded ring.
This internal bonding removes the O-H donor from intermolecular hydrogen bonding, lowering the boiling point.
In the para isomer the groups are too far apart, so every OH hydrogen-bonds to neighbours, building a network that raises the boiling point.
keyConcept: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding lowers boiling point by reducing intermolecular attractions, unlike intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
commonMistake: Reversing which isomer bonds intramolecularly, or attributing the difference to polarity or molar mass.

optionExplanations.0: This reverses the geometry and the effect; only the ortho isomer bonds intramolecularly, and such bonding lowers, not raises, boiling point.
optionExplanations.2: The ortho arrangement does not make the molecule non-polar; the volatility difference is due to hydrogen bonding.
optionExplanations.3: The two isomers have identical molecular formulae and molar masses, so dispersion forces cannot distinguish them.

shortExplanation: Four electrons are transferred in the reaction as written, so delta G = -nFE = -(4)(96500)(1.23) = -475 kJ.
solutionSteps: Determine n from the balanced equation: 2 H2 release 4 electrons, so n = 4.
Apply delta G = -nFE = -(4)(96500 C/mol)(1.23 V).
Compute -4.75e5 J, approximately -475 kJ.
keyConcept: Read the electron count from the balanced equation as written, then apply delta G = -nFE with the sign giving a negative value for positive E.
commonMistake: Using n = 2 (per mole of H2) instead of n = 4, or dropping the negative sign.

optionExplanations.0: This uses n = 2 (per mole of H2 or water) instead of n = 4, halving the magnitude.
optionExplanations.1: This overcounts the charge as n = 8, doubling the true value.
optionExplanations.3: This has the correct magnitude but a positive sign, dropping the negative sign in delta G = -nFE.

solutionSteps: Combine delta G = -nFE and delta G = -RT ln K to get log K = nE/[(2.303RT)/F].
Substitute the 298 K value 0.0592 V: log K = (2)(0.30)/0.0592.
Compute log K = 0.60/0.0592 = 10.1, so K = about 1e10.
keyConcept: The equilibrium constant follows log K = nE/0.0592 at 298 K; a positive E gives K greater than 1.
commonMistake: Using n = 1, dropping the sign, or confusing the ln and log10 constants.

optionExplanations.0: This has the right magnitude but a negative exponent, a sign slip; a positive E gives K much greater than 1.
optionExplanations.1: This uses n = 1, giving log K about 5, ignoring the two electrons transferred.
optionExplanations.2: This doubles the exponent to about 20 by applying a factor of 2 twice.

shortExplanation: delta S_surr = -delta H/T = +120000/300 = +400 J/K/mol, so delta S_universe = -200 + 400 = +200 J/K/mol > 0, meaning the reaction is spontaneous.
solutionSteps: Compute delta S_surr = -delta H/T = -(-120000 J/mol)/300 K = +400 J/K/mol (convert kJ to J).
Add the system term: delta S_universe = -200 + 400 = +200 J/K/mol.
Since delta S_universe > 0, the reaction is spontaneous at 300 K.
keyConcept: A process is spontaneous when the total entropy change of the universe (system plus surroundings) is positive.
commonMistake: Judging spontaneity from the system entropy alone, mishandling the sign of delta S_surr, or misreading a positive delta S_universe as non-spontaneous.

optionExplanations.0: This counts only delta S_surr (+400) and neglects the negative system term.
optionExplanations.1: This gets the correct +200 but applies the second law backwards; a positive value means the reaction is spontaneous.
optionExplanations.3: This judges spontaneity from delta S_system (-200) alone, ignoring the entropy exported to the surroundings.

shortExplanation: K = 1e2 while Q = (10)^2/(0.10 x 0.10) = 1e4. Since Q > K, delta G is positive and the reaction shifts to the left.
solutionSteps: Find K from delta G = -2.303RT log K: log K = 11.4/5.71 = 2.0, so K = 1e2.
Compare: Q (1e4) > K (1e2), so delta G = -11.4 + 5.71 log(1e4) = +11.4 kJ/mol > 0.
Conclude the reaction proceeds to the left.
keyConcept: Reaction direction depends on delta G = delta G-standard + 2.303RT log Q; when Q > K the forward reaction is non-spontaneous.
commonMistake: Judging direction from delta G-standard alone, inverting Q, or assuming Q = K.

optionExplanations.1: This assumes Q equals K, but Q (1e4) does not equal K (1e2), so the system is not at equilibrium.
optionExplanations.2: This judges direction from the standard free energy only; the actual direction depends on delta G with Q included.
optionExplanations.3: This inverts the reaction quotient (reactants over products), giving Q < K and the opposite conclusion.

shortExplanation: Because delta G adds but E does not, E3 = (n1 E1 + n2 E2)/(n1 + n2) = [(1)(0.77) + (2)(-0.44)]/3 = -0.037 V.
solutionSteps: Recognise electrode potentials are intensive and cannot be added; delta G = -nFE is the additive quantity.
Write delta G for each step: -(1)F(0.77) and -(2)F(-0.44).
keyConcept: Combine half-reactions with different electron counts by adding delta G values, giving an electron-weighted average of potentials.
commonMistake: Adding or simple-averaging the potentials directly instead of weighting by electron number.

optionExplanations.0: This computes the correct weighted numerator (-0.11) but fails to divide by the total of 3 electrons.
optionExplanations.1: This adds the two potentials directly, treating E as an additive quantity.
optionExplanations.4: This takes the simple arithmetic mean of the two potentials, ignoring their different electron counts.

shortExplanation: Charge Q = 5.00 x 1930 = 9650 C gives 0.100 mol electrons, so 0.050 mol H2 and 0.025 mol O2; total 0.075 mol x 22.4 = 1.68 L.
solutionSteps: Compute charge Q = I t = 5.00 A x 1930 s = 9650 C.
Moles of electrons = 9650/96500 = 0.100 mol.
At the cathode, 2 H+ + 2 e- -> H2, so n(H2) = 0.100/2 = 0.050 mol.
At the anode, 2 H2O -> O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e-, so n(O2) = 0.100/4 = 0.025 mol.
Total gas = 0.075 mol; at STP V = 0.075 x 22.4 = 1.68 L.
keyConcept: Convert charge to moles of electrons, then apply the correct electron count per gas (2 for H2, 4 for O2), giving a 2:1 volume ratio.
commonMistake: Counting only one electrode's gas, assuming equal moles of H2 and O2, or using wrong electron counts.

optionExplanations.0: This counts only the cathode gas H2 (0.050 mol, 1.12 L), omitting the oxygen at the anode.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes equal moles of H2 and O2, ignoring the different electron stoichiometry at the two electrodes.
optionExplanations.2: This counts only the anode gas O2 (0.025 mol, 0.56 L), omitting the hydrogen at the cathode.

shortExplanation: Protonating the terminal CH2 puts the positive charge on the more substituted C2, giving the more stable tertiary carbocation. Water then bonds there and loss of H+ yields the tertiary alcohol, so the -OH sits on the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov).
solutionSteps: Add H+ to the terminal =CH2 carbon of the double bond.
The positive charge lands on C2, the more substituted carbon, giving a tertiary carbocation (more stable than the primary alternative).
Water bonds to C2; loss of H+ gives the alcohol.
The -OH is on C2, so the product is 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
keyConcept: Markovnikov acid-catalysed hydration proceeds through the most stable carbocation, placing -OH on the more substituted carbon.
commonMistake: Assuming anti-Markovnikov addition and putting the -OH on the terminal (less substituted) carbon, as if a primary carbocation had formed.

optionExplanations.0: Assumes the carbocation forms at the secondary C3 rather than the more stable tertiary C2.
optionExplanations.3: Straightens the branched skeleton into a linear five-carbon chain, ignoring the methyl branch.
optionExplanations.4: Anti-Markovnikov: places -OH on the terminal carbon via the less stable primary carbocation.

shortExplanation: SN2 is second order overall, rate = k[R-Br][CN-], so raising the cyanide concentration increases the rate. The other changes each slow substitution or divert it to elimination.
solutionSteps: Write the SN2 rate law: rate = k[R-Br][CN-].
Note the reaction is first order in nucleophile.
Increasing [CN-] therefore increases the rate.
keyConcept: SN2 is bimolecular, so its rate depends on the concentration of both the substrate and the nucleophile.
commonMistake: Assuming a more polar (protic) solvent always speeds the reaction up, when hydrogen bonding actually deactivates the anionic nucleophile.

optionExplanations.0: Fluoride is a poorer leaving group than bromide because the C-F bond is much stronger, slowing substitution.
optionExplanations.1: A polar protic solvent hydrogen-bonds to and stabilises the anion, lowering its reactivity and slowing SN2.
optionExplanations.3: A tertiary carbon is too hindered for backside attack, making SN2 extremely slow.

shortExplanation: Fischer esterification proceeds by acyl-oxygen cleavage: the alcohol's oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon and is retained in the ester, while the water expelled comes from the acid. The 18O therefore ends up in the single-bonded bridging -O- of the ester.
solutionSteps: Identify that the alcohol oxygen (18O) attacks the carbonyl carbon of the acid.
Recognise acyl-oxygen cleavage: the -OH lost as water comes from the carboxylic acid.
Conclude the alcohol's 18O is retained as the ester's single-bonded (alkoxy) oxygen.
The water released contains ordinary 16O.
keyConcept: In Fischer esterification the carboxylic acid supplies the oxygen that leaves as water, and the alcohol oxygen becomes the ester's bridging -O-.
commonMistake: Assuming the alcohol's C-O bond breaks so its oxygen leaves in the water, when in fact the acid provides the water oxygen.

optionExplanations.0: The mechanism is regiospecific, so the label does not scramble between the two products.
optionExplanations.2: Assumes the alcohol's oxygen leaves as water; the acid actually supplies that oxygen.
optionExplanations.3: The label sits in the single-bond bridging oxygen, not the carbonyl oxygen, which derives from the acid.

shortExplanation: Ranking by activating/deactivating strength: the nitro group is a strong deactivator, chlorine deactivates by induction, benzene is the reference, methyl is a weak activator, and hydroxyl is a strong activator. Least to most reactive is nitrobenzene < chlorobenzene < benzene < toluene < phenol.
solutionSteps: Classify -NO2 as a strong electron-withdrawing deactivator (least reactive).
Classify -Cl as a net deactivator by induction, below benzene.
Take benzene as the reference point.
Classify -CH3 as a weak activator (hyperconjugation/induction).
Classify -OH as a strong activator via oxygen lone-pair donation (most reactive).
keyConcept: Electrophilic aromatic substitution rate depends on how much a substituent activates or deactivates the ring by electronic effects.
commonMistake: Assuming that ortho/para-directing halogens must be activating; halogens deactivate the ring even though they direct ortho/para.

optionExplanations.0: Makes chlorobenzene least reactive, overweighting chlorine's induction and underestimating the stronger resonance withdrawal by -NO2.
optionExplanations.1: This is the reverse ordering (most to least reactive).
optionExplanations.2: Places phenol below toluene; oxygen lone-pair donation makes -OH the stronger activator.

shortExplanation: The aldehyde first adds one methanol to give a hemiacetal, then a second methanol displaces water to give the acetal. Overall RCHO + 2 CH3OH gives RCH(OCH3)2 + H2O; the acid is a catalyst and the reaction is reversible.
solutionSteps: Add the first methanol to the aldehyde to form a hemiacetal (no water lost).
Under acid catalysis, a second methanol displaces water to form the acetal.
Sum the overall equation: two methanol incorporated, one water released.
Note HCl is regenerated (catalyst) and the acetal hydrolyses back in aqueous acid.
keyConcept: Acetal formation is an acid-catalysed, reversible condensation incorporating two alcohol molecules and releasing one water.
commonMistake: Treating the acid catalyst as a consumed reactant, or assuming the acetal is stable to warm aqueous acid.

optionExplanations.0: That describes the hemiacetal (addition only); the isolated acetal needs a second methanol and loss of water.
optionExplanations.3: The acid is a catalyst regenerated at the end of the cycle, not consumed.
optionExplanations.4: Acetals are readily hydrolysed back to the aldehyde by warm aqueous acid; they are stable only to base.

shortExplanation: Each ester linkage forms by condensation, losing one water. A single linear chain of 12 monomer units has 12 - 1 = 11 linkages, so 11 water molecules are released.
solutionSteps: Count the monomer units: 6 diacid + 6 diol = 12 units.
A linear chain of n units has n - 1 linkages.
Compute 12 - 1 = 11 linkages.
Each linkage releases one water, giving 11 water molecules.
keyConcept: In linear step-growth condensation polymerisation, n monomer units form n - 1 linkages, each expelling one small molecule.
commonMistake: Counting one water per monomer (12) and forgetting that n units linked in a line form only n - 1 linkages.

optionExplanations.0: Counts one water per monomer (12) instead of one per linkage (11).
optionExplanations.1: Counts one water per repeat unit, ignoring that the alternating chain has nearly twice as many linkages.
optionExplanations.3: Assumes two waters per linkage, double-counting the single water expelled at each ester bond.

shortExplanation: At fixed molality, freezing-point depression depends only on the van't Hoff factor i (total particles per formula unit). Al2(SO4)3 gives 2 Al3+ + 3 SO4^2- = 5 particles, the most, so it has the largest depression and lowest freezing point.
solutionSteps: Recall ΔTf = i·Kf·m, so at fixed m and Kf the depression scales with i.
Count particles: glucose i = 1, NaCl i = 2, CaCl2 i = 3, K2SO4 i = 3, Al2(SO4)3 i = 5.
The largest i gives the largest ΔTf.
Al2(SO4)3 (i = 5) has the lowest freezing point.
keyConcept: Freezing-point depression is a colligative property governed by the total number of dissolved particles, not their size or charge.
commonMistake: Assuming a heavier molecule or a more highly charged ion depresses the freezing point more; only the particle count matters.

optionExplanations.1: CaCl2 gives i = 3, fewer particles than the five from Al2(SO4)3.
optionExplanations.2: Glucose is a non-electrolyte (i = 1), the fewest particles, so it has the highest freezing point.
optionExplanations.4: K2SO4 gives i = 3; the sulfate charge is irrelevant, and 3 is less than 5.

solutionSteps: Rearrange Π = cRT to c = Π/(RT).
Find moles: n = c x V = 0.0100 x 0.500 = 5.00e-3 mol.
Compute molar mass: M = mass/n = 1.50/5.00e-3 = 300 g/mol.
keyConcept: Osmotic pressure Π = cRT lets a measured pressure give the solute concentration and hence its molar mass.
commonMistake: Dividing concentration by volume instead of multiplying when finding moles, or ignoring the volume entirely.

optionExplanations.0: Divides concentration by volume (n = c/V) instead of multiplying, giving too many moles and M = 75.
optionExplanations.1: Treats the molar concentration as the number of moles, ignoring the 0.500 L volume.
optionExplanations.2: Applies a van't Hoff factor of 2 to a compound explicitly stated to be non-dissociating.

shortExplanation: By Raoult's law P_X = 0.20 x 100 = 20 kPa and P_Y = 0.80 x 25 = 20 kPa, giving a total of 40 kPa. The vapour mole fraction of X is 20/40 = 0.50, enriched because X is the more volatile component.
solutionSteps: Apply Raoult's law: P_X = x_X·P°X = 0.20 x 100 = 20 kPa.
Apply Raoult's law: P_Y = x_Y·P°Y = 0.80 x 25 = 20 kPa.
Total pressure = 20 + 20 = 40 kPa (Dalton's law).
keyConcept: The vapour above an ideal solution is enriched in the more volatile component; y_X = P_X/P_total with partial pressures from Raoult's law.
commonMistake: Assuming the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, ignoring enrichment in the more volatile component.

optionExplanations.1: Assumes the vapour composition equals the liquid composition (0.20), ignoring enrichment.
optionExplanations.2: This is the mole fraction of Y in the liquid (1 - 0.20), reporting the wrong quantity.
optionExplanations.3: Uses P_Y = P°Y = 25 kPa without weighting Y by its mole fraction, giving 20/45 = 0.44.

shortExplanation: The van't Hoff factor is i = ΔTf/(Kf·m) = 0.2046/(1.86 x 0.100) = 1.10. For HA giving H+ and A-, i = 1 + α, so α = 0.10, i.e. 10% dissociation.
solutionSteps: For HA giving 1 + α particles, write i = 1 + α.
Solve α = i - 1 = 0.10.
Express as 10% dissociation.
keyConcept: For a weak acid dissociating into two ions, the van't Hoff factor relates to the degree of dissociation by i = 1 + α.
commonMistake: Using the fully-dissociated depression (i = 2) as the reference denominator instead of the relation i = 1 + α.

optionExplanations.0: Uses the complete-dissociation value (i = 2) as denominator, α = 0.2046/0.372 = 0.55.
optionExplanations.3: Reports the undissociated fraction (1 - α = 0.90) instead of the dissociated fraction.
optionExplanations.4: Equates the van't Hoff factor itself (1.10) with the degree of dissociation, ignoring the +1 term.

shortExplanation: Initial partial pressures are 1.20 atm CO and 0.80 atm O2. CO is limiting: it needs 0.60 atm O2, leaving 0.20 atm O2 in excess and forming 1.20 atm CO2. Final total = 1.20 + 0.20 = 1.40 atm.
solutionSteps: Find initial partial pressures: P_CO = 0.60 x 2.00 = 1.20 atm, P_O2 = 0.40 x 2.00 = 0.80 atm.
Apply the 2:1 CO:O2 ratio: 1.20 atm CO needs 0.60 atm O2.
Identify CO as limiting; 0.80 - 0.60 = 0.20 atm O2 remains.
Form 1.20 atm CO2 (1:1 with CO).
Sum final pressures: 1.20 + 0.20 = 1.40 atm.
keyConcept: At constant T and V, partial pressures act like moles; a limiting-reactant analysis on pressures gives the final total pressure.
commonMistake: Forgetting the leftover excess O2 when summing final partial pressures, or misidentifying the limiting reactant.

optionExplanations.0: Assumes the total pressure is unchanged, overlooking that the reaction reduces the total moles of gas.
optionExplanations.1: Assumes O2 is limiting (all 0.80 atm used), which would require 1.60 atm of CO.
optionExplanations.4: Counts only the 1.20 atm CO2 and forgets the 0.20 atm of unreacted excess O2.

shortExplanation: Using 1.00 kg water as basis: 4.00 mol solute has mass 1000 g, so the solution mass is 2000 g. Its volume is 2000/1.25 = 1600 mL = 1.600 L, giving molarity 4.00/1.600 = 2.50 mol/L.
solutionSteps: Take 1.00 kg water as basis, containing 4.00 mol solute.
Compute solute mass: 4.00 x 250 = 1000 g.
Total solution mass = 1000 + 1000 = 2000 g.
Volume = mass/density = 2000/1.25 = 1600 mL = 1.600 L.
Molarity = 4.00/1.600 = 2.50 mol/L.
keyConcept: Converting molality to molarity requires the total solution mass (solvent plus solute) and the solution density to find the volume.
commonMistake: Using water's density instead of the solution density, or omitting the solute mass from the total.

optionExplanations.1: Uses water's density (1.0 g/mL) for the 2000 g solution instead of the given 1.25 g/mL.
optionExplanations.2: Uses the invalid shortcut molarity = molality x density, which has no dimensional basis.
optionExplanations.4: Assumes 1 kg water equals 1 L of solution, ignoring the added solute mass and density.

shortExplanation: Dividing each mass percent by the atomic mass gives moles C = 3.33, H = 6.7, O = 3.33. Dividing by the smallest (3.33) gives a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, so the empirical formula is CH2O.
solutionSteps: Divide all by the smallest value (3.33).
Obtain the ratio C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.
Write the empirical formula CH2O.
keyConcept: An empirical formula comes from converting mass percentages to moles and reducing to the simplest whole-number ratio.
commonMistake: Reporting a multiple of the simplest ratio (a molecular formula) instead of reducing to the empirical formula.

optionExplanations.0: The correct 1 : 2 : 1 ratio was not reduced to simplest whole numbers; the empirical formula is CH2O.
optionExplanations.1: Takes oxygen's mass as 32 (O2) instead of 16, distorting the ratio to 2 : 4 : 1.
optionExplanations.4: Uses the mass percentages directly as mole numbers, skipping division by the atomic masses.

shortExplanation: The anhydrous residue is 4.92 - 2.52 = 2.40 g = 0.0200 mol MgSO4, and the water lost is 2.52/18 = 0.140 mol. The ratio x = 0.140/0.0200 = 7, so the hydrate is MgSO4·7H2O.
solutionSteps: Residue mass = 4.92 - 2.52 = 2.40 g.
Moles MgSO4 = 2.40/120 = 0.0200 mol.
x = moles water / moles salt = 0.140/0.0200 = 7.
keyConcept: The water of crystallisation x is the mole ratio of water lost to anhydrous salt remaining after heating.
commonMistake: Using the whole hydrate mass as the anhydrous salt mass, or swapping the residue and water-lost values.

optionExplanations.0: Uses M(MgSO4) = 88 (only two sulfate oxygens counted) instead of 120, lowering x to about 5.
optionExplanations.1: Takes M(H2O) = 16 (ignoring the two hydrogens), giving too few water moles and x near 8.
optionExplanations.3: Uses the full 4.92 g as the anhydrous salt mass, overcounting salt moles (x near 3.4).

shortExplanation: Moles of acid = 9.80/98 = 0.100 mol. Each H3PO4 has 4 oxygen atoms, so oxygen moles = 0.400 mol, and multiplying by NA gives 0.400 x 6.0e23 = 2.4e23 oxygen atoms.
solutionSteps: Compute moles of acid: n = 9.80/98 = 0.100 mol.
Each formula unit has 4 oxygen atoms, so moles of O = 4 x 0.100 = 0.400 mol.
Multiply by NA: 0.400 x 6.0e23 = 2.4e23 oxygen atoms.
keyConcept: Atom count equals (mass/molar mass) x (atoms per formula unit) x Avogadro's constant.
commonMistake: Counting molecules instead of oxygen atoms, i.e. omitting the factor of 4 oxygen atoms per formula unit.

optionExplanations.1: Treats the sample as one full mole then multiplies by four oxygens (1 x 4 x NA).
optionExplanations.2: Gives the number of H3PO4 molecules (0.100 x NA), omitting the factor of 4 oxygens per molecule.
optionExplanations.4: Counts all 8 atoms per formula unit rather than only the 4 oxygens.

shortExplanation: Equal gas volumes are proportional to moles. Carbon balance: 20 cm3 hydrocarbon gives 60 cm3 CO2, so x = 3. Oxygen consumed = 150 - 50 = 100 cm3, so x + y/4 = 5, giving y = 8. The hydrocarbon is C3H8.
solutionSteps: Use Avogadro's law so volume ratios equal mole ratios.
Carbon balance: x = CO2 volume / hydrocarbon volume = 60/20 = 3.
Oxygen consumed = 150 - 50 = 100 cm3.
With x = 3, y/4 = 2, so y = 8, giving C3H8.
keyConcept: In gas-volume stoichiometry, volumes at constant T and P substitute directly for moles in the balanced combustion equation.
commonMistake: Using the CO2 volume rather than the O2 actually consumed in the oxygen balance, or misreading which volume represents consumed oxygen.

optionExplanations.0: Uses the water coefficient y/2 instead of y/4 in the oxygen balance, giving y = 4.
optionExplanations.1: Subtracts the CO2 volume from initial oxygen (150 - 60 = 90) to find oxygen consumed, giving y = 6.
optionExplanations.3: Mistakes the 110 cm3 remaining gas for oxygen consumed, giving an impossible y = 10.

shortExplanation: The gas volume gives M = 0.86/(0.224/22.4) = 86 g/mol. Combustion gives C : H : O = 0.0400 : 0.0600 : 0.0200 = 2 : 3 : 1, so the empirical formula is C2H3O (mass 43). Since 86/43 = 2, the molecular formula is C4H6O2.
solutionSteps: Ratio C : H : O = 2 : 3 : 1, empirical formula C2H3O (mass 43).
Scale by 86/43 = 2 to get C4H6O2.
keyConcept: Combustion analysis gives the empirical formula, and the molar mass from the gas volume scales it to the molecular formula.
commonMistake: Stopping at the empirical formula without using the molar mass to scale up to the molecular formula.

optionExplanations.1: This is only the empirical formula; the molar mass (86) was not used to scale it up.
optionExplanations.2: Guesses a saturated ester CnH2nO2 from M near 86 instead of using the measured hydrogen (only 6 H).
optionExplanations.3: Omits the oxygen, treating the compound as a hydrocarbon and ignoring the 0.32 g of oxygen.

shortExplanation: Cu2+ (E° = +0.34 V) has a more positive reduction potential than water, so copper deposits at the cathode. Sulfate cannot be oxidised, so water is oxidised to O2 at the anode, releasing H+ and lowering the pH.
solutionSteps: At the cathode, compare Cu2+ (+0.34 V) with water/H+ (0.00 V); Cu2+ is reduced to copper.
At the anode, note sulfate's sulfur is already at +6 and cannot be oxidised.
Water is oxidised: 2H2O -> O2 + 4H+ + 4e-.
The liberated H+ makes the solution more acidic, so pH decreases.
keyConcept: Electrolysis products are set by discharge preferences (reduction potentials), and H+ released at the anode lowers the pH.
commonMistake: Thinking pH rises, when the anode reaction 2H2O -> O2 + 4H+ + 4e- actually makes the solution more acidic.

optionExplanations.0: Correct electrode products but wrongly claims pH rises; the anode releases H+, lowering the pH.
optionExplanations.1: Predicts hydrogen at the cathode, but Cu2+ has a more positive reduction potential and is discharged first.
optionExplanations.4: Predicts SO2 at the anode, but sulfate sulfur is already at its maximum +6 and cannot be oxidised.

shortExplanation: The sum of oxidation states equals the ion charge. For S2O3^2-, 2x - 6 = -2 gives x = +2. For S4O6^2-, 4y - 12 = -2 gives y = +2.5. The averages are +2 and +2.5.
solutionSteps: For thiosulfate: 2x + 3(-2) = -2, so 2x = +4 and x = +2.
For tetrathionate: 4y + 6(-2) = -2, so 4y = +10 and y = +2.5.
The +2.5 is a non-integer average over inequivalent sulfur atoms.
Report +2 for thiosulfate and +2.5 for tetrathionate.
keyConcept: Average oxidation state comes from balancing the sum of oxidation numbers against the ion's charge, and may be fractional.
commonMistake: Ignoring the ionic charge and setting the atom sum to zero, giving +3 and +3.

optionExplanations.1: Assumes sulfur is fully oxidised (+6) as in sulfate, ignoring the actual atom-to-charge balance.
optionExplanations.2: Ignores the -2 ionic charge, setting the atom sum to zero to get +3 and +3.
optionExplanations.3: Correct magnitudes but assigned to the wrong ions; the higher average belongs to the tetrathionate product.

shortExplanation: Dichromate gains 6 electrons (Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O) and ethanol loses 4 electrons oxidising to ethanoic acid. Balancing electrons (LCM 12) gives dichromate : ethanol = 2 : 3.
solutionSteps: Write the reduction half: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O (6 electrons gained).
Write the oxidation half: the -CH2OH carbon goes -1 to +3, losing 4 electrons.
Balance electrons with LCM 12: 2 dichromate provide 12 e-, 3 ethanol require 12 e-.
Read off the ratio 2 : 3.
keyConcept: The mole ratio in a redox equation follows from balancing electrons lost against electrons gained.
commonMistake: Stopping ethanol oxidation at the aldehyde (2 electrons) instead of the carboxylic acid (4 electrons).

optionExplanations.0: Ignores the electron balance and assumes equal moles.
optionExplanations.1: This is the correct ratio inverted (ethanol : dichromate).
optionExplanations.2: Treats dichromate as a 2-electron oxidant instead of the full 6 electrons.

shortExplanation: An oxidant works when its reduction potential is more positive than the couple being oxidised. Fe3+ (+0.77 V) exceeds I2/I- (+0.54 V) so it oxidises iodide, but is below Br2/Br- (+1.07 V) so it cannot oxidise bromide.
solutionSteps: State the rule: oxidation is feasible when the oxidant's E° exceeds the target couple's E°.
Compare Fe3+ (+0.77 V) with I2/I- (+0.54 V): 0.77 > 0.54, so iodide is oxidised.
Compare Fe3+ with Br2/Br- (+1.07 V): 0.77 < 1.07, so bromide is not oxidised.
Fe3+ has exactly the required selectivity.
