optionExplanations.1: Only about 1% of treated patients benefit, not 25%; this reads a relative reduction as an absolute proportion.
optionExplanations.2: The absolute gap is only 1 percentage point, confusing 'percent' with 'percentage points'.
optionExplanations.3: The placebo baseline is 4%, not 25%; this mistakes the relative reduction for the baseline risk.
optionExplanations.4: This uses the relative reduction in the NNT formula (1/0.25 = 4) instead of the absolute reduction.

shortExplanation: Exactly one of Omar and Raj goes, giving two cases. Either Omar and Nia go with the rest staying, or Pia and Raj go with the rest staying. In both, at least one of Omar and Pia is absent, so Tom, who goes only if both do, never goes.
solutionSteps: From 'exactly one of Omar and Raj', split into Case 1 (Omar in, Raj out) and Case 2 (Omar out, Raj in).
Case 1: 'if Pia then Raj' forces Pia out, so Nia in; Tom out since Pia is out; arrangement Nia and Omar.
Case 2: 'if Nia then Omar' forces Nia out, so Pia in; Tom out since Omar is out; arrangement Pia and Raj.
In both arrangements Tom is excluded, so Tom does not go.
keyConcept: Split on an exclusive constraint into cases and keep only what holds in every case.
commonMistake: Treating something true in only one arrangement (Nia goes, or Raj is out) as though it must be true in all.

optionExplanations.1: Raj goes in Case 2, so his exclusion is not forced.
optionExplanations.2: In Case 1 Omar goes but Pia does not, so 'if Omar then Pia' is false and not necessary.
optionExplanations.3: Each valid arrangement contains exactly two members, not three.
optionExplanations.4: Nia goes in Case 1 but stays home in Case 2, so her going is not forced.

shortExplanation: Revenue per copy is revenue divided by copies: hardback 800/40 = 20 and audiobook 500/25 = 20, so both earn 20 euro per copy. Paperback (9) and e-book (5) differ, and profit cannot be judged without cost data.
solutionSteps: Compute revenue per copy for each format: 800/40 = 20, 1,080/120 = 9, 1,000/200 = 5, 500/25 = 20.
Compare: hardbacks and audiobooks both give 20 euro per copy.
Check the other claims: paperbacks lead revenue (1,080), e-books lead volume (200), and no cost data exist for profit.
Conclude only the equal per-copy revenue of hardbacks and audiobooks must be true.
keyConcept: Distinguish total revenue, units sold, and revenue per unit; per-unit figures require dividing revenue by copies.
commonMistake: Assuming the highest-volume or highest-revenue format also leads on the other measure, or inferring profit without cost data.

optionExplanations.0: Profitability cannot be judged without cost data, and audiobooks actually earn 20 euro per copy.
optionExplanations.1: E-books lead volume (200k) but paperbacks lead revenue (1,080k), so the rankings differ.
optionExplanations.2: Paperbacks earned 1,080k versus e-books' 1,000k, so e-books do not lead on revenue.
optionExplanations.3: Paperbacks earn 9 per copy versus 20 for hardbacks, so hardbacks earn more per copy.

shortExplanation: The two pumps are redundant, so the pump subsystem fails only if both fail: P = 1 - (0.2)(0.2) = 0.96. The controller is required (in series), so multiply: 0.90 x 0.96 = 0.864.
solutionSteps: Compute the chance both pumps fail: 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04.
So at least one pump works with probability 1 - 0.04 = 0.96.
The controller is required, so multiply its 0.90 by the pump subsystem's 0.96.
keyConcept: Redundant components use the complement of joint failure; required components multiply as a series factor.
commonMistake: Omitting the required controller factor, or treating the two pumps as both required instead of redundant.

optionExplanations.0: 0.960 is only the pump subsystem's reliability and omits the controller factor of 0.90.
optionExplanations.1: 0.996 treats every component including the controller as redundant.
optionExplanations.3: 0.720 counts only a single pump, ignoring the backup.
optionExplanations.4: 0.576 treats both pumps as required, ignoring the redundancy.

shortExplanation: This is the valid form 'all M are P; some S are M; therefore some S are P'. The gym members who are athletes exist and must follow a strict diet, so at least one gym member follows a strict diet.
solutionSteps: Note statement 2 guarantees some gym members are professional athletes.
By statement 1, all professional athletes follow a strict diet.
So those athlete gym members follow a strict diet.
Conclude at least one gym member follows a strict diet.
keyConcept: Valid syllogism (Darii): all M are P and some S are M yield some S are P.
commonMistake: Strengthening 'some' to 'all', reversing an 'all A are B' premise, or drawing an unsupported negative conclusion.

optionExplanations.0: From 'all athletes follow a strict diet' one cannot infer all diet-followers are athletes.
optionExplanations.2: Nothing is stated about non-athlete gym members' diets, so this negative is unsupported.
optionExplanations.3: The athlete gym members both follow a strict diet and are athletes, so this denies a guaranteed overlap.
optionExplanations.4: Statement 2 says only some gym members are athletes, so nothing follows about every member.

shortExplanation: The columnist infers causation from a correlation. The strongest weakener reverses the causal arrow: if councils install extra cameras only after thefts have already surged, then rising theft drives camera installation, fully explaining the correlation without the columnist's claim.
solutionSteps: Identify the inference: cameras correlate with more thefts, so cameras cause thefts.
Recognise that reversing the causal direction would undermine this.
Note that installing cameras only after a theft surge means theft causes cameras.
Conclude the correlation is explained without cameras causing thefts, weakening the claim.
keyConcept: Reverse causation: the correlation can arise because the supposed effect actually drives the supposed cause.
commonMistake: Choosing an option that reinforces the correlation, or one about an unrelated outcome such as arrest rates.

optionExplanations.1: No change without cameras and high theft with them tends to strengthen the correlation, not weaken the causal claim.
optionExplanations.2: Residents' approval is about opinion, irrelevant to the causal relationship.
optionExplanations.3: The falling cost of cameras says nothing about whether cameras cause thefts.
optionExplanations.4: Higher arrest rates concern catching thieves, not whether cameras increase thefts committed.

shortExplanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the average of the two leg speeds. The ascent at 20 km/h already consumes the entire time a 40 km/h round-trip average allows, leaving zero time for the descent, so no finite descending speed can reach the target.
solutionSteps: Let the one-way distance be d, so the round trip is 2d.
For a 40 km/h average over 2d, the total time must be 2d/40 = d/20.
The ascent at 20 km/h alone takes d/20 = the full time budget.
That leaves zero time for the descent, which would require infinite speed.
Therefore no finite descending speed can achieve a 40 km/h average.
keyConcept: Average speed over equal distances is the time-weighted (harmonic) mean of the leg speeds, dominated by the slower leg.
commonMistake: Averaging the two leg speeds arithmetically, as if going twice as fast down could offset going slowly up.

optionExplanations.0: Setting the descent speed equal to the desired average ignores that the slow ascent has already used up the entire time budget.
optionExplanations.1: Comes from setting the arithmetic mean of the leg speeds, (20 + x)/2 = 40; average speed over equal distances is not the arithmetic mean.
optionExplanations.2: Assumes that because the target is double the ascent speed, the descent must be double the target, a spurious proportionality.

shortExplanation: The rule requires BOTH conditions: the project cannot attract adequate private funding AND its benefits are shared with the general public rather than captured by one backer. Only the soil-microbiology study, which no private investor will back and whose findings are published openly for all farmers, meets both.
solutionSteps: Note the rule is a conjunction: condition (i) no adequate private funding, and condition (ii) benefits shared with the general public.
Test each project against both conditions.
The soil-micro-organism study attracts no private investment (satisfies i) and its openly published findings benefit all farmers (satisfies ii).
Every other project has private finance available or captures benefit for one backer, failing at least one condition.
keyConcept: A biconditional rule with two required conditions is satisfied only when every condition holds simultaneously.
commonMistake: Treating a project as qualifying because it produces some public benefit, while ignoring that both conditions of the conjunction must hold.

optionExplanations.0: The pharmaceutical company is willing to finance it (fails the no-private-funding condition) and the sole patent captures the benefit for one backer (fails the shared-benefit condition).
optionExplanations.2: It has already secured venture-capital funding, so it fails the no-private-funding condition; the free public version is a lure.
optionExplanations.4: Its results would be public, but competing private firms are willing to finance it, so it fails the no-private-funding condition.

shortExplanation: The stem has the form 'all D are P; e is P; therefore e is D' — it affirms the consequent, which is invalid because poor performance could have other causes. The parallel flaw is the argument 'all sapphires scratch glass; this scratches glass; therefore this is a sapphire'.
solutionSteps: Identify the stem's form: All D are P; e is P; therefore e is D (affirming the consequent).
Recognise this is invalid because P can hold for reasons other than D.
Match to the argument sharing this exact invalid form, not merely the topic or conclusion.
The argument 'all sapphires scratch glass; this scratches glass; therefore this is a sapphire' affirms the consequent identically.
keyConcept: Parallel-reasoning tasks require matching the logical form, not surface vocabulary or the conclusion reached.
commonMistake: Matching arguments by shared topic or by reaching a similar conclusion instead of by shared logical structure.

optionExplanations.0: This is valid modus tollens: denying the consequent validly yields denial of the antecedent.
optionExplanations.2: This is valid modus ponens: affirming the antecedent 'is a sapphire' validly concludes 'scratches glass'.
optionExplanations.3: This is a fallacy, but a different one — denying the antecedent, not affirming the consequent.

shortExplanation: To justify treating the swimmers differently, the principle must turn on the one feature that differs between them: X acted knowingly while Y did not. Making personal responsibility the criterion bans the responsible swimmer and clears the blameless one, exactly reproducing the panel's decision.
solutionSteps: Identify what differs between the two cases: X took the substance knowingly, Y unknowingly; substance and concentration are identical.
The justifying principle must hinge on that difference.
A responsibility-based principle sanctions the athlete who is responsible (X) and clears the one who is not (Y).
This exactly matches banning X and clearing Y.
keyConcept: A principle justifies differential treatment only if it tracks the specific feature on which the two cases actually differ.
commonMistake: Choosing a fair-sounding principle that is orthogonal to, or contradicts, the one difference the scenario establishes.

optionExplanations.0: Strict liability would require banning both swimmers, since both exceeded the threshold, so it cannot justify differential treatment.
optionExplanations.2: The scenario never states that performance effects differed between the swimmers, so this does not track the knowing/unknowing distinction.
optionExplanations.4: The concentration is identical for both, so a concentration-based principle predicts identical, not different, treatment.

shortExplanation: Every finance-committee member is entitled to vote, but no external consultant may vote. Anyone who may vote therefore cannot be an external consultant, so no finance-committee member is an external consultant.
solutionSteps: Note that every finance-committee member is entitled to vote on the budget.
Note that no external consultant may vote on the budget.
Anyone entitled to vote cannot be an external consultant.
Therefore no finance-committee member can be an external consultant.
keyConcept: Combining a universal permission with a universal prohibition forces the two groups to be disjoint.
commonMistake: Assuming that groups overlapping on the audit board must overlap everywhere, or converting 'some A are C' into 'all C are A'.

optionExplanations.0: Some audit-board members are external consultants who may not vote, so not every audit-board member may vote.
optionExplanations.1: This is impossible: finance members may all vote and consultants may not, so no finance member can be a consultant.
optionExplanations.4: The passage says only that some audit-board members are consultants; it does not follow that every consultant is on the audit board.

shortExplanation: The clues force the relative order Q, R, P, S among four runners. The only remaining runner, T, must be first, because placing T anywhere else would make Q first, which the clues forbid. The unique order is T, Q, R, P, S.
solutionSteps: From clue 2, Q is ahead of R; from clue 1, R is immediately ahead of P; from clue 3, S is after P.
This gives the forced relative sequence Q, R, P, S.
Insert the fifth runner T; if T were not first, Q would be first.
Clue 2 says Q is not first, so T must be first.
The unique order is T first, Q second, R third, P fourth, S fifth.
keyConcept: Chaining ordering constraints can force a unique sequence once the free element is placed to satisfy every clue.
commonMistake: Failing to test where the unconstrained runner T must go, and overlooking that any other placement violates 'Q is not first'.

optionExplanations.0: In the forced order Q finishes second, not fourth.
optionExplanations.1: R finishes third; S is the runner in fifth place.
optionExplanations.3: Clue 1 puts R immediately ahead of P, so P is fourth and R third — P is never ahead of R.

shortExplanation: The conclusion is about total ingredient cost, but the evidence is only about price per kilogram. A lower price per kilogram lowers total cost only if the mass of margarine used does not rise enough to cancel the saving, so the argument assumes no substantially greater mass is needed.
solutionSteps: Note the conclusion concerns total ingredient cost, while the premise concerns price per kilogram.
Total cost = price per kilogram multiplied by mass used.
A lower price per kilogram lowers total cost only if the mass used stays comparable.
Apply the negation test: if far more margarine were required, total cost could rise and the argument fails.
So the argument depends on the mass not rising substantially.
keyConcept: A necessary assumption is one whose negation defeats the argument; a per-unit saving translates to a total saving only if quantity is held roughly constant.
commonMistake: Assuming a lower price per kilogram automatically lowers total cost without checking that the quantity used stays similar.

optionExplanations.0: Future price trends are not needed; a per-kilogram saving already exists now, and the argument concerns the present substitution.
optionExplanations.2: Nutritional health is irrelevant to a comparison of ingredient costs.
optionExplanations.3: Whether customers can taste the difference bears on sales and revenue, not on whether ingredient costs fall.

shortExplanation: The respondents are subscribers to a runners' magazine who then chose to reply, a doubly self-selected group of exercise enthusiasts. Generalising from them to 'most adults in the country' is unsound because the sample is unrepresentative of adults in general.
solutionSteps: Identify the sample: subscribers to a runners' magazine who voluntarily replied.
Recognise this group is self-selected twice over and skewed towards exercisers.
The conclusion generalises to all adults in the country.
The leap fails because the sample cannot represent adults in general.
Note the defect is bias, not size: 6,000 respondents is a large sample.
keyConcept: A sample that is unrepresentative of the target population undermines a generalisation regardless of how large the sample is.
commonMistake: Blaming sample size when the real problem is that a large but biased, self-selected sample cannot represent the whole population.

optionExplanations.0: No necessary-versus-sufficient condition is confused in this argument; that flaw is not present.
optionExplanations.1: This describes the fallacy of division (whole-to-part), which the argument does not commit.
optionExplanations.4: The sample was large (6,000 replies), so 'too small' is not the defect; a large biased sample is still misleading.

shortExplanation: For t minutes both pipes run together at 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 per minute; then pipe B runs alone at 1/30 per minute for the remaining (18 - t) minutes. Setting the total filled to 1 gives t = 8 minutes.
solutionSteps: Let pipe A be open for t minutes.
Combined rate of both pipes = 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 of the cistern per minute.
Pipe B alone runs at 1/30 per minute for the remaining (18 - t) minutes.
Write the equation t*(1/12) + (18 - t)*(1/30) = 1.
Multiply by 60: 5t + 2(18 - t) = 60, so 3t = 24 and t = 8.
keyConcept: Work-rate problems add reciprocal rates during shared time, then account separately for each single-pipe phase.
commonMistake: Adding the rates as 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/10 instead of 1/12, or dropping the second single-pipe phase entirely.

optionExplanations.0: This reports how long both pipes together would take to fill the cistern (12 minutes), ignoring the second phase.
optionExplanations.3: 9 is half of 18, from wrongly assuming pipe A was open for exactly half the total time.
optionExplanations.4: This comes from adding the rates incorrectly as 1/10 instead of 1/12, which yields t = 6.

shortExplanation: The greatest overlap is min(96, 72) = 72, feasible since 54 delegates can speak neither. The least overlap is 96 + 72 - 150 = 18, since the two groups sum to 168 and must overlap by at least that excess. The difference is 72 - 18 = 54.
solutionSteps: Greatest b: fit German speakers inside French speakers, giving b = min(96, 72) = 72 (54 delegates speak neither).
Least b: since 96 + 72 = 168 exceeds 150, the overlap is at least 168 - 150 = 18.
Least b = 18, achieved when no delegate speaks neither language.
Difference = 72 - 18 = 54.
keyConcept: For two subsets of a universe, the minimum overlap is (sum of sizes - universe) when positive, and the maximum overlap is the smaller subset size.
commonMistake: Reporting a single extreme value of b instead of the difference between the greatest and least.

optionExplanations.0: 24 is the difference of the two group sizes (96 - 72), not the overlap difference.
optionExplanations.1: 18 is only the least possible value of b, not the difference between greatest and least.
optionExplanations.3: 90 comes from adding the greatest and least values (72 + 18) instead of subtracting them.

shortExplanation: Helmets reduce head-injury risk per cyclist (a rate), but the reported rise is in the absolute number of injuries (a count). If many more people cycle after the law, total exposure grows, so the absolute number of head injuries can rise even while each cyclist is safer.
solutionSteps: Distinguish the risk per cyclist (a rate) from the total number of injuries (a count).
Helmets lower the rate per cyclist.
A large increase in the number of cyclists raises total exposure.
Higher exposure can raise the absolute count even as the per-cyclist rate falls, resolving the discrepancy.
keyConcept: A falling per-unit rate is compatible with a rising absolute total when the population exposed grows enough.
commonMistake: Attacking helmet effectiveness instead of explaining how the total number of injuries could rise while each cyclist is safer.

optionExplanations.1: Variation in helmet effectiveness with collision speed does not explain why the total number of head injuries rose.
optionExplanations.3: If many rode without helmets, their rate would resemble the pre-law situation, explaining no rise above the previous level.
optionExplanations.4: That helmets do not protect other body parts is irrelevant, since the discrepancy concerns head injuries specifically.

shortExplanation: The council infers causation purely from a before-after change. It is most weakened by evidence that night-time accidents were already falling by about 30% every two years before the lamps were fitted, so the observed fall is just the continuation of a pre-existing trend and need not be due to the lighting.
solutionSteps: Identify the causal claim: brighter lighting caused the 30% fall.
The evidence is only a before-after change on one road.
A pre-existing 30%-per-two-years downward trend would produce the same fall without the lamps.
That undermines the inference that the lighting caused the reduction, defeating the town-wide rollout case.
keyConcept: A before-after change supports causation only if the outcome would not have changed anyway; a matching prior trend removes that support.
commonMistake: Accepting a causal claim from a simple before-after comparison without ruling out an existing trend.

optionExplanations.1: The cost of the scheme is irrelevant to whether the lighting caused the fall in accidents.
optionExplanations.2: Unchanged daytime accidents act as a control that, if anything, strengthens the causal case rather than weakening it.
optionExplanations.3: Drivers' subjective feelings of safety give no reason to doubt the causal claim and mildly support it.

shortExplanation: Statement (ii) makes a first-class average plus a completed research project sufficient for the scholarship. By its contrapositive, anyone not awarded it lacks one of those. Anna did complete a research project, so the missing ingredient must be the first-class average.
solutionSteps: Statement (ii): first-class average AND research project implies the scholarship.
Take the contrapositive: no scholarship implies no first-class average OR no research project.
Anna was not awarded the scholarship, so at least one required part is missing.
Anna did complete a research project, so the missing part is the first-class average.
Conclude Anna does not have a first-class average.
keyConcept: The contrapositive of a sufficient condition lets you deduce which required ingredient is absent when the outcome fails.
commonMistake: Treating the sufficient condition as necessary and denying the antecedent, or inventing unstated reasons for the outcome.

optionExplanations.0: This denies the antecedent of the sufficient condition; without the project she might still fail to qualify.
optionExplanations.2: Nothing in the premises mentions declining the award; turning it down is invented information.
optionExplanations.4: The premises show only that Anna lacks a first-class average, not that any first-class student was refused the award.

shortExplanation: Take 100 samples in 2023 with 60 positive. In 2024 there are 150 samples and 60 x 1.20 = 72 positives, so the rate is 72/150 = 48%. The positivity rate falls by 60 - 48 = 12 percentage points because the denominator grew faster than the numerator.
solutionSteps: Assume 100 samples in 2023, of which 60 are positive (60%).
In 2024 the number of samples is 100 x 1.5 = 150.
Positives in 2024 are 60 x 1.20 = 72.
Positivity rate = 72/150 = 48%.
The rate falls by 60 - 48 = 12 percentage points.
keyConcept: A rate changes according to how numerator and denominator grow; if the denominator grows faster, the rate falls.
commonMistake: Confusing a change in the positive count with a change in the rate, or reporting a relative change as a change in percentage points.

optionExplanations.0: 72 is the 2024 positive count, not the rate; treating the 20% rise in positives as a rise in the rate ignores the larger rise in samples.
optionExplanations.1: 75% comes from swapping which quantity grew by which percentage.
optionExplanations.3: The rate is unchanged only if numerator and denominator grow by the same factor; here they grow by 20% and 50%.

shortExplanation: G is fixed on Wednesday. 'Exactly two presentations between H and L' places them three days apart, so H and L are either Monday and Thursday or Tuesday and Friday. Only the Tuesday-Friday option lets 'J before K' hold with K off Friday, forcing J Monday, H Tuesday, G Wednesday, K Thursday, L Friday.
solutionSteps: Fix G on Wednesday (day 3).
Two presentations between H and L means they are three days apart, with H before L: either (Monday, Thursday) or (Tuesday, Friday).
Try H Monday, L Thursday: free days Tuesday and Friday take J and K; K cannot be Friday, so K Tuesday and J Friday, making J later than K — violates 'J before K'.
So H Tuesday, L Friday; free days Monday and Thursday take J and K; 'J before K' forces J Monday, K Thursday.
Unique schedule: J Monday, H Tuesday, G Wednesday, K Thursday, L Friday, so K presents on Thursday.
keyConcept: Fixing an anchor and a spacing constraint narrows placements to a few cases; ordering rules then eliminate all but the unique valid schedule.
commonMistake: Adopting the Monday-Thursday placement for H and L without checking that keeping K off Friday then violates 'J before K'.

optionExplanations.0: The constraints explicitly forbid K on Friday, and Friday is taken by L.
optionExplanations.3: L on Thursday belongs to the rejected Monday-Thursday arrangement, which fails 'J before K' once K is kept off Friday.
optionExplanations.4: H on Monday belongs to that same rejected arrangement.

shortExplanation: The time an item spends in the factory is waiting time plus processing time. The new machine halved processing time, so for the total to rise, waiting must have grown more. Tripling the order volume created long queues, so items now wait far longer before processing despite the faster machine.
solutionSteps: Total dwell time = waiting (queue) time + processing time.
The new machine halved the processing time.
For the total to rise, waiting time must have increased by more than the processing time fell.
Accepting roughly three times as many orders lengthens the queue enough to outweigh the halved processing time.
keyConcept: Throughput speed only affects processing time; total time in a system also depends on queueing, which grows with arrival volume.
commonMistake: Seizing on any negative detail without checking it is large and consistent enough to outweigh a full doubling of processing speed.

optionExplanations.0: The old machine's age says nothing about why times rose after the change.
optionExplanations.1: A brief daily warm-up still leaves the machine at least as fast as the old one for most of the day.
optionExplanations.4: Occasional breakdowns repaired within a day cannot systematically outweigh a doubling of processing speed.

shortExplanation: The argument supports 'most trustworthy' by appealing to 'most reliable', then supports 'most reliable' by appealing back to 'most trustworthy'. The conclusion is used to prove itself, offering no independent evidence — circular reasoning that begs the question.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: the paper is the most trustworthy.
Note the support offered: its reporting is the most reliable.
Note the support for that: it is the most trustworthy paper.
The two claims are interchangeable, so the reasoning runs in a circle with no independent evidence.
keyConcept: Begging the question occurs when the conclusion is assumed within its own supporting premise.
commonMistake: Mislabelling circular reasoning as another named fallacy that the argument does not actually commit.

optionExplanations.0: The argument never appeals to a lack of counter-evidence, so it is not an appeal to ignorance.
optionExplanations.1: No external authority is cited; the paper merely restates its own claim in different words.
optionExplanations.3: Popularity is never invoked; the argument does not claim the paper is widely believed.

shortExplanation: The argument leans on the analogy that a brain is like a computer, where adding memory reliably raises capacity without limit. It is weakened most by a relevant disanalogy: beyond a point, adding neurons disrupts the tuned connections between existing neurons, so mental performance can deteriorate rather than grow.
solutionSteps: Identify the analogy: brain is like a computer, and adding units of memory raises capacity without limit.
The inference needs this 'more units, more capacity' relationship to transfer to brains.
Point out a relevant difference: brain capacity depends on how neurons are connected, not merely their number.
If adding neurons disrupts connections and can reduce performance, the analogy's key property fails and the inference collapses.
keyConcept: An analogy is weakened only by a difference in a relevant respect — one that touches the property the argument relies on.
commonMistake: Assuming that any true difference between two things weakens an analogy, rather than only a difference in the relevant respect.

optionExplanations.0: A difference in current arithmetic speed does not touch the claim about improving capacity by adding units.
optionExplanations.1: Differences between individual people's memories do not address whether adding neurons raises capacity.
optionExplanations.3: How each is manufactured has no bearing on the scaling inference.

shortExplanation: By alligation, each stock's amount is proportional to the other stock's distance from the target. Blend X pairs with |70 - 45| = 25 and Blend Y with |45 - 30| = 15, so X : Y = 5 : 3. Of 800 g, Blend X is 5/8 x 800 = 500 g.
solutionSteps: Compute each distance from the 45% target: Blend X at 30% is 15 away, Blend Y at 70% is 25 away.
By alligation, X : Y = (Y's distance) : (X's distance) = 25 : 15 = 5 : 3.
Blend X = 5/8 of 800 g = 500 g (Blend Y = 300 g).
keyConcept: In alligation, each component is used in proportion to the opposite component's distance from the target concentration.
commonMistake: Pairing each stock with its own distance from the target instead of the opposite stock's distance, inverting the ratio.

optionExplanations.0: 360 g is the Arabica content of the whole blend (45% of 800), not the mass of Blend X.
optionExplanations.1: Assuming an equal split because 45% is near the midpoint ignores that 45% is closer to X's 30%, so more X is needed.
optionExplanations.2: 300 g comes from inverting the alligation ratio to X : Y = 3 : 5.

shortExplanation: The board's principle is that a rule accepted by all participants must be enforced equally on everyone, even when this overrides the best performance. The cycling federation stripping the winner for breaking an agreed technical specification matches on every element: an agreed rule, the top performer penalised, and the rule binding all regardless of outcome.
solutionSteps: State the board's principle: equal enforcement of an agreed rule outweighs individual merit.
Look for a case with an agreed rule, the best performer penalised, and the justification that the rule binds everyone.
The cycling case has all three: an agreed specification, the first rider stripped, and the rule applied to every competitor.
It is structurally identical to the board's decision.
keyConcept: Principle-matching requires the same underlying rationale, here equal enforcement of an agreed rule over merit, not merely a similar setting.
commonMistake: Matching on surface features such as sport or officials rather than on the underlying principle of equal enforcement.

optionExplanations.0: This rewards the best performance on a chosen measure, close to the opposite of letting an agreed rule override the best work.
optionExplanations.1: This changes a rule in response to majority opinion rather than applying an accepted rule uniformly.
optionExplanations.2: This rests on the finality of an official's on-field decision, not on equal enforcement of an agreed rule.
optionExplanations.3: This makes a compassionate exception to a rule, whereas the board's principle forbids exceptions.

shortExplanation: Convert ownership counts to proportions: 52/400 = 13%, 80/500 = 16%, 66/300 = 22%, 30/250 = 12%. The 45-59 group's 22% is the highest, so a greater proportion of that group owns an electric car than any other.
solutionSteps: Compute each group's ownership proportion: 18-29 is 52/400 = 13%, 30-44 is 80/500 = 16%.
Compare the proportions; 22% for the 45-59 group is the highest.
So a greater proportion of the 45-59 group own an electric car than any other group.
keyConcept: Comparisons of prevalence across groups of different sizes require proportions, not absolute counts.
commonMistake: Equating the largest absolute count of owners with the highest ownership proportion or with 'enthusiasm'.

optionExplanations.1: The proportions run 13%, 16%, 22%, 12% — they rise then fall, so ownership does not rise steadily with age.
optionExplanations.2: Expressed intention is not actual behaviour and ignores current ownership; the data cannot predict future ownership.
optionExplanations.3: The 30-44 group has the most owners in absolute number but only the second-highest rate; count does not measure enthusiasm.
optionExplanations.4: Total owners = 228, so a majority needs more than 114, but 30-44 has only 80.

shortExplanation: The main conclusion is the claim that everything else supports. Signalled by 'should ... therefore', the recommendation that governments treat separated cycle lanes as a core public-health measure is supported by the safety, uptake and air-quality points and supports none of them.
solutionSteps: Identify candidate statements and the connective 'should ... therefore'.
Test each: does it support the others, or is it supported by them?
The safety, uptake and air-quality claims form a chain leading to the recommendation.
The recommendation is supported by all the rest and supports nothing further, so it is the main conclusion.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the statement supported by the others while itself providing support to none.
commonMistake: Selecting a prominent empirical claim or a mid-chain inference instead of the final recommendation.

optionExplanations.0: This is a mid-chain inference that feeds the next step, not the ultimate point.
optionExplanations.1: This is an intermediate conclusion in the causal chain, used to help justify the final recommendation.
optionExplanations.2: The injury-reduction claim is an intermediate conclusion used as evidence for later steps.
optionExplanations.3: This is a premise introduced by 'because' to explain the injury-reduction claim.

shortExplanation: The plan works only if the reason children under-brush is that they lack a toothbrush. If the real barrier is something else, such as no toothpaste or no supervision, then giving out brushes will not change behaviour, so it is crucial to establish whether the absence of a toothbrush is the actual constraint.
solutionSteps: The plan links under-brushing to a remedy of giving out toothbrushes.
This link holds only if lacking a toothbrush is why children under-brush.
If the binding constraint is something else, free brushes will not raise brushing.
So the key thing to establish is whether children who under-brush do so because they have no toothbrush.
keyConcept: To judge an intervention, check whether it removes the actual constraint causing the problem.
commonMistake: Assuming that supplying a tool solves the problem without confirming the tool's absence is the true barrier.

optionExplanations.0: The premise that brushing twice a day reduces decay is already accepted, so confirming it adds nothing.
optionExplanations.1: Affordability bears on sustaining the plan, not on whether it would reduce decay if carried out.
optionExplanations.2: The relative price of the brushes is irrelevant to whether distributing them reduces decay.

shortExplanation: The first premise presents cutting research and raising fees as the only two options. Having ruled out raising fees, it concludes cutting research is unavoidable. But the pair is not exhaustive — alternative funding or savings elsewhere exist — so this is a false dilemma.
solutionSteps: Identify the disjunctive premise: either cut research or raise fees.
The argument rules out raising fees and concludes cutting research is forced.
This is valid only if the two options are genuinely exhaustive.
Other options exist, so presenting only two is a false dilemma.
keyConcept: A false dilemma presents a limited set of options as exhaustive when further alternatives exist.
commonMistake: Labelling the argument with an unrelated fallacy instead of noticing the missing third option.

optionExplanations.0: No authority's opinion is cited anywhere in the argument.
optionExplanations.1: There is no inference from a property of individual students to a property of the whole group.
optionExplanations.2: The term 'burden' is used in a single, consistent sense, so there is no equivocation.

shortExplanation: Daily revenue is customers multiplied by mean spend: P = 800, Q = 900, R = 750, S = 600 euros. The busiest shop R (250 customers) takes 750, while the highest-mean-spend shop Q (6.00 each) takes 900, so R takes less than Q.
solutionSteps: Compute each shop's revenue as customers x mean spend.
The busiest shop is R with 250 customers, taking 750.
The highest mean spend is Q at 6.00, taking 900.
Since 750 < 900, the busiest shop takes less than the highest-mean-spend shop, matching the claim.
keyConcept: Total revenue combines volume and per-customer spend; the highest count and the highest spend need not coincide.
commonMistake: Assuming high spend per customer implies high customer numbers, or that revenue tracks customer count.

optionExplanations.1: The two highest-mean-spend shops, Q and S, serve 270 customers, fewer than P and R's 450.
optionExplanations.2: The shop with the fewest customers is S (120) with mean spend 5.00, but the lowest mean spend is R's 3.00.
optionExplanations.3: S takes only 600 euros, below 700, so not every shop takes at least 700.
optionExplanations.4: R serves more customers than P but takes less revenue (750 vs 800), so revenue does not rise with customer numbers.

shortExplanation: In the first hour both pipes fill 1/6 + 1/4 = 5/12 of the tank. Pipe Y alone fills the remaining 7/12 at 1/4 per hour, taking 7/3 hours (2 h 20 min), for a total of 3 hours 20 minutes.
solutionSteps: Express rates as tank per hour: X = 1/6, Y = 1/4.
First hour, both open: 1/6 + 1/4 = 5/12 filled.
Remaining fraction: 1 - 5/12 = 7/12.
Time for Y alone: (7/12) / (1/4) = 7/3 h = 2 h 20 min.
Total time: 1 h + 2 h 20 min = 3 h 20 min.
keyConcept: Combine rates as fractions of the job per hour, then divide remaining work by the acting rate.
commonMistake: Assuming both pipes run for the whole job, which gives 2 h 24 min and ignores that X is closed after 1 hour.

optionExplanations.0: 3 h 30 min overestimates Y's time for the remaining 7/12, which actually takes 2 h 20 min.
optionExplanations.1: 2 h 24 min (12/5 h) is the time if both pipes ran together for the entire job, ignoring that X closes after 1 hour.
optionExplanations.2: 2 h 48 min does not match the correct remaining fraction of 7/12 at Y's rate.

shortExplanation: The conclusion that fewer cars will enter follows only if some current solo drivers actually change their behaviour when charges rise. If none did, car numbers would be unchanged, so this responsiveness is a necessary assumption.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: raising parking charges will cut cars entering downtown.
Identify the gap: higher charges reduce cars only if drivers respond.
Apply the negation test to each candidate assumption.
Negating 'at least some drivers would not drive in' leaves car numbers unchanged, destroying the inference.
Confirm the responsiveness of current drivers is required.
keyConcept: A necessary assumption is one whose negation breaks the argument's inference.
commonMistake: Choosing a claim that is stronger than needed (that the measure is the most effective) rather than the minimal responsiveness the conclusion requires.

optionExplanations.0: The argument claims only that charges reduce cars, not that this is the most effective of all measures.
optionExplanations.1: The source of congestion (commuters vs delivery vehicles) concerns a different conclusion than the number of cars entering.
optionExplanations.2: How the extra revenue is spent has no bearing on whether higher charges themselves reduce cars entering.

shortExplanation: The argument chains several unsupported steps from allowing calculators to an incompetent profession, treating each transition as inevitable. Presenting an extreme outcome as the certain consequence of a small first step is the slippery-slope flaw.
solutionSteps: Trace the chain: calculators to no mental arithmetic to no estimation to undetected errors to an incompetent profession.
Note that none of the intermediate links is justified.
Recognise that a modest first step is claimed to force an extreme final outcome.
Identify this as the slippery-slope pattern.
keyConcept: A slippery-slope argument asserts an inevitable cascade of worsening consequences without supporting the connecting steps.
commonMistake: Mislabelling the flaw as a composition or hasty-generalisation error when no part-to-whole or sampling reasoning occurs.

optionExplanations.0: The argument does not mistake a necessary condition for a sufficient one; that diagnosis does not fit the chain structure.
optionExplanations.1: There is no inference from members to a group, so this is not a fallacy of composition.
optionExplanations.2: No sample of students is cited, so this is not a hasty generalisation.
optionExplanations.3: Nothing is said about the character or motives of calculator supporters, so it is not an ad hominem.

shortExplanation: The unique solution is Ben on floor 1 with espresso, Ada on floor 2 with tea, Cara on floor 3 with latte, and Dan on floor 4 with water. So the espresso drinker (floor 1) is necessarily below the tea drinker (floor 2).
solutionSteps: Place Ada on floor 2 (clue 2).
Cara drinks latte, so she is not the floor-1 espresso drinker; with Dan above her, Cara cannot be floor 4, so Cara is floor 3 and Dan floor 4.
The remaining floor 1 goes to Ben, so Ben drinks espresso.
Ada did not order water, so Ada drinks tea and Dan drinks water.
Compare: espresso is floor 1, tea is floor 2, so espresso is on a lower floor than tea.
keyConcept: Combine positional and exclusion clues to fix a unique arrangement, then test each candidate statement against it.
commonMistake: Assuming the highest floor must take the tea instead of using the clue that places tea with Ada.

optionExplanations.0: Ben is forced onto floor 1 by the espresso and ordering clues, not floor 3.
optionExplanations.2: Dan drinks water, not tea; the tea belongs to Ada.
optionExplanations.3: The water drinker is Dan on floor 4, not floor 2.
optionExplanations.4: Cara is on floor 3, above Ada on floor 2, so this reverses the actual order.

shortExplanation: Knowing the two numbers differ restricts the sample space to the 30 non-double outcomes. All six sums of 7 already have different numbers, so the conditional probability is 6/30 = 1/5.
solutionSteps: Start with 36 equally likely ordered outcomes.
Exclude the 6 doubles, leaving 30 outcomes.
List sums of 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) - all 6 have different numbers.
Compute 6/30 = 1/5.
keyConcept: Conditioning on an event means recomputing probability over the restricted sample space.
commonMistake: Using 6/36 = 1/6 over the full sample space, ignoring the information that the numbers differ.

optionExplanations.0: 1/3 comes from wrongly taking only 18 different-number outcomes instead of 30.
optionExplanations.1: 7/36 misuses the target sum as a count of outcomes over the full space.
optionExplanations.2: 1/6 is 6/36 over the unrestricted space, ignoring the given condition.
optionExplanations.4: 6/35 removes only one outcome instead of all six doubles.

shortExplanation: The reference argument has the valid form All A are B; No B are C; therefore No A are C. The copper-wire argument reproduces this exactly, matching structure rather than subject matter.
solutionSteps: Abstract the reference: All A are B (choir can read music); No B are C (readers are not beginners); therefore No A are C.
Note the middle term B is predicate of the first premise and subject of the second.
Test each option for the same form.
The copper-wire argument fits with A = copper wires, B = conductors, C = perfect insulators.
keyConcept: Parallel-reasoning questions match logical form, not content.
commonMistake: Picking an argument that merely shares surface wording or a negative premise but has a different underlying structure.

optionExplanations.1: This is an all-affirmative chain with no negative premise, a different valid form.
optionExplanations.2: Its negative premise involves the wrong pair of terms and the inference is invalid.
optionExplanations.3: It uses a particular premise and particular conclusion, unlike the all-universal reference.
optionExplanations.4: It has two negative premises, which is an invalid structure and does not parallel the reference.

shortExplanation: The claim infers causation from a mere correlation. A dose-response gradient - more plants tracking steadily lower stress - is a recognised hallmark of a genuine causal effect and provides the strongest support.
solutionSteps: Note the argument moves from correlation (plant owners report less stress) to causation.
Recall that a graded dose-response relationship strengthens a causal inference.
Check that increasing plant count matches declining stress across the range.
Select the dose-response option as the strongest support.
keyConcept: A dose-response gradient is strong evidence that an association is causal.
commonMistake: Treating any additional favourable association, or a circular restatement of the correlation, as if it strengthened the causal claim.

optionExplanations.0: This merely restates the original correlation as the conclusion, adding no new support.
optionExplanations.1: This describes reverse causation (calm people choose plants), which undermines the claim.
optionExplanations.3: Greater job satisfaction is a separate outcome and does not show plants cause lower stress.
optionExplanations.4: Workers finding plant-filled offices pleasant is an appeal to opinion, not evidence of reduced stress.

shortExplanation: Four options restate recorded facts or follow necessarily from them. Only the causal claim goes beyond the data, since the groups differ in age and commuting distance - confounders that could explain the sick-leave difference - so causation cannot be reliably concluded.
solutionSteps: Check each option against what the passage recorded.
Confirm the BMI, age, and distance comparisons are directly stated.
Confirm the existence of regular cyclists follows from the data.
Identify the causal claim as unsupported because the study is observational and confounded.
keyConcept: Observational correlations with confounders do not establish causation.
commonMistake: Accepting a causal conclusion from group differences without ruling out confounders like age and commute distance.

optionExplanations.0: This directly restates the recorded BMI comparison, so it can be concluded.
optionExplanations.1: The passage explicitly states the cyclists were younger, so it can be concluded.
optionExplanations.2: The passage explicitly states cyclists more often lived within 5 km, so it can be concluded.
optionExplanations.3: The data describe such a group, so its members must exist; this can be concluded.

shortExplanation: R's claim that P is a knight forces P and R to share a type, making Q's 'different types' claim false, so Q is a knave. P's statement that Q is a knave is then true, so P is a knight and therefore R is too - exactly two knights.
solutionSteps: R says P is a knight, so R and P must be the same type.
Since P and R share a type, Q's claim that they differ is false, so Q is a knave.
P said Q is a knave, which is now true, so P is a knight.
Because R shares P's type, R is also a knight.
Count: P and R are knights, Q is a knave - exactly two.
keyConcept: A statement asserting another's type links the two speakers' truth-values; test assignments for consistency.
commonMistake: Assuming a uniform all-knaves solution without checking that it leads to a contradiction.

optionExplanations.0: This undercounts; a consistent assignment forces both P and R to be knights.
optionExplanations.1: All knaves fails: it makes P both a knave and a knight, a contradiction.
optionExplanations.3: Q cannot be a knight, since P and R sharing a type makes Q's claim false.
optionExplanations.4: The statements do fix a unique solution, so it is not indeterminate.

shortExplanation: True 'fallow' calls have probability 0.15 x 0.80 = 0.12; false ones 0.85 x 0.20 = 0.17. By Bayes' theorem the probability the animal was really fallow is 0.12 / 0.29, about 41%.
solutionSteps: Compute the true-positive path: 0.15 x 0.80 = 0.12.
Compute the false-positive path: 0.85 x 0.20 = 0.17.
Total probability of a 'fallow' report: 0.12 + 0.17 = 0.29.
Apply Bayes: 0.12 / 0.29 = 0.41, about 41%.
keyConcept: Bayes' theorem weights the test accuracy by the base rate; rare conditions produce many false positives.
commonMistake: Base-rate neglect: taking the 80% hit rate as the answer and ignoring how rare fallow deer are.

optionExplanations.0: 0.12 is the joint probability of fallow and a 'fallow' call, missing the normalising denominator.
optionExplanations.1: 15% is only the prior proportion of fallow deer, using none of the report.
optionExplanations.2: About 59% is the probability the animal was actually a red deer, the complementary conditional.
optionExplanations.4: 80% is the ranger's hit rate, which ignores the low base rate of fallow deer.

shortExplanation: This is the valid form Ferio: No cold-blooded animals are mammals and some pond animals are cold-blooded, so those pond animals are not mammals. Hence some animals in this pond are not mammals.
solutionSteps: Note premise 2 gives some pond animals that are cold-blooded.
Note premise 1 says no cold-blooded animal is a mammal.
Conclude those particular pond animals are not mammals.
State the valid particular-negative conclusion: some pond animals are not mammals.
keyConcept: The Ferio syllogism (No M are P; Some S are M) validly yields Some S are not P.
commonMistake: Inflating 'some are not mammals' into a universal 'none are mammals', or converting into a claim about mammals.

optionExplanations.1: This contradicts the premises, since the pond contains cold-blooded animals that cannot be mammals.
optionExplanations.2: Nothing guarantees any pond animal is a mammal; a particular-negative does not license a particular-affirmative.
optionExplanations.3: Only the cold-blooded pond animals are shown not to be mammals; others might be, so 'no' is too strong.
optionExplanations.4: This illicitly converts the conclusion into a claim about mammals rather than pond animals.

shortExplanation: The critic moves from 'the restaurant scores well on the measures a rating is meant to judge' to 'the rating stands'. This works only if an assessment should be settled solely by considerations relevant to the quality it measures, so the owner's politics are set aside.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: the three-star rating stands.
Identify the reason: the restaurant is excellent on cooking, service and value.
Find the bridging principle: only relevant considerations should govern the assessment.
Confirm this excludes the irrelevant fact of the owner's politics.
keyConcept: The operative principle in an argument is the general rule that licenses moving from its reason to its conclusion.
commonMistake: Choosing an overly broad absolute (never let feelings affect any decision) instead of the narrow relevance-only rule the argument needs.

optionExplanations.0: This is an empirical claim about customer psychology, not the normative rule licensing the inference.
optionExplanations.1: An absolute ban on all feelings is far stronger than the argument needs; only irrelevant considerations are barred.
optionExplanations.2: This invents an impartiality-through-no-acquaintance condition the argument never uses.
optionExplanations.3: This concerns reputation in general, not the basis on which an evaluation should be conducted.

shortExplanation: The straight strip 1-2-3-4 folds into a band of four side faces, in which faces two apart end up opposite. Faces 1 and 3 are two apart, so face 3 is directly opposite face 1.
solutionSteps: Recognise the strip 1-2-3-4 wraps into a band of four side faces.
In such a band, faces two positions apart are opposite: 1 opposite 3, 2 opposite 4.
Note the tabs 5 and 6 form the top and bottom faces, opposite each other.
Conclude face 1 is opposite face 3.
keyConcept: In a four-square strip of a cube net, each face is opposite the one two positions along the band.
commonMistake: Treating an adjacent square in the strip, or the far end of the strip, as the opposite face.

optionExplanations.0: Face 2 is directly below face 1 in the strip, so they share an edge and are adjacent, never opposite.
optionExplanations.1: Face 5 is joined to an edge of face 1, so it is adjacent, and it pairs with face 6 as top/bottom.
optionExplanations.2: Face 6 folds to the cap opposite face 5, not opposite face 1.
optionExplanations.4: Face 4 is the far end of the strip, but ends of a four-strip are not opposite; face 4 pairs with face 2.

shortExplanation: From the fourth term onward each term is the sum of the previous three: 1+2+4=7, 2+4+7=13, 4+7+13=24, 7+13+24=44. The next term is 13+24+44 = 81.
solutionSteps: Test the sum-of-previous-three rule: 1+2+4 = 7.
Apply the rule to the last three terms: 13+24+44 = 81.
keyConcept: Identify a recurrence that fits every term from the stated starting point, not just the first few.
commonMistake: Fitting a simpler rule such as doubling or Fibonacci to the earliest terms, which then breaks later.

optionExplanations.0: 88 = 2 x 44 continues doubling, but doubling already fails at 4 to 7.
optionExplanations.1: 84 assumes the gaps double, forcing a geometric pattern onto the differences.
optionExplanations.3: 64 = 44 + 20 assumes the last gap repeats, treating the sequence as arithmetic.
optionExplanations.4: 68 = 24 + 44 uses a Fibonacci rule, which does not reproduce the earlier terms.

shortExplanation: The argument slides from 'number of cases detected' to 'how likely people are to develop the condition'. The newly introduced routine screening can raise the recorded count without any change in the true rate, so the rise does not establish higher incidence.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: people are four times as likely to develop condition X.
Note the evidence is only the fourfold rise in recorded cases.
Observe the passage supplies a rival cause: new routine screening finds previously missed mild cases.
Conclude the rise may be a detection artefact, not a real rise in occurrence.
keyConcept: Ascertainment (detection) bias: more testing raises recorded cases without changing the true incidence.
commonMistake: Assuming the flaw must be a missing per-capita rate or a two-point comparison rather than the stated screening effect.

optionExplanations.0: A missing per-head denominator matters only if the population changed, which is not stated; the screening test is the decisive issue.
optionExplanations.2: Comparing two single years is a minor concern and does not undo a fourfold change with a stated systematic cause.
optionExplanations.3: Failing to rule out genetic causes still concedes incidence rose; the deeper problem is that the rise itself is unestablished.
optionExplanations.4: Cases diagnosed elsewhere would make the clinic figures an undercount, which does not explain away a real rise.

shortExplanation: The graph plots net change, which is positive every year, so the running total of customers rises each year. The end-of-2023 total is therefore the largest of any year shown; the falling line only means the yearly increase got smaller.
solutionSteps: Note the plotted quantity is net change (gains minus losses), positive every year.
A positive net change each year means the cumulative total rises every year.
So the total is greatest at the end of the final year, 2023.
Interpret the declining line as smaller yearly gains, not a falling total.
keyConcept: A positive rate of change means the underlying level keeps rising, even when the rate itself is falling.
commonMistake: Reading a downward-sloping change line as a fall in the total (confusing rate with level).

optionExplanations.0: From 2019 to 2023 the net-change line falls, so the yearly gain decreased, not increased.
optionExplanations.1: After 2019 the line stays positive, so the total rose between 2019 and 2023 rather than falling.
optionExplanations.3: The largest yearly gain is at the 2019 peak, not in 2016 where the line merely starts.
optionExplanations.4: A positive net change each year means the total kept increasing, so it did not stay the same.

shortExplanation: The conclusion that congestion falls rests on new cycling trips being trips not made by car. This follows only if a substantial share of the extra cyclists would otherwise have driven, so that is the necessary assumption.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: cycle lanes reduce motor-traffic congestion.
Identify the gap: new cycling trips cut congestion only if they replace car trips.
Apply the negation test: if few new cyclists would otherwise have driven, car use barely changes.
Confirm that a substantial share switching from cars is required.
keyConcept: The needed assumption supplies the missing link and is minimal, not the strongest possible version.
commonMistake: Choosing the maximal claim (every new cyclist gives up the car completely) rather than the modest 'substantial proportion'.

optionExplanations.0: This is far stronger than needed; only enough trips must shift, not every cyclist abandoning the car.
optionExplanations.1: Cycling need not be faster; people may switch for cost, health, or environmental reasons.
optionExplanations.3: Whether car journeys were rising beforehand is an irrelevant background trend.
optionExplanations.4: Whether another scheme would work better is an opportunity-cost aside irrelevant to this argument.

shortExplanation: A crude death rate reflects both care quality and how ill the patients were. If Hospital A takes the highest-risk referrals while B operates only on low-risk patients, A can have a higher crude mortality yet still give the sickest patients the best chance.
solutionSteps: Note that crude mortality depends on the patients' baseline risk (case-mix).
Suppose A receives the highest-risk cases and B only low-risk cases.
Then A's higher crude rate reflects sicker patients, not worse care.
So sending the most seriously ill to A is consistent with A having the higher rate.
keyConcept: Unequal case-mix means crude death rates cannot be compared directly across hospitals.
commonMistake: Comparing raw mortality rates without adjusting for how ill each hospital's patients were.

optionExplanations.0: More experienced surgeons at B would deepen the paradox, making the recommendation harder to explain.
optionExplanations.1: Earlier discharge of survivors is irrelevant to a fixed 30-day mortality measure.
optionExplanations.2: A larger volume of operations does not by itself explain a higher rate or the referral advice.
optionExplanations.4: Catchment size is irrelevant to patients' risk profile unless it changed case severity, which is not stated.

shortExplanation: Each remainder is exactly one less than its divisor, so N + 1 is a common multiple of 5, 6 and 7. The lowest common multiple is 210, and since N < 300, N + 1 = 210 gives N = 209.
solutionSteps: Note remainders 4, 5, 6 are each one less than 5, 6, 7.
So N + 1 is divisible by 5, 6 and 7.
Compute LCM(5,6,7) = 210.
Since N < 300, set N + 1 = 210, giving N = 209.
keyConcept: When each remainder is one short of its divisor, N + 1 is a common multiple of the divisors.
commonMistake: Ignoring the 'one short' offset and choosing 210, which leaves remainder 0 with each divisor.

optionExplanations.1: 174 is exactly divisible by 6, so it fails the remainder-5-with-6 condition.
optionExplanations.2: 120 is the product of the remainders, which has no basis and is divisible by 5 and 6.
optionExplanations.3: 210 is the LCM itself and leaves remainder 0, ignoring the one-short offset.
optionExplanations.4: 119 leaves no remainder with 7, satisfying only two of the three conditions.

shortExplanation: The only evidence for causation is the order of events: the rate cut came first, the spending rise second. Concluding causation from mere succession, without excluding coincidence or another cause, is the post hoc fallacy.
solutionSteps: Identify the evidence: the rate cut preceded the spending rise.
Identify the conclusion: the cut caused the rise.
Note that succession alone does not establish causation.
Recognise the failure to exclude coincidence or a common cause as the post hoc fallacy.
keyConcept: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: treating temporal sequence as proof of causation.
commonMistake: Mislabelling the flaw as reverse causation, which is chronologically impossible here.

optionExplanations.0: Reverse causation is impossible here, since the January cut precedes the February rise.
optionExplanations.1: Sample size is a secondary quibble; even a full year would not fix the succession-to-causation error.
optionExplanations.2: The argument never claims the cut is the only way to raise spending, so this false-dilemma charge does not apply.
optionExplanations.4: The argument does not confuse a percentage change with an absolute change.

shortExplanation: Success requires sterility, and sterility implies no colonies. Colonies appeared, so the culture was not sterile; since success needs sterility, the experiment did not succeed.
solutionSteps: Translate: success implies sterile; sterile implies no colonies.
Colonies appeared, so by contrapositive the culture was not sterile.
Since success requires sterility and sterility failed, success is impossible.
Conclude the experiment did not succeed.
keyConcept: Chain contrapositives: denying a necessary condition denies the outcome that requires it.
commonMistake: Affirming the consequent by assuming no colonies would guarantee success, though sterility is only necessary.

optionExplanations.0: Sterility is necessary for success and the culture was not sterile, so success is impossible.
optionExplanations.2: This affirms the consequent; sterility is necessary, not sufficient, for success.
optionExplanations.3: The premises mention no 'seal', so this introduces an unstated cause.
optionExplanations.4: Colonies appeared, and sterile implies no colonies, so the culture was not sterile.

shortExplanation: The pharmacist had good reason to believe the ten-fold dose could seriously harm the patient, so she suspended action until the doubt was resolved. A principle that a professional should not follow a possibly harmful instruction until the doubt is cleared exactly justifies her refusal.
solutionSteps: Identify the facts: a ten-fold dose gave good reason to suspect serious harm, and she withheld the medicine.
Identify the conclusion: her refusal was the right decision.
Find a principle whose antecedent matches the harm suspicion and whose consequent endorses suspending action.
Confirm the harm-doubt principle licenses the conclusion.
keyConcept: A principle-support answer must have an antecedent matching the facts and a consequent matching the conclusion.
commonMistake: Selecting a principle that judges by outcome, which was unknown when the decision was made, or one that supports the opposite conclusion.

optionExplanations.1: This would require handing over exactly what was prescribed, supporting the opposite conclusion.
optionExplanations.2: Judging only by outcomes cannot justify a decision made before the outcome was known.
optionExplanations.3: This concerns explaining risks to the patient, a feature absent from the case.
optionExplanations.4: This forbids making the patient wait, supporting the opposite conclusion.

shortExplanation: A multiple of 15 must be divisible by both 3 and 5. Statement 1 forces divisibility by 3 (digit sum) and by 5 (ends in 5), so it alone answers yes. Statement 2 gives a multiple of 45, which is automatically a multiple of 15, so it alone also answers yes. Each statement alone is sufficient.
solutionSteps: Note 15 = 3 x 5, so N is a multiple of 15 iff divisible by both 3 and 5.
Statement 1: digit sum divisible by 3 gives 3 | N; ending in 5 gives 5 | N; hence 15 | N.
Statement 2: 45 = 3 x 15, so every multiple of 45 is a multiple of 15; hence 15 | N.
Both statements independently give a definite yes.
keyConcept: In data sufficiency, either statement can be independently conclusive; sufficiency does not require combining them.
commonMistake: Assuming both clues are needed together and overlooking that each alone settles the question.

optionExplanations.1: Statement 1 is also sufficient, since the digit-sum and last-digit tests together force divisibility by 15.
optionExplanations.2: The information is more than enough; both statements are conclusive, not insufficient.
optionExplanations.3: Each statement is independently conclusive, so they are not sufficient only in combination.
optionExplanations.4: Statement 2 is also sufficient, since a multiple of 45 must be a multiple of 15.

shortExplanation: Ana proposed to reduce examinations and use somewhat more coursework. Bruno rebuts abolishing all examinations, a far more extreme position she never held. Attacking a distorted, stronger version of the opponent's view is the straw man fallacy.
solutionSteps: State Ana's actual position: reduce examinations, use a little more coursework.
State Bruno's target: abolishing all examinations.
Note Bruno refutes the extreme version, not Ana's moderate proposal.
Identify this misrepresentation as a straw man.
keyConcept: A straw man rebuts a distorted, more extreme version of the opponent's actual claim.
commonMistake: Labelling the error a false dilemma when the underlying fault is misrepresenting the opponent's proposal.

optionExplanations.1: The apparent two-option framing is a by-product of the misrepresentation, not the primary flaw.
optionExplanations.2: Employer trust is offered as a consequence of abolition, not an illegitimate appeal to authority.
optionExplanations.3: Bruno never claims coursework cannot be marked reliably, so this invented assumption is not his flaw.
optionExplanations.4: Bruno appeals to consequences of abolition, not to the system's long standing, so it is not an appeal to tradition.

shortExplanation: The differences between terms are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, each double the last, so the next difference is 32 and the next term is 33 + 32 = 65. Equivalently the terms are 2^n + 1.
solutionSteps: Compute differences: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 - each doubles.
The next difference is 32.
Check the closed form 2^n + 1: 2^6 + 1 = 65.
keyConcept: Look at the pattern of differences; here they form a geometric sequence, matching 2^n + 1.
commonMistake: Repeating the last difference instead of doubling it, or dropping the '+1' from the 2^n structure.

optionExplanations.0: 66 = 2 x 33 uses a multiply-by-two step but drops the '-1' of the recurrence.
optionExplanations.2: 64 = 2^6 recognises the powers of two but forgets the '+1'.
optionExplanations.3: 50 = 17 + 33 mistakes the sequence for a Fibonacci-type sum.
optionExplanations.4: 49 = 33 + 16 repeats the last difference instead of doubling it to 32.

shortExplanation: The red-green pair can only sit at positions 2 and 3, since placing it at either end forces yellow next to the end-anchored blue, which is forbidden. That leaves blue and yellow at the two ends in either order, so the green house is always house 3.
solutionSteps: The red house is immediately left of green, so the pair occupies (1,2), (2,3) or (3,4).
If the pair is at (1,2), houses 3 and 4 hold blue and yellow; blue must be at an end (house 4), forcing yellow to 3, adjacent to blue — forbidden.
If the pair is at (3,4), houses 1 and 2 hold blue and yellow; blue at an end (house 1) forces yellow to 2, adjacent to blue — forbidden.
So the pair sits at (2,3), leaving houses 1 and 4 (the ends, never adjacent) for blue and yellow in either order.
In both surviving arrangements red is house 2 and green is house 3, so green is always house 3.
keyConcept: In a 'must be true' constraint puzzle, eliminate impossible placements first, then keep only what holds across every surviving arrangement.
commonMistake: Fixing blue or yellow to a specific end when two mirror-image arrangements both remain valid, so those positions are not forced.

optionExplanations.0: Blue and yellow occupy the two ends (houses 1 and 4), which are never adjacent, so this is never true.
optionExplanations.1: Yellow is house 4 in only one of the two valid arrangements, so it need not be true.
optionExplanations.3: Blue is house 1 in only one of the two valid arrangements, so it need not be true.
optionExplanations.4: The red house is always house 2, an interior position, so it is in fact never at an end.

shortExplanation: The Vice-Chancellor uses a rise in a proxy (satisfaction scores) as evidence for a rise in the target (teaching quality). This inference works only if the score increase reflects genuinely better teaching rather than tactics that lift scores without improving teaching.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: teaching quality has improved.
Identify the evidence: student-satisfaction scores rose.
Note that satisfaction score is a proxy standing in for the unobserved target, teaching quality.
Apply the negation test: if the scores rose without any real teaching improvement (e.g. grade inflation, easier assessment), the conclusion collapses.
So the argument must assume the score rise reflects genuine improvement.
keyConcept: An argument that reasons from a proxy to the thing it stands for necessarily assumes the proxy is valid — that a change in the indicator tracks a change in the target.
commonMistake: Reaching for an over-strong claim (financial incentives are the best method, or there were no prior incentives) instead of the minimal proxy-validity assumption the inference actually needs.

optionExplanations.0: The argument needs only that quality improved, not that incentives are the most effective possible method; negating this comparative claim leaves the conclusion intact.
optionExplanations.3: This is far stronger than needed; the conclusion does not require zero prior incentives, so it is not a necessary assumption.
optionExplanations.4: This is about whether the scheme caused the rise, a causal-attribution claim; the conclusion is about what the rise shows regarding quality, not what caused it.

shortExplanation: The ten hospitals were chosen because their infection rates were at an extreme in a single year, and such rates fluctuate around a stable average. Values selected for being unusually high tend to fall back toward the mean the next year even with no intervention, which fully explains the larger-than-average drop without crediting the protocol.
solutionSteps: Note the hospitals entered the programme because they had the highest rates in one year.
Recognise that infection rates fluctuate year to year around a stable long-term average.
An extreme high reading is partly due to chance and tends to be followed by a lower one — regression to the mean.
This mechanism alone predicts a larger-than-average fall at exactly these hospitals.
So it supplies a complete rival explanation, undermining the claim that the protocol caused the fall.
keyConcept: Regression to the mean: subjects selected for an extreme value on a fluctuating measure tend to move back toward the average on remeasurement, with no intervention needed.
commonMistake: Assuming any co-occurring background change weakens the claim, or mistaking the elimination of confounders for a weakener when it actually strengthens the argument.

optionExplanations.0: Cost bears on whether the protocol is worthwhile, not on whether it reduced infections, so it leaves the effectiveness claim untouched.
optionExplanations.1: Ruling out other simultaneous changes removes rival explanations, which strengthens the causal claim rather than weakening it.
optionExplanations.2: A general fact about which operations carry more infection risk is not tied to any change between the two years and gives no reason to doubt the protocol.
optionExplanations.3: The ten hospitals fell by more than the region, so a small region-wide fall does not explain their larger drop; this is consistent with the argument.

shortExplanation: Tracking the six positions through each roll from the start Top=1, South=2, East=3, the top face becomes 4 after the first East move, 2 after the North move, and 6 after the second East move.
solutionSteps: Set the start positions: Top=1, South=2, East=3, so Bottom=6, North=5, West=4.
A roll East cycles top->east, east->bottom, bottom->west, west->top; north and south stay fixed.
After rolling East, the new top is the old west = 4.
A roll North cycles top->north, north->bottom, bottom->south, south->top; east and west stay fixed. New top is the old south = 2.
Roll East again: the new top is the current west = 6.
Check that opposite faces still sum to 7 at each step.
keyConcept: Track all six face positions and apply a fixed cyclic swap for each roll direction, keeping opposite faces paired (sum 7) as a running check.
commonMistake: Stopping the sequence one move early or reporting a side/bottom face instead of the top.

optionExplanations.0: 4 is the top after only the first roll East, not after all three moves.
optionExplanations.1: 3 is the face pointing South at the end, not the top face.
optionExplanations.3: 5 is on the hidden bottom after the first two rolls, not the final top.
optionExplanations.4: 2 is the top after only the first two rolls; it ignores the third move, which brings 6 to the top.

shortExplanation: With L proportional to w*d^2/l, take the ratio of the two beams so the constant cancels: L2 = 900 * (4/6) * (15/10)^2 * (3/5) = 810 kg. The length ratio is inverted because load is inversely proportional to length.
solutionSteps: Write the joint variation: L = k*w*d^2/l.
Form the ratio L2 = L1 * (w2/w1) * (d2/d1)^2 * (l1/l2) so k cancels.
Simplify factors: (2/3) * (9/4) * (3/5).
keyConcept: For joint/inverse variation, comparing two cases as a ratio cancels the constant; square any factor tied to a squared quantity and invert any inverse-proportion factor.
commonMistake: Forgetting to square the depth ratio, or using the length ratio the wrong way up — a longer beam must support less, so the factor is 3/5, not 5/3.

optionExplanations.1: 1350 kg omits the length factor entirely; because the second beam is longer, the 3/5 factor must reduce the load.
optionExplanations.2: 540 kg uses the depth to the first power, dropping the required square on the depth ratio.
optionExplanations.3: 2250 kg treats length as directly proportional, using 5/3 instead of 3/5, so a longer beam wrongly supports more.
optionExplanations.4: 360 kg squares the width instead of the depth, attaching the square to the wrong variable.

shortExplanation: The original is modus tollens: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P (P = divisible by 6, Q = divisible by 3). The only option with the identical form has: if mammal then four-chambered heart; not four-chambered heart; therefore not a mammal.
solutionSteps: Strip the original to its logical skeleton: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
Recognise this valid form as modus tollens (denying the consequent).
Test each option for the same skeleton, ignoring subject matter.
The mammal argument denies the consequent (no four-chambered heart) to deny the antecedent (not a mammal) — an exact match.
keyConcept: Parallel-reasoning questions require matching the abstract logical structure, not the topic or mere validity.
commonMistake: Matching on validity alone or on the surface presence of an 'if-then', while overlooking the specific pattern (denying vs affirming the consequent or antecedent).

optionExplanations.1: This denies the antecedent (if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q), an invalid form and a different structure.
optionExplanations.2: This is a hypothetical syllogism chaining two conditionals across three terms, with no negation of a component.
optionExplanations.3: This is modus ponens (if P then Q; P; therefore Q), valid but starting from affirming the antecedent, not denying the consequent.
optionExplanations.4: This affirms the consequent (if P then Q; Q; therefore P), an invalid form and the opposite move to the original.

shortExplanation: The argument goes from 'new capacity exceeds current peak demand' to 'congestion disappears', which holds only if peak demand stays roughly the same. If the wider road attracts additional drivers (induced demand), demand can rise to meet the new capacity and congestion returns.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: peak-time congestion will disappear.
Note the reasoning: new capacity (up 50%) will exceed current demand (only 30% above old capacity).
Observe this depends on demand not rising after the lane opens.
Apply the negation test: if peak demand rises substantially with the extra lane, the conclusion fails.
So the argument assumes demand will not rise substantially.
keyConcept: A demand-versus-capacity argument silently assumes demand is fixed; induced demand can defeat that assumption.
commonMistake: Treating engineering feasibility, cost-worthiness, or irrelevant comparisons as the load-bearing assumption instead of the fixed-demand premise.

optionExplanations.0: Whether the benefit justifies the cost is a value judgement about desirability, not a premise the factual conclusion needs.
optionExplanations.1: How this road compares with others has no bearing on whether congestion on this particular road will clear.
optionExplanations.2: The availability of alternative routes is not required; the conclusion concerns this road's demand-versus-capacity balance.
optionExplanations.4: Whether existing lanes must be narrowed is an engineering detail; the argument already stipulates capacity rises by 50%.

shortExplanation: The word 'significant' is used first in its statistical sense (an effect unlikely to be due to chance) and then in its everyday sense (important or sizeable). Trading on these two meanings of one term is the fallacy of equivocation.
solutionSteps: Note the first sentence uses 'significant' in its technical, statistical sense.
Recognise that statistical significance says nothing about how large or clinically important the effect is.
See that the second sentence switches to the everyday sense of 'significant' as 'important'.
The conclusion follows only if the two senses are treated as one — equivocation.
