keyConcept: Equivocation: an argument trades on two different meanings of a single key term to make an invalid inference appear valid.
commonMistake: Mislabelling the flaw as division, appeal to authority, unrepresentative sampling, or reversed causation — none of which this passage commits.

optionExplanations.0: This describes the fallacy of division, but the argument never reasons from a group average to individual patients.
optionExplanations.1: An appeal to authority would rest the claim on who asserts it; here a (defective) chain of reasoning is offered instead.
optionExplanations.2: An unrepresentative-sample objection concerns generalising from an atypical group; the defect here is verbal, not statistical.
optionExplanations.4: There is no reversal of cause and effect; the argument does not claim better health produced the blood-pressure change.

shortExplanation: No statistics-degree holder works nights, so every night-shift worker lacks that degree. At least one night-shift worker is a manager, so at least one manager lacks a statistics degree.
solutionSteps: From 'no statistics-degree holder works the night shift', every night-shift worker holds no statistics degree.
From 'some night-shift workers are managers', at least one night-shift worker is a manager.
That person is both a manager and a night-shift worker, so holds no statistics degree.
Therefore at least one manager does not hold a statistics degree, which follows necessarily.
keyConcept: Chaining a universal exclusion with an existential premise yields a guaranteed particular conclusion, without inflating 'some' into 'all'.
commonMistake: Converting a 'some' statement into an 'all' statement, or drawing conclusions the premises do not force.

optionExplanations.0: Only some night-shift workers are stated to be managers, so it does not follow that every night-shift worker is a manager.
optionExplanations.1: 'Some night-shift workers are managers' does not give 'all managers work nights'; that illicitly converts the premise.
optionExplanations.2: Every biologist holds a statistics degree and no such person works nights, so no biologist can work the night shift.
optionExplanations.3: The night-shift manager guaranteed by the premises holds no statistics degree, so at least one manager lacks it; this must be true.
optionExplanations.4: A biologist could still be a manager on a non-night shift, so the premises do not force that no biologist is a manager.

shortExplanation: Dividing defects by units produced gives rates of 2% (X), 5% (Y) and 6% (Z). Factory Z has the highest defect rate while also producing the fewest units, so both parts of that statement hold.
solutionSteps: Compute each defect rate: X = 40/2000 = 2%.
Z has the highest rate and its 800 units are the fewest produced, so both halves of the statement are true.
keyConcept: Compare proportions (defects divided by output), not raw defect counts, when judging relative quality.
commonMistake: Confusing absolute defect counts with defect rates, or output volume with defect contribution.

optionExplanations.0: The largest producer is Y at 5%, but the highest rate belongs to Z at 6%, so greater output does not drive the highest rate.
optionExplanations.2: Judging reliability by raw defect count (150) ignores the rate; Y's 5% is below Z's 6%.
optionExplanations.3: Similar defect counts (40 vs 48) come from very different outputs, giving rates of 2% and 6%, so quality is not similar.
optionExplanations.4: Despite the smallest output, Z had 48 defects, more than X's 40, so Z is not the smallest contributor to the total.

shortExplanation: Since a Mathematics distinction guarantees an offer, K's lack of an offer means K has no distinction (contrapositive). Rule 3 then requires that K, lacking the distinction, has relevant work experience.
solutionSteps: Rule 1: a Mathematics distinction guarantees an offer.
K was not offered a place, so by contrapositive K has no Mathematics distinction.
Rule 3: every applicant has a distinction or relevant work experience (or both).
K lacks the distinction, so K must have relevant work experience.
keyConcept: Combine the contrapositive of a sufficient-condition rule with a disjunctive rule to force the remaining alternative.
commonMistake: Reading rule 2 backwards — being denied a place does not prove the interview was failed, since denial can arise for other reasons.

optionExplanations.0: If K had the distinction, rule 1 would guarantee an offer, contradicting that K was not offered a place.
optionExplanations.1: The rules do not determine the interview result, so 'passed' is not forced.
optionExplanations.2: Rule 2 says failing the interview leads to no offer, but the converse does not hold, so a failed interview is not forced.
optionExplanations.3: This contradicts the deduction that K must have relevant work experience via rule 3.

shortExplanation: The €5 million projection multiplies the new €2.50 toll by last year's 2,000,000 crossings. This is valid only if roughly the same number of cars keep crossing after the price rise.
solutionSteps: Find last year's crossings: €4,000,000 / €2.00 = 2,000,000 cars.
The projection assumes the new revenue = €2.50 * 2,000,000 = €5,000,000.
This holds only if the number of crossings stays about the same.
Negation test: if crossings decline after the rise, revenue falls short of €5 million and the conclusion fails.
So the argument assumes traffic will not decline.
keyConcept: A revenue projection that reuses the old quantity at a new price assumes demand is unaffected by the price change.
commonMistake: Confusing the use of the funds (repair cost) or the necessity of the plan with the arithmetic assumption the revenue estimate actually needs.

optionExplanations.0: Whether the toll is the only funding option is irrelevant to whether raising it yields €5 million.
optionExplanations.1: Drivers' opinion of fairness is not required; revenue can reach €5 million even if drivers resent the toll, provided they still cross.
optionExplanations.2: The argument needs future traffic to hold up, not that the current toll deters nobody.
optionExplanations.4: This confuses the cost of the repairs with the calculation of revenue raised; the revenue conclusion is independent of repair cost.

shortExplanation: The study has no comparison group, so it cannot show the remedy caused the improvement. If an inert placebo capsule produces the identical 70% improvement, the effect cannot be credited to the remedy's active ingredients.
solutionSteps: Note the design has no control group, only patients who took the remedy.
The conclusion is causal: the remedy is effective.
A placebo group improving by the same 70% shows the improvement occurs without any active ingredient.
So expectation and natural fluctuation, not the remedy, can explain the result, undercutting the causal claim.
keyConcept: An uncontrolled before-after result cannot establish causation; a placebo control that matches the effect removes the ingredient as the cause.
commonMistake: Mistaking cost, tradition, chemical content, or a small dropout for something that bears on whether the remedy caused the improvement.

optionExplanations.1: A dispensing fee bears on who enrolled or on cost, not on whether the remedy caused the improvement.
optionExplanations.2: Containing plant compounds does not show any of them relieves headaches; chemical content is not clinical effect.
optionExplanations.3: Long traditional use is an appeal to tradition and is not evidence of efficacy.
optionExplanations.4: A dropout of 10 of 200 does not explain the improvement among those who completed the study.

shortExplanation: The argument treats the absence of evidence that aspartame causes cancer as proof that it does not — the appeal to ignorance. Not having found an effect is not the same as having shown there is none.
solutionSteps: Identify the premise: no study has shown aspartame causes cancer.
Identify the conclusion: aspartame certainly does not cause cancer and is entirely safe.
Recognise the leap from 'no evidence of harm' to 'evidence of no harm'.
This is the appeal to ignorance; studies may have been too few, small, or short to detect the effect, so the certainty is unwarranted.
keyConcept: Appeal to ignorance (argumentum ad ignorantiam): absence of evidence for a claim is wrongly treated as evidence against it.
commonMistake: Mislabelling the flaw as post hoc, hasty generalisation, equivocation, or composition — none of which this argument commits.

optionExplanations.1: No causal claim is drawn from a temporal sequence, so post hoc does not fit.
optionExplanations.2: The argument makes no claim about sampling from a body of studies, so unrepresentative sampling misreads it.
optionExplanations.3: No key term shifts meaning between premises and conclusion, so equivocation is not the flaw.
optionExplanations.4: There is no part-to-whole inference, so the fallacy of composition does not apply.

shortExplanation: Using speed times teeth conserved at each mesh: A to B gives 1200 * 15/45 = 400 rpm anticlockwise, C shares B's shaft at 400 rpm anticlockwise, and C to D gives 400 * 20/40 = 200 rpm clockwise. Two meshes reverse direction twice, restoring gear A's sense.
solutionSteps: At a mesh, driven speed = driver speed * (driver teeth / driven teeth).
A to B: 1200 * 15/45 = 400 rpm; B turns opposite to A, so anticlockwise.
C is on B's shaft, so C also turns at 400 rpm anticlockwise.
C to D: 400 * 20/40 = 200 rpm; D turns opposite to C, so clockwise.
Two meshes give two reversals, returning D to gear A's clockwise sense.
keyConcept: Speed scales inversely with tooth count at each mesh; each mesh reverses rotation, and gears on a shared shaft rotate together.
commonMistake: Inverting a tooth ratio (mixing up driver and driven) or miscounting the reversals, which flips the reported direction.

optionExplanations.1: 3600 rpm inverts the A-B tooth ratio (using 45/15), confusing which gear is the driver.
optionExplanations.2: The 200 rpm speed is right but the direction is wrong; two mesh reversals restore gear A's clockwise sense.
optionExplanations.3: 400 rpm stops at gear C and ignores the C-D reduction stage.
optionExplanations.4: 800 rpm inverts the C-D tooth ratio (using 40/20), treating the larger driven gear as if it sped the shaft up.

shortExplanation: The positive starch test means the sample was not heated (biconditional), which forces the biuret test to be negative (disjunction), which by modus tollens means the sample does not contain protein.
solutionSteps: Statement 4 gives a positive starch test.
Statement 2 is a biconditional, so a positive starch test means the sample was not heated.
Statement 3 says biuret negative or heated; since not heated, the biuret test is negative.
Statement 1 says protein implies a positive biuret test; the biuret test is negative, so by modus tollens the sample has no protein.
keyConcept: Chain a biconditional, a disjunctive syllogism, and modus tollens to propagate a single known fact through the conditions.
commonMistake: Misreading the biconditional to conclude the sample was heated, or affirming the consequent to conclude it contains protein.

optionExplanations.0: The biconditional makes a positive starch test equivalent to 'not heated', so the sample was not heated.
optionExplanations.2: 'Not heated' is correct but 'biuret positive' is false, and a conjunction with a false part is false.
optionExplanations.3: Statement 3 with 'not heated' forces the biuret test to be negative, not positive.
optionExplanations.4: The biuret test is negative, and statement 1 then forces the sample to lack protein, so it cannot contain protein.

shortExplanation: Survival is measured from the date of diagnosis. If the test merely moves that date three years earlier without delaying death, screen-detected patients automatically show longer post-diagnosis survival while dying at the same time — lead-time bias. The argument must assume the extra survival is a real postponement of death.
solutionSteps: Note the conclusion is causal: screening will prolong lives.
Observe that 'survival after diagnosis' is timed from the diagnosis date.
Recognise that detecting the tumour earlier starts the survival clock sooner.
Apply the negation test: if the extra measured survival is only earlier counting, with deaths on the same dates, the conclusion fails.
So the argument assumes the longer survival is a genuine delay of death, not lead-time bias.
keyConcept: Lead-time bias: earlier detection lengthens measured survival-from-diagnosis even when the date of death is unchanged, so longer post-diagnosis survival need not mean lives are prolonged.
commonMistake: Confusing a desirable property of the test (perfect sensitivity) or the disease's importance with the assumption the causal conclusion actually requires.

optionExplanations.1: How important tumour T is relative to other causes of death is irrelevant to whether screening prolongs the lives of those who have it.
optionExplanations.2: Perfect detection would make the test better but is not required; the inference about detected patients can stand even if some cases are missed.
optionExplanations.3: This is far stronger than needed; the argument requires earlier detection to postpone death, not a universal three-year ceiling on symptomatic survival.
optionExplanations.4: Relative cost bears on value for money, not on whether the programme prolongs life.

shortExplanation: Removing bacterium B halts and partly reverses the weight gain, and re-colonising restores it. This reversibility-plus-re-challenge in the same animals is the strongest experimental demonstration that B is causing the effect.
solutionSteps: The claim is causal: bacterium B causes excess weight gain.
The strongest support manipulates the putative cause and observes the effect track it.
Eliminating B stops and reverses the weight gain (reversibility).
Re-colonising with B brings the weight gain back (re-challenge).
The same animals serve as their own controls, ruling out many alternative explanations.
keyConcept: Demonstrating that removing a cause abolishes the effect and reinstating it restores the effect is powerful evidence of causation.
commonMistake: Treating a cross-species association or an unrelated property of the organism as strong causal evidence, or overlooking that a temperature difference introduces a confounder.

optionExplanations.1: A differing ambient temperature is a confounder affecting metabolism and weight, so it would weaken the attribution to B, not strengthen it.
optionExplanations.2: Culturability is a laboratory convenience that says nothing about whether B affects body weight.
optionExplanations.3: A cross-sectional association in humans is weak and open to reverse causation, so it is not strong causal evidence.
optionExplanations.4: The relative cost of rearing the two groups is irrelevant to causation.

shortExplanation: A high group average does not guarantee that every member beats every rival, since some members may lie below the mean. Inferring a specific fact about the individual Dr Rossi from a fact about the aggregate is the fallacy of division.
solutionSteps: Note the premise is about the department's average output being highest.
Note the conclusion is about a specific individual, Dr Rossi, beating every rival.
Recognise that a group can have the highest mean while containing below-average members.
So distributing the aggregate property onto an individual member is the fallacy of division.
keyConcept: Fallacy of division: wrongly inferring that a property of a group as a whole (or its average) must hold of each individual member.
commonMistake: Confusing division with its mirror image, composition, which reasons from the parts to the whole.

optionExplanations.1: This describes composition (part-to-whole), the converse fallacy; the argument reasons from the whole/average to a part.
optionExplanations.2: No one's identity or authority is used to dismiss a claim, so there is no ad hominem.
optionExplanations.3: No causal claim is made; the mistake is distributing an average onto an individual, not inferring causation from correlation.
optionExplanations.4: The error is not about sample size; the departmental average could be perfectly well established.

shortExplanation: Each operation multiplies the surviving disinfectant by 48/60 = 4/5, so after n operations the fraction is (4/5)^n. Since (4/5)^3 = 0.512 is still above 0.5 while (4/5)^4 = 0.4096 is below, four operations are required.
solutionSteps: Each operation removes 12 of the 60 well-mixed litres and replaces them with water.
So it multiplies the remaining original disinfectant by 48/60 = 4/5.
After n operations the surviving fraction is (4/5)^n.
Require (4/5)^n < 1/2.
keyConcept: Repeated draw-and-replace mixing decays the original substance geometrically by a fixed ratio each step, not linearly.
commonMistake: Treating removal as additive (12 litres each time) or misreading 0.512 as already below one-half after three operations.

optionExplanations.0: This treats removal as linear; each replacement re-dilutes what remains, so the loss is geometric.
optionExplanations.1: 5 over-counts by one; the first power below 0.5 is the fourth, not the fifth.
optionExplanations.3: After three operations the fraction is 0.512, still above one-half, so three operations are not enough.
optionExplanations.4: Since 4/5 < 1, the fraction decreases toward zero and must eventually drop below one-half.

shortExplanation: Since the batch was not released, the seals cannot be intact (modus tollens on rule 2). The disjunction in rule 3 then forces the cold chain to have been broken, and rule 1 gives that the batch is destroyed.
solutionSteps: Rule 2 says intact seals lead to release; the batch was not released, so by modus tollens the seals are not intact.
Rule 3 says the cold chain was broken or the seals are intact; the seals are not intact, so the cold chain was broken.
Rule 1 says a broken cold chain leads to destruction.
So by modus ponens the batch is destroyed.
keyConcept: Chain modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism, and modus ponens to force a definite outcome from conditional rules.
commonMistake: Stopping short of the full chain, or inferring 'cold chain not broken' from 'not released', which is a denying-the-antecedent slip.

optionExplanations.0: A definite conclusion does follow — the batch is destroyed — so the premises are not indeterminate.
optionExplanations.2: This contradicts rule 4, which states the batch was not released.
optionExplanations.3: Modus tollens on rules 2 and 4 shows the seals are not intact, so this is false.
optionExplanations.4: The deduction establishes that the cold chain was broken, the opposite of this option.

shortExplanation: The leap from a trial result in Country X to a prediction for Country Y works only if the vaccine's protective effect is transportable — not substantially lower in Country Y's population. If a different strain or immune profile made it much less effective there, the 80% figure would not carry over.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: vaccinated people in Country Y will have roughly 80% lower risk.
Note the evidence comes from a trial in Country X.
The inference requires the effect to transfer to Country Y's population.
Negation test: if effectiveness in Country Y were substantially lower, the 80% would not carry over and the conclusion fails.
So the argument assumes no such efficacy-reducing difference between the populations.
keyConcept: Transporting a study result to a new population assumes the effect is not substantially different there (external transportability).
commonMistake: Confusing relative risk reduction with disease burden, population coverage with individual efficacy, or internal representativeness with transportability to a different population.

optionExplanations.0: The existence of a cheaper or better alternative is a comparative decision point; the conclusion only claims the vaccine cuts risk by 80%.
optionExplanations.1: Whether the whole population can be vaccinated concerns how many are protected, not the per-person efficacy the conclusion asserts.
optionExplanations.3: Internal representativeness bears on generalising the trial to Country X itself; the contested step is trial-to-Country-Y.
optionExplanations.4: A relative risk reduction can hold whether the disease is common or rare, so equal incidence is not required.

shortExplanation: The counting method changed at the same time: automatic turnstiles that double-count repeat entries can inflate the recorded figure even if real usage was unchanged. This makes the apparent 30% rise a possible measurement artifact, attacking the very evidence the causal claim rests on.
solutionSteps: The argument infers causation from a single datum: a 30% rise in recorded visits.
The strongest weakener undermines the datum itself, not just offers a rival cause.
The switch to automatic turnstiles that double-count repeat entries occurred at the start of the same year.
So the recorded rise may reflect a counting change rather than a real increase in use, undercutting the evidence.
keyConcept: When an argument rests on a measured figure, a simultaneous change in how the figure is measured can explain the change as an artifact.
commonMistake: Assuming any co-occurring change weakens the argument without checking the direction of its effect, or confusing a cost or descriptive fact with the causal reasoning.

optionExplanations.0: A competing free-Wi-Fi source would draw people away from libraries, predicting fewer visits, so it does not explain the rise.
optionExplanations.1: A budget overrun bears on value for money, not on whether the Wi-Fi caused the rise.
optionExplanations.3: The relative age of users versus non-users is a static descriptive fact that says nothing about why visits changed over the year.
optionExplanations.4: What visitors did once inside does not bear on whether the Wi-Fi attracted them.

shortExplanation: This is the gambler's fallacy. The low probability of four girls in a row applies only as a prediction before any births; once they have occurred, the fifth birth is independent and the chance of a boy stays one half regardless of the streak.
solutionSteps: Note the births are stated to be independent.
'Four girls in a row is unlikely' is a low probability attached to the whole sequence in advance.
Once four girls have occurred, the fifth birth is a fresh independent event.
So the probability of a boy remains one half; the past streak carries no memory and cannot make a boy 'due'.
keyConcept: Gambler's fallacy: for independent events, past outcomes do not change the probability of the next outcome.
commonMistake: Transferring the low prior probability of a whole sequence onto the next single event.

optionExplanations.0: The father reasons about a single next event, not a population proportion, so 'unrepresentative sample' misdescribes the error.
optionExplanations.1: The argument stipulates equal probability; correcting the real-world ratio would leave the independence error untouched.
optionExplanations.3: 'Likely' is used consistently to mean 'probable' throughout, so there is no equivocation.
optionExplanations.4: There is no cause-and-effect relationship being reversed; the flaw concerns probability and independence.

shortExplanation: Each partner's weight is capital times months invested: Anna 144,000, Bianca 144,000, Carla 54,000, totalling 342,000. Bianca's share is 144,000/342,000 = 8/19.
keyConcept: Profit-sharing by capital times time weights both the amount contributed and its duration together.
commonMistake: Weighting by capital only or time only, or crediting Carla with the full 12 months when she withdrew after 6.

optionExplanations.0: 4/13 weights by time only (12:8:6), dropping the capital factor.
optionExplanations.1: 4/11 credits Carla's capital for all 12 months instead of 6, giving 144:144:108.
optionExplanations.3: 6/13 weights by capital only (12:18:9), dropping the time factor.
optionExplanations.4: 1/3 splits equally, ignoring both the differing capitals and durations.

shortExplanation: The absolute-value equation splits into x^2 - 4 = 3 and x^2 - 4 = -3, giving x^2 = 7 and x^2 = 1. These yield x = ±sqrt(7) and x = ±1, four distinct real values.
solutionSteps: Split |x^2 - 4| = 3 into x^2 - 4 = 3 and x^2 - 4 = -3.
From x^2 - 4 = 3 get x^2 = 7, so x = ±sqrt(7).
From x^2 - 4 = -3 get x^2 = 1, so x = ±1.
All four values sqrt(7), -sqrt(7), 1, -1 are distinct, so there are 4 solutions.
keyConcept: An absolute-value equation |A| = k with k > 0 splits into A = k and A = -k; each positive x^2 value gives two opposite roots.
commonMistake: Solving only one case, or forgetting that each x^2 value produces two opposite roots.

optionExplanations.2: The four values do not coincide, so none of them repeat.
optionExplanations.3: This counts only one case (x^2 = 7 alone or x^2 = 1 alone), which gives just two roots.
optionExplanations.4: This ignores that each x^2 value yields two opposite roots.

shortExplanation: The total number of committees is C(9,4) = 126. Subtracting those with 0 women (5) and exactly 1 woman (40) leaves 81 with at least 2 women, giving probability 81/126 = 9/14.
solutionSteps: Count all committees: C(9,4) = 126.
Count committees with 0 women: C(5,4) = 5.
Count committees with exactly 1 woman: C(4,1)·C(5,3) = 4·10 = 40.
Committees with at least 2 women: 126 - 5 - 40 = 81.
Probability = 81/126 = 9/14.
keyConcept: For 'at least' events, subtract the complementary cases (fewer than 2 women) from the total.
commonMistake: Computing the probability of exactly one woman and reporting it as the answer.

optionExplanations.1: This equals 40/126, the probability of exactly one woman only.
optionExplanations.3: This corresponds to the complement (0 or 1 woman) after a simplification slip.
optionExplanations.4: This over-counts and is not obtained from a correct case analysis.

shortExplanation: Setting t = log2(x) turns the equation into t + 1/t = 5/2, whose roots are t = 2 and t = 1/2. These give x = 4 and x = sqrt(2), with product 4·sqrt(2) = 4√2.
solutionSteps: Let t = log2(x); by change of base logx(2) = 1/t.
The equation becomes t + 1/t = 5/2, i.e. 2t^2 - 5t + 2 = 0.
Solve to get t = 2 or t = 1/2.
Convert back: x = 2^2 = 4 and x = 2^(1/2) = sqrt(2), both valid.
Product = 4·sqrt(2) = 4√2 (equivalently 2^(2 + 1/2) = 2^(5/2)).
keyConcept: The substitution t = log2(x) with logx(2) = 1/t reduces the equation to a quadratic; the product of solutions equals 2^(sum of t-values).
commonMistake: Adding the two solutions or misapplying exponent laws when combining them.

optionExplanations.1: This keeps only t = 2 and mishandles the exponents to reach 2^3.
optionExplanations.2: This reports only the single solution sqrt(2), keeping just t = 1/2.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the product of the t-values (2·1/2 = 1) as an exponent, misapplying the exponent law.
optionExplanations.4: This adds the two solutions (4 + sqrt(2)) instead of multiplying them.

shortExplanation: With simultaneous draws, use combinations: choosing 1 of 4 defective and 2 of 8 good gives C(4,1)·C(8,2) = 112 favourable outcomes out of C(12,3) = 220, so the probability is 112/220 = 28/55.
solutionSteps: Favourable outcomes: C(4,1)·C(8,2) = 4·28 = 112.
Total outcomes: C(12,3) = 220.
Probability = 112/220 = 28/55.
keyConcept: Drawing without replacement from a fixed set requires combinations (hypergeometric counting), not independent-trial probabilities.
commonMistake: Treating the draws as independent with replacement and applying a binomial formula.

optionExplanations.0: This omits the C(8,2) factor for the two good components.
optionExplanations.1: This halves the favourable count, forgetting a factor in the pair count.
optionExplanations.3: This treats the draws as independent with p = 1/3, a with-replacement error.
optionExplanations.4: This just reports the defective fraction 4/12, ignoring the 'exactly one of three' condition.

shortExplanation: The right side x + 2 requires x >= -2. Solving both sign cases gives roots x = 3, x = -2, and x = 1, all valid, so there are three distinct solutions.
solutionSteps: Require x + 2 >= 0, so x >= -2.
Case x^2 - 4 >= 0: x^2 - x - 6 = 0 gives x = 3 or x = -2, both valid.
Case x^2 - 4 < 0: x^2 + x - 2 = 0 gives x = 1 or x = -2; only x = 1 lies in this range.
Distinct valid solutions are x = -2, 1, 3, giving three in total.
keyConcept: Absolute-value equations split by sign; each candidate must be checked against the domain condition and its case's validity range.
commonMistake: Solving only one sign case, or double-counting x = -2 as if it were two separate roots.

optionExplanations.1: This counts all four algebraic roots without noticing x = -2 repeats and without the x >= -2 check.
optionExplanations.2: This wrongly requires x > -2 strictly, discarding x = -2 and keeping too few.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes no solution exists, skipping the case analysis.
optionExplanations.4: This solves only the case x^2 - 4 = x + 2, missing the sign-flipped case that yields x = 1.

shortExplanation: The law of cosines gives BC^2 = 64 + 25 - 40 = 49, so BC = 7. The law of sines then gives 2R = 7/sin 60°, so R = 7/sqrt(3) = 7√3/3.
solutionSteps: Law of sines: 2R = a/sin A = 7/(sqrt(3)/2) = 14/sqrt(3).
keyConcept: The circumradius satisfies 2R = a/sin A, where a is the side opposite angle A.
commonMistake: Forgetting to halve 2R, or omitting the sin A denominator.

optionExplanations.0: This multiplies by sin A instead of dividing by it.
optionExplanations.1: This reports 2R = 14√3/3 as R, forgetting to halve.
optionExplanations.2: This divides by an extra factor of 2, using R = a/(4 sin A).
optionExplanations.3: This sets R = a/2, forgetting the sin A denominator.

shortExplanation: Substituting u = 2^x turns the equation into u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0, giving u = 1 or u = 4, so x = 0 or x = 2. Their sum is 2.
solutionSteps: Notice 2^(2x) = (2^x)^2, so let u = 2^x (with u > 0). The equation becomes u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0.
Factor: (u - 1)(u - 4) = 0, so u = 1 or u = 4.
Convert back to x: 2^x = 1 gives x = 0, and 2^x = 4 gives x = 2.
Sum of the real solutions = 0 + 2 = 2.
keyConcept: The substitution u = 2^x converts an exponential equation into a quadratic; solve for u, then take logs (base 2) to recover the x-values before answering.
commonMistake: Reporting the sum of the u-roots (1 + 4 = 5) instead of the sum of the x-values (0 + 2 = 2).

optionExplanations.0: This is the sum of the u-roots (1 + 4 = 5), the values before converting back to x.
optionExplanations.1: 6 would require x-values summing to 6, such as 2 and 4. But 2^x = 4 gives x = 2 (not 4), and the other root 2^x = 1 gives x = 0, so neither solution equals 4 and the true sum is 2.
optionExplanations.2: This mis-solves 2^x = 4 as x = 4 (confusing base and exponent); correctly, 2^x = 4 means x = 2.
optionExplanations.4: This reports only one solution (x = 0) and forgets to add the second solution x = 2.

shortExplanation: The product is odd only when both numbers are odd. There are C(5,2) = 10 all-odd pairs out of C(10,2) = 45, so P(odd) = 2/9 and P(even) = 1 - 2/9 = 7/9.
solutionSteps: The product is even unless both chosen numbers are odd.
All-odd pairs: C(5,2) = 10 (from the five odd numbers).
Total pairs: C(10,2) = 45.
P(product odd) = 10/45 = 2/9, so P(product even) = 1 - 2/9 = 7/9.
keyConcept: A product is even unless every factor is odd; use the complement of the all-odd case.
commonMistake: Reporting the probability of an odd product, or assuming even and odd are equally likely.

optionExplanations.2: This is the probability the product is odd (both numbers odd), the complement.
optionExplanations.3: This mis-counts the favourable or total pairs.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes even and odd products are equally likely, but only an all-odd pair gives an odd product.

shortExplanation: At steady state the amount just after a dose satisfies L = 60 + 0.25L, so 0.75L = 60 and L = 80 mg. This equals the infinite geometric sum 60/(1 - 0.25).
solutionSteps: Let L be the amount just after a dose in steady state.
Each day the previous amount decays to 25%, then 60 mg is added: L = 60 + 0.25L.
Solve: 0.75L = 60, so L = 80 mg.
Equivalently, sum the geometric series 60/(1 - 0.25) = 80 mg.
keyConcept: A repeated dose with fractional retention reaches a steady state L = dose/(1 - retained fraction), the sum of an infinite geometric series.
commonMistake: Using the eliminated fraction (0.75) instead of the retained fraction (0.25) in the sum.

optionExplanations.0: This equals a single dose, ignoring the drug carried over from previous doses.
optionExplanations.1: This is the trough level just before the next dose (0.25 × 80), not the level immediately after.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the eliminated fraction 0.75 instead of the retained fraction 0.25, giving 60/(1 - 0.75).
optionExplanations.4: This adds only the first two doses, truncating the geometric series after two terms.

shortExplanation: Vieta's formulas give p + q + r = 3/2 and pq + pr + qr = 2. Then p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (3/2)^2 - 2·2 = 9/4 - 4 = -7/4.
solutionSteps: By Vieta's: p + q + r = 3/2 and pq + pr + qr = 4/2 = 2.
Use the identity p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (p+q+r)^2 - 2(pq+pr+qr).
keyConcept: Vieta's formulas for ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d give sum of roots = -b/a and pairwise sum = c/a; combine with the square-of-sum identity.
commonMistake: Forgetting to divide the coefficients by the leading coefficient, or omitting the -2(pairwise sum) term.

optionExplanations.0: This computes only (p+q+r)^2 = 9/4, forgetting to subtract the pairwise term.
optionExplanations.1: This forgets to divide the pairwise sum by the leading coefficient, giving 9/4 - 2·4.
optionExplanations.3: This reads coefficients directly as symmetric sums, ignoring the leading coefficient 2.
optionExplanations.4: This adds rather than subtracts the pairwise term, giving 9/4 + 4.

shortExplanation: Rearranging gives (x - 4)/(x + 3) >= 0. The quotient is non-negative for x < -3 and for x >= 4, so the solution set is (-infinity, -3) ∪ [4, +infinity).
solutionSteps: Combine over a common denominator: (x - 4)/(x + 3) >= 0.
Critical values: x = 4 (numerator zero, included) and x = -3 (denominator zero, excluded).
Sign chart: quotient positive for x < -3 and x > 4, zero at x = 4.
Solution: (-infinity, -3) ∪ [4, +infinity).
keyConcept: Rational inequalities must be rearranged to compare with zero and analysed with a sign chart; a zero denominator is always excluded, a zero numerator is included when the inequality is non-strict.
commonMistake: Multiplying both sides by (x + 3) without accounting for its sign, losing a branch of the solution.

optionExplanations.0: This multiplies by (x + 3) as if always positive, losing the branch where the denominator is negative.
optionExplanations.1: This includes x = -3, but the expression is undefined there.
optionExplanations.3: This excludes x = 4, but the non-strict inequality includes it since the numerator is zero there.
optionExplanations.4: This selects the interval between the critical values, where the quotient is actually negative.

shortExplanation: Rewriting to common bases gives x + 3y = 11 and 2x - y = 1. Solving yields x = 2 and y = 3, so x + y = 5.
solutionSteps: First equation: 2^x·2^(3y) = 2^(x+3y) = 2^11, so x + 3y = 11.
Second equation: 3^(2x)/3^y = 3^(2x-y) = 3^1, so 2x - y = 1.
From the second, y = 2x - 1; substitute: x + 3(2x - 1) = 11, so 7x = 14, x = 2.
Then y = 3, so x + y = 5.
keyConcept: Rewrite all terms to a common base so exponents can be equated, forming a linear system.
commonMistake: Failing to expand 8 = 2^3 or 9 = 3^2, dropping the exponent factor.

optionExplanations.0: This treats 8^y as 2^y, dropping the exponent 3, so the first equation reads x + y = 11.
optionExplanations.2: This solves correctly but reports x alone instead of the requested sum x + y.
optionExplanations.3: This just adds the right-hand exponents 11 and 1 without solving the system.
optionExplanations.4: This treats 9^x as 3^x, dropping the exponent 2, giving x + y = 6.

shortExplanation: The geometric condition (a + d)^2 = a(a + 4d) gives d = 2a = 6, so the terms are 3, 9, 27 and the common ratio is 3.
solutionSteps: The three terms are a = 3, a + d, and a + 4d.
Geometric condition: (a + d)^2 = a(a + 4d).
Expand: a^2 + 2ad + d^2 = a^2 + 4ad, so d^2 - 2ad = 0, i.e. d(d - 2a) = 0.
Since d ≠ 0, d = 2a = 6; terms are 3, 9, 27.
Common ratio = 9/3 = 3.
keyConcept: Three consecutive geometric terms satisfy (middle)^2 = (first)·(third); the ratio is a later term divided by the preceding one.
commonMistake: Reporting the common difference (6) or a term value (9) instead of the ratio, or inverting the ratio.

optionExplanations.0: This computes d/a = 2, confusing that relationship with the geometric ratio.
optionExplanations.2: This inverts the ratio, dividing an earlier term by a later one.
optionExplanations.3: This reports the second geometric term (9) instead of the ratio.
optionExplanations.4: This reports the arithmetic common difference d = 6 instead of the geometric ratio.

solutionSteps: Sum of squares: a^2/(1 - r^2) = 40.5.
keyConcept: The squares of a geometric series form another geometric series with ratio r^2; combine the two sum formulas and factor 1 - r^2 = (1 - r)(1 + r).
commonMistake: Mishandling the 1 - r^2 factorisation or confusing r with r^2.

optionExplanations.0: This confuses r with r^2 or misreads the ratio of the two sums.
optionExplanations.2: This comes from mishandling the 1 - r^2 factorisation as (1 - r)^2.
optionExplanations.3: With this ratio the terms fall off too slowly and the sum of squares would exceed 40.5.
optionExplanations.4: This gives (1 - r)/(1 + r) = 1/3, not 1/2, so the sum of squares would not be 40.5.

shortExplanation: The power of the point gives PT^2 = PA·PB, so 64 = 4·PB and PB = 16 m. The chord AB = PB - PA = 16 - 4 = 12 m.
solutionSteps: Apply the tangent-secant relation: PT^2 = PA·PB.
Solve 8^2 = 4·PB, so PB = 64/4 = 16 m.
AB is the chord: AB = PB - PA = 16 - 4 = 12 m.
keyConcept: Power of a point: for a tangent PT and secant meeting the circle at A then B from external point P, PT^2 = PA·PB.
commonMistake: Reporting PB instead of subtracting the external segment PA to get the chord AB.

optionExplanations.0: This reports PB, the full distance to the far edge, without subtracting PA.
optionExplanations.2: This adds PA + PB, treating the answer as the total secant path.
optionExplanations.3: This takes the arithmetic mean of PA and PB, with no geometric basis.
optionExplanations.4: This reports the tangent length PT itself, ignoring the power-of-a-point relation.

shortExplanation: The circle has centre (1, 2) and radius 5. The centre-to-line distance is 3, so the chord length is 2·sqrt(25 - 9) = 8.
solutionSteps: Complete the square: (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 25, centre (1, 2), radius 5.
Distance from centre to 3x + 4y - 26 = 0: |3 + 8 - 26|/sqrt(9 + 16) = 15/5 = 3.
Half-chord = sqrt(r^2 - d^2) = sqrt(25 - 9) = 4.
Full chord = 2·4 = 8.
keyConcept: A chord's length is 2·sqrt(r^2 - d^2), where d is the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line.
commonMistake: Forgetting to double the half-chord, or adding d^2 instead of subtracting it.

optionExplanations.0: This returns the half-chord (4), forgetting to double it.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes the line passes through the centre and returns the diameter 2r.
optionExplanations.2: This computes 2·sqrt(r^2 + d^2), adding d^2 instead of subtracting.
optionExplanations.3: This uses 2d, mistaking twice the centre-to-line distance for the chord.

shortExplanation: Using cos 2x = 2cos^2 x - 1, the equation factors as (2cos x - 1)(cos x + 1) = 0, giving cos x = 1/2 (x = π/3, 5π/3) and cos x = -1 (x = π): three solutions.
solutionSteps: Substitute cos 2x = 2cos^2 x - 1: 2cos^2 x + cos x - 1 = 0.
Factor: (2cos x - 1)(cos x + 1) = 0.
cos x = 1/2 gives x = π/3 and x = 5π/3 on [0, 2π).
cos x = -1 gives x = π.
Total: three solutions.
keyConcept: The double-angle identity converts cos 2x into a quadratic in cos x, which factors to give the base angles.
commonMistake: Dropping one factor, or miscounting solutions of cos x = -1 in the interval.

optionExplanations.1: This mis-expands cos 2x and picks up a spurious extra root.
optionExplanations.2: This keeps only cos x = 1/2, overlooking the cos x = -1 branch.
optionExplanations.3: This counts cos x = -1 as giving two solutions, but it yields only x = π.
optionExplanations.4: This counts roots over a doubled range such as 0 <= x < 4π.

shortExplanation: The area gives sin A = 1/2; since A is obtuse, A = 150° and cos A = -sqrt(3)/2. The cosine rule then gives BC^2 = 64 + 25 + 40√3 = 89 + 40√3.
solutionSteps: Area = (1/2)·8·5·sin A = 20 sin A = 10, so sin A = 1/2.
Since A is obtuse, A = 150° and cos A = -sqrt(3)/2.
keyConcept: The area formula fixes sin A; the obtuse condition selects the negative cosine, which the cosine rule then uses.
commonMistake: Taking the acute angle (A = 30°) and using a positive cosine, contrary to the obtuse condition.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the acute solution A = 30° with cos A = +sqrt(3)/2, ignoring that A is obtuse.
optionExplanations.1: This sets cos A = -1/2, confusing the value of sin A with cos A.
optionExplanations.3: This omits the cosine term, effectively treating A as 90°.
optionExplanations.4: This drops the factor of 2, using AB·AC·cos A instead of 2·AB·AC·cos A.

shortExplanation: The axial cross-section is an isosceles triangle with base 10, equal sides 13, and height 12. The inscribed sphere's radius equals this triangle's inradius: Area/semiperimeter = 60/18 = 10/3 cm.
solutionSteps: Slant height = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = 13 cm.
Axial section: isosceles triangle, base 2·5 = 10, equal sides 13, height 12.
So the sphere radius = 10/3 cm.
keyConcept: A sphere inscribed in a cone has radius equal to the inradius of the cone's axial cross-sectional triangle.
commonMistake: Dividing the area by the full perimeter instead of the semiperimeter.

optionExplanations.0: This takes half the base radius, wrongly assuming the sphere spans half the base width.
optionExplanations.1: This divides by the full perimeter instead of the semiperimeter.
optionExplanations.2: This uses the vertical height in place of the slant length in the tangency relation.
optionExplanations.3: This uses an incorrect similar-triangle ratio Rh/L.

shortExplanation: A circle tangent to both axes has centre (r, r); passing through (2, 1) gives r^2 - 6r + 5 = 0, so r = 1 or r = 5. The centres (1, 1) and (5, 5) are sqrt(32) = 4√2 apart.
solutionSteps: Centre is (r, r) with radius r for tangency to both axes.
Expand: r^2 - 6r + 5 = 0, so r = 1 or r = 5.
Centres are (1, 1) and (5, 5).
Distance = sqrt(4^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(32) = 4√2.
keyConcept: A circle tangent to both axes in the first quadrant has centre (r, r) and radius r; a passing-through condition yields a quadratic in r.
commonMistake: Mis-solving the quadratic, or taking only one coordinate difference in the distance.

optionExplanations.0: This mis-solves the quadratic as r = 1, 3, giving centres (1, 1) and (3, 3).
optionExplanations.1: This mis-places the centres at (0, 0) and (6, 6).
optionExplanations.3: This takes only one coordinate difference (5 - 1 = 4), ignoring the second dimension.
optionExplanations.4: This adds the two radii (1 + 5) instead of finding the distance between centres.

shortExplanation: The expected winnings equal the total prize money divided by the number of tickets: (300 + 4·50 + 10·10)/200 = 600/200 = €3.00.
solutionSteps: Each ticket has probability 1/200 of winning any given prize.
This sums to €3.00, equal to total prizes €600 divided by 200 tickets.
keyConcept: The fair price equals the expected value: total prize money divided by the number of tickets (every prize tier contributes).
commonMistake: Dividing by the number of prizes or including only some prize tiers.

optionExplanations.0: This divides €600 by the number of prizes (15) instead of the number of tickets.
optionExplanations.1: This counts only the €300 grand prize, ignoring the €50 and €10 prizes.
optionExplanations.2: This includes the grand prize and the four €50 prizes but forgets the ten €10 prizes.
optionExplanations.4: This divides €600 by 100 rather than by the 200 tickets.

shortExplanation: Arrange B, C, D, E in 4! = 24 ways, creating five gaps. Placing the three identical A's in three of the five gaps gives C(5,3) = 10 ways, so the total is 24·10 = 240.
solutionSteps: Arrange the four distinct non-A letters: 4! = 24 ways.
These create five gaps (before, between, after).
Place at most one A per gap: choose 3 of 5 gaps, C(5,3) = 10 (A's identical).
keyConcept: The gap method keeps identical items non-adjacent: arrange the others first, then choose gaps by combination.
commonMistake: Using a permutation instead of a combination for the identical A's, or ignoring the non-adjacency condition.

optionExplanations.0: This treats the three A's as one block 'AAA', counting arrangements where they are all together.
optionExplanations.1: This is the total number of unrestricted arrangements (7!/3!), ignoring non-adjacency.
optionExplanations.3: This treats the identical A's as distinguishable, using P(5,3) = 60 instead of C(5,3) = 10.
optionExplanations.4: This is the complementary count (at least two A's adjacent), 840 - 240.

solutionSteps: Joint P(Y and defective) = 0.40·0.05 = 0.020.
Bayes: P(Y | defective) = 0.020/0.032 = 0.625.
keyConcept: Bayes' theorem inverts a conditional: divide the joint probability by the total probability of the evidence.
commonMistake: Reporting the prior, the defect rate, or the joint probability without normalising.

optionExplanations.1: This is the prior P(Y), ignoring the defective evidence.
optionExplanations.2: This is P(defective | Y), the machine's defect rate, inverting the conditional.
optionExplanations.3: This is P(X | defective), the posterior for the other machine.
optionExplanations.4: This is the joint probability P(Y and defective), omitting the division by P(defective).

shortExplanation: With X ~ B(5, 1/4), passing means X >= 4. P(X=5) = 1/1024 and P(X=4) = 15/1024, summing to 16/1024 = 1/64.
solutionSteps: Model correct answers as X ~ B(5, 1/4).
keyConcept: 'At least 4 of 5' under independent guessing is a binomial tail: sum P(X=4) and P(X=5) with p = 1/4.
commonMistake: Omitting the binomial coefficient, or adding only one of the two passing cases.

optionExplanations.0: This drops the binomial coefficient and the fifth question's factor, treating four-correct as one fixed outcome.
optionExplanations.2: This counts only the all-five-correct outcome, omitting the exactly-four case.
optionExplanations.3: This counts only P(X=4), omitting P(X=5); passing needs both.
optionExplanations.4: This uses p = 1/2 as if each question had two options, but each has four.

shortExplanation: Choose the one student who gets their own sheet (C(5,1) = 5) and derange the other four (D4 = 9): (5·9)/120 = 45/120 = 3/8.
solutionSteps: Total orderings: 5! = 120.
Choose which single student gets their own sheet: C(5,1) = 5.
The remaining four sheets must be a derangement: D4 = 9.
Favourable count = 5·9 = 45, so probability = 45/120 = 3/8.
keyConcept: Exactly one fixed point: choose the fixed element, then derange the rest so none of them is fixed.
commonMistake: Using the wrong derangement value for four objects, or omitting the choice of which student is fixed.

optionExplanations.0: This treats it as a plain 1-in-5 chance, ignoring that the other four must all be misplaced.
optionExplanations.1: This uses an incorrect derangement count D4 = 8 instead of 9.
optionExplanations.2: This omits the factor C(5,1) for choosing which student is the fixed point.
optionExplanations.4: This is the probability that no student gets their own sheet (a full derangement), a different event.

shortExplanation: Choosing 3 of 10 marbles gives C(10,3) = 120 equally likely selections. Exactly two red means C(4,2)*C(6,1) = 6*6 = 36 favourable selections, so the probability is 36/120 = 3/10.
solutionSteps: Count total ways to draw 3 from 10: C(10,3) = 120.
Count ways to pick 2 red from 4: C(4,2) = 6.
Count ways to pick 1 blue from 6: C(6,1) = 6.
Multiply favourable counts: 6*6 = 36.
Divide by the total: 36/120 = 3/10.
keyConcept: Hypergeometric counting: multiply the combinations for each colour, then divide by the total number of unordered selections.
commonMistake: Treating the draws as ordered or using the wrong denominator, which distorts the count of favourable outcomes.

optionExplanations.0: 1/5 = 24/120 miscounts the favourable outcomes.
optionExplanations.2: 1/6 treats the draws as ordered or uses the wrong denominator.
optionExplanations.3: 2/5 = 48/120 over-counts the favourable selections.

shortExplanation: Dividing the two readings, 24/3 = 8 = e^(3k), so e^k = 2 (mass doubles each hour). Stepping back two hours from t = 2 divides by e^(2k) = 4, giving m0 = 3/4 = 0.75 g.
solutionSteps: Divide the readings to eliminate m0: m(5)/m(2) = 24/3 = 8.
Since m(5)/m(2) = e^(3k), set e^(3k) = 8, so e^k = 2.
Relate the start to t = 2: m(2) = m0*e^(2k), so m0 = 3/e^(2k).
Compute e^(2k) = 4, so m0 = 3/4 = 0.75 g.
keyConcept: Taking a ratio of two exponential readings cancels m0 and isolates the growth factor.
commonMistake: Multiplying by the growth factor when going backwards in time instead of dividing.

optionExplanations.0: 1.5 divides the t = 2 reading by only one factor of e^k, back-extrapolating one hour instead of two.
optionExplanations.1: 6 multiplies by the growth factor going backwards instead of dividing.
optionExplanations.2: 0.375 steps back using the 3-hour factor e^(3k) = 8 instead of the 2-hour factor e^(2k) = 4.

shortExplanation: The remainder theorem gives p(1) = -4, so a + b = -3; the factor theorem gives p(-1) = 0, so a - b = 5. Solving yields a = 1, b = -4, and p(x) = (x + 1)^2(2x - 3), whose non-(-1) root is x = 3/2.
solutionSteps: Apply the remainder theorem: p(1) = 2 + a + b - 3 = -4, so a + b = -3.
Apply the factor theorem: p(-1) = -2 + a - b - 3 = 0, so a - b = 5.
Solve the system: a = 1, b = -4.
Write p(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 3 and factor out (x + 1).
Factor fully: p(x) = (x + 1)^2(2x - 3), so the other root solves 2x - 3 = 0, giving x = 3/2.
keyConcept: Remainder and factor theorems turn division conditions into linear equations for the unknown coefficients.
commonMistake: Solving 2x - 3 = 0 as x = 3 by failing to divide by the leading coefficient 2.

optionExplanations.1: -3/2 reads the linear factor as (2x + 3) rather than (2x - 3), a sign slip.
optionExplanations.3: 1/2 mis-derives the linear factor as (2x - 1), usually from an arithmetic error in b.
optionExplanations.4: 3 comes from solving 2x - 3 = 0 without dividing by the leading coefficient 2.

shortExplanation: By Vieta, alpha + beta = 6 and alpha*beta = 7. The squared roots sum to (alpha + beta)^2 - 2*alpha*beta = 36 - 14 = 22 and multiply to (alpha*beta)^2 = 49, giving x^2 - 22x + 49 = 0.
solutionSteps: Read off Vieta's relations: alpha + beta = 6, alpha*beta = 7.
Sum the new roots: alpha^2 + beta^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 - 2*alpha*beta = 36 - 14 = 22.
Multiply the new roots: alpha^2*beta^2 = (alpha*beta)^2 = 49.
Build the monic quadratic x^2 - Sx + P = 0 with S = 22, P = 49: x^2 - 22x + 49 = 0.
keyConcept: A monic quadratic is x^2 - (sum of roots)x + (product of roots), and alpha^2 + beta^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 - 2*alpha*beta.
commonMistake: Using (alpha + beta)^2 directly as alpha^2 + beta^2, omitting the -2*alpha*beta correction.

optionExplanations.0: The +22x sign is wrong; the linear coefficient is minus the sum of the roots.
optionExplanations.1: The -36x uses (alpha + beta)^2 = 36 as the sum of squares, omitting the -2*alpha*beta term.
optionExplanations.4: The -50x uses (alpha + beta)^2 + 2*alpha*beta = 50, taking the correction term with the wrong sign.

shortExplanation: Substituting u = 3x - 2 into g(3x - 2) = 6x + 1 recovers g(x) = 2x + 5. Solving 2x + 5 = 4 gives g^(-1)(4) = -1/2.
solutionSteps: Set u = 3x - 2, so x = (u + 2)/3.
Substitute into the composite: g(u) = 6*(u + 2)/3 + 1 = 2u + 5.
Hence g(x) = 2x + 5.
Solve g(x) = 4: 2x + 5 = 4, so 2x = -1 and x = -1/2.
keyConcept: Recover an inner-composed function by back-substituting the inner argument, then invert by solving the output equation.
commonMistake: Inverting the whole composition or the wrong function instead of the recovered g.

optionExplanations.0: 2 inverts f instead of g, computing f^(-1)(4) = (4 + 2)/3.
optionExplanations.1: 13 evaluates g(4) = 2*4 + 5 rather than its inverse.
optionExplanations.4: 1/2 ignores f and treats the composition 6x + 1 as g, computing (4 - 1)/6.

shortExplanation: The remainder theorem gives P(1) = 12, so a + b = 5; the factor theorem gives P(-2) = 0, so 2a - b = 1. Solving yields a = 2, b = 3, and the remainder on division by (x - 2) is P(2) = 28.
solutionSteps: Apply the remainder theorem: P(1) = 1 + a + b + 6 = 12, so a + b = 5.
Apply the factor theorem: P(-2) = -8 + 4a - 2b + 6 = 0, so 2a - b = 1.
Solve the system: a = 2, b = 3.
keyConcept: The remainder on division by (x - c) equals P(c), so the answer is found by evaluating the recovered polynomial at x = 2.
commonMistake: Reporting the remainder for (x - 1) again instead of recomputing P(2).

optionExplanations.0: 0 would require (x - 2) to be a factor, but P(2) = 28.
optionExplanations.1: 12 just repeats the remainder for division by (x - 1).
optionExplanations.3: 20 comes from an arithmetic slip in evaluating P(2), such as omitting a term.

shortExplanation: Set y = (2x + 1)/(x - 3) and solve for x: y(x - 3) = 2x + 1 leads to x(y - 2) = 3y + 1, so x = (3y + 1)/(y - 2). Thus the inverse is (3x + 1)/(x - 2).
solutionSteps: Write y = (2x + 1)/(x - 3) and clear the denominator: y(x - 3) = 2x + 1.
Expand: yx - 3y = 2x + 1.
Collect x terms: yx - 2x = 3y + 1, so x(y - 2) = 3y + 1.
Solve: x = (3y + 1)/(y - 2), then rename to get f^(-1)(x) = (3x + 1)/(x - 2).
keyConcept: Find an inverse of a rational function by swapping y and x roles and algebraically isolating the variable.
commonMistake: Taking the reciprocal of f(x) instead of solving y = f(x) for x.

optionExplanations.2: (2x + 1)/(x + 3) merely flips a sign and is not obtained by solving for x.
optionExplanations.3: (3x - 1)/(x + 2) has sign errors from mishandling the rearrangement.
optionExplanations.4: (x - 3)/(2x + 1) is the reciprocal of f(x), not its inverse.

shortExplanation: The threshold fraction is 7.5/240 = 1/32 = (1/2)^5, so exactly 5 half-lives elapse to reach 7.5 mg, at 5*8 = 40 hours. At 40 h the mass equals 7.5 mg, still satisfying 'at least 7.5 mg', so 40 is the greatest valid whole hour.
solutionSteps: Form the remaining fraction: 7.5/240 = 1/32.
Recognise 1/32 = (1/2)^5, so 5 half-lives are needed.
Multiply by the half-life: 5*8 = 40 hours.
Note that at 40 h the mass is exactly 7.5 mg, meeting the 'at least' threshold, so the measurement is still valid.
keyConcept: Express the target as a power of 1/2 to read off the number of half-lives directly.
commonMistake: Miscounting the halving steps, an off-by-one error in the number of half-lives.

optionExplanations.0: 24 mis-simplifies the ratio to 1/8 = (1/2)^3, giving only 3 half-lives.
optionExplanations.1: 32 counts one halving step too few (4 instead of 5), landing on 4*8.
optionExplanations.2: 48 counts one half-life too many (6 half-lives), overshooting the threshold.

shortExplanation: Iterating a(n+1) = 3*a(n) - 4 from a(1) = 5 gives 5, 11, 29, 83, 245, 731, so a(6) = 731. Equivalently a(n) = 3^n + 2, so a(6) = 729 + 2 = 731.
solutionSteps: Confirm with the closed form: fixed point x = 2 gives a(n) = 3^n + 2, so a(6) = 729 + 2 = 731.
keyConcept: A linear recurrence a(n+1) = r*a(n) + c has closed form a(n) = (a - fixed point)*r^(n-1) + fixed point, here 3^n + 2.
commonMistake: Dropping the constant term from the closed form and reporting only 3^6.

optionExplanations.0: 729 uses only 3^n, dropping the +2 from the fixed point.
optionExplanations.2: 245 is a(5), stopping one iteration short.
optionExplanations.3: 727 takes the wrong sign for the fixed point, using 3^n - 2.

shortExplanation: New recipients form a geometric sequence 6, 18, 54, ... with a = 6, r = 3. The cumulative total is S(n) = 3(3^n - 1) = 3^(n+1) - 3; setting this to 2184 gives 3^(n+1) = 2187 = 3^7, so n = 6.
solutionSteps: Identify the daily new recipients: 6, 18, 54, ..., geometric with a = 6, r = 3.
Write the cumulative sum: S(n) = 6(3^n - 1)/(3 - 1) = 3^(n+1) - 3.
Recognise 2187 = 3^7, so n + 1 = 7 and n = 6.
keyConcept: The sum of a geometric series is a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1); solve by matching the target to a power of the ratio.
commonMistake: Mis-simplifying the sum to 3^n - 3, causing an off-by-one error in the exponent.

optionExplanations.2: 9 also uses a doubling model and rounds the non-integer solution upward.
optionExplanations.3: 7 mis-simplifies the sum as 3^n - 3, solving 3^n = 2187 for n = 7.
optionExplanations.4: 8 models the spread with ratio 2 instead of 3, solving 2^n = 365.

solutionSteps: Set them equal: 10a + 45d = 20a + 190d.
Simplify to 2a + 29d = 0.
keyConcept: S(30) = 15(2a + 29d), and the equal-sums condition forces exactly that bracket to vanish.
commonMistake: Reducing S(30) to 15(2a + 29d) but failing to see the bracket is exactly zero.

optionExplanations.0: Twice S(10) treats partial sums additively, ignoring that the third block of terms is negative.
optionExplanations.2: The claim that the first term and difference are needed misses that S(10) = S(20) already supplies the relation S(30) depends on.
optionExplanations.3: Equal to S(10) over-extends the vanishing of the middle block to the last block; the last block equals minus the first, so they cancel.

shortExplanation: The mass after t days is M0*(1.5)^(t/10). Setting (1.5)^(t/10) = 3 and using log(1.5) = log3 - log2 = 0.176 gives t = 10*0.477/0.176 = 27.1, about 27 days.
solutionSteps: Model the growth: mass = M0*(1.5)^(t/10).
Set (1.5)^(t/10) = 3 and take base-10 logs: (t/10)*log(1.5) = log3.
Solve t = 10*(0.477/0.176) = 27.1, rounding to 27 days.
keyConcept: Convert a repeated-multiplier growth model to a logarithmic equation to solve for the time exponent.
commonMistake: Treating the exponent as a plain multiplier, e.g. writing 1.5*(t/10) = 3.

optionExplanations.2: 4 inverts the ratio, computing 10*log(1.5)/log3.
optionExplanations.3: 16 models '50% increase' as a doubling, using log3/log2.
optionExplanations.4: 20 linearises the exponent, writing 1.5*(t/10) = 3.

shortExplanation: After n years the value is 1.25^n, so we need the least whole n with 1.25^n > 2, i.e. n > log2/log1.25 = 0.301/0.097 = 3.10. The least such whole number is 4.
solutionSteps: Write the growth factor after n years as 1.25^n.
Require 1.25^n > 2 and take logs: n*log(1.25) > log2.
Round up to the next whole year: n = 4 (1.25^3 = 1.953 < 2, 1.25^4 = 2.441 > 2).
keyConcept: For a 'first exceeds' compound-growth question, take logs and round the threshold UP to the next whole period.
commonMistake: Rounding the log result down and reporting 3 years, when 1.25^3 is still below 2.

optionExplanations.0: 2 gives 1.25^2 = 1.5625, far short of doubling.
optionExplanations.2: 3 uses 1.25^3 = 1.953, which is still less than 2; n must round up.
optionExplanations.4: 5 overshoots; the value first exceeds double at year 4.

shortExplanation: The circle has centre (0,0) and radius 2√2. Tangency means the distance |c|/√2 from the centre to x - y + c = 0 equals the radius, giving |c| = 4, so c = 4 or c = -4.
solutionSteps: Write the line as x - y + c = 0 and note the circle has centre (0,0), radius 2√2.
Apply the point-to-line distance: |0 - 0 + c|/√(1^2 + (-1)^2) = |c|/√2.
Set the distance equal to the radius: |c|/√2 = 2√2.
Solve |c| = 2√2*√2 = 4, so c = 4 or c = -4.
keyConcept: A line is tangent to a circle exactly when the perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius.
commonMistake: Omitting the √2 in the distance formula and setting |c| equal to the radius directly.

optionExplanations.0: ±4√2 divides by 2 instead of √2, taking √(1^2 + 1^2) as 2.
optionExplanations.1: ±2√2 sets |c| equal to the radius directly, dropping the √2 from the distance formula.
optionExplanations.4: ±8 uses the diameter as the required perpendicular distance instead of the radius.

shortExplanation: By the sine rule sin B = b sin A / a = √6*(√2/2)/2 = √3/2. Since b sin A < a < b this is the ambiguous case, so B = 60° or B = 120°, giving C = 75° or C = 15° — two triangles.
solutionSteps: Apply the sine rule: sin B = b sin A / a = √6*sin45°/2.
Check the ambiguous case: b sin A = √3 < a = 2 < b = √6, so two triangles exist.
Solve sin B = √3/2: B = 60° or B = 120°, both valid since A + B < 180°.
keyConcept: In the SSA configuration with b sin A < a < b, the sine rule yields two valid triangles from the acute and obtuse solutions for B.
commonMistake: Keeping only one solution for B and missing the second triangle.

optionExplanations.1: One triangle with C = 15° keeps only the obtuse B = 120°, discarding the acute solution.
optionExplanations.2: 'No such triangle' wrongly treats the data as impossible, but a valid triangle clearly exists.
optionExplanations.3: One triangle with C = 75° keeps only the acute B = 60°, discarding the obtuse solution.

shortExplanation: The 120° angle is opposite the longest side x + 4. The cosine rule with cos120° = -1/2 gives (x + 4)^2 = 3x^2 + 6x + 4, which reduces to x^2 - x - 6 = 0, whose positive root is x = 3.
solutionSteps: Place the largest angle opposite the longest side x + 4.
Apply the cosine rule: (x + 4)^2 = x^2 + (x + 2)^2 - 2x(x + 2)cos120°.
Use cos120° = -1/2, turning the last term into +x(x + 2): right side = 3x^2 + 6x + 4.
Solve x^2 - x - 6 = (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0; since x > 0, x = 3.
keyConcept: The cosine rule with cos120° = -1/2 introduces a positive product term, so the equation for the largest angle is not Pythagorean.
commonMistake: Dropping the cosine term and treating the largest angle as a right angle.

optionExplanations.0: 7 reports the longest side x + 4 instead of x.
optionExplanations.1: 6 uses Pythagoras (as if the angle were 90°), dropping the cosine term.
optionExplanations.4: 5 reports the middle side length instead of x.

shortExplanation: Substituting cos^2 x = 1 - sin^2 x gives 2sin^2 x - sin x - 1 = 0, which factors as (2 sin x + 1)(sin x - 1) = 0. So sin x = -1/2 (x = 7π/6, 11π/6) or sin x = 1 (x = π/2), summing to 7π/2.
solutionSteps: Replace cos^2 x with 1 - sin^2 x to get -2sin^2 x + sin x + 1 = 0.
Rearrange to 2sin^2 x - sin x - 1 = 0.
Factor: (2 sin x + 1)(sin x - 1) = 0, so sin x = -1/2 or sin x = 1.
Solve on [0, 2π): sin x = -1/2 gives 7π/6 and 11π/6; sin x = 1 gives π/2.
Sum the roots: π/2 + 7π/6 + 11π/6 = 21π/6 = 7π/2.
keyConcept: Convert to a single trig function with the Pythagorean identity, then factor the resulting quadratic in sin x.
commonMistake: Dropping the sin x = 1 root or mis-factoring the quadratic and landing on the wrong angles.

optionExplanations.0: 5π/2 mis-factors as (2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1), giving sin x = 1/2 and sin x = -1.
optionExplanations.1: 3π solves sin x = -1/2 correctly but discards the sin x = 1 root x = π/2.
optionExplanations.3: 3π/2 places the sin x = -1/2 roots at the +1/2 positions (π/6, 5π/6).

shortExplanation: Angle APB is a right angle exactly when P lies on the circle with AB as diameter, centre (4,3) and r^2 = 10. Setting y = 0 gives (x - 4)^2 = 1, so x = 3 or x = 5.
solutionSteps: Recognise the Thales condition: APB = 90° means P is on the circle with diameter AB.
Find the centre (midpoint of AB): (4, 3).
Solve x = 3 or x = 5, both distinct from A and B.
keyConcept: The locus of points seeing a fixed segment at a right angle is the circle having that segment as diameter (Thales' theorem).
commonMistake: Forgetting the (0 - 3)^2 term when substituting y = 0.

optionExplanations.0: (4 ± √10, 0) omits the (0 - 3)^2 term, solving (x - 4)^2 = 10.
optionExplanations.1: (4 ± √31, 0) uses the full length |AB| as radius instead of half of it.
optionExplanations.2: (4, 0) only assumes a single point, missing that the circle meets the x-axis twice.

shortExplanation: Completing the square gives centre (4,3), radius 3. The distance from the origin to the centre is 5, so the tangent length is √(5^2 - 3^2) = √16 = 4.
solutionSteps: Complete the square: (x - 4)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 9, so centre (4,3), r = 3.
Compute the distance OC = √(4^2 + 3^2) = 5.
Apply the tangent-length relation t^2 = OC^2 - r^2 = 25 - 9 = 16.
Take the square root: t = 4.
keyConcept: The tangent length from an external point satisfies t^2 = (distance to centre)^2 - r^2, by the right-angle at the point of tangency.
commonMistake: Subtracting the radius directly from OC instead of combining them in quadrature.

optionExplanations.0: 5 is the distance OC to the centre, not the tangent length; the radius must still be removed in quadrature.
optionExplanations.1: 2 = OC - r treats the tangent as a straight-line difference of distances.
optionExplanations.3: 3 is the circle's radius, not the tangent length.

shortExplanation: 'Red or king' overlaps, so P = P(red) + P(king) - P(red and king) = 26/52 + 4/52 - 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13.
solutionSteps: Count red cards: 26; kings: 4.
Identify the overlap: 2 red kings.
Apply the addition rule: P = (26 + 4 - 2)/52.
Simplify: 28/52 = 7/13.
keyConcept: For non-mutually-exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
commonMistake: Adding the two probabilities without subtracting the two red kings counted in both sets.

optionExplanations.0: 15/26 = 30/52 adds without subtracting the overlap, treating the events as mutually exclusive.
optionExplanations.2: 8/13 = 32/52 adds the intersection instead of subtracting it, double-counting the red kings.
optionExplanations.4: 1/2 = 26/52 counts only red cards, ignoring the two black kings.

shortExplanation: Six people around a circle give (6-1)! = 120 arrangements. Gluing Anna and Marco into a block gives (5-1)!*2 = 48 adjacent arrangements, so the non-adjacent count is 120 - 48 = 72.
solutionSteps: Count total circular arrangements: (6-1)! = 120.
Glue Anna and Marco into one block, leaving 5 units: (5-1)! = 24 circular arrangements.
Multiply by the block's 2 internal orders: 24*2 = 48 adjacent arrangements.
Subtract from the total: 120 - 48 = 72.
keyConcept: Circular arrangements of n distinct people number (n-1)!; count 'not adjacent' as the complement of the glued-block adjacent count.
commonMistake: Forgetting to multiply the block by 2 for its internal order, or using linear n! instead of (n-1)!.

optionExplanations.1: 48 is the number of arrangements where Anna and Marco DO sit together, the complement of what is asked.
optionExplanations.2: 96 forgets to multiply the block by 2, undercounting the adjacent cases as 24.
optionExplanations.3: 480 uses linear permutations (n!) instead of circular (n-1)!.

shortExplanation: The equally likely ordered outcomes BB, BG, GB, GG each have probability 1/4. Conditioning on 'at least one boy' removes GG, leaving three outcomes of which one is BB, so the probability is (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3.
solutionSteps: List the equally likely ordered outcomes: BB, BG, GB, GG.
Apply the condition 'at least one boy', which removes only GG.
Count remaining outcomes: BB, BG, GB (three), of which one is BB.
Compute P(BB | at least one boy) = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3.
keyConcept: Conditional probability restricts the sample space; 'at least one boy' does not identify which child, so ordering information is retained.
commonMistake: Answering 1/2 by imagining one particular child is known to be a boy.

optionExplanations.0: 1/2 treats it as 'one particular child is a boy', wrongly discarding ordering information.
optionExplanations.1: 2/3 is the probability of exactly one boy given at least one boy, not two boys.
optionExplanations.3: 1/4 is the unconditional probability of two boys, ignoring the given information.

shortExplanation: Independent (not mutually exclusive) events have P(A and B) = 0.3*0.5 = 0.15. By inclusion-exclusion, P(A or B) = 0.3 + 0.5 - 0.15 = 0.65.
solutionSteps: Compute the intersection using independence: P(A and B) = 0.3*0.5 = 0.15.
Apply the addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
keyConcept: Independence gives P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B); it is not the same as mutual exclusivity, so the intersection is non-zero.
commonMistake: Assuming the events are mutually exclusive and skipping the subtraction of the intersection.

optionExplanations.1: 0.95 adds the intersection instead of subtracting it.
optionExplanations.2: 0.80 = 0.3 + 0.5 assumes mutual exclusivity, but independent events with positive probability overlap.
optionExplanations.4: 0.15 is the intersection P(A and B), not the union.

shortExplanation: After eliminating 2 of 5 options, 3 remain, so P(correct) = 1/3 and P(wrong) = 2/3. The expected mark is (1/3)(+3) + (2/3)(-1) = 1 - 2/3 = +1/3.
solutionSteps: Update the probabilities after elimination: P(correct) = 1/3, P(wrong) = 2/3.
Weight each outcome by its score: (1/3)(+3) + (2/3)(-1).
Compare to 0 from blanking: +1/3 > 0, so guessing is worthwhile.
keyConcept: Expected value weights each outcome's score by its updated conditional probability after eliminating options.
commonMistake: Using the pre-elimination probabilities 1/5 and 4/5, or omitting the -1 penalty.

optionExplanations.1: +2/3 uses P(wrong) = 1/3, as if only one wrong option remained.
optionExplanations.2: -1/5 uses the original five options with P(correct) = 1/5 and P(wrong) = 4/5.
optionExplanations.3: +1 counts only the gain (1/3)(3) and omits the -1 penalty term.

shortExplanation: Of 216 ordered outcomes, 6*5*4 = 120 are all-different, and 5*4*3 = 60 of those contain no six. So all-different with at least one six number 120 - 60 = 60, giving 60/216 = 5/18.
solutionSteps: Count total ordered outcomes: 6^3 = 216.
Count all-different outcomes: 6*5*4 = 120.
Count all-different outcomes with no six (from {1,2,3,4,5}): 5*4*3 = 60.
Subtract to require at least one six: 120 - 60 = 60.
keyConcept: Handle 'all different AND at least one six' by counting all-different outcomes and subtracting those avoiding six.
commonMistake: Reporting the all-different probability alone, ignoring the 'at least one six' requirement.

optionExplanations.0: 25/216 corresponds to a different scenario and does not enforce 'all different'.
optionExplanations.1: 5/9 = 120/216 is the probability of merely all-different, ignoring the six requirement.
optionExplanations.4: 5/36 = 30/216 halves the correct favourable count of 60.

shortExplanation: For a frequency table the mean is the total of (value x frequency) divided by the total frequency. Total goals = 48 over 30 matches, so the mean is 48/30 = 1.6 goals per match.
solutionSteps: Multiply each goal value by its frequency: (0x6)+(1x9)+(2x8)+(3x5)+(4x2).
Sum to get total goals = 0+9+16+15+8 = 48.
Add the frequencies to get total matches = 6+9+8+5+2 = 30.
Divide: mean = 48/30 = 1.6.
keyConcept: Mean of grouped data = sum of (value x frequency) divided by total frequency.
commonMistake: Averaging the category labels themselves, or dividing by the number of distinct categories instead of the total number of matches.

optionExplanations.1: This multiplies frequencies by the position labels 1-5 instead of the actual goal values 0-4, an off-by-one error giving 78/30 = 2.6.
optionExplanations.2: This averages the five goal categories (0+1+2+3+4)/5 as if each occurred equally often, ignoring the frequency weighting.
optionExplanations.3: This is the median (average of the 15th and 16th ordered values), not the mean.
optionExplanations.4: This divides the total goals by the 5 goal categories instead of by the 30 matches, giving 48/5 = 9.6.

shortExplanation: Work with totals. All 50 students total 50 x 60 = 3000; Class B totals 20 x 66 = 1320, so Class A totals 1680 over 30 students, a mean of 56.
solutionSteps: Total marks for all 50 students = 50 x 60 = 3000.
Class B total = 20 x 66 = 1320.
Class A total = 3000 - 1320 = 1680.
Class A mean = 1680/30 = 56.
keyConcept: A combined mean must be weighted by group size; convert means to totals before combining.
commonMistake: Treating the overall mean as the simple average of the two class means, ignoring that the classes have different sizes.

optionExplanations.1: This swaps the two class sizes, weighting Class A by 20 and Class B by 30, giving 1020/20 = 51.
optionExplanations.3: This wrongly assumes Class A's mean equals the overall mean of 60.
optionExplanations.4: This simply quotes Class B's mean of 66, assuming both classes share the same mean.

shortExplanation: The frequency-weighted mean is 87/40 = 2.175, while both the median and the mode equal 2. So the mean exceeds the median and the mode, which are equal to each other.
solutionSteps: Median: cumulative counts 4, 13, 25 place the 20th and 21st values in the '2 children' group, so median = 2.
Mode: the largest frequency (12) is at 2 children, so mode = 2.
Compare: 2.175 > 2 = 2, so the mean exceeds the equal median and mode.
keyConcept: In a right-skewed distribution the upper tail pulls the mean above the median and mode.
commonMistake: Averaging the six category labels (giving 2.5) instead of computing the frequency-weighted mean.

optionExplanations.0: The value 2.5 averages the six category labels and ignores the frequencies; the weighted mean is 2.175.
optionExplanations.2: This confuses the modal value (most frequent, 2) with the largest data value recorded (5).
optionExplanations.3: This reverses the skew; the high-side tail pulls the mean above the median, not below it.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes a symmetric distribution where all three measures coincide, but the tail pulls the mean above 2.

shortExplanation: Only the total changes. Correcting 39 to 93 adds 54 and correcting 70 to 40 subtracts 30, a net +24. The corrected total 1184 over 20 marks gives a mean of 59.2.
solutionSteps: Original total = 20 x 58 = 1160.
First correction 39 to 93: change = +54.
Second correction 70 to 40: change = -30.
Net change = +54 - 30 = +24, so corrected total = 1184.
Corrected mean = 1184/20 = 59.2.
keyConcept: Correcting data values changes only the total; the mean shifts by (net change)/n.
commonMistake: Applying only one of the two corrections, or reversing the direction of the changes.

optionExplanations.0: This reverses the sign of both corrections for a net -24, giving 56.8.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes the two corrections cancel, but +54 and -30 do not cancel.
optionExplanations.3: This applies only the first correction (+54), giving 60.7 and ignoring the second error.
optionExplanations.4: This applies only the second correction (-30), giving 56.5 and missing the larger upward correction.

shortExplanation: With ages a<=b<=c<=d<=e summing to 50, the median forces c = 9 and the unique mode 7 forces a = b = 7. Minimising d at 10 (since d = 9 would tie the mode) gives the maximum oldest age e = 17.
solutionSteps: Mean 10 gives total = 5 x 10 = 50.
The median is the middle value, so c = 9.
Since 7 is the only mode and 7 < 9, it must sit at the two lowest spots: a = b = 7.
Remaining d + e = 50 - 7 - 7 - 9 = 27 with 9 <= d <= e.
To maximise e, minimise d; d = 9 would tie the mode at two 9s, so d = 10.
Then e = 27 - 10 = 17, and {7, 7, 9, 10, 17} satisfies every condition.
keyConcept: To maximise the largest value under fixed mean, median and mode, minimise every other value within the constraints.
commonMistake: Allowing a second 9 in the fourth position, which creates a tie and violates that 7 is the only mode.

optionExplanations.0: This forces d = 11 (above the mean) so e = 16, confusing the mean with the median.
optionExplanations.1: This uses {7, 7, 9, 9, 18}, but the second 9 makes 9 also a mode, violating the unique-mode condition.
optionExplanations.3: This spreads the top two ages evenly ({7, 7, 9, 12, 15}) instead of pushing the oldest to its extreme.
optionExplanations.4: This places 8 in the fourth position without re-ordering, so the value used as the median is not actually the middle value.

shortExplanation: Under y = 1.25x + 5 the mean transforms fully to 1.25 x 52 + 5 = 70, but the standard deviation is unaffected by the +5 shift and only scaled by 1.25, giving 1.25 x 8 = 10.
solutionSteps: Adding a constant to every value shifts the data but does not change the spread.
Multiplying every value by 1.25 scales the spread by 1.25.
New standard deviation = 1.25 x 8 = 10.
keyConcept: Under y = ax + b, the mean becomes a(mean)+b while the standard deviation becomes |a| times the old one; the additive constant does not affect spread.
commonMistake: Adding the constant 5 to the standard deviation, or scaling it by 1.25 squared (which applies to variance).

optionExplanations.0: The mean 65 omits the +5 shift; the standard deviation of 10 is correct but the mean must include the addition.
optionExplanations.2: This adds 5 to the standard deviation as well; adding a constant leaves the spread unchanged.
optionExplanations.3: This scales the standard deviation by 1.25 squared, a factor that applies to the variance, not the standard deviation.
optionExplanations.4: This leaves the standard deviation at 8, ignoring that multiplying every value by 1.25 scales it to 10.

shortExplanation: The cleaned region is an annular sector: the fraction 120/360 of the ring between radii 40 cm and 10 cm. Its area is (1/3)·π(40^2 − 10^2) = (1/3)(1500π) = 500π cm^2.
solutionSteps: Identify the region as a sector of a ring with outer radius 40 and inner radius 10.
Take the fraction swept: 120/360 = 1/3.
keyConcept: Area of an annular sector = (theta/360)·π(R^2 − r^2), using the difference of squares of the radii.
commonMistake: Squaring the difference of the radii (40 − 10)^2 instead of taking the difference of the squares R^2 − r^2.

optionExplanations.0: This computes (1/3)π(40 − 10)^2, treating the 30 cm blade length as a radius instead of using R^2 − r^2.
optionExplanations.1: This halves the swept angle to 60 degrees, misreading the given 120 degrees.
optionExplanations.2: This uses the reflex angle 240 degrees rather than the 120 degrees actually swept.
optionExplanations.3: This is the full annulus area π(40^2 − 10^2), omitting the 120/360 fraction.

shortExplanation: The inside edge gives 2(100) + 2πr = 400, so r = 100/π. The area is the rectangle 100·(200/π) plus one full circle π(100/π)^2 = 20000/π + 10000/π = 30000/π m^2.
solutionSteps: Perimeter: 2(100) + 2(πr) = 400, so 2πr = 200 and r = 100/π.
Rectangle width = diameter = 2r = 200/π.
Rectangle area = 100 x 200/π = 20000/π.
The two semicircular ends form one full circle: π(100/π)^2 = 10000/π.
keyConcept: Two semicircular ends of equal radius combine into a single full circle; use the perimeter to find the radius first.
commonMistake: Double-counting the ends as two full circles, or forgetting one of the two semicircular ends.

optionExplanations.1: This adds two full circles (2πr^2) rather than one, double-counting the curved ends.
optionExplanations.2: This includes only one semicircular end (1/2 πr^2), forgetting the identical second end.
optionExplanations.3: This is the area of the two ends alone (one circle), omitting the rectangular middle.
optionExplanations.4: This is the rectangle only (100 x 200/π), omitting the two semicircular ends.

shortExplanation: The shared face is internal, so the exposed surface is the cone's curved surface πrl plus the hemisphere's curved surface 2πr^2. With slant height l = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 10, the total is 60π + 72π = 132π cm^2.
