keyConcept: Internal resistance is a fixed property of the battery; the current must be recomputed for each load, and internal power is I^2 r.
commonMistake: Reusing the first current, ignoring internal resistance when finding the current, or computing external or total power instead of internal.

optionExplanations.0: This finds the current as ε/R = 6 A, ignoring internal resistance, then multiplies by r.
optionExplanations.1: This computes I^2 R = 32 W, the external power, mislabelled as internal.
optionExplanations.2: This reuses the first-arrangement current (2.0 A) instead of recomputing for the 2.0 Ω load.
optionExplanations.4: This computes the total power εI = 48 W, not the internally dissipated part.

shortExplanation: Node analysis (Millman's theorem) gives the node voltage as 4.0 V, so the load current is V/R = 4.0/2.0 = 2.0 A.
solutionSteps: Apply Millman: V = (ε1/r1 + ε2/r2)/(1/r1 + 1/r2 + 1/R).
Denominator: 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/2 = 1.
keyConcept: Two EMF sources across common nodes are handled by node analysis (Millman's theorem), not by naively adding EMFs or resistances.
commonMistake: Averaging or adding the EMFs, ignoring one battery, or treating the parallel sources as a single series loop.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the mean EMF (9 V) across only the load, ignoring both internal resistances.
optionExplanations.1: This considers only the 12 V battery, ignoring the 6 V battery's contribution.
optionExplanations.2: This adds the EMFs and places all resistances in series, treating parallel batteries as one loop.
optionExplanations.3: This treats the EMFs as opposing in a single loop and ignores the load resistor.

shortExplanation: The 3 μF and 6 μF in parallel give 9 μF, in series with 9 μF gives 4.5 μF, so the series charge is 54 μC. The parallel block then sits at 6.0 V, and the 6 μF capacitor holds 6*6 = 36 μC.
solutionSteps: Parallel combination: 3 + 6 = 9 μF.
Series with 9 μF: C_eq = (9*9)/(9 + 9) = 4.5 μF.
Series charge: Q = C_eq*V = 4.5*12 = 54 μC.
Voltage across parallel block: 54 μC / 9 μF = 6.0 V.
Charge on 6 μF: Q = 6 μF * 6.0 V = 36 μC.
keyConcept: Series capacitors share the same charge; within a parallel block the voltage is common and charge divides in proportion to capacitance.
commonMistake: Assigning the whole series charge to one capacitor, applying the full battery voltage, or splitting the charge equally.

optionExplanations.0: This gives the charge on the 3.0 μF capacitor (3.0*6.0), not the 6.0 μF one.
optionExplanations.2: This assigns the whole series charge (54 μC) to the 6.0 μF capacitor.
optionExplanations.3: This applies the full 12 V across the 6.0 μF capacitor, ignoring the series drop.
optionExplanations.4: This splits the 54 μC equally between the two parallel capacitors instead of by capacitance.

shortExplanation: Wires A and B attract (toward A) with 2e-4 N/m, and wires B and C repel (also toward A) with 4e-4 N/m; both point the same way, so the net force per unit length is 6e-4 N/m.
solutionSteps: Force from A (parallel currents attract): f_AB = μ0*10*10/(2π*0.10) = 2e-4 N/m toward A.
Force from C (antiparallel currents repel, C on opposite side): f_BC = μ0*10*20/(2π*0.10) = 4e-4 N/m toward A.
Both contributions point toward A, so they add: 2e-4 + 4e-4 = 6e-4 N/m.
keyConcept: The net force on a wire is the vector sum of forces from each neighbour, using f = μ0 I1 I2/(2πd); parallel currents attract and antiparallel repel.
commonMistake: Getting the directions wrong and subtracting the contributions, or using the wrong current for a neighbour.

optionExplanations.1: This uses 20 A for both neighbours, overstating wire A's current.
optionExplanations.2: This subtracts the two contributions, mistaking them as opposing; both push B toward A.
optionExplanations.3: This includes only the force from wire C, ignoring wire A.
optionExplanations.4: This drops the factor of 2 in the force law, doubling each force.

shortExplanation: The circulated charge is q = NΔΦ/R, which depends only on the total flux change. Reversal makes ΔB = 0.80 T, giving q = 200*5.0e-3*0.80/8.0 = 0.10 C.
solutionSteps: Integrate Faraday's law: q = ∫I dt = NΔΦ/R, independent of the rate of change.
Reversal gives ΔB = 0.40 − (−0.40) = 0.80 T.
Flux change per turn: ΔΦ = AΔB = 5.0e-3*0.80 = 4.0e-3 Wb.
keyConcept: The total charge through a coil is NΔΦ/R and depends only on the net flux change, not on how quickly it happens.
commonMistake: Using ΔB = 0.40 T (missing the reversal), omitting the number of turns, or forgetting to divide by resistance.

optionExplanations.0: This takes ΔB = 0.40 T instead of the full 0.80 T from the reversal.
optionExplanations.1: This omits the number of turns, using single-turn flux.
optionExplanations.3: This applies an extra factor of 2 on top of the already-doubled ΔB.
optionExplanations.4: This computes the flux-linkage change but forgets to divide by the resistance.

shortExplanation: At constant voltage the charge rises from 400 μC to 1200 μC, so the battery moves ΔQ = 800 μC through 100 V, doing W = ΔQ*V = 80 mJ.
solutionSteps: Voltage fixed at 100 V; capacitance rises from 4.0 μF to κ*4.0 = 12 μF.
Initial charge: Q0 = C0*V = 400 μC; final charge: Q = 12 μF*100 V = 1200 μC.
Extra charge moved: ΔQ = 1200 − 400 = 800 μC.
Battery work: W = ΔQ*V = 8.0e-4*100 = 80 mJ.
keyConcept: At constant voltage the battery does work ΔQ*V; only half of this goes into extra stored energy, the rest into the mechanical work of drawing in the slab.
commonMistake: Confusing the battery's work with the change in stored energy, or using the full charge instead of the extra charge delivered.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the full final charge Q*V instead of the extra charge ΔQ delivered.
optionExplanations.1: This reports the initial stored energy (1/2)C0 V^2.
optionExplanations.3: This reports the increase in stored energy (40 mJ); the battery does more, also supplying the mechanical work.
optionExplanations.4: This reports the final stored energy (1/2)κC0 V^2 = 60 mJ.

shortExplanation: R2 and R3 in parallel give 2.0 Ω, so the total resistance is 6.0 Ω and the current through R1 is 2.0 A. The power in R1 is I^2 R1 = 16 W.
solutionSteps: Parallel combination: R2 || R3 = (6.0*3.0)/(6.0 + 3.0) = 2.0 Ω.
Total resistance: 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω.
Current through R1: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A.
keyConcept: All battery current flows through the series resistor R1; its power is I^2 R1 once the total-circuit current is found.
commonMistake: Using the parallel resistance instead of R1, or reporting the total battery power instead of the power in R1.

optionExplanations.0: This would require I = 1.0 A, from mishandling the resistor combination.
optionExplanations.1: This is the total power delivered by the battery (IV), not the power in R1.
optionExplanations.2: This uses the parallel combination's 2.0 Ω instead of R1, or halves the correct value.
optionExplanations.3: This does not correspond to any correct current-and-resistance combination for R1.

shortExplanation: Frequency is fixed by the source and does not change at a boundary, so the wavelength in bone is λ = v_bone/f = 4050/(1.5e6) = 2.7 mm.
solutionSteps: Frequency stays constant across the boundary at 1.5 MHz.
Apply v = fλ in bone: λ = v_bone/f.
keyConcept: At a boundary the frequency is unchanged; speed and wavelength change together, with λ = v/f.
commonMistake: Assuming the wavelength or frequency is carried unchanged across the boundary, or averaging the two speeds.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the arithmetic mean of the two speeds, which has no physical basis.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes the frequency halves on entering bone; frequency is fixed by the source.
optionExplanations.2: This is the wavelength in soft tissue, assuming wavelength is carried unchanged.
optionExplanations.3: This inverts λ = v/f, wrongly shortening the wavelength as speed rises.

shortExplanation: The lowest-frequency minimum has the largest wavelength, with path difference ΔL = λ/2. So λ = 1.70 m and f = v/λ = 340/1.70 = 200 Hz.
solutionSteps: Destructive interference for in-phase sources: ΔL = (n + 1/2)λ.
Lowest frequency means longest wavelength, so smallest n = 0: ΔL = λ/2.
keyConcept: For in-phase sources a minimum occurs when the path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths; the lowest frequency uses ΔL = λ/2.
commonMistake: Using a higher-order minimum, applying the maximum condition, or using a quarter-wavelength path difference.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the next-order minimum ΔL = 3λ/2, a genuine minimum but not the lowest frequency.
optionExplanations.1: This sets ΔL = 2λ, which gives a maximum and a higher order.
optionExplanations.2: This applies the constructive condition ΔL = λ (a maximum) instead of destructive.
optionExplanations.3: This uses ΔL = λ/4, a 90-degree phase difference rather than the 180 degrees needed for a minimum.

shortExplanation: Consecutive resonance lengths differ by λ/2, and the constant end correction cancels: λ/2 = 51.0 − 16.0 = 35.0 cm. So λ = 0.70 m and v = fλ = 350 m/s.
solutionSteps: Successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2, with the end correction cancelling in the difference.
keyConcept: Taking the difference of consecutive resonance lengths gives λ/2 and eliminates the unknown end correction.
commonMistake: Assuming a spacing of λ/4 or λ, or treating a single measured length as exactly λ/4 and ignoring the end correction.

optionExplanations.0: This assumes consecutive resonances differ by λ/4 rather than λ/2.
optionExplanations.1: This treats the second length as λ/4 (the fundamental), which is wrong for higher resonances.
optionExplanations.2: This treats the first length as exactly λ/4, ignoring the end correction.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes consecutive resonances are a full wavelength apart.

shortExplanation: By the displacement method, f = (D^2 − d^2)/(4D) = (90^2 − 30^2)/(4*90) = 20.0 cm, corresponding to conjugate distances of 30 cm and 60 cm.
solutionSteps: The two lens positions are conjugate points: u = (D − d)/2 and v = (D + d)/2.
Apply the displacement formula: f = (D^2 − d^2)/(4D).
keyConcept: In the lens-displacement method, f = (D^2 − d^2)/(4D), where D is the object-screen separation and d the distance between the two focusing positions.
commonMistake: Using f = D/4 (valid only when the positions merge), dropping the factor of 4, or confusing an object distance with the focal length.

optionExplanations.0: This uses f = D/4, valid only in the limiting case d = 0, overestimating f.
optionExplanations.1: This drops the factor of 4, using (D^2 − d^2)/(2D).
optionExplanations.3: This takes f = D/2; no relation gives the focal length as half the separation.
optionExplanations.4: This is the smaller object distance (D − d)/2, mistaken for the focal length.

shortExplanation: Subtracting the two photoelectric equations eliminates the work function and gives hc = 1240 eV·nm, then φ = 3.0 eV. The threshold wavelength is λ0 = hc/φ = 1240/3.0 ≈ 413 nm.
solutionSteps: Write eV_s = hc/λ − φ for both measurements and subtract: e(V2 − V1) = hc(1/λ2 − 1/λ1).
Find work function: φ = hc/λ1 − eV1 = 4.0 − 1.0 = 3.0 eV.
Threshold: λ0 = hc/φ = 1240/3.0 ≈ 413 nm.
keyConcept: Two stopping-potential measurements determine both hc and the work function; the threshold wavelength satisfies hc/λ0 = φ.
commonMistake: Equating the work function to a stopping-potential energy, or a sign error that adds instead of subtracts the kinetic energy.

optionExplanations.0: This sets φ = eV2 = 2.0 eV, confusing kinetic energy with the work function.
optionExplanations.2: This makes a sign error, adding the kinetic energy to get φ = 5.0 eV.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes the threshold is simply the longer tested wavelength, but both tested wavelengths eject electrons.
optionExplanations.4: This sets φ = eV1 = 1.0 eV, again confusing kinetic energy with the work function.

shortExplanation: A 12.5 eV electron can excite the atom to at most n = 3 (needing 12.09 eV, versus 12.75 eV for n = 4). Downward transitions among levels 1, 2 and 3 give C(3,2) = 3 distinct wavelengths.
solutionSteps: Each electron carries 12.5 eV of kinetic energy.
Excitation from n=1 to n requires ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/n^2): 10.2 eV for n=2, 12.09 eV for n=3, 12.75 eV for n=4.
Since 12.09 ≤ 12.5 < 12.75, the highest populated level is n = 3.
Distinct emission lines = C(3,2) = 3 (transitions 3→2, 3→1, 2→1).
keyConcept: The available electron energy caps the highest accessible level; the number of spectral lines is the number of level pairs, C(n,2).
commonMistake: Overestimating the top level (n=4 or n=5), counting only one transition, or counting only transitions ending at the ground state.

optionExplanations.0: This counts a single de-excitation, overlooking that different atoms follow different downward routes.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes excitation to n = 4, which needs 12.75 eV, exceeding the available energy.
optionExplanations.2: This assumes excitation to n = 5, which is far above the available energy.
optionExplanations.3: This counts only transitions ending on the ground state, omitting 3→2.

shortExplanation: Only the front reflection has a π phase change, so the bright-fringe condition is 2nt = (m + 1/2)λ. The smallest non-zero thickness (m = 0) is t = λ/(4n) = 532/(4*1.33) = 100 nm.
solutionSteps: Front reflection (air-to-film) gives a π phase change; back reflection (film-to-air) gives none.
Net half-wave shift makes constructive reflection require 2nt = (m + 1/2)λ.
Smallest non-zero thickness uses m = 0: 2nt = λ/2, so t = λ/(4n).
keyConcept: In thin-film reflection, a π phase change at only one surface shifts the constructive condition to 2nt = (m + 1/2)λ, using the wavelength inside the film.
commonMistake: Ignoring the phase change, ignoring the refractive index, or dropping the factor of 2 for the double traversal.

optionExplanations.0: This ignores both the refractive index and the phase change, using 2t = λ.
optionExplanations.2: This omits the phase change, using 2nt = λ, which actually gives a dark fringe here.
optionExplanations.3: This drops the factor of 2 for the double traversal, setting nt = λ.
optionExplanations.4: This ignores the refractive index, using the vacuum wavelength in t = λ/4.

shortExplanation: Treat the beam as a rigid body in equilibrium and take torques about support B to eliminate its reaction. This gives R_A x 4.0 = 200 x 2.0 + 600 x 3.0 = 2200 N.m, so R_A = 550 N.
solutionSteps: Weight of beam W_beam = 20 x 10 = 200 N, acting at the centre 2.0 m from each end.
Weight of block W_load = 60 x 10 = 600 N, acting 1.0 m from A and hence 3.0 m from B.
Take torques about B (this removes R_B): R_A x 4.0 = 200 x 2.0 + 600 x 3.0.
keyConcept: For a rigid body in static equilibrium both the net force and the net torque about any point are zero; choosing the pivot at an unknown reaction eliminates it.
commonMistake: Assuming the two supports share the total weight equally; equal sharing only holds for a symmetric load, but here the block is off-centre so the nearer support carries more.

optionExplanations.1: This is the reaction at the far support B, not at A; the support nearer the load must carry more.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes the near support carries the entire load plus half the beam weight, but the load is shared between both supports according to their lever arms.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes the supports share the total 800 N equally, which only holds for a symmetric load.

shortExplanation: A smooth wall gives only a horizontal reaction, so torques about the foot give the wall reaction N_w = (100 + 300)/tan(theta) = 200 N, which equals the required friction. With ground normal 500 N, the minimum coefficient is 200/500 = 0.40.
solutionSteps: Vertical equilibrium: ground normal N_g = 200 + 300 = 500 N.
Horizontal equilibrium: friction f = wall reaction N_w.
Take torques about the foot: N_w(L sin theta) = 200(L/2 cos theta) + 300(L cos theta).
Cancel L: N_w = (100 + 300)/tan(theta) = 400/2 = 200 N.
Required friction f = 200 N, so mu_min = f/N_g = 200/500 = 0.40.
keyConcept: A frictionless wall exerts a purely horizontal (normal) force; the ladder's own weight acts at its midpoint, giving it half the lever arm of a load at the top.
commonMistake: Multiplying by tan(theta) instead of dividing by it; the horizontal reaction scales as cos/sin = 1/tan(theta) because the wall's height above the foot sets the lever arm.

optionExplanations.0: This multiplies by tan(theta) instead of dividing, using N_w = 400 x 2 = 800 N.
optionExplanations.2: This omits the 1/tan(theta) geometry factor, as if the ladder stood at 45 degrees.
optionExplanations.4: This treats the ladder's own weight as acting at the top with the full lever arm, but a uniform ladder's weight acts at its midpoint.

shortExplanation: For floating equilibrium the cube's density equals the volume-weighted average of the two liquid densities. With x the fraction in water, 800 = 1000x + 700(1 - x) = 700 + 300x, giving x = 1/3.
solutionSteps: Let x be the fraction of volume in water and (1 - x) the fraction in oil.
Weight equals total upthrust; divide by (Volume x g): rho_cube = rho_water x + rho_oil (1 - x).
Solve: 300x = 100, so x = 1/3 in water (two-thirds sits in oil).
keyConcept: When a body floats spanning two fluids, its density is the volume-weighted mean of the fluid densities, since both layers contribute buoyancy.
commonMistake: Ignoring the oil's buoyancy and treating the cube as floating in water alone, which gives the submerged fraction as rho_cube/rho_water = 0.8.

optionExplanations.1: This assumes the cube splits equally between the liquids by symmetry, but the split is fixed by the density balance.
optionExplanations.2: This is the fraction in the oil, (rho_water - rho_cube)/(rho_water - rho_oil) = 200/300, with the two fractions swapped.
optionExplanations.4: This ignores the oil layer and treats the cube as floating in water alone, giving rho_cube/rho_water = 0.8.

shortExplanation: Torricelli's law gives the efflux speed v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 1.25) = 5.0 m/s from the 1.25 m head. The jet then falls 0.80 m to the ground in t = 0.40 s, so the range is 5.0 x 0.40 = 2.0 m.
solutionSteps: Efflux speed from depth below surface: v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 1.25) = 5.0 m/s, horizontal.
Projectile fall time from hole to ground: t = sqrt(2 y / g) = sqrt(2 x 0.80 / 10) = 0.40 s.
Horizontal range = v x t = 5.0 x 0.40 = 2.0 m.
keyConcept: The exit speed depends only on the depth of water above the hole (Torricelli), while the horizontal range is a projectile problem whose fall time is set by the hole's height above the ground.
commonMistake: Using the hole's depth below the surface as the projectile's fall height; the fall time is set by the hole's height above the ground (0.80 m), a separate distance.

optionExplanations.1: This takes the efflux speed from the full surface-to-ground head instead of just the depth above the hole.
optionExplanations.2: This omits the factor 2 in Torricelli's law, using v = sqrt(g h).
optionExplanations.3: This uses the 1.25 m depth as the fall height, but the fall time is set by the 0.80 m above the ground.

shortExplanation: Continuity with A1 = 2 A2 gives v2 = 2 v1. The piezometer difference is a pressure drop P1 - P2 = rho g (delta h) = 6000 Pa, and Bernoulli gives 3 v1^2 = 12, so v1 = 2.0 m/s and the narrow-section speed is v2 = 4.0 m/s.
solutionSteps: Continuity: A1 v1 = A2 v2 with A1 = 2 A2, so v2 = 2 v1.
Pressure drop from piezometer heights: P1 - P2 = rho g (delta h) = 1000 x 10 x 0.60 = 6000 Pa.
Narrow-section speed v2 = 2 v1 = 4.0 m/s.
keyConcept: Continuity and Bernoulli must be applied together; the piezometer height difference measures the static-pressure drop between two moving streams, not a free efflux.
commonMistake: Applying Torricelli's formula directly to the height difference, which ignores the continuity relation linking the two speeds.

optionExplanations.0: This misuses Torricelli to get the wide-section speed and then doubles it, combining two errors.
optionExplanations.1: This is the speed in the wide section; continuity requires the fluid to speed up in the constriction.
optionExplanations.3: This drops the factor 1/2 in Bernoulli's kinetic terms, giving 3 v1^2 = 6.

shortExplanation: The submerged fraction equals the density ratio, so floating 80% under water gives rho_block = 800 kg/m^3. In oil of the same density, the ratio is 1.0, so the block is neutrally buoyant and effectively fully submerged.
solutionSteps: For a floating body, submerged fraction = rho_block / rho_liquid.
In water: 0.80 = rho_block / 1000, so rho_block = 800 kg/m^3.
In oil: ratio = 800 / 800 = 1.0, requiring 100% submersion to float.
The block is neutrally buoyant, on the point of sinking.
keyConcept: A floating object's submerged fraction is the ratio of its density to the surrounding liquid's density; when the two are equal the object is neutrally buoyant.
commonMistake: Multiplying the two submerged fractions (0.8 x 0.8); flotation depends on the density ratio, not a product of fractions.

optionExplanations.0: This multiplies the fractions 0.8 x 0.8, but flotation depends on rho_block/rho_liquid.
optionExplanations.2: In the less dense oil the block sits lower (more submerged), not higher.
optionExplanations.4: The submerged fraction changes with the liquid; 80% applies only in water.

shortExplanation: Continuity gives the narrow-section speed v2 = (8.0/2.0)(1.0) = 4.0 m/s. Bernoulli then gives P2 = 200000 + (1/2)(1000)(1 - 16) = 192500 Pa = 192.5 kPa, since the faster flow has lower pressure.
solutionSteps: Bernoulli (horizontal): P2 = P1 + (1/2)rho(v1^2 - v2^2).
keyConcept: Where a streamline flow speeds up (in the constriction), its static pressure falls, as required by Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe.
commonMistake: Getting the sign of the Bernoulli term wrong and concluding the pressure rises in the narrow section.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the wrong sign, giving a higher pressure in the narrow section.
optionExplanations.1: This uses too large a speed difference (as if v2 were 5 m/s).
optionExplanations.2: This assumes the pressure is unchanged, ignoring that the faster flow lowers pressure.

shortExplanation: The fixed points (0 C, 20 X) and (100 C, 220 X) give the linear relation X = 20 + 2C. Setting X = C gives C = 20 + 2C, so C = -20, and both scales read -20.
solutionSteps: Fit a linear relation through (0 C, 20 X) and (100 C, 220 X): slope = (220 - 20)/(100 - 0) = 2.
So X = 20 + 2C.
Set the readings equal, X = C: C = 20 + 2C.
keyConcept: Two temperature scales are related by a straight line fixed by two common reference points; a coincident reading is where that line meets X = C.
commonMistake: Recalling the Fahrenheit-Celsius coincidence (-40) by rote and transferring it to a different scale.

optionExplanations.0: This is the intercept (the X value when C = 0), not the point of coincidence.
optionExplanations.1: This is where Fahrenheit and Celsius coincide, wrongly transferred to this scale.
optionExplanations.4: At the ice point C = 0 but X = 20, so the scales do not agree there.

shortExplanation: The 21000 J available from cooling the water to 0 C exceeds the 16800 J needed to melt all the ice, so all the ice melts. The 4200 J surplus warms the full 250 g of water, giving T = 4.0 C.
solutionSteps: Heat if water cools to 0 C: 200 x 4.2 x 25 = 21000 J.
Heat to melt all the ice: 50 x 336 = 16800 J.
Since 21000 > 16800, all the ice melts with 4200 J to spare.
Energy balance: 200 x 4.2 x (25 - T) = 50 x 336 + 50 x 4.2 x T.
keyConcept: In calorimetry, first compare available heat with the latent heat needed to melt all the ice; if it melts, the surplus warms the total mass of water including the melt-water.
commonMistake: Warming only the original water and forgetting that the 50 g of melt-water must also be raised to the final temperature.

optionExplanations.0: This stops at the melting point without checking that the available 21000 J exceeds the 16800 J needed to melt the ice.
optionExplanations.1: This warms only the original 200 g and forgets the 50 g of melt-water.
optionExplanations.2: This treats the ice as merely cold water, ignoring the latent heat of fusion.

shortExplanation: The liquid expands by V0 x beta x deltaT and the glass cavity by V0 x (3 alpha) x deltaT, since a solid's volume coefficient is three times its linear one. Overflow = 1000 x 50 x (4.3e-4 - 3.0e-5) = 20.0 cm^3.
solutionSteps: Liquid expansion: deltaV_L = V0 x beta_L x deltaT.
Cavity expansion: deltaV_g = V0 x (3 alpha) x deltaT, since the volume coefficient is 3 x linear.
Overflow = V0 x deltaT x (beta_L - 3 alpha).
keyConcept: The volume expansion coefficient of a solid is three times its linear coefficient, and only the difference between liquid and container expansions overflows.
commonMistake: Using the glass's linear coefficient alpha instead of the volume coefficient 3 alpha for the cavity.

optionExplanations.1: This uses the linear coefficient alpha for the glass instead of 3 alpha.
optionExplanations.3: This adds the two expansions instead of subtracting them.
optionExplanations.4: This neglects the vessel's expansion entirely, using beta_L alone.

shortExplanation: In series the same heat current flows, so each rod's temperature drop is proportional to its resistance R = L/(kA), giving R_A : R_B = 1:3. The 80 C total drop splits as 20 C across A and 60 C across B, so the junction is at 100 - 20 = 80 C.
solutionSteps: In series the heat current is the same through both rods.
Thermal resistance R = L/(kA); with equal L and A, R is proportional to 1/k.
Total drop 80 C splits in this ratio: 20 C across A, 60 C across B.
Junction temperature = 100 - 20 = 80 C.
keyConcept: For rods in series, the temperature drop across each is proportional to its thermal resistance, so the poorer conductor takes the larger drop.
commonMistake: Making the temperature drop proportional to conductivity rather than to resistance, which puts the larger drop on the wrong rod.

optionExplanations.0: This over-weights rod B's resistance, pushing the junction almost to the hot face.
optionExplanations.1: This makes the drop proportional to conductivity, giving a 60 C drop across A.
optionExplanations.2: This is the arithmetic mean of the end temperatures, ignoring the unequal resistances.
optionExplanations.3: This puts the whole drop across rod A, associating the larger drop with the better conductor.

shortExplanation: Internal energy is a state function, so from path I, deltaU = 200 - 140 = 60 J. Along path II with 90 J of work, Q = deltaU + W = 60 + 90 = 150 J absorbed.
solutionSteps: Along path I: deltaU = Q - W = 200 - 140 = 60 J.
deltaU depends only on the endpoints, so it is 60 J for any path from A to B.
Along path II: Q = deltaU + W = 60 + 90 = 150 J, absorbed.
keyConcept: The change in internal energy depends only on the initial and final states, while heat and work are path-dependent.
commonMistake: Treating heat as a state function and assuming Q is the same as along path I.

optionExplanations.0: This treats Q as a state function equal to the path-I value; only deltaU is path-independent.
optionExplanations.1: This has the right magnitude but wrong sign, from misapplying the first-law sign convention.
optionExplanations.2: This sets Q = deltaU, forgetting the 90 J of work done along path II.
optionExplanations.3: This sets Q = W, assuming deltaU = 0, but the fixed endpoints require deltaU = 60 J.

shortExplanation: Total moles are conserved as the gas redistributes between a 300 K vessel and a 500 K vessel at a common pressure. Equating initial and final moles gives P = 2 P0 T1/(T0 + T1) = 2(1.0e5)(500)/800 = 1.25e5 Pa.
solutionSteps: Initial moles: n_tot = 2 P0 V / (R T0), each vessel of volume V.
Final moles at common P: n_tot = PV/(R T0) + PV/(R T1).
Equate: P(1/T0 + 1/T1) = 2 P0 / T0.
keyConcept: With the valve open the two vessels share one pressure but keep their own temperatures; conserving total moles across the two temperatures fixes the common pressure.
commonMistake: Applying Gay-Lussac's law to all the gas as if it were uniformly heated to 500 K.

optionExplanations.0: This swaps the two temperatures, giving an unphysical pressure fall when a vessel is heated.
optionExplanations.1: This heats all the gas to 500 K, giving P = P0(500/300).
optionExplanations.2: This assumes the pressure is unchanged, ignoring that heating raises the common pressure.
optionExplanations.3: This treats all the gas as being at the mean temperature 400 K.

shortExplanation: At constant pressure Q = (7/2)R per mole, which splits into work R, rotational energy R, and translational energy (3/2)R. The translational fraction is (3/2)/(7/2) = 3/7.
solutionSteps: At constant pressure, Q = n C_p deltaT with C_p = (7/2)R for a diatomic gas.
Per mole the (7/2)R splits into: work W = R deltaT, rotational (2/2)R deltaT = R deltaT, translational (3/2)R deltaT.
Translational fraction = (3/2)/(7/2) = 3/7 (about 0.43).
keyConcept: By equipartition, only 3 of the diatomic gas's degrees of freedom are translational, and at constant pressure part of the heat also does external work.
commonMistake: Confusing the translational share with C_v/C_p = 5/7, which counts the rotational energy as translational.

optionExplanations.0: This ignores both the work done by the gas and the rotational modes.
optionExplanations.1: 2/7 = R/C_p is the fraction of heat doing external work, not the translational share.
optionExplanations.2: 5/7 = C_v/C_p is the fraction going into total internal energy, counting rotation as translation.
optionExplanations.4: 3/5 divides translational by internal energy alone, dropping the work term.

shortExplanation: Using V = emf - Ir at the two points, subtracting gives r = 0.60 ohm and emf = 12.0 V. The short-circuit current is emf/r = 12.0/0.60 = 20 A.
solutionSteps: Terminal voltage: V = emf - Ir.
Two points: 10.8 = emf - 2r and 9.0 = emf - 5r.
Subtract: 1.8 = 3r, so r = 0.60 ohm.
Short-circuit current = emf/r = 12.0/0.60 = 20 A.
keyConcept: A real cell obeys V = emf - Ir; two current-voltage points determine both the EMF and the internal resistance, and the short-circuit current is emf/r.
commonMistake: Treating a terminal voltage as the EMF instead of solving for the true EMF of 12.0 V.

optionExplanations.0: This takes the terminal voltage 9.0 V as the EMF.
optionExplanations.1: This takes the terminal voltage 10.8 V as the EMF.
optionExplanations.2: This uses a terminal voltage divided by its current as the internal resistance, confusing load with internal resistance.
optionExplanations.3: This merely restates the larger quoted current, ignoring that a smaller load raises the current further.

shortExplanation: Maximum power transfer occurs when R equals the internal resistance, R = 3.0 ohm. Then I = 24/6.0 = 4.0 A and P = I^2 R = 16 x 3.0 = 48 W.
solutionSteps: Maximum power in R occurs at R = r = 3.0 ohm.
Power: P = I^2 R = 4.0^2 x 3.0 = 48 W (equivalently emf^2/(4r) = 576/12).
keyConcept: The maximum-power-transfer condition is R = r, at which only half the total power reaches the load.
commonMistake: Ignoring the internal resistance when computing the current, which overstates the delivered power.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the terminal-voltage squared over the total resistance with the wrong values.
optionExplanations.1: This computes emf^2/R while ignoring internal resistance in the current.
optionExplanations.2: This corresponds to a larger R, raising efficiency but not the delivered power (confusing power with efficiency).
optionExplanations.4: This is the total power delivered by the EMF; half is lost in the internal resistance.

shortExplanation: From R = V^2/P the lamps have resistances 240 ohm and 360 ohm. In series the current is 120/600 = 0.20 A, so the higher-resistance '40 W' lamp dissipates 0.20^2 x 360 = 14.4 W and glows brighter.
solutionSteps: Resistances: '60 W' lamp = 120^2/60 = 240 ohm; '40 W' lamp = 120^2/40 = 360 ohm.
Series total = 600 ohm; shared current I = 120/600 = 0.20 A.
Power in the '40 W' lamp = I^2 R = 0.20^2 x 360 = 14.4 W.
Power in the '60 W' lamp = 0.20^2 x 240 = 9.6 W, so the '40 W' lamp is brighter.
keyConcept: In series, components carry the same current, so power P = I^2 R is greatest in the higher-resistance (lower-rated) lamp.
commonMistake: Assuming the lamp with the higher power rating is always brighter, which fails in a series connection.

optionExplanations.1: This is the power in the '60 W' lamp; in series the higher-resistance lamp dissipates more.
optionExplanations.2: This assumes the lamp still runs at its rated power, which applies only at its rated 120 V.
optionExplanations.3: This is the total power of both lamps together, not the power in one lamp.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes the 120 V divides equally, but it divides in proportion to resistance.

shortExplanation: At constant volume the resistance scales as R proportional to L^2, so tripling the length raises R by a factor of 9. At fixed voltage P = V^2/R, so the power falls to P/9.
solutionSteps: Constant volume: A = volume/L, so R = rho L/A = rho L^2/volume, i.e. R proportional to L^2.
Tripling L increases R by a factor of 3^2 = 9.
At fixed voltage, P = V^2/R, so power falls by the same factor of 9, to P/9.
keyConcept: Stretching a wire at constant volume thins it, so resistance grows as the square of the length; at fixed voltage power is inversely proportional to resistance.
commonMistake: Forgetting that the cross-section shrinks when the wire is stretched, so treating R as merely proportional to L.

optionExplanations.1: This treats resistance as inversely proportional to length, reversing the dependence.
optionExplanations.2: This finds the 9x resistance change but reports it as the power change, assuming P proportional to R.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes the area is unchanged, ignoring the thinning of the wire.
optionExplanations.4: This mis-scales the area as 1/L^2, making R proportional to L^3.

shortExplanation: The arm ratios 10/20 and 15/30 are equal, so the bridge is balanced and no current flows through the 25 ohm link. The network is then 30 ohm in parallel with 45 ohm = 18 ohm, giving I = 9.0/18 = 0.50 A.
solutionSteps: Compare arm ratios: (A-B)/(B-C) = 10/20 = 0.5 and (A-D)/(D-C) = 15/30 = 0.5.
They are equal, so the bridge is balanced and the 25 ohm resistor carries no current.
Branch A-B-C = 10 + 20 = 30 ohm; branch A-D-C = 15 + 30 = 45 ohm.
Supply current I = 9.0/18 = 0.50 A.
keyConcept: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the two arm ratios are equal; the bridge resistor then carries no current and can be removed.
commonMistake: Failing to recognise the balance and mis-combining the branches, or forgetting one of the two parallel paths.

optionExplanations.0: This uses only the A-D-C branch (9.0/45) and ignores the parallel path.
optionExplanations.1: This places the two branches in series rather than in parallel (9.0/75).
optionExplanations.2: This adds all five resistors in a single series loop (9.0/100).
optionExplanations.4: This uses only the A-B-C branch (9.0/30) and ignores the parallel path.

shortExplanation: The voltmeter's 60 kohm in parallel with R2 gives 60 || 60 = 30 kohm. The divider is then 20 kohm and 30 kohm, so the reading is 16 x 30/(20 + 30) = 9.6 V, below the true 12.0 V.
solutionSteps: Voltmeter in parallel with R2: 60 || 60 = 30 kohm.
Divider now has upper 20 kohm and lower 30 kohm.
This is below the undisturbed 12.0 V because the meter loads the divider.
keyConcept: A real voltmeter of finite resistance loads the divider arm it measures, pulling the reading below the ideal (open-circuit) value.
commonMistake: Neglecting the loading effect and quoting the undisturbed 12.0 V as if the voltmeter were ideal.

optionExplanations.0: This is the p.d. across the upper resistor after loading (16 - 9.6), not across R2.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes the 16 V divides equally, but the resistors are unequal.
optionExplanations.2: This places the voltmeter across the upper resistor instead of across R2.
optionExplanations.3: This is the undisturbed p.d., ignoring the loading effect of a real voltmeter.

shortExplanation: The current is I = V/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A over t = 240 s, so charge Q = It = 480 C. The heat dissipated is E = VIt = 12 x 2.0 x 240 = 5760 J.
solutionSteps: Current: I = V/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A.
Time: t = 4.0 min = 240 s.
Charge: Q = It = 2.0 x 240 = 480 C.
Energy: E = VIt = 12 x 2.0 x 240 = 5760 J (equally I^2 R t = 4.0 x 6.0 x 240).
keyConcept: Charge is current times time, and electrical energy converted to heat is P t = VIt = I^2 R t.
commonMistake: Failing to convert 4.0 minutes to 240 seconds before computing charge and energy.

optionExplanations.1: The charge is right, but this halves the energy.
optionExplanations.2: This uses t = 4.0 s instead of 240 s, not converting minutes to seconds.
optionExplanations.3: This confuses the current with the charge and greatly under-counts the energy.
optionExplanations.4: This uses a current of 1.0 A, as if R were 12 ohm.

shortExplanation: Each wavelength is lambda = v/f using that wave's own speed. The radio wave gives (3.0e8)/(1.0e8) = 3.0 m, and the ultrasound gives 1500/(1.5e6) = 1.0 mm.
solutionSteps: Radio wave at c = 3.0e8 m/s: lambda = (3.0e8)/(100e6) = 3.0 m.
Ultrasound at 1500 m/s in tissue: lambda = 1500/(1.5e6) = 1.0e-3 m = 1.0 mm.
Each uses the correct speed for its own medium.
keyConcept: Wavelength depends on the wave's speed as well as its frequency; different wave types in different media can have the higher frequency yet the longer wavelength.
commonMistake: Assuming the higher-frequency wave must have the shorter wavelength, ignoring the very different wave speeds.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the speed of sound in air rather than the given tissue speed for the ultrasound.
optionExplanations.1: This assigns the shorter wavelength to the higher-frequency wave, ignoring the different speeds.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the speed of light for the ultrasound.
optionExplanations.4: This applies the tissue speed to the radio wave.

shortExplanation: Reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference, energy-without-matter transport and medium-dependent speed occur for all progressive waves. Only polarisation, shown by the intensity falling to zero as a filter is rotated, is unique to transverse waves.
solutionSteps: List the general wave behaviours: reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference, energy transfer, medium-dependent speed.
All of these occur for both transverse and longitudinal waves, so none distinguishes them.
Polarisation confines oscillations to one plane, possible only when they are perpendicular to travel.
Extinction as a filter is rotated proves the wave can be polarised, hence it is transverse.
keyConcept: Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; longitudinal waves cannot.
commonMistake: Believing that reflection, refraction or diffraction is a signature of transverse waves, when all waves show these.

optionExplanations.0: Reflection and refraction occur for all waves.
optionExplanations.1: Every progressive wave transfers energy without a net transfer of matter.
optionExplanations.3: Both wave types diffract; sound diffracts around obstacles just as light does.
optionExplanations.4: The speed of both transverse and longitudinal waves depends on the medium.

shortExplanation: For a string fixed at both ends, successive resonances differ by the fundamental, so f1 = 490 - 420 = 70 Hz. Since f1 = v/(2L), the length is L = 140/(2 x 70) = 1.0 m.
solutionSteps: A string fixed at both ends resonates at integer multiples of the fundamental.
Successive resonances differ by f1: f1 = 490 - 420 = 70 Hz.
Fundamental fits half a wavelength: lambda1 = 2L, so f1 = v/(2L).
keyConcept: A string fixed at both ends has harmonics at integer multiples of the fundamental, so the spacing between adjacent resonances is the fundamental frequency.
commonMistake: Assuming the lowest observed resonance is itself the fundamental, rather than finding the fundamental from the resonance spacing.

optionExplanations.1: This uses lambda1 = L instead of lambda1 = 2L for the fundamental.
optionExplanations.2: This applies a quarter-wavelength (fixed-free) boundary condition to a string fixed at both ends.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes 420 Hz is the fundamental.
optionExplanations.4: This sets the string length equal to one full wavelength of the 420 Hz mode.

shortExplanation: Snell's law gives the refraction angle sin r = 0.64/1.50 = 0.4285, so r = 25.4 degrees from the top-face normal. At the vertical side face the incidence angle is the complement, 64.6 degrees, which exceeds the critical angle arcsin(1/1.50) = 41.8 degrees, so total internal reflection occurs.
solutionSteps: At the top face: sin 40 = 1.50 sin r, so sin r = 0.64/1.50 = 0.4285 and r = 25.4 degrees.
The side face normal is perpendicular to the top face normal, so the side incidence angle is 90 - 25.4 = 64.6 degrees.
Critical angle for glass-air: arcsin(1/1.50) = 41.8 degrees.
Since 64.6 > 41.8, the ray is totally internally reflected.
keyConcept: The normals of perpendicular faces are perpendicular, so the internal angle at the side face is the complement of the refraction angle; TIR occurs when it exceeds the glass-air critical angle.
commonMistake: Using the refraction angle directly as the side-face incidence angle, overlooking that the side-face normal is perpendicular to the top-face normal.

optionExplanations.0: The side angle is right but the critical angle is computed for glass-water instead of glass-air.
optionExplanations.2: Total internal reflection does occur when light goes from glass toward air beyond the critical angle, exactly this case.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the refraction angle directly as the side-face incidence angle, missing the perpendicular-normal geometry.
optionExplanations.4: This carries the external 40 degree angle into the glass, ignoring refraction.

shortExplanation: With the real-is-positive convention f = +15 cm and u = +10 cm, so 1/v = 1/15 - 1/10 = -1/30 and v = -30 cm. The image is virtual and upright, 30 cm behind the mirror, with magnification |v/u| = 30/10 = 3.
solutionSteps: Assign f = +15 cm (concave) and u = +10 cm.
Apply the mirror equation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/15 - 1/10 = (2 - 3)/30 = -1/30.
Solve: v = -30 cm; the negative sign means the image is 30 cm behind the mirror, hence virtual and upright.
Compute magnification: m = |v/u| = 30/10 = 3.
keyConcept: An object closer than the focal length of a concave mirror produces an enlarged, upright, virtual image behind the mirror.
commonMistake: Assuming no image forms when the object is inside the focal length, or inverting the magnification ratio to u/v.

optionExplanations.0: An object inside the focal length still forms an image: an enlarged virtual one behind the mirror.
optionExplanations.1: The image position is right but this inverts the magnification (u/v = 0.33 instead of v/u = 3).
optionExplanations.3: This drops the negative sign on v, wrongly calling a virtual image behind the mirror a real, inverted one.
optionExplanations.4: This adds instead of subtracting the object term (1/v = 1/f + 1/u), a mis-rearrangement of the mirror equation.

shortExplanation: Maxima coincide when m1*480 = m2*600, giving m1:m2 = 5:4, so the smallest orders are 5 and 4. The coincidence position is y = 5 * 480e-9 * 1.5 / 0.50e-3 = 7.2 mm.
solutionSteps: Bright fringes satisfy y = m*lambda*D/d, so coincidence requires m1*lambda1 = m2*lambda2.
Take the smallest integers: m1 = 5 (480 nm), m2 = 4 (600 nm).
keyConcept: Two interference patterns coincide at the lowest common multiple of their fringe spacings, found from the smallest integer orders satisfying m1*lambda1 = m2*lambda2.
commonMistake: Taking the first coincidence as one fringe spacing of either colour, or as the difference of the two spacings.

optionExplanations.0: This is the difference of the two fringe spacings (1.80 - 1.44), treating coincidence like a beat spacing.
optionExplanations.1: This is just the fringe spacing of the 480 nm light, not the first coincidence.
optionExplanations.2: This is just the fringe spacing of the 600 nm light, not the first coincidence.
optionExplanations.3: This assigns a 4th-order 480 nm fringe, which coincides with no 600 nm maximum.

shortExplanation: The open pipe's third harmonic 3f1 = 900 Hz gives f1 = 300 Hz = v/(2L). The equal-length closed pipe has fundamental v/(4L) = 150 Hz and resonates only at odd multiples 150, 450, 750, 1050 Hz, so the highest below 1000 Hz is 750 Hz.
solutionSteps: Open pipe: 3f1 = 900 Hz, so f1 = 300 Hz = v/(2L).
Closed pipe of the same length: fundamental = v/(4L) = f1/2 = 150 Hz.
A closed pipe resonates only at odd harmonics: 150, 450, 750, 1050 Hz, ...
Select the highest value not exceeding 1000 Hz: 750 Hz.
keyConcept: A pipe closed at one end has fundamental v/(4L) and supports only odd harmonics; an open pipe has fundamental v/(2L) and supports all harmonics.
commonMistake: Treating the closed pipe as supporting all harmonics, or ignoring the 1000 Hz ceiling.

optionExplanations.1: This treats the closed pipe as supporting all harmonics of 150 Hz, but only odd harmonics exist.
optionExplanations.2: This uses the correct odd series but reports 1050 Hz, ignoring the 1000 Hz limit.
optionExplanations.3: This gives the closed pipe's fundamental rather than its highest resonance below 1000 Hz.
optionExplanations.4: This wrongly assumes closing one end raises the fundamental to 600 Hz instead of lowering it to 150 Hz.

shortExplanation: Each photon carries E = hc/lambda = 1240/248 = 5.0 eV. The maximum kinetic energy is KE_max = E - phi = 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0 eV, so the stopping potential is 3.0 V.
solutionSteps: Compute photon energy: E = hc/lambda = 1240/248 = 5.0 eV.
Apply the photoelectric equation: KE_max = E - phi = 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0 eV.
Set eV_s = KE_max, so V_s = 3.0 V.
keyConcept: The stopping potential equals the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy in eV: eV_s = hc/lambda - phi.
commonMistake: Using the whole photon energy or the work function itself as the stopping potential instead of their difference.

optionExplanations.0: This sets the stopping potential equal to the work function, not the electrons' kinetic energy.
optionExplanations.1: This uses the entire photon energy, forgetting the work function must first be paid to release the electron.
optionExplanations.2: This adds the work function to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.
optionExplanations.4: This divides the photon energy by the work function rather than subtracting.

shortExplanation: Photon energies add, so 1/lambda2 = 1/lambda_abs - 1/lambda1 = 1/120 - 1/200 = 1/300, giving lambda2 = 300 nm.
solutionSteps: Energy is conserved: E_abs = E1 + E2.
Since E is proportional to 1/lambda, write 1/120 = 1/200 + 1/lambda2.
Therefore lambda2 = 300 nm.
keyConcept: In a two-step de-excitation, photon energies (not wavelengths) sum to the absorbed energy, and energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
commonMistake: Adding or subtracting wavelengths directly instead of conserving energy through reciprocals.

optionExplanations.0: This is the arithmetic mean of the two wavelengths, which has no basis in energy conservation.
optionExplanations.1: This subtracts the wavelengths directly, but it is energy, not wavelength, that is conserved.
optionExplanations.2: This adds the reciprocals (1/120 + 1/200), giving the sum rather than the remaining energy.
optionExplanations.4: This adds the two wavelengths, treating wavelength as the conserved additive quantity.

shortExplanation: A charged particle curves on a radius r = mv/(qB), so the light, singly-charged beta electron has the smallest radius and is deflected most, oppositely to the positive alpha. The neutral gamma rays feel no magnetic force and pass straight through.
solutionSteps: For comparable speeds, the path radius scales as m/q.
The beta particle (charge -e, tiny mass) has the smallest m/q, so it curves most sharply.
The alpha (charge +2e) has opposite charge, so it curves the opposite way, and its large mass gives a much bigger radius (least deflected of the charged particles).
Gamma rays are uncharged, so qvB = 0 and they are undeflected.
keyConcept: Magnetic deflection depends on charge sign and on the radius mv/(qB); neutral radiation is undeflected.
commonMistake: Thinking speed alone causes deflection, or that charge magnitude alone determines the deflection while ignoring mass.

optionExplanations.0: Gamma rays are uncharged and feel no magnetic force regardless of speed.
optionExplanations.1: Equal speed does not give equal deflection, since radius depends on m/q, which differs enormously.
optionExplanations.2: Alpha and beta have opposite charges and deflect in opposite directions, and gamma is undeflected.
optionExplanations.4: Although the alpha has twice the charge, its far larger mass gives a large radius, so it deflects least.

shortExplanation: The mass number drops by 24, so there are 24/4 = 6 alpha decays, lowering Z from 90 to 78. To reach Z = 82 requires 82 - 78 = 4 beta-minus decays. So 6 alpha and 4 beta particles are emitted.
solutionSteps: Only alpha decay changes A, by -4 each: number of alphas = (232 - 208)/4 = 6.
Six alphas lower Z by 6*2 = 12, from 90 to 78.
Beta-minus decay raises Z by +1 each with no change in A.
Reach the final Z = 82: number of betas = 82 - 78 = 4.
keyConcept: Alpha decay changes A by -4 and Z by -2; beta-minus decay changes Z by +1 with A unchanged.
commonMistake: Miscounting alphas by dividing by 3, swapping the two counts, or ignoring that alphas already lowered Z before beta decay.

optionExplanations.0: This divides the mass-number change by 3, as if an alpha changed A by 3.
optionExplanations.1: This interchanges the alpha and beta counts.
optionExplanations.2: This halves the required atomic-number correction, giving 2 betas instead of 4.
optionExplanations.3: This takes the beta count as 90 - 82 = 8, ignoring that the alphas already lowered Z and that beta raises Z.

shortExplanation: Activity falls by a factor 800/100 = 8 = 2^3 in 30 minutes, so the half-life is 10 minutes. A further 20 minutes is 2 half-lives, so 100 Bq halves twice: 100 -> 50 -> 25 Bq.
solutionSteps: Find the number of halvings in 30 min: 800/100 = 8 = 2^3, so 3 half-lives.
Half-life = 30/3 = 10 minutes.
A further 20 minutes = 2 half-lives.
Halve twice from 100 Bq: 100 -> 50 -> 25 Bq.
keyConcept: Each half-life multiplies activity by 1/2; the number of half-lives elapsed sets the decay factor.
commonMistake: Using the wrong half-life or an off-by-one number of halvings.

optionExplanations.1: This takes the half-life as 5 minutes, giving four halvings of 100 Bq.
optionExplanations.2: This counts only one half-life in 20 minutes, effectively a 20-minute half-life.
optionExplanations.3: This reports the 30-minute reading, ignoring the further 20 minutes of decay.
optionExplanations.4: This counts three halvings in the further 20 minutes, an off-by-one error.

shortExplanation: Total binding energy is per-nucleon value times nucleon number. Before: two deuterons at 2*1.1 = 2.2 MeV each, total 4.4 MeV. After: one helium-4 at 4*7.1 = 28.4 MeV. Energy released = 28.4 - 4.4 = 24 MeV.
solutionSteps: Total binding energy of each deuteron = 2 * 1.1 = 2.2 MeV; two give 4.4 MeV.
Total binding energy of helium-4 = 4 * 7.1 = 28.4 MeV.
Energy released = increase in total binding energy = 28.4 - 4.4 = 24 MeV.
keyConcept: Fusion energy released equals the increase in total binding energy (per-nucleon value times nucleon count) between reactants and product.
commonMistake: Using the per-nucleon difference alone, or forgetting the reactants already carried binding energy that must be subtracted.

optionExplanations.0: This uses only the per-nucleon difference (7.1 - 1.1) without multiplying by the nucleon count.
optionExplanations.1: This gives only the helium-4 total binding energy, forgetting to subtract the deuterons' binding energy.
optionExplanations.2: This multiplies the per-nucleon difference by 2 nuclei instead of by the 4 nucleons of helium.
optionExplanations.3: This adds the reactant and product binding energies instead of subtracting them.

shortExplanation: By E = mc^2, the mass-loss rate is dm/dt = P/c^2 = 3.6e26 / (9e16) = 4.0e9 kg/s.
solutionSteps: Relate radiated power to mass loss: P = (dm/dt) c^2.
Rearrange: dm/dt = P/c^2.
Substitute: c^2 = (3.0e8)^2 = 9e16 m^2/s^2.
Compute: dm/dt = 3.6e26 / 9e16 = 4.0e9 kg/s.
keyConcept: Mass-energy equivalence links radiated power to rate of rest-mass loss via dm/dt = P/c^2.
commonMistake: Multiplying by c^2 instead of dividing, dividing by c instead of c^2, or slipping a power of ten in squaring c.

optionExplanations.0: This multiplies power by c^2 instead of dividing, inverting E = mc^2.
optionExplanations.1: This uses c^2 = 9e17, a power-of-ten slip in squaring 3e8.
optionExplanations.2: This divides by c rather than c^2, using E = mc.
optionExplanations.4: This multiplies power by c, both a rearrangement and a dimensional error.

shortExplanation: Balancing field magnitudes at distance x from +q: kq/x^2 = k(9q)/(0.40 - x)^2 gives (0.40 - x)/x = 3, so x = 0.10 m = 10 cm from the +q charge.
solutionSteps: For two like charges the null lies between them, nearer the weaker charge.
Set magnitudes equal: kq/x^2 = k(9q)/(0.40 - x)^2.
Cancel k and q, then take the square root: (0.40 - x)/x = 3.
Solve: 0.40 - x = 3x, so x = 0.10 m = 10 cm from +q.
keyConcept: Between two like charges the field null sits where the inverse-square fields balance; the distance ratio equals the square root of the charge ratio.
commonMistake: Using the charge ratio directly instead of its square root, or placing the null at the midpoint or nearer the larger charge.

optionExplanations.0: For two like charges the null lies between them; it lies outside only for unlike charges.
optionExplanations.1: The midpoint ignores that fields of unequal magnitude cannot cancel halfway.
optionExplanations.3: This sets the distance ratio equal to the charge ratio (1/9), omitting the required square root.
optionExplanations.4: This places the null nearer the larger charge, but it must lie closer to the weaker one.

shortExplanation: The field is E = V/d = 200/0.020 = 1.0e4 V/m, giving acceleration a = eE/m = 1.76e15 m/s^2. Over transit time t = L/v0 = 1.33e-9 s, the deflection is y = (1/2)a*t^2 = 1.6 mm.
solutionSteps: Field between plates: E = V/d = 200/0.020 = 1.0e4 V/m.
Transverse acceleration: a = eE/m = (1.6e-19)(1.0e4)/(9.1e-31) = 1.76e15 m/s^2.
Transit time along the plates: t = L/v0 = 0.040/(3.0e7) = 1.33e-9 s.
keyConcept: Motion between charged plates is projectile-like: use the separation d for the field but the plate length L for the transit time.
commonMistake: Using L for the field or d for the transit time, or omitting the factor 1/2 in y = (1/2)a*t^2.

optionExplanations.0: This mis-converts 2.0 cm to 0.2 m, making the field ten times too small.
optionExplanations.1: This uses E = V/L instead of E = V/d, halving the acceleration.
optionExplanations.3: This uses transit time t = d/v0 instead of L/v0.
optionExplanations.4: This omits the factor 1/2, doubling the true deflection.

shortExplanation: At equilibrium T*cos(theta) = mg and T*sin(theta) = BIL, so tan(theta) = BIL/(mg). Solving, I = mg*tan(theta)/(BL) = (0.040*10*0.75)/(0.50*0.20) = 3.0 A.
solutionSteps: The horizontal magnetic force is F = BIL; the weight mg acts down; tension T acts along the threads.
Resolve: T*cos(theta) = mg (vertical) and T*sin(theta) = BIL (horizontal).
Divide to eliminate T: tan(theta) = BIL/(mg).
keyConcept: For a horizontal force and weight balanced by a thread, tan(theta) equals the ratio of horizontal force to weight.
commonMistake: Using sin or cos of the angle instead of tan, inverting the tangent, or equating BIL directly to mg.

optionExplanations.0: This uses cos(theta) instead of tan(theta), misidentifying the force components.
optionExplanations.1: This uses sin(theta) instead of tan(theta), treating the magnetic force as along the thread.
optionExplanations.2: This inverts the tangent, writing tan(theta) = mg/(BIL).
optionExplanations.3: This sets BIL = mg, ignoring that only the horizontal component is balanced through the angle.

shortExplanation: An ion passes undeflected when qE = qvB; the charge cancels, giving v = E/B = (3.0e4)/(0.20) = 1.5e5 m/s.
solutionSteps: Set the electric and magnetic forces equal and opposite: qE = qvB.
Cancel q: E = vB.
keyConcept: Crossed E and B fields act as a velocity selector, passing v = E/B independent of the ion's charge and mass.
commonMistake: Assuming the speed depends on charge-to-mass ratio, inverting the ratio, or multiplying the fields.

optionExplanations.0: The charge and mass cancel in qE = qvB, so the selected speed is independent of ion species.
optionExplanations.1: This introduces a spurious factor of one half, giving E/(2B).
optionExplanations.2: This inverts the ratio to B/E, solving the balance the wrong way round.
optionExplanations.4: This multiplies the fields (EB), a dimensional error.

shortExplanation: By Faraday's law |EMF| = N*A*(dB/dt) = 200 * 7.85e-3 * 2.0 = 3.1 V, with A = pi*(0.050)^2 and dB/dt = 0.40/0.20 = 2.0 T/s. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the increasing flux.
solutionSteps: Rate of field change: dB/dt = (0.50 - 0.10)/0.20 = 2.0 T/s.
EMF magnitude: |EMF| = N*A*(dB/dt) = 200 * 7.85e-3 * 2.0 = 3.1 V.
Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the increasing flux.
keyConcept: Faraday's law gives |EMF| = N*A*(dB/dt) for a coil in a changing field, and Lenz's law fixes the current's sense to oppose the change.
commonMistake: Using the final field value instead of its change, omitting the number of turns, or using the diameter as the radius.

optionExplanations.1: This uses the final field value (0.50/0.20 = 2.5 T/s) instead of the change 0.40 T.
optionExplanations.2: The magnitude is right but a current reinforcing the flux would violate Lenz's law and energy conservation.
optionExplanations.3: This omits the number of turns N, using the single-turn EMF.
optionExplanations.4: This treats 5.0 cm as the diameter, quartering the area.

shortExplanation: Acceleration gives v = sqrt(2eV/m) = 1.33e7 m/s. In the field r = mv/(eB) = (9.1e-31 * 1.33e7)/(1.6e-19 * 2.0e-3) = 3.8e-2 m = 3.8 cm.
solutionSteps: Work-energy: eV = (1/2)m*v^2, so v = sqrt(2eV/m) = sqrt(2*1.6e-19*500/9.1e-31) = 1.33e7 m/s.
In the magnetic field, magnetic force = centripetal force: evB = m*v^2/r.
Solve for radius: r = mv/(eB).
keyConcept: The accelerating p.d. sets the speed via eV = (1/2)mv^2, and the magnetic field gives r = mv/(eB).
commonMistake: Omitting the factor 1/2, reporting the diameter, or using 2.0 T instead of 2.0 mT.

optionExplanations.0: This omits the factor 1/2, making the speed too small by sqrt(2).
optionExplanations.1: This gives the diameter (2r) instead of the radius.
optionExplanations.2: The kinetic energy is eV regardless of the accelerator's length, so the radius is fully determined.
optionExplanations.3: This uses B = 2.0 T instead of 2.0 mT, making the radius a thousand times too small.

shortExplanation: Each neighbour repels with F = k*q^2/a^2 = (9.0e9)(2.0e-6)^2/(0.20)^2 = 0.90 N. The two forces are 60 degrees apart, so the resultant is 2F*cos(30 degrees) = sqrt(3)*F = 1.6 N.
solutionSteps: Compute the pair force: F = k*q^2/a^2 = (9.0e9)(2.0e-6)^2/(0.20)^2 = 0.90 N.
The two repulsive forces on the chosen charge are separated by the 60-degree interior angle.
Resultant of two equal forces 60 degrees apart: 2F*cos(30 degrees) = sqrt(3)*F.
keyConcept: The net force is the vector sum of the two Coulomb forces; for equal forces 60 degrees apart the resultant is sqrt(3) times each.
commonMistake: Using only one neighbour's force, or adding the two forces as if parallel or perpendicular.

optionExplanations.0: This gives only the force from one neighbour, ignoring the second charge.
optionExplanations.2: This adds the two magnitudes arithmetically, as if the forces were parallel.
optionExplanations.3: This multiplies the pair force by 3, treating the net as three equal contributions.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes the forces are perpendicular (sqrt(2)*F) instead of 60 degrees apart.

shortExplanation: Conserving momentum with east positive: (3.0)(+6.0) + (2.0)(-4.0) = +10 kg m/s. Dividing by the total mass 5.0 kg gives +2.0 m/s, i.e. 2.0 m/s east.
solutionSteps: Take east as positive and compute total momentum: (3.0)(+6.0) + (2.0)(-4.0) = 18 - 8 = +10 kg m/s.
Total mass after coupling = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 kg.
Common velocity v = +10/5.0 = +2.0 m/s, i.e. 2.0 m/s east.
keyConcept: In a perfectly inelastic collision, total signed momentum is conserved and the combined body's velocity is total momentum divided by total mass.
commonMistake: Adding momentum magnitudes without signs, forgetting to divide by total mass, or averaging the speeds.

optionExplanations.0: This adds momentum magnitudes (18 + 8) before dividing, ignoring the opposite directions.
optionExplanations.2: The magnitude is right but the sign is reversed, wrongly making the pair move west.
optionExplanations.3: This reports the net momentum (10 kg m/s) as a velocity, forgetting to divide by total mass.
optionExplanations.4: This averages the two velocities, ignoring the unequal masses.

shortExplanation: Zero initial momentum gives the fragments equal-magnitude momenta, so kinetic energy p^2/(2*mass) is inversely proportional to mass. The energies are in ratio 3:1, so the lighter fragment carries 3/(3+1) = 3/4.
solutionSteps: Momentum conservation: m*v_light = 3m*v_heavy, so both carry equal-magnitude momentum p.
Each kinetic energy is p^2/(2*mass), inversely proportional to mass.
Energy ratio light:heavy = (1/m):(1/3m) = 3:1.
Lighter fragment's fraction = 3/(3+1) = 3/4.
keyConcept: In an explosion from rest, fragments share equal-magnitude momentum, so kinetic energy splits inversely with mass.
commonMistake: Comparing only speeds squared without mass weighting, or assuming the energy splits equally.

optionExplanations.0: This compares only squared speeds (9:1), forgetting to weight each energy by mass.
optionExplanations.1: This is the heavier fragment's fraction, wrongly assuming less mass means less energy.
optionExplanations.2: This makes the same squared-speed error but assigns the ratio to the wrong fragment.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes energy is shared equally, but only momentum magnitude is equal.

shortExplanation: Each second, 3.0 kg of water loses its horizontal velocity from 20 m/s to 0. The force equals the rate of change of momentum: 3.0 kg/s * 20 m/s = 60 N, so the water pushes on the wall with 60 N.
solutionSteps: The water's speed change on impact is 20 - 0 = 20 m/s (no rebound).
Rate of momentum change = (mass flow rate) * (change in speed) = 3.0 * 20 = 60 kg m/s per second.
By impulse-momentum this equals the force on the water; by Newton's third law the water exerts 60 N on the wall.
keyConcept: For a steady jet, force = (mass flow rate) * (change in velocity).
commonMistake: Using a kinetic-energy expression, assuming rebound, or using an average velocity.

optionExplanations.0: This is (1/2)*(mass flow rate)*(speed)^2, a power, not a force.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes elastic rebound giving a 40 m/s change, but the water does not rebound.
optionExplanations.2: This uses (mass flow rate)*(speed)^2, an energy-based expression with wrong dimensions.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the average velocity (10 m/s) instead of the total change in speed.

shortExplanation: For a 1D elastic collision with B at rest, v_A' = ((m_A - m_B)/(m_A + m_B))u_A = -2.0 m/s and v_B' = (2m_A/(m_A + m_B))u_A = +4.0 m/s. So A rebounds at 2.0 m/s backward and B moves at 4.0 m/s forward.
solutionSteps: Use the elastic formulas: v_A' = ((m_A - m_B)/(m_A + m_B))u_A and v_B' = (2m_A/(m_A + m_B))u_A.
Compute v_B' = (2.0/3.0)(6.0) = +4.0 m/s (forward).
Check: momentum 1.0(-2.0) + 2.0(4.0) = 6.0 and KE 2 + 16 = 18 J both match the initial values.
keyConcept: In a 1D elastic collision with a heavier stationary target, the lighter incoming ball rebounds backward.
commonMistake: Applying the equal-mass result, swapping the two balls' speeds, or dropping the negative sign on the lighter ball.

optionExplanations.0: A stopping while B takes 6.0 m/s is the equal-mass result, not valid here where m_B > m_A.
optionExplanations.1: The speeds are assigned to the wrong balls and A is not reversed.
optionExplanations.3: The speeds are correct but A's direction is not reversed; the lighter ball must recoil.
optionExplanations.4: A common 2.0 m/s is the inelastic (sticking) result, which does not conserve kinetic energy.

shortExplanation: Momentum conservation gives common velocity v = (2.0*6.0)/6.0 = 2.0 m/s. Initial KE = (1/2)(2.0)(6.0)^2 = 36 J and final KE = (1/2)(6.0)(2.0)^2 = 12 J, so 36 - 12 = 24 J is dissipated.
solutionSteps: Find the common velocity: v = (2.0*6.0)/(2.0 + 4.0) = 2.0 m/s.
Initial kinetic energy: (1/2)(2.0)(6.0)^2 = 36 J.
Final kinetic energy: (1/2)(6.0)(2.0)^2 = 12 J.
Energy converted to heat and deformation = 36 - 12 = 24 J.
keyConcept: In a perfectly inelastic collision momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; the loss is the initial minus final kinetic energy.
commonMistake: Reporting the retained energy instead of the loss, or using an averaged velocity.

optionExplanations.0: Losing exactly half only applies when a body sticks to an equal mass, not here.
optionExplanations.1: This is the retained kinetic energy, not the amount dissipated.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes all kinetic energy is lost, which momentum conservation forbids.
optionExplanations.4: This averages the speeds to 3.0 m/s; the correct common velocity is 2.0 m/s.

shortExplanation: Sliding: V = sqrt(2*mu*g*d) = sqrt(2*0.50*10*0.90) = 3.0 m/s just after impact. Momentum conservation in the embedding: (0.010)u = (1.00)(3.0), so u = 300 m/s.
solutionSteps: Sliding phase (friction): (1/2)(M+m)V^2 = mu*(M+m)*g*d, so V^2 = 2*mu*g*d = 2*0.50*10*0.90 = 9.0.
Therefore V = 3.0 m/s just after impact.
Embedding phase (perfectly inelastic, momentum conserved): m*u = (M+m)V.
keyConcept: Treat the two phases separately: kinetic energy is dissipated in the embedding, but momentum is conserved there, and work-energy governs the sliding.
commonMistake: Equating the bullet's kinetic energy directly to friction work, or slipping a factor of ten in the mass ratio.

optionExplanations.0: This equates the bullet's KE to friction work, wrongly assuming energy is conserved during embedding.
optionExplanations.1: This inverts the mass ratio, dividing instead of multiplying in the momentum step.
optionExplanations.2: This is the common speed just after impact (V), not the bullet's pre-impact speed.
optionExplanations.3: This is the correct method with a factor-of-ten mass slip (mass ratio 1000 rather than 100).

shortExplanation: With zero total momentum the centre of mass stays fixed, so the boat displacement = (m_person/(m_person + m_boat))*L = (60/180)(3.0) = 1.0 m.
solutionSteps: No external horizontal force and starting from rest: the centre of mass does not move.
Let the boat move x opposite to the walk; the person moves (3.0 - x) relative to the water.
Fix the centre of mass: 60(3.0 - x) = 120x, so 180 = 180x.
Solve: x = 1.0 m.
keyConcept: When total momentum is zero, the centre of mass stays put and the two bodies' displacements are inversely proportional to their masses.
commonMistake: Confusing a fixed centre of mass with a fixed boat, or assigning the person's displacement to the boat.

optionExplanations.1: This assumes the person and boat move equal distances, ignoring the mass ratio.
optionExplanations.2: This confuses a fixed centre of mass with a stationary boat.
optionExplanations.3: This assumes the boat moves a full boat-length, ignoring the person's own motion relative to the water.
optionExplanations.4: This is the person's displacement relative to the water, assigned wrongly to the boat.

shortExplanation: Surface field g = GM/r^2, so g_X/g_E = 3/2^2 = 3/4. Hence g_X = 10 * 0.75 = 7.5 N/kg.
solutionSteps: Use g = GM/r^2 and take ratios: g_X/g_E = (M_X/M_E)/(r_X/r_E)^2.
Substitute the ratios: = 3 / 2^2 = 3/4.
Compute: g_X = 10 * 3/4 = 7.5 N/kg.
keyConcept: Surface gravitational field is proportional to mass and inversely proportional to the square of the radius.
commonMistake: Not squaring the radius, ignoring the radius entirely, or inverting the ratio.

optionExplanations.0: This inverts the ratio, putting mass in the denominator and radius squared in the numerator.
optionExplanations.1: This uses the radius to the first power instead of squaring it.
optionExplanations.2: This scales only with mass and ignores the radius.
optionExplanations.4: This accounts only for the radius and ignores the tripled mass.

shortExplanation: For circular orbits Kepler's third law gives T^2 proportional to r^3, so T scales as r^(3/2). Multiplying the radius by 4 multiplies the period by 4^(3/2) = 8, giving 8 x 2 = 16 hours.
solutionSteps: Set gravity equal to the centripetal requirement: GMm/r^2 = 4 pi^2 m r / T^2.
Rearrange to T^2 proportional to r^3, so T proportional to r^(3/2).
Radius factor is 4, so period factor is 4^(3/2) = 2^3 = 8.
Multiply: T_B = 8 x 2 = 16 hours.
keyConcept: Kepler's third law: orbital period scales as radius to the 3/2 power.
commonMistake: Applying the wrong power of the radius ratio, for example treating the period as linear in radius or applying the r^3 dependence directly to T.

optionExplanations.0: This uses T proportional to r^(1/2) (a factor of 2), confusing orbital-speed scaling with period scaling.
optionExplanations.1: This applies T proportional to r^3 (a factor of 64), wrongly putting the r^3 dependence of T^2 onto T itself.
optionExplanations.2: This treats the period as linear in radius (a factor of 4) instead of r^(3/2).

shortExplanation: Orbital period scales as r^(3/2). Reducing the radius to R/4 multiplies the period by (1/4)^(3/2) = 1/8, so the new period is 24/8 = 3 hours.
solutionSteps: Use T proportional to r^(3/2).
Radius factor is 1/4, so period factor is (1/4)^(3/2) = 1/8.
Multiply: T = 24 x 1/8 = 3 hours.
keyConcept: Kepler's third law: smaller orbital radius means a shorter period, scaling as r^(3/2).
commonMistake: Assuming every Earth satellite keeps the 24-hour geostationary period, or using the wrong power of the radius ratio.

optionExplanations.0: This treats the period as linear in radius (factor 1/4), ignoring the 3/2 power.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes the period is unchanged, wrongly treating any Earth satellite as geostationary.
optionExplanations.2: This uses T proportional to r^(1/2), giving 24/2 = 12 hours instead.

shortExplanation: For a conical pendulum the tension's vertical component balances gravity and its horizontal component supplies the centripetal force, giving T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g). Substituting yields 2 pi sqrt(1.0/10) = 2.0 s.
solutionSteps: Vertical balance: tension cos(theta) = mg.
Horizontal balance: tension sin(theta) = m omega^2 r with r = L sin(theta).
Divide the two to get omega^2 = g/(L cos(theta)).
Period T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g) = 2 pi sqrt(2.0 x 0.50/10) = 2 pi sqrt(0.10) = 2.0 s.
keyConcept: In a conical pendulum the string angle links gravity and the centripetal force, so the period depends on L cos(theta)/g.
commonMistake: Placing cos(theta) in the wrong position (dividing instead of multiplying) or using sin(theta), or dropping the factor of 2 pi.

optionExplanations.0: This comes from dividing by cos(theta) instead of multiplying, using 2 pi sqrt(L/(g cos(theta))).
optionExplanations.1: This uses sin 60 degrees instead of cos 60 degrees when resolving the tension.
optionExplanations.2: This is the simple-pendulum result 2 pi sqrt(L/g), ignoring the cone angle.

shortExplanation: The mass at the equator needs centripetal acceleration a = 4 pi^2 R/T^2 = 0.034 m/s^2 directed inward. Newton's second law gives mg - N = ma, so the scale reads less than mg by ma = 100 x 0.034 = 3.4 N.
solutionSteps: Compute the centripetal acceleration: a = 4 pi^2 R/T^2 = 4 pi^2 x 6.4e6/(86400)^2 = 0.034 m/s^2.
Apply Newton's second law toward the centre: mg - N = ma.
The deficit is mg - N = ma = 100 x 0.034 = 3.4 N.
keyConcept: Part of gravity provides the centripetal force for a rotating body, so the supporting (scale) force falls short of mg by ma.
commonMistake: Assuming rotation has no effect, or reporting the acceleration itself as a force by forgetting to multiply by the mass.

optionExplanations.1: This assumes rotation has no effect, ignoring that gravity must supply the centripetal force so N is less than mg.
optionExplanations.2: This reports the centripetal acceleration as the force, omitting the 100 kg mass factor.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the diameter 2R instead of the radius R, doubling the acceleration.

shortExplanation: For a surface-skimming orbit the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(R/g), and at the surface g is proportional to R at fixed density, so R/g is constant. The period depends only on mean density, so with equal densities T_Y = T_X.
solutionSteps: For a surface orbit gravity provides the centripetal force: v^2 = gR, so T = 2 pi sqrt(R/g).
At the surface g = GM/R^2 and for a uniform sphere M = (4/3) pi R^3 rho, so g = (4/3) pi G rho R.
Thus g is proportional to R, making R/g independent of R.
The period depends only on density: T = sqrt(3 pi/(G rho)), so equal densities give T_Y = T_X.
keyConcept: For a surface-skimming orbit the period depends only on the planet's mean density, not its size.
commonMistake: Scaling the period with radius while forgetting that surface gravity also grows with radius and cancels the radius dependence.

optionExplanations.1: This assumes T proportional to R, ignoring that stronger surface gravity offsets the larger circumference.
optionExplanations.2: This applies T proportional to R^2, over-counting the radius dependence and ignoring the change in g.
optionExplanations.4: This assumes T proportional to sqrt(R), forgetting that g also increases with R and cancels the radius dependence.

shortExplanation: In a freely orbiting station the astronaut and the scale accelerate together toward the Earth at the local field strength, so there is no contact force between them. The scale reads 0 N even though gravity there is still non-zero (about 2.45 N/kg).
solutionSteps: A scale reads the normal contact force it exerts (apparent weight).
In orbit both astronaut and scale are in free fall with the same acceleration g' = 9.8 x (R/2R)^2 = 2.45 N/kg.
With no relative acceleration between them, the normal force is zero.
The scale therefore reads 0 N.
keyConcept: Apparent weightlessness: in free-fall orbit there is no contact force, so a scale reads zero even though gravity is not zero.
commonMistake: Reporting the actual gravitational force at altitude as the scale reading, ignoring the free-fall condition.

optionExplanations.0: This confuses mass with weight (as if g = 1 N/kg) and ignores free fall.
optionExplanations.1: This gives the true gravitational force at altitude, 80 x 2.45, but the free-fall station makes the normal force zero.
optionExplanations.3: This uses the surface value 80 x 9.8, ignoring both the reduced g and the free-fall condition.

shortExplanation: At constant speed the useful output is the rate of gain of potential energy, P_out = mgv = 50 x 10 x 0.40 = 200 W. Efficiency = output/input = 200/250 = 80%.
solutionSteps: Output power equals force times velocity with force equal to the weight: P_out = mgv = 50 x 10 x 0.40 = 200 W.
Form the ratio output over input: 200/250.
Efficiency = 0.80 = 80%.
keyConcept: Efficiency is useful output power divided by total input power, always less than 100%.
commonMistake: Omitting g so mass is treated as weight, or inverting the efficiency ratio to give a value above 100%.

optionExplanations.0: This omits g, using 50 x 0.40 = 20 W as the output, giving 20/250 = 8%.
optionExplanations.2: This uses the weight mg = 500 N as if it were the output power, forgetting to multiply by the speed.
optionExplanations.3: This inverts the ratio to input/output = 250/200 = 125%, wrongly exceeding 100%.

shortExplanation: The elastic energy stored is (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(800)(0.15)^2 = 9.0 J. At the top all of it becomes gravitational potential energy, mgh = 9.0 J, so h = 9.0/(0.20 x 10) = 4.5 m.
solutionSteps: Elastic energy stored: E = (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(800)(0.0225) = 9.0 J.
At the highest point the ball is at rest, so mgh = 9.0 J.
keyConcept: Conservation of energy: stored elastic energy converts fully to gravitational potential energy at the highest point.
commonMistake: Dropping the factor of 1/2 in the spring energy, or forgetting g in mgh.

optionExplanations.1: This omits the factor of 1/2 in the elastic energy, using kx^2 = 18 J so h = 9.0 m.
optionExplanations.2: This forgets g and divides the energy by mass alone, 9.0/0.20 = 45 m.
optionExplanations.3: This uses x rather than x^2 in the elastic energy, giving 60 J and h = 30 m.

shortExplanation: Elastic energy stored is (1/2)kx^2. From 1.6 J at 4.0 cm, k = 2000 N/m; the total to reach 8.0 cm is 6.4 J, so the extra work is 6.4 - 1.6 = 4.8 J.
solutionSteps: Total work to reach 8.0 cm: (1/2)(2000)(0.08)^2 = 6.4 J.
Additional work = 6.4 - 1.6 = 4.8 J.
keyConcept: Elastic energy grows as the square of extension, so equal further stretches require increasing amounts of work.
commonMistake: Assuming the second equal stretch needs the same work as the first, or forgetting to subtract the work already done.

optionExplanations.0: This assumes an equal further extension needs equal work, treating the force as constant.
optionExplanations.1: This assumes work is proportional to extension, doubling the first value, ignoring the x^2 dependence.
optionExplanations.2: This gives the total work to reach 8.0 cm, forgetting to subtract the 1.6 J already done.

shortExplanation: At constant speed the driving force balances the along-slope weight component mg sin(theta) = 600 N plus the 500 N resistance, giving 1100 N. Power = force x speed = 1100 x 20 = 22 kW.
solutionSteps: Weight component along the slope: mg sin(theta) = 1200 x 10 x (1/20) = 600 N.
Add resistance: total driving force = 600 + 500 = 1100 N.
Power = force x speed = 1100 x 20 = 22000 W = 22 kW.
keyConcept: For steady motion up an incline the engine balances both the gravity component along the slope and the resistive force; power equals force times speed.
commonMistake: Using the full weight instead of its along-slope component, or omitting one of the two opposing forces.

optionExplanations.0: This includes only the resistance, 500 x 20 = 10 kW, ignoring gravity on the slope.
optionExplanations.1: This uses the full weight mg = 12000 N plus resistance instead of the along-slope component.
optionExplanations.2: This includes only the gravitational component, 600 x 20 = 12 kW, ignoring resistance.

shortExplanation: Where kinetic and potential energy are equal, each is half the total, so PE = (1/2)(1/2)mv0^2. Setting mgh = (1/4)mv0^2 gives h = v0^2/(4g) = 400/40 = 10 m, exactly half the maximum height.
solutionSteps: Total energy equals the initial kinetic energy (1/2)mv0^2.
At the crossover KE = PE, so each equals half the total: mgh = (1/4)mv0^2.
keyConcept: Energy conservation: when kinetic equals potential energy, the potential energy is one quarter of the initial kinetic energy.
